themes.name: Business and the meaning of a word
themes.canonicalName: Business and the meaning of a word

characters.name: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come

quotations.text: Marley was dead, to begin with. There is no doubt whatever about that.
quotations.context: The opening sentences of the book.
quotations.analysis: The phrase 'to begin with' is doing two jobs: it dates the death and it flags the fact as a premise the reader has to accept before anything else can be built on it. Dickens spends the next paragraph arguing about doornails precisely so that the death itself slips past unexamined.

quotations.text: Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster.
quotations.context: The first full description of Scrooge, before any action.
quotations.analysis: Three of the four terms are about being closed rather than being cruel, and the flint image concedes that the fire is in there and simply has never been struck. An oyster is also something that can be opened, which is a quiet promise the book will keep in eighty pages.

quotations.text: He carried his own low temperature always about with him; he iced his office in the dog-days, and didn’t thaw it one degree at Christmas.
quotations.context: Continuing the opening portrait of Scrooge.
quotations.analysis: The cold is not something he suffers but something he emits, which makes his effect on the people round him a physical fact rather than an opinion about his manners. 'One degree' turns the sentence into a measurement, the language Scrooge himself would use.

quotations.text: a good time; a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time; the only time I know of, in the long calendar of the year, when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely
quotations.speaker: Fred
quotations.context: Fred answering his uncle's demand to know what reason he has to be merry.
quotations.analysis: Fred's whole defence arrives as a single unbroken sentence with the clauses piling up, which is the opposite of Scrooge's clipped questions and refusals. He then concedes the accounting point — Christmas has never put gold or silver in his pocket — and argues that it has done him good anyway, meeting his uncle on his own ground and declining to stay there.

quotations.text: “Are there no prisons?” asked Scrooge.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: His first reply to the two gentlemen collecting for the poor.
quotations.analysis: He answers a request for money with a question about institutions, which moves the conversation from particular people to public provision and lets him leave without giving anything. Four words also make him sound reasonable, and the book has to spend three staves undoing that impression.

quotations.text: “If they would rather die,” said Scrooge, “they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Told that many would rather die than go to the workhouse.
quotations.analysis: The phrase belongs to political economy rather than to malice: it treats people as a quantity in excess of a total. Dickens stores it carefully, and in Stave III has the Ghost of Christmas Present quote it back word for word while Scrooge is looking at a child who may be the one it applies to.

quotations.text: There’s more of gravy than of grave about you, whatever you are!
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Explaining to Marley's ghost why he will not believe in it.
quotations.analysis: A pun under that much pressure is a sign of nerve, and it tells us the man is not stupid, only committed. Dickens needs this joke: a Scrooge with no wit could be frightened into reform, and reform by fright alone is exactly what the last stave has to disprove.

quotations.text: “I wear the chain I forged in life,” replied the Ghost. “I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it.
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: Answering Scrooge's question about why he is fettered.
quotations.analysis: Free will is named twice in one sentence, which removes any suggestion that this is a punishment imposed from outside. The chain is made of cash-boxes, ledgers and keys, so what he is wearing is not a penalty for his trade but his trade itself, simply weighed.

quotations.text: “Business!” cried the Ghost, wringing its hands again. “Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence were, all, my business.
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: After Scrooge says that Marley was always a good man of business.
quotations.analysis: The argument is won by repeating a single word until its meaning shifts under it: five uses of 'business' in three sentences, each one widening the term. Marley does not tell Scrooge to stop being a man of business; he tells him he has been doing a small part of the job and calling it the whole.

quotations.text: “It is required of every man,” the Ghost returned, “that the spirit within him should walk abroad among his fellow-men, and travel far and wide; and, if that spirit goes not forth in life, it is condemned to do so after death.
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: Explaining what kind of afterlife he is serving.
quotations.analysis: The punishment is exactly the neglected duty, performed compulsorily and too late — the ghost is not in torment for anything he did but for a journey he declined to make. It also quietly explains the plot: Scrooge is about to be walked round London against his will.

quotations.text: “The school is not quite deserted,” said the Ghost. “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Past
quotations.context: Arriving at the schoolroom of Scrooge's boyhood.
quotations.analysis: The ghost describes the boy in the present tense and in the third person, so that Scrooge hears his own childhood reported as a piece of news about a stranger. 'Solitary' has already been used of the adult oyster, and the repetition makes the loneliness a continuous condition rather than a result.

quotations.text: He has the power to render us happy or unhappy; to make our service light or burdensome; a pleasure or a toil.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Defending Fezziwig after the spirit remarks that the ball cost only a few pounds.
quotations.analysis: Dickens notes that Scrooge says this 'speaking unconsciously like his former, not his latter self' — the argument for decent employment comes out of Scrooge's own mouth before he has agreed to it. It also states the case in the vocabulary of power and service, not charity, which is why it will hold in the final stave.

quotations.text: “It matters little,” she said softly. “To you, very little. Another idol has displaced me; and, if it can cheer and comfort you in time to come as I would have tried to do, I have no just cause to grieve.”
quotations.speaker: Belle
quotations.context: Releasing the young Scrooge from their engagement.
quotations.analysis: She accuses him of idolatry and then immediately withdraws her own standing to complain about it, which leaves him nothing to push against. 'Idol' is the strongest word in the sentence and the only religious one in a scene otherwise conducted entirely in the language of contracts.

quotations.text: “Come in!” exclaimed the Ghost. “Come in! and know me better, man!”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: Scrooge's first sight of the second spirit, among heaped food.
quotations.analysis: An invitation, not a summons — the opposite of Stave I, where Scrooge spent the whole evening refusing to come in or let anyone else. The word 'man' at the end is a greeting between equals, and it is the first time anyone in the book has addressed him with that kind of warmth.

quotations.text: He told me, coming home, that he hoped the people saw him in the church, because he was a cripple, and it might be pleasant to them to remember upon Christmas Day who made lame beggars walk and blind men see.
quotations.speaker: Bob Cratchit
quotations.context: Bob reporting what Tiny Tim said on the way back from church.
quotations.analysis: Tim has thought about how he is looked at and decided what he wants the looking to do, which makes him an agent in the scene rather than an object of pity. The thought reaches the reader at two removes — the child told his father, the father tells his wife — so the boy's dignity is never staged for effect.

quotations.text: “God bless us every one!” said Tiny Tim, the last of all.
quotations.speaker: Tiny Tim
quotations.context: The end of the Cratchits' Christmas toast.
quotations.analysis: 'The last of all' places him at the end of a queue of speakers, the smallest voice in the room, and Dickens gives the line no emphasis whatever. It returns as the last sentence of the book, by which time the reader has been shown a future in which it was not said.

quotations.text: This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want. Beware of them both, and all of their degree, but most of all beware this boy, for on his brow I see that written which is Doom, unless the writing be erased.
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: Revealing the two children clinging beneath his robe.
quotations.analysis: The spirit has just said the children are Man's, not his, which places the responsibility before the allegory arrives. Ignorance is ranked above Want as the greater danger, which is a specific political claim about schooling rather than relief, and 'unless the writing be erased' leaves the sentence open in a book whose whole subject is whether a foreseen end can still be changed.

quotations.text: “Are there no prisons?” said the Spirit, turning on him for the last time with his own words. “Are there no workhouses?”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: The spirit's final words, immediately after showing Ignorance and Want.
quotations.analysis: Nothing is added and nothing is explained; the whole rebuke consists of Scrooge's own sentences handed back at the right moment. Dickens has waited two staves to use them, and the delay is what gives the repetition its force — the reader recognises the words before Scrooge does.

quotations.text: Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of the things that May be only?
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: At the neglected grave, before he is made to read the name on it.
quotations.analysis: The question the whole book turns on, and the silent spirit refuses to answer it. Scrooge is asking about grammar — the difference between a future tense and a conditional — and the novella's position is that the difference is entirely made of what he does on Christmas morning.

quotations.text: I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future. The Spirits of all Three shall strive within me.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Clutching at the robe of the last spirit, beside his own headstone.
quotations.analysis: He promises to keep all three tenses running at once, which is a precise description of what the book has just done to him. 'Try' is the honest word in the sentence: the vow is made in terror at a graveside, and Dickens leaves a whole stave to test whether it survives daylight.

quotations.text: I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy, I am as giddy as a drunken man.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Christmas morning, tangled in his own stockings.
quotations.analysis: The same device that fixed him in Stave I — hard as flint, solitary as an oyster — comes back running in the other direction, four similes where there had been four. Two of them, the schoolboy and the drunken man, restore exactly the parts of a life the earlier staves showed him losing.

quotations.text: Scrooge was better than his word. He did it all, and infinitely more; and to Tiny Tim, who did not die, he was a second father.
quotations.context: The narrator's account of what followed.
quotations.analysis: 'Who did not die' is slipped in as a subordinate clause, as though it were incidental, and it is the single most important fact in the book. Dickens measures the conversion by other people's outcomes rather than by Scrooge's feelings, which is why the sentence is about what he was to somebody rather than what he became.

quotations.text: And so, as Tiny Tim observed, “God Bless Us, Every One!”
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novella.
quotations.analysis: The book closes by handing its last words to its smallest character, and by putting them in the past tense of reported speech — 'observed' — as though the blessing were a settled matter of record. The capitals are new since Stave III: the same four words, now printed as a title.

themes.name: What a man who can make anything will make
Kings, bosses and the habit of obedience
Slavery, in the sixth century and the nineteenth

techniques.name: A narrator who cannot hear himself

quotations.text: It was in Warwick Castle that I came across the curious stranger whom I am going to talk about.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the book, spoken by the frame narrator.
quotations.analysis: A tourist's sentence, flat and unhurried, before anything strange has been allowed in. The frame is doing quiet work: it lets the impossible story arrive as somebody else's manuscript, so the reader can decide for himself what to believe.

quotations.text: So I am a Yankee of the Yankees—and practical; yes, and nearly barren of sentiment, I suppose—or poetry, in other words.
quotations.context: Hank Morgan introducing himself at the start of his manuscript.
quotations.analysis: He offers his lack of poetry as a qualification. Everything the novel goes on to test is in that boast: the man who is proud of having no sentiment will be the one deciding what a life is worth on the last afternoon.

quotations.text: Why, I could make anything a body wanted—anything in the world, it didn’t make any difference what
quotations.context: Describing his training at the arms factory in Hartford.
quotations.analysis: Stated as a workman's pride, and it is the novel's whole premise. Twain puts the emphasis on anything twice, and the second half of the book is a demonstration of what that word includes.

quotations.text: I will blot out the sun, and he shall never shine again
quotations.context: The message Hank sends to the king, timed against an eclipse he has worked out from the date.
quotations.analysis: Knowledge used as a threat, in the voice of the magicians he has been deriding. The sentence wins him the kingdom and sets the terms of his rule: he will govern by doing things nobody around him can explain.

quotations.text: the very first official thing I did, in my administration—and it was on the very first day of it, too—was to start a patent office
quotations.context: Listing the beginnings of his civilisation.
quotations.analysis: Before schools, before medicine, before food: the machinery for owning ideas. It is a joke about American priorities and a serious statement of Twain's own, made while he was bankrupting himself on a patented typesetter.

quotations.text: a country without a patent office and good patent laws was just a crab, and couldn’t travel any way but sideways or backways
quotations.context: The reason given, immediately afterwards.
quotations.analysis: The image is homely and the doctrine is absolute. Twain's habit of putting a nineteenth-century certainty into a farmyard simile is what lets the reader enjoy the opinion and doubt it at the same time.

quotations.text: Any kind of royalty, howsoever modified
quotations.context: The Boss setting out his view of hereditary rule.
quotations.analysis: The opening of the novel's plainest political statement, and it is made by a man who has just accepted the second-highest office in the kingdom. Twain lets the contradiction stand without comment for another thirty chapters.

quotations.text: unlimited power is the ideal thing when it is in safe hands
quotations.context: Hank explaining why he has not simply abolished the monarchy.
quotations.analysis: The clause that gives the book away. He means his own hands, and the novel's last chapters are the argument against the sentence — delivered not as a rebuttal but as a body count.

quotations.text: a man is a man, at bottom
quotations.context: Hank on what training does and does not reach.
quotations.analysis: The democratic premise stated in five words, and it is the belief that makes his schools worth building. The novel gives it the best evidence it has — the king in the smallpox hut — and then asks whether it survives the sand-belt.

quotations.text: I was become a stockholder in a corporation where nine hundred and ninety-four of the members furnished all the money and did all the work
quotations.context: Working out what the population of Britain actually consists of.
quotations.analysis: A company report as social analysis: nine hundred and ninety-four workers, six shareholders. Twain's arithmetic here is the model for the economic chapters later, where the same point is made to a blacksmith who cannot bear it.

quotations.text: The blunting effects of slavery upon the slaveholder’s moral perceptions are known and conceded
quotations.context: After the king, travelling in disguise, has failed to see what is wrong with a slave gang.
quotations.analysis: Written by a man who grew up in a slaveholding town in Missouri, about a country thirteen centuries away. The sentence is careful and general, and the chapters around it are neither.

quotations.text: Fifty-four what? Men? No, minds—the capablest in the world
quotations.context: The Boss's proclamation to the massed knighthood, offering terms.
quotations.analysis: The confidence is technical and entirely justified: fifty-four trained people with electricity and machine guns can beat thirty thousand. What the sentence cannot see is that being right about this is the disaster.

quotations.text: Dismember me this animal, and return him in a basket to the base-born knave who sent him
quotations.context: Clarence acting out the answer the knights will send, to save the trouble of sending the message.
quotations.analysis: A boy performs the enemy's reply in Malory's own idiom, and is exactly right. It is the novel's best joke and its most chilling moment: the negotiation is over before it starts, and both sides know it.

quotations.text: How empty is theory in presence of fact!
quotations.context: Hank, after Clarence's demonstration.
quotations.analysis: He means the flag of truce. The line applies far better to everything else he has built: the schools, the newspapers and the republic have all just been shown to be theory, and the fact arriving over the hill is armed.

quotations.text: we were in a trap
quotations.context: After the battle, with the dead heaped around the cave.
quotations.analysis: Four words, and the victory turns into the ending. The fifty-four cannot leave because of what they have made, and the plague that kills them comes from the men they killed — the plainest statement in Twain of what a decisive weapon does to the man holding it.

themes.name: Money, law and a woman's signature
themes.canonicalName: Money, law and a woman's signature

themes.name: Reputation and what a man will risk
Duties to others and duties to oneself
Inheritance, sickness and the sins of fathers
Work, and who is allowed to do it

quotations.text: Is that my little lark twittering out there?
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: His first words in the play, called from the study without coming out.
quotations.analysis: The first thing said to Nora is not her name, and it is a question about a noise rather than a person. Ibsen puts the whole marriage in the opening exchange: a man who addresses his wife as wildlife, from another room, and a woman who answers in the character he has named.

quotations.text: It was I who saved Torvald’s life.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Pulling Mrs Linde down beside her on the sofa, after being told she knows nothing of real trouble.
quotations.analysis: The emphasis is placed on the pronoun, and it is the first sentence in the play in which Nora is the subject of a serious verb. She has been treated as an expense for two scenes and now produces the one fact that would reverse the household's opinion of her, and immediately makes her friend promise to keep it.

quotations.text: The law cares nothing about motives.
quotations.speaker: Krogstad
quotations.context: Answering Nora's claim that saving a life must count for something.
quotations.analysis: Six words, and they are the play's legal position stated correctly by its least admired character. Ibsen gives the blackmailer the accurate account of how the statute works, so that Nora's outrage has nothing to push against except the law itself.

quotations.text: Then it must be a very foolish law.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Her immediate reply to Krogstad.
quotations.analysis: She dismisses the entire legal code in eight words and then changes the subject, which in Act I reads as childishness. The last act picks the same sentence up and turns it into a programme: she will go away and find out whether the law is right or she is.

quotations.text: Almost everyone who has gone to the bad early in life has had a deceitful mother.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Explaining to Nora, minutes after Krogstad has left the house, why a dishonest parent ruins children.
quotations.analysis: He delivers it as professional experience and it lands on the woman standing in front of him, who has just been threatened over a forged signature. The scene ends with Nora refusing to let the children in, which is the first thing she decides entirely on her own.

quotations.text: He suffers from a diseased moral character, Mrs. Helmer; but even he began talking of its being highly important that he should live.
quotations.speaker: Doctor Rank
quotations.context: Explaining who else is waiting to see Helmer.
quotations.analysis: A dying physician diagnoses a man's ethics as a medical condition, and the sentence turns on the word but: even the morally diseased want to go on living. Ibsen is putting Rank's spine and Krogstad's reputation into the same vocabulary, which is the play's quiet joke about inheritance.

quotations.text: Do you suppose I am going to make myself ridiculous before my whole staff, to let people think that I am a man to be swayed by all sorts of outside influence?
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Refusing to reinstate Krogstad at his wife's request.
quotations.analysis: The reason he gives is not that Krogstad is dishonest but that reversing himself would look like being led by someone. A few lines later he admits the real objection is that the man calls him by his first name in front of the clerks, and a marriage is destroyed on that point of etiquette.

quotations.text: As soon as I am quite certain that the worst has come, I shall send you my card with a black cross on it, and then you will know that the loathsome end has begun.
quotations.speaker: Doctor Rank
quotations.context: Telling Nora how she will know that he is dying.
quotations.analysis: He arranges his own death as a piece of correspondence, so that nobody has to be present for it. The card with the black cross is the play's most economical stage property: it converts a man into a piece of paper in a letterbox, which is precisely what Krogstad's letter does to Nora.

quotations.text: How should you understand it? A wonderful thing is going to happen!
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: To Mrs Linde, who has asked what she is waiting for.
quotations.analysis: She never says what the wonderful thing is, and the refusal is not coyness: naming it would require her to admit she has been counting on her husband to sacrifice himself. The phrase recurs half a dozen times and means something different each time she uses it.

quotations.text: You should have let it alone; you must prevent nothing. After all, it is splendid to be waiting for a wonderful thing to happen.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: On being told that Mrs Linde has written to Krogstad and will see him tomorrow.
quotations.analysis: She forbids the one intervention that might save her, because the catastrophe has become the test she wants her husband to pass. It is the clearest evidence that by Act II Nora is no longer trying to avoid discovery; she is waiting for it.

quotations.text: Two on the same piece of wreckage would stand a better chance than each on their own.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Linde
quotations.context: Proposing to Krogstad in the Helmers' sitting room while the dance goes on upstairs.
quotations.analysis: A proposal expressed as arithmetic, offered by a woman who has already once chosen security over love and does not pretend otherwise. This is the only negotiation in the play conducted by two people who tell each other the truth, and Ibsen stages it in the same room that has held eight years of concealment.

quotations.text: Helmer must know all about it. This unhappy secret must be disclosed; they must have a complete understanding between them, which is impossible with all this concealment and falsehood going on.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Linde
quotations.context: Stopping Krogstad from asking for his letter back.
quotations.analysis: She takes the decision that ends the marriage, and she takes it on a principle rather than out of malice: a household running on a secret is worse off than one facing a scandal. Everything Nora suffers in the last twenty minutes is set in motion by the only person in the play who has been supporting herself.

quotations.text: Now you have destroyed all my happiness. You have ruined all my future. It is horrible to think of! I am in the power of an unscrupulous man; he can do what he likes with me, ask anything he likes of me, give me any orders he pleases⁠—I dare not refuse. And I must sink to such miserable depths because of a thoughtless woman!
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Moments after reading Krogstad's letter.
quotations.analysis: Count the possessives: my happiness, my future, my house. The forgery was committed to keep him alive and his response is a list of his own losses, which is the exact information Nora has been waiting eight years to receive.

quotations.text: Yes, it is true! I am saved! Nora, I am saved!
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Opening the second letter, which encloses the bond.
quotations.analysis: He says it twice and both times in the first person singular, then adds her name as an afterthought rather than as a subject. Nora's question in reply, what about her, gets the answer that she is saved too, and the pronouns have already decided the end of the play.

quotations.text: He called me his doll-child, and he played with me just as I used to play with my dolls.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: At the table, explaining how she came to have no opinions of her own.
quotations.analysis: The word the play is named for is used by Nora only in the last ten minutes, and she applies it first to her father. What she is describing is not cruelty but an inheritance of arrangements, which is why the speech is delivered flatly rather than as an accusation.

quotations.text: But our home has been nothing but a playroom. I have been your doll-wife, just as at home I was Papa’s doll-child; and here the children have been my dolls. I thought it great fun when you played with me, just as they thought it great fun when I played with them. That is what our marriage has been, Torvald.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Continuing the same speech, a few lines later.
quotations.analysis: Three generations are lined up in one sentence: she was played with, she was played with again, and she has been doing it to her own children. The charge is not that her husband was a tyrant but that nothing in the house was ever serious, and she includes herself in the indictment.

quotations.text: Before all else, you are a wife and a mother.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Answering Nora's claim that she has duties to herself.
quotations.analysis: He states it as a definition rather than an argument, which is what makes it answerable. The phrase before all else is then taken from him word for word in Nora's reply, and the theft of the construction is the point at which she stops being managed.

quotations.text: Duties to myself.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Asked what duties could possibly outrank those to husband and children.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and they are the sentence that caused the play to be banned, rewritten and argued about across Europe. Ibsen places them as a flat answer to a rhetorical question, with no justification attached, so that the audience has to supply the argument or refuse it.

quotations.text: I don’t believe that any longer. I believe that before all else I am a reasonable human being, just as you are⁠—or, at all events, that I must try and become one. I know quite well, Torvald, that most people would think you right, and that views of that kind are to be found in books; but I can no longer content myself with what most people say, or with what is found in books. I must think over things for myself and get to understand them.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Rejecting the definition of herself as wife and mother first.
quotations.analysis: She does not claim that most people are wrong, only that she can no longer take their word or a book's for it. The demand is not for rights but for the chance to find out what she thinks, which is a smaller and much harder thing to refuse.

quotations.text: According to it a woman has no right to spare her old dying father, or to save her husband’s life. I can’t believe that.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Explaining what she has learned about the law since Krogstad explained it to her.
quotations.analysis: She has taken Krogstad's legal lesson from Act I and turned it into a test the law has to pass, not one she has to. The last four words do all the work: not a claim about what the law is, but a refusal to accept it, which is where the play leaves the question.

quotations.text: I would gladly work night and day for you, Nora⁠—bear sorrow and want for your sake. But no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Told that the wonderful thing she waited for was his taking the blame himself.
quotations.analysis: The first clause offers a lifetime of labour and the second withholds the one thing that was actually asked for, and he sees no contradiction between them. Honour is being described as a possession a man cannot spend, which is the same logic his household has applied to money all along.

quotations.text: It is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Her reply, immediately after Helmer says no man would sacrifice his honour for love.
quotations.analysis: The sentence answers a claim about human nature with a fact about how many people have already done it. It also enlarges the play in one line, taking a quarrel in a Norwegian sitting room and setting it against every household the audience has come from.

quotations.text: Ah, Torvald, the most wonderful thing of all would have to happen.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Asked whether they might ever be more than strangers.
quotations.analysis: The phrase has been running through the play attached to a rescue she expected from her husband, and here it is transferred to something neither of them can arrange: a change in both of them. She says two lines later that she no longer believes in wonderful things happening, which is what makes the ending a departure rather than an ultimatum.

quotations.text: The sound of a door shutting is heard from below.
quotations.speaker: Stage direction
quotations.context: The last line of the play, printed as a stage direction after Helmer's final half-sentence.
quotations.analysis: Ibsen gives the curtain to a noise offstage rather than to a speech, and to a door that the audience never sees. The sentence is passive and impersonal, which leaves Helmer alone on stage with a hope he has just voiced and a sound that answers it.

themes.name: Night, sleep and the morning story

quotations.text: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour Draws on apace; four happy days bring in Another moon: but, O, methinks, how slow This old moon wanes!
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: The opening lines, four days before the wedding.
quotations.analysis: The play starts a clock and immediately complains about it, which is how the whole comedy will run: everything is dated to the moon. The image Theseus reaches for — an old woman withering away a young man's inheritance — puts impatience and money in the first speech of a play about who may marry whom.

quotations.text: Hippolyta, I woo'd thee with my sword, And won thy love, doing thee injuries; But I will wed thee in another key,
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: To his bride, in the same opening speech.
quotations.analysis: He describes a conquest as a courtship without appearing to notice the difference, and 'doing thee injuries' is left in the sentence as a plain fact. 'In another key' is a musical term, so the change he promises is one of tone rather than of relation — which is precisely the question Oberon and Titania will act out in the wood.

quotations.text: I beg the ancient privilege of Athens, As she is mine, I may dispose of her: Which shall be either to this gentleman Or to her death, according to our law
quotations.speaker: Egeus
quotations.context: Asking the duke to enforce his right over his daughter.
quotations.analysis: 'Dispose of' is a term for property, and the alternatives offered are a husband or an execution, in that order and in the same sentence. Egeus is not presented as a monster: he is invoking something he calls ancient and the duke agrees it exists, which is what makes the first scene of a comedy cold.

quotations.text: To you your father should be as a god; One that composed your beauties, yea, and one To whom you are but as a form in wax By him imprinted and within his power To leave the figure or disfigure it.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Advising Hermia to obey, before setting out her choices.
quotations.analysis: The image makes a daughter a seal impression rather than a person, and the pun on figure and disfigure lets destruction sound like a matter of craft. It is offered as kindly counsel, which is the point: the play's cruelty is spoken in the register of good sense.

quotations.text: The course of true love never did run smooth;
quotations.speaker: Lysander
quotations.context: Comforting Hermia after the duke's judgement.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted line in the play is a young man consoling his girlfriend by telling her that their situation is an old story, and he is about to list the ways love goes wrong as if reciting from a book. What follows is not comfort but a catalogue of obstacles, ending in the image of darkness swallowing light.

quotations.text: And ere a man hath power to say 'Behold!' The jaws of darkness do devour it up: So quick bright things come to confusion.
quotations.speaker: Lysander
quotations.context: The end of his list of the ways love is thwarted.
quotations.analysis: Three heavy monosyllables — jaws, darkness, devour — arrive in a comedy fifteen minutes old. 'Quick' means living as well as fast, so the line describes both a flash of lightning and a short life, and it is the closest this play comes to the tragedy the mechanicals will perform badly in the last act.

quotations.text: Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; And therefore is wing'd Cupid painted blind:
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Alone, deciding to betray Hermia's escape plan to Demetrius.
quotations.analysis: She works out the play's theory of love before any magic has appeared, and then acts on it in the worst available way. The rhymed couplets she has slipped into mark the moment a character stops talking to other people and starts constructing an argument for herself.

quotations.text: Let me play the lion too: I will roar, that I will do any man's heart good to hear me;
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: At the casting, having already asked to play Pyramus and Thisbe.
quotations.analysis: 'Too' is the joke: he has accepted the lead and wants the other parts as well, including the one with no words. Quince talks him out of it by explaining that a convincing lion would get the company hanged, which is the first of the play's several reminders that theatre in 1595 was a licensed activity.

quotations.text: Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania.
quotations.speaker: Oberon
quotations.context: The first meeting of the fairy king and queen in the play.
quotations.analysis: Six words establish that this marriage is in the middle of a long argument, and the greeting inverts a courtesy — well met — into its opposite. Everything the fairies do for the rest of the night is a move in a quarrel that began before the audience arrived.

quotations.text: And thorough this distemperature we see The seasons alter: hoary-headed frosts Far in the fresh lap of the crimson rose,
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: In the middle of her account of the damage the quarrel has done.
quotations.analysis: The speech puts flooded fields, rotted corn and human disease on the domestic argument's account, which is a far larger claim than any mortal in the play makes. It also dates the comedy for the first audience: the mid-1590s were years of ruined harvests and abnormal weather, and this is the play noticing.

quotations.text: Set your heart at rest: The fairy land buys not the child of me. His mother was a votaress of my order:
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: Refusing to hand over the changeling boy.
quotations.analysis: Her reason for keeping the child is not possessiveness but a promise to a dead friend, and the speech that follows is the warmest thing in the play — two women laughing on a beach at the shape of the sails. The boy himself never appears, and after Act IV nobody mentions him again.

quotations.text: It fell upon a little western flower, Before milk-white, now purple with love's wound, And maidens call it love-in-idleness.
quotations.speaker: Oberon
quotations.context: Describing how Cupid's arrow missed an imperial votaress and struck a flower.
quotations.analysis: The drug that drives the rest of the plot is given an origin story in three lines, and its colour is a wound. 'Love-in-idleness' is a real country name for the wild pansy, so the enchantment arrives dressed as folklore rather than as sorcery — which is how the play prefers its magic.

quotations.text: I'll put a girdle round about the earth In forty minutes.
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: Sent to fetch the flower from wherever it grows.
quotations.analysis: The boast fixes the scale of the wood: the errand crosses the world and takes less time than an act. It also quietly sets the play's clock against the audience's, since forty minutes is roughly how long the fairies are then offstage.

quotations.text: I am your spaniel; and, Demetrius, The more you beat me, I will fawn on you: Use me but as your spaniel, spurn me, strike me, Neglect me, lose me; only give me leave, Unworthy as I am, to follow you.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Pursuing Demetrius into the wood after he has told her to go away.
quotations.analysis: Four imperatives in a row, all of them asking to be hurt, and the one thing she requests is permission rather than affection. Oberon overhears this, which is why he intervenes — the play's only act of supernatural kindness is provoked by a woman debasing herself in front of a stranger.

quotations.text: Your wrongs do set a scandal on my sex: We cannot fight for love, as men may do; We should be wood and were not made to woo.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: After Demetrius threatens to do her mischief in the wood.
quotations.analysis: She identifies the rule she is breaking and states the cost of breaking it in one couplet. 'Wood' puns on wooed and on the old word for mad, and also names the place she is standing in — three meanings in a monosyllable, all of them about a woman who has come to the wrong place to do the wrong thing.

quotations.text: reason and love keep little company together now-a-days; the more the pity that some honest neighbours will not make them friends.
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: Replying to the fairy queen's declaration of love, while wearing an ass's head.
quotations.analysis: The play's thesis is delivered in prose by the only character who has not been given the drug, and he treats the failure of reason and love as a neighbourly dispute that a bit of mediation might settle. It is also a polite way of telling a queen that she is not making sense.

quotations.text: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: Watching the four lovers converge, having caused the confusion himself.
quotations.analysis: The line is usually quoted as detached wisdom; on stage it is an author admiring his own mistake. Puck has just proposed that they stay and watch, which makes the lovers' worst hour into an entertainment with two spectators — the same arrangement the audience is in.

quotations.text: So we grow together, Like to a double cherry, seeming parted, But yet an union in partition; Two lovely berries moulded on one stem;
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Accusing Hermia of joining the men in mocking her.
quotations.analysis: The most tender description of friendship in the play is made in the course of ending one, and every image in it is of two things that cannot be separated. 'Union in partition' is a paradox held together only by the grammar, which is what the friendship has become by this point in the night.

quotations.text: O, when she's angry, she is keen and shrewd! She was a vixen when she went to school; And though she be but little, she is fierce.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Hiding behind the men as Hermia loses her temper.
quotations.analysis: The line most often printed on posters is an insult delivered while retreating, and the evidence for it is what Hermia was like at school — the two women have known each other since childhood and are now using that knowledge as ammunition. Hermia's reply picks out the only word that matters to her: 'Little' again.

quotations.text: My Oberon! what visions have I seen! Methought I was enamour'd of an ass.
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: Waking after Oberon has taken the changeling boy and released her.
quotations.analysis: She calls it a vision, he says nothing about what he did, and the boy is never mentioned again by either of them. Her next line — that her eyes now loathe his visage — is aimed at a man asleep three feet away, and the comedy depends on the audience finding that funny rather than looking at it too closely.

quotations.text: The eye of man hath not heard, the ear of man hath not seen, man's hand is not able to taste, his tongue to conceive, nor his heart to report, what my dream was.
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: Alone on stage, waking after the others have gone.
quotations.analysis: The senses have been shuffled, which is exactly right for someone describing an experience the available vocabulary does not cover; the pattern is a garbled echo of St Paul on what the eye has not seen. The mangling is the meaning — this is the only character who admits that something happened which cannot be tidied into a morning story.

quotations.text: The lunatic, the lover and the poet Are of imagination all compact:
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Dismissing the lovers' account of the night before the entertainment begins.
quotations.analysis: 'All compact' means made entirely of, so the three are not compared but identified. The speech is the rational case against everything the audience has just watched, delivered by a character out of Greek myth in a play with fairies in it, and Hippolyta's reply — that all four tell the same story — is the only answer it gets.

quotations.text: And as imagination bodies forth The forms of things unknown, the poet's pen Turns them to shapes and gives to airy nothing A local habitation and a name.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: The continuation of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: He intends this as evidence that poets are unreliable, and produces the best description of writing in Shakespeare while doing it. 'A local habitation and a name' is what a stage gives a story — an address and a cast list — so the sceptic accidentally states the terms on which the theatre he is standing in operates.

quotations.text: The best in this kind are but shadows; and the worst are no worse, if imagination amend them.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Answering Hippolyta's complaint that the mechanicals' play is the silliest stuff she ever heard.
quotations.analysis: The defence of bad acting is also a defence of all acting, and it is made by the man who has just explained that imagination is not to be trusted. Hippolyta's answer is the sharper one: then it must be your imagination and not theirs, which puts the work of the theatre squarely on the people watching.

quotations.text: If we shadows have offended, Think but this, and all is mended, That you have but slumber'd here While these visions did appear.
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: The epilogue, spoken after the fairies have blessed the house.
quotations.analysis: 'Shadows' is Theseus's word for actors four hundred lines earlier, so the epilogue picks up the court's own dismissal and turns it into an apology. The offer is the one the characters have already accepted about themselves — call it a dream — and the rhymed tetrameter is the fairies' metre, which means the excuse is being made by the people who caused the trouble.

quotations.text: Persons attempting to find a motive in this narrative will be prosecuted; persons attempting to find a moral in it will be banished; persons attempting to find a plot in it will be shot.
quotations.context: The single sentence printed on its own page before the novel begins.
quotations.analysis: Three legal punishments escalate from prosecution to execution across one sentence, which is the same escalation the book's river towns run on. The joke is also a set of instructions: it is precisely the motive, the moral and the plot that readers have been arguing about ever since, and the notice knows it.

quotations.text: The shadings have not been done in a haphazard fashion, or by guesswork; but painstakingly, and with the trustworthy guidance and support of personal familiarity with these several forms of speech.
quotations.context: The note on dialect, printed immediately after the Notice.
quotations.analysis: Having just forbidden the reader to look for anything, Twain makes one claim in earnest, and it is about accuracy of ear. The effect is to put speech under warranty before the first chapter: how a character talks is going to be offered as evidence, so the reader is warned not to treat any voice in the book as neutral.

quotations.text: You don’t know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain’t no matter. That book was made by Mr. Mark Twain, and he told the truth, mainly. There was things which he stretched, but mainly he told the truth.
quotations.context: The opening of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The narrator reviews his own author in the third sentence, and grades him: mainly truthful, some stretching. That sets the terms for everything after it — this book will be judged by whether it tells the truth rather than whether it is well made — and it establishes at once that Huck's honesty and Huck's accuracy are not the same thing.

quotations.text: She said it was wicked to say what I said; said she wouldn’t say it for the whole world; she was going to live so as to go to the good place. Well, I couldn’t see no advantage in going where she was going, so I made up my mind I wouldn’t try for it.
quotations.context: Miss Watson has told Huck about heaven and hell, and he has said he wishes he were in the second one.
quotations.analysis: He rejects salvation on grounds of company, which is a child's reason and also the book's whole ethical method: Huck decides everything by who is in the room. The same calculation will produce his decision in Chapter 31, where he chooses hell again, and for exactly the same reason.

quotations.text: “Well, I b’lieve you, Huck. I⁠—I run off.”
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: On Jackson's Island, after Huck has sworn not to tell.
quotations.analysis: The hesitation is printed into the line — the pronoun is said twice with a dash between — and it is the only time in the book Jim stammers. He is handing a white child the power to have him hunted, and the novel measures the size of that in two syllables and a piece of punctuation.

quotations.text: “Yes; en I’s rich now, come to look at it. I owns mysef, en I’s wuth eight hund’d dollars. I wisht I had de money, I wouldn’ want no mo’.”
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: Telling Huck about his speculations in livestock and the bank that failed.
quotations.analysis: He performs the entire logic of slavery in three clauses: the man is the property, so running makes him the owner of an asset worth eight hundred dollars that he cannot sell or spend. The joke is exact and the final wish — that he had the money instead of merely being it — is the most desolate sentence in the chapter.

quotations.text: En all you wuz thinkin’ ’bout wuz how you could make a fool uv ole Jim wid a lie. Dat truck dah is trash; en trash is what people is dat puts dirt on de head er dey fren’s en makes ’em ashamed.
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: After Huck, reunited in the fog, has tried to convince him that the whole terrifying night was a dream.
quotations.analysis: Jim turns the leaves and rubbish on the raft into a definition and then applies it to a person, so the rebuke is built out of what is physically in front of them. It is the only moment in the book where an adult states a moral principle plainly, and it comes from the man the law counts as property; Huck's apology follows, and he records it as the hardest thing he ever did.

quotations.text: Jim said it made him all over trembly and feverish to be so close to freedom. Well, I can tell you it made me all over trembly and feverish, too, to hear him, because I begun to get it through my head that he was most free⁠—and who was to blame for it? Why, me.
quotations.context: Watching for the lights of Cairo, where the Ohio would carry them into free states.
quotations.analysis: The same four words describe two opposite feelings, and the repetition is what makes the passage work: Huck can feel exactly what Jim feels and has been taught to file it as guilt. 'Who was to blame' treats another man's liberty as damage, which is the vocabulary the whole book is trying to get out of and never quite does.

quotations.text: Then I thought a minute, and says to myself, hold on; s’pose you’d a done right and give Jim up, would you felt better than what you do now? No, says I, I’d feel bad⁠—I’d feel just the same way I do now.
quotations.context: Alone on the raft after turning two slave hunters away with a story about smallpox in the family.
quotations.analysis: He tests his moral training empirically and it fails: the two courses of action produce the same feeling, so the rule cannot be doing any work. Huck's conclusion is that he may as well stop bothering about right and wrong altogether, which is the funniest and bleakest joke in the novel — the failure of a corrupt ethics leaves him with no ethics he can name.

quotations.text: a feud is this way: A man has a quarrel with another man, and kills him; then that other man’s brother kills him; then the other brothers, on both sides, goes for one another; then the cousins chip in⁠—and by and by everybody’s killed off, and there ain’t no more feud. But it’s kind of slow, and takes a long time.
quotations.speaker: Buck Grangerford
quotations.context: Explaining to Huck what his family has been doing for thirty years.
quotations.analysis: The definition is delivered as a process with a predictable end state, like a recipe, and the last sentence complains about the pace rather than the outcome. Buck cannot say what the quarrel was about — a lawsuit, somebody lost — and he will be killed within two chapters, which makes his tone the exact measure of how thoroughly the thing has been inherited.

quotations.text: Not a sound anywheres⁠—perfectly still⁠—just like the whole world was asleep, only sometimes the bullfrogs a-cluttering, maybe.
quotations.context: The opening of the dawn passage, a few pages before the duke and the king come aboard.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built entirely out of negatives and qualifications, which is how Huck describes anything he loves: he will not commit to the silence without adding the frogs. This is the last unspoiled morning in the book — within four pages two men will climb onto the raft — and Twain gives it the most careful prose Huck ever produces.

quotations.text: It’s lovely to live on a raft. We had the sky up there, all speckled with stars, and we used to lay on our backs and look up at them, and discuss about whether they was made or only just happened.
quotations.context: Describing the nights before the two confidence men arrive.
quotations.analysis: Two people on a raft conduct a cosmological debate in the flattest possible terms — made, or only just happened — and neither of them wins. It is the only conversation in the book between equals, and Twain has placed it in the middle of the chapter that ends with the raft being taken over.

quotations.text: I was born and raised in the South, and I’ve lived in the North; so I know the average all around. The average man’s a coward.
quotations.speaker: Colonel Sherburn
quotations.context: On his own porch, facing the mob that has come to lynch him for shooting Boggs.
quotations.analysis: The speech works because it is true and because the man delivering it has just committed murder in front of a child. Twain gives the book's sharpest analysis of crowd cowardice to a killer and then gives nobody the reply, which leaves the reader holding an argument they cannot comfortably accept or refute.

quotations.text: “Well, that’s what I’m a-saying; all kings is mostly rapscallions, as fur as I can make out.”
quotations.speaker: Huckleberry Finn
quotations.context: On the raft, after Jim asks whether the two impostors are typical of royalty.
quotations.analysis: Huck defends the frauds by generalising them, and then runs through Henry the Eighth and half the English succession to prove it — which is his one piece of book learning and it is all wrong. The comedy conceals the point: the duke and the king are not a departure from how power behaves in this novel, they are a small provincial version of it.

quotations.text: Oh, Huck, I bust out a-cryin’ en grab her up in my arms, en say, ‘Oh, de po’ little thing! De Lord God Amighty fogive po’ ole Jim, kaze he never gwyne to fogive hisself as long’s he live!’ Oh, she was plumb deef en dumb, Huck, plumb deef en dumb⁠—en I’d ben a-treat’n her so!
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: Late at night on the raft, after Huck has woken to find him mourning for his wife and children.
quotations.analysis: The story is told as a piece of evidence against himself: he struck a four-year-old for disobedience she could not hear. Twain gives Jim a scene of self-accusation of exactly the kind he gives Huck, and the repetition of 'plumb deef en dumb' is the sound of a man still, years later, working out what happened.

quotations.text: “Good-bye. I’m going to do everything just as you’ve told me; and if I don’t ever see you again, I shan’t ever forget you and I’ll think of you a many and a many a time, and I’ll pray for you, too!”⁠—and she was gone.
quotations.speaker: Mary Jane Wilks
quotations.context: Leaving the house on Huck's instructions, so that the fraud can be exposed without her present.
quotations.analysis: She promises to pray for a boy who has spent three days lying to her, and Huck's reaction is to say that she could no more pray for Judas than for him. The novel gives him a person to protect for the first time since Jim, and the test matters because Jim is not there: it is the one decision he makes for somebody he has known for three days.

quotations.text: You can’t pray a lie⁠—I found that out.
quotations.context: Kneeling to pray for the strength to give Jim up, and finding the words will not come.
quotations.analysis: Five words and a discovery, reported in the past tense as though it were a fact about the world rather than about him. The sentence is the hinge of the book: Huck has established that he cannot deceive God, which leaves him nothing to hide behind when he sits down twenty lines later with the letter in his hand.

quotations.text: It was a close place. I took it up, and held it in my hand. I was a-trembling, because I’d got to decide, forever, betwixt two things, and I knowed it.
quotations.context: Holding the letter that would tell Miss Watson where Jim is.
quotations.analysis: Four short sentences, no subordination, and one adverb doing all the work: 'forever'. Huck understands the stakes exactly — he has just spent a page remembering Jim standing his watch and calling him honey — and the physical detail of the trembling hand is the only description in a passage otherwise made entirely of thought.

quotations.text: “All right, then, I’ll go to hell”⁠—and tore it up.
quotations.speaker: Huckleberry Finn
quotations.context: The decision, spoken aloud to himself on the raft.
quotations.analysis: The most moral act in American fiction is recorded as a sin by the person committing it, and the sentence gives two thirds of its length to the damnation and one clause to the deed. 'All right, then' is the tone of a boy conceding an argument he has lost, which is precisely what has happened: his conscience won, and he did the right thing anyway.

quotations.text: It was awful thoughts and awful words, but they was said. And I let them stay said; and never thought no more about reforming.
quotations.context: Immediately after tearing up the letter.
quotations.analysis: 'Let them stay said' treats speech as something that could have been withdrawn and deliberately was not, which is as close as Huck comes to claiming a decision. He then reclassifies himself as wicked by profession, and the novel lets the misdescription stand — there is nobody in the book qualified to correct him.

quotations.text: Well, it made me sick to see it; and I was sorry for them poor pitiful rascals, it seemed like I couldn’t ever feel any hardness against them any more in the world. It was a dreadful thing to see. Human beings can be awful cruel to one another.
quotations.context: Watching a mob carry the tarred and feathered duke and king through the town on a rail.
quotations.analysis: He pities two men who sold his friend for forty dollars, which is the clearest evidence in the book that his sympathy operates independently of desert. The final sentence is the only general statement Huck makes in the whole novel, and it is about the crowd rather than about the frauds.

quotations.text: it don’t make no difference whether you do right or wrong, a person’s conscience ain’t got no sense, and just goes for him anyway
quotations.context: Walking home after the mob has gone past, feeling to blame for something he did not do.
quotations.analysis: This is the finding of the experiment he ran in Chapter 16, now stated as a law. It also quietly protects the ending: a conscience that punishes indiscriminately is not a moral instrument at all, which is why Huck's decision on the raft has to be understood as made against his conscience rather than by it.

quotations.text: Well, den, is Jim gywne to say it? No, sah⁠—I doan’ budge a step out’n dis place ’dout a doctor, not if it’s forty year!
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: After Tom is shot in the leg during the escape, with the raft waiting and the river open.
quotations.analysis: He reasons it out first — would Tom leave a man to die? — and answers with the one thing he has that is entirely his own, which is his word. The choice costs him his liberty within the hour, and Twain places it in the middle of the section most often accused of throwing the novel's moral seriousness away.

quotations.text: But I reckon I got to light out for the Territory ahead of the rest, because Aunt Sally she’s going to adopt me and sivilize me, and I can’t stand it. I been there before.
quotations.context: The last sentences of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book ends where it began, with a boy running from a woman who wants to improve him, and the circle is the point: nothing in four hundred pages has changed his position. 'I been there before' is the flattest possible last line, and the Territory he proposes to light out for is Indian land the United States is in the process of taking.

quotations.text: To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: The first sentence of the collection.
quotations.analysis: The present tense is the surprising part: Watson is writing long afterwards and the habit still holds. Naming her by a definite article rather than a name turns a person into a category of one, and the sentence works as an announcement that the book will begin with the case its hero lost.

quotations.text: He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: Watson explaining what Irene Adler did and did not mean to Holmes.
quotations.analysis: 'I take it' is a hedge, and it is Watson's, not Doyle's: the narrator is offering an assessment he cannot verify about a man he lives with. The machine image will be contradicted within twenty pages by the same narrator noticing that Holmes has kept a photograph.

quotations.text: You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Before the stair-counting demonstration, in the sitting room at Baker Street.
quotations.analysis: The two verbs are almost synonyms in ordinary use, and Holmes prises them apart to make an ability sound like a discipline anyone could acquire. It is also a piece of self-promotion aimed at the man who writes the accounts, which is how the phrase came to be repeated for a century.

quotations.text: It is a capital mistake to theorise before one has data. Insensibly one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Refusing to speculate about an anonymous note before reading it properly.
quotations.analysis: The second sentence is the useful one, and it describes an error of character rather than of method — 'insensibly' concedes that nobody notices themselves doing it. Doyle, trained as a doctor, is describing diagnosis, and the collection's guilty parties are usually people who decided early what a fact meant.

quotations.text: I am lost without my Boswell.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Stopping Watson from leaving as a client arrives.
quotations.analysis: He does not say he needs an assistant; he says he needs a biographer. The joke concedes the whole structure of the book — that Holmes's work only exists for us because a companion writes it up — and it flatters Watson at the exact moment Holmes wants him to stay.

quotations.text: And that was how a great scandal threatened to affect the kingdom of Bohemia, and how the best plans of Mr. Sherlock Holmes were beaten by a woman’s wit.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: The closing sentence of the first story.
quotations.analysis: Watson gives the defeat the cadence of a triumph, with the long balanced clauses of a case closed. Note what the sentence does not say: the photograph is still in Adler's keeping, and the only thing actually recovered is Holmes's opinion of women.

quotations.text: It is quite a three pipe problem, and I beg that you won’t speak to me for fifty minutes.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: In the stalls at a concert, before the night's work at the bank.
quotations.analysis: Thinking is given a unit of measurement and a duration, which is a very Victorian way of describing genius — as a quantity of labour rather than a flash. The fifty minutes also buys Doyle a scene break, and the reader is kept outside the reasoning until the cellar.

quotations.text: My life is spent in one long effort to escape from the commonplaces of existence. These little problems help me to do so.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: After the arrest, yawning, as the case ends.
quotations.analysis: The motive stated here is not justice, money or curiosity but boredom, and it is offered as the ordinary condition of his life rather than an affectation. 'Little problems' reduces a bank robbery and a ruined pawnbroker to a distraction, which is the coldest thing Holmes says in the collection.

quotations.text: Depend upon it, there is nothing so unnatural as the commonplace.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Arguing that ordinary life is stranger than anything a novelist would invent.
quotations.analysis: It inverts the usual defence of realism: the commonplace is not the safe ground but the anomaly. Placed at the head of the collection's least violent case — a stepfather in false whiskers protecting an annuity — the remark functions as a working instruction for reading the rest.

quotations.text: The law cannot, as you say, touch you
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: To James Windibank, having proved that he courted his own stepdaughter in disguise.
quotations.analysis: He concedes the legal point and then, in the same breath, tells Windibank that no man ever deserved punishment more, before reaching for a hunting crop. The story ends with the crime proved, the criminal untouchable and the victim never told — a combination Doyle repeats often enough that it cannot be an accident.

quotations.text: There is nothing more deceptive than an obvious fact
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: On the train to Herefordshire, discussing the case against young McCarthy.
quotations.analysis: The line sets up the story's mechanism exactly: a son quarrels with his father, the father is found dead, and everybody stops there. Doyle is describing how circumstantial cases are built, and the story that follows is really about the difference between what happened and what a jury would believe.

quotations.text: You know my method. It is founded upon the observation of trifles.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Explaining to Watson how he read the ground by the pool.
quotations.analysis: 'Founded upon' is a builder's phrase, and the claim is that the small things are the foundation rather than the ornament. The sentence is also a piece of brand management — Holmes speaks of his method as an established system, to a man whose published accounts are what established it.

quotations.text: None of those which come to me are. I am the last court of appeal.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Answering a client who says his case is no ordinary one.
quotations.analysis: He describes himself in the language of a legal hierarchy while standing entirely outside it, and the claim is about position rather than skill: people reach him when the institutions have already failed. The story then makes the boast unbearable, since this client is dead within hours.

quotations.text: It was only by trying begging as an amateur that I could get the facts upon which to base my articles.
quotations.speaker: Neville St. Clair
quotations.reference: The Man with the Twisted Lip
quotations.context: Explaining how a journalist came to spend years as a beggar in the City.
quotations.analysis: The word 'amateur' is the hinge: he begins as a professional writer imitating a beggar and ends as a professional beggar imitating a gentleman, and the change is measured only in income. Doyle lets the man tell it himself, so the reader gets the whole social argument in the voice of someone who would rather not be making it.

quotations.text: My name is Sherlock Holmes. It is my business to know what other people don’t know.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
quotations.context: To a salesman in the Covent Garden market, having just won a bet about geese.
quotations.analysis: Two flat declarative sentences, one giving a name and one giving a trade, as though the second followed from the first. 'Business' is doing a lot of work: knowledge is stock, and the scene he has just played out was a small commercial transaction conducted with a sovereign and a wager.

quotations.text: I suppose that I am commuting a felony, but it is just possible that I am saving a soul.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
quotations.context: After letting James Ryder run out of the door at Christmas.
quotations.analysis: He names his own offence accurately and in legal language, then sets a soul against it on the other side of a 'but'. The balance of the sentence is the whole of his private jurisdiction: a man with no warrant weighing a prosecution against a life, and telling only Watson.

quotations.text: It is not cold which makes me shiver
quotations.speaker: Helen Stoner
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: At Baker Street before seven in the morning, moved nearer the fire.
quotations.analysis: Holmes has offered a physical explanation and she corrects it, which is the first sign that this client can be relied on to report accurately. Doyle gets a whole atmosphere out of a denial: the word 'terror' is never needed because the body has already supplied it.

quotations.text: When a doctor does go wrong he is the first of criminals. He has nerve and he has knowledge.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: Discussing Dr Grimesby Roylott with Watson, himself a doctor.
quotations.analysis: The observation is made to a physician by a man whose own qualifications are the same two — nerve and knowledge — which places Holmes and Roylott uncomfortably close together. Doyle had been a practising doctor, and the remark reads as a professional's assessment of what his training would equip him to do.

quotations.text: Violence does, in truth, recoil upon the violent, and the schemer falls into the pit which he digs for another.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: Standing over Roylott's body with the snake still in the room.
quotations.analysis: He reaches for a proverb and a psalm at the one moment in the collection where he has actually caused a death, and the borrowed wisdom does the work of not saying so. Holmes admits privately afterwards that he is indirectly responsible and that it will not weigh heavily on him.

quotations.text: I have lost my thumb and I have lost a fifty-guinea fee, and what have I gained?
quotations.speaker: Victor Hatherley
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Engineer's Thumb
quotations.context: On the train back to London, the house burnt and the gang gone.
quotations.analysis: He totals the case as a balance sheet and finds it in deficit, which is the only story in the collection to end that way. Holmes answers 'Experience', and the joke does not quite cover the fact that the detective arrived after everything and caught nobody.

quotations.text: It is very good of Lord St. Simon to honour my head by putting it on a level with his own
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Noble Bachelor
quotations.context: After the departing aristocrat has said the case will need wiser heads than either of theirs.
quotations.analysis: The client intended a courtesy and has delivered an insult, and Holmes returns it by taking the words literally. It is the collection's sharpest joke about rank, made by a man who has solved the case before the peer finished stating it and who declines to be thanked for it.

quotations.text: No, the debt is not to me. You owe a very humble apology to that noble lad, your son, who has carried himself in this matter as I should be proud to see my own son do, should I ever chance to have one.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Beryl Coronet
quotations.context: To Alexander Holder, who has had his son arrested for the theft.
quotations.analysis: The case is solved by physical evidence but judged on character, and the judgement falls on the client rather than the thief. The closing clause is the one glimpse of a private life the collection allows Holmes, and he offers it as a measure of someone else's conduct rather than a confidence.

quotations.text: I can’t make bricks without clay.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
quotations.context: Waiting for Violet Hunter's next letter, with nothing to work on.
quotations.analysis: He has just barked the same word three times, and the sentence that follows turns detection into a trade with raw materials and a supplier. The clay comes from a governess who is already inside the house, which makes her the working investigator of the story's first half.

quotations.text: It is my belief, Watson, founded upon my experience, that the lowest and vilest alleys in London do not present a more dreadful record of sin than does the smiling and beautiful countryside.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
quotations.context: Looking out of a train window at isolated houses in Hampshire.
quotations.analysis: The reason he gives is not moral but architectural: isolation, and the impunity it grants. It closes the collection by reversing the expected geography of Victorian crime fiction — the city is dangerous because it is crowded, the country because nobody is near enough to hear.

quotations.text: “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice “without pictures or conversations?”
quotations.context: The second sentence of the book, as Alice looks over her sister’s shoulder.
quotations.analysis: Carroll puts a judgement about books at the front of a book, and the judgement is a child’s test of quality: pictures and conversations. What follows is made almost entirely of both, so the opening is a specification that the rest of the text meets exactly.

quotations.text: “Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?” and sometimes, “Do bats eat cats?”
quotations.context: Falling down the rabbit-hole, growing sleepy.
quotations.analysis: The question reverses because Alice is going to sleep, and the reversal is the first sign that Wonderland runs on grammar rather than on events. She herself supplies the reason it does not matter which way round it is put — she cannot answer either — which is the exact logic the Hatter will later use against her.

quotations.text: “Curiouser and curiouser!” cried Alice (she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English)
quotations.context: Immediately after eating the cake, as she shoots up to nine feet.
quotations.analysis: Alice knows the comparative is wrong and says so in the same breath, so the nonsense is not outside language but one step past its usual limit. The doubling also gives the sentence an upward motion that matches what her body is doing, which is why no other word would serve.

quotations.text: But if I’m not the same, the next question is, Who in the world am I? Ah, that’s the great puzzle!
quotations.context: Alone in the hall, fanning herself with the Rabbit’s fan.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is a syllogism: if I am not the same, then I am someone else, so which one? Alice tests it against the only evidence a child has — Ada’s ringlets, Mabel’s ignorance, the multiplication table — and the test fails on all three, which is why the chapter ends with her in a pool of her own tears.

quotations.text: “Speak English!” said the Eaglet. “I don’t know the meaning of half those long words, and, what’s more, I don’t believe you do either!”
quotations.context: Interrupting the Dodo’s proposal for a Caucus-race.
quotations.analysis: The Eaglet does what nobody else in the book will do: it demands that an official voice be translated. Carroll gives the demand to the smallest bird present and immediately undercuts it — the Eaglet hides a smile — so the challenge to pompous language is itself a piece of social manoeuvring.

quotations.text: At last the Dodo said, “everybody has won, and all must have prizes.”
quotations.context: Ending the Caucus-race, in which the runners began when they liked and stopped when the Dodo said so.
quotations.analysis: A result is announced for a contest that had no start, no course and no finish. The sentence is perfectly formed and entirely empty, and it is the first of several occasions on which Wonderland uses correct official phrasing to settle something that was never in dispute.

quotations.text: “Who are you?” said the Caterpillar.
quotations.context: The Caterpillar’s first words, spoken from the mushroom.
quotations.analysis: Four words, and the book has spent four chapters making them unanswerable. Coming from a creature about to dissolve into a chrysalis and re-form as something else, the question is also a professional one, which is why Alice’s complaint about changing size gets so little sympathy.

quotations.text: “I can’t explain myself, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m not myself, you see.”
quotations.context: Answering the Caterpillar’s demand that she explain herself.
quotations.analysis: ‘Explain myself’ is a dead metaphor that Alice revives by taking it at full strength: to explain herself she would have to have a self to explain. The politeness of the phrasing — ‘I’m afraid, sir’ — keeps a genuinely frightening admission inside the manners of a well-brought-up child.

quotations.text: “Oh, you can’t help that,” said the Cat: “we’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.”
quotations.context: The Cheshire Cat, in a tree, after Alice objects that she does not want to go among mad people.
