quotations.analysis: The Cat includes itself and Alice in the same sentence, which converts an insult into a description of the premises. It then offers a proof by comparison with a dog, and the proof is formally respectable: the only thing wrong with it is that the premises about dogs are invented.

quotations.text: “That depends a good deal on where you want to get to,” said the Cat.
quotations.context: Answering Alice’s request for directions from the fork in the wood.
quotations.analysis: The Cat gives the only genuinely sound advice in the book, and it is useless to Alice because she has no destination. The exchange quietly names the book’s method: nothing underground can be navigated by a traveller who has not decided what she wants.

quotations.text: “Well! I’ve often seen a cat without a grin,” thought Alice; “but a grin without a cat! It’s the most curious thing I ever saw in my life!”
quotations.context: Watching the Cat vanish slowly, ending with the smile.
quotations.analysis: Alice separates a property from the thing that has it and notices that the result is impossible rather than merely odd. Her method here is the book’s in miniature: she states the ordinary case first, then the departure from it, and treats the gap as evidence worth recording.

quotations.text: “No room! No room!” they cried out when they saw Alice coming. “There’s plenty of room!” said Alice indignantly
quotations.context: Arriving at the tea-party, where three creatures are crowded into one corner of a large table.
quotations.analysis: The lie is contradicted by the furniture in the same sentence, and Alice answers it with a fact rather than an argument. Carroll establishes in two lines that this table runs on assertion, which is why the riddle that follows is allowed to have no answer.

quotations.text: The Hatter opened his eyes very wide on hearing this; but all he said was, “Why is a raven like a writing-desk?”
quotations.context: The Hatter’s first remark to Alice, dropped into a conversation about hair-cutting.
quotations.analysis: A riddle is a contract: you ask, I try, you tell me. The Hatter breaks it at every stage, and when Alice asks for the answer he says he has not the slightest idea. The joke is not the raven; it is a form of words that keeps its shape after its purpose has been removed.

quotations.text: “I’ve had nothing yet,” Alice replied in an offended tone, “so I can’t take more.”
quotations.context: The March Hare has just invited her to take more tea.
quotations.analysis: Alice is right and is told she is wrong, and the correction — that you cannot take less than nothing — is true of arithmetic and false of tea. It is the clearest case in the book of a creature winning an argument by changing which system the words belong to.

quotations.text: the Queen was in a furious passion, and went stamping about, and shouting “Off with his head!” or “Off with her head!” about once in a minute.
quotations.context: During the croquet game, in which the hoops keep walking away.
quotations.analysis: Carroll gives the rate rather than the drama: about once a minute. Turning a death sentence into a statistic drains it of menace, and the reader learns before Alice does that these orders are noise — the King has been quietly pardoning everybody behind the Queen’s back.

quotations.text: “We called him Tortoise because he taught us,” said the Mock Turtle angrily: “really you are very dull!”
quotations.context: Explaining why the old Turtle who taught him was called Tortoise.
quotations.analysis: The pun is delivered angrily, as though Alice were the slow one, and that is what makes the scene work: in Wonderland the person who has to have the joke explained is always at fault. The Mock Turtle’s whole education runs on the same principle, which is why he mourns it.

quotations.text: ‘Take care of the sense, and the sounds will take care of themselves.’
quotations.context: One of the Duchess’s morals, delivered with her chin in Alice’s shoulder.
quotations.analysis: The Duchess has inverted the proverb about pounds and pence, and the inversion is a fair description of Carroll’s own practice: mind the meaning and the sound follows. Coming from a woman who finds a moral in everything and observes none of them, it is advice the book both offers and mistrusts.

quotations.text: “I could tell you my adventures⁠—beginning from this morning,” said Alice a little timidly: “but it’s no use going back to yesterday, because I was a different person then.”
quotations.context: Offering to tell the Gryphon and the Mock Turtle her adventures.
quotations.analysis: This is the same question the Caterpillar asked, answered at last — not by working out who she is, but by accepting that yesterday’s Alice is no longer available for comparison. Her timidity over saying it is the measure of how large the admission is.

quotations.text: “Begin at the beginning,” the King said gravely, “and go on till you come to the end: then stop.”
quotations.context: Instructing the White Rabbit to read the verses offered as evidence.
quotations.analysis: The King’s only contribution to jurisprudence is a rule about reading aloud, delivered gravely as though it settled something. It is also the book’s sole piece of usable advice, and Carroll gives it to the least competent person in the room.

quotations.text: “No, no!” said the Queen. “Sentence first⁠—verdict afterwards.”
quotations.context: The Queen’s response to the King’s call for the jury to consider its verdict.
quotations.analysis: Every element of due process is present in the trial and only the order has gone; the Queen’s correction is procedural rather than mad. Alice’s reply, that the idea is stuff and nonsense, is the first time she names the problem instead of arguing inside it.

quotations.text: “Who cares for you?” said Alice, (she had grown to her full size by this time.) “You’re nothing but a pack of cards!”
quotations.context: The end of the trial, with Alice grown back to her full size.
quotations.analysis: ‘Nothing but’ does the work: the court is reduced to the material it is made of. Alice had noticed as much in Chapter VIII and kept it to herself; saying it aloud is what ends the dream, because the cards have no power once nobody agrees to treat them as a court.

books.title: American Ghost Stories
books.author: F. Marion Crawford, Ambrose Bierce, Ellen Glasgow and others

themes.name: The house as the haunted thing
Who is allowed to tell it

quotations.text: “Henry had words with Edward in the study the night before Edward died,” said Caroline Glynn.
quotations.context: The first line of Freeman's story. Edward lies dead in the house.
quotations.analysis: A murder story's opening in the grammar of a family complaint. Had words is exactly what a sister would say, and it puts the crime, if there is one, inside the ordinary vocabulary of a household quarrel.

quotations.text: Even the shock of death—for her brother Edward lay dead in the house—could not disturb her outward serenity of demeanor.
quotations.context: Describing Emma, the married sister and the family beauty, in her rocking-chair.
quotations.analysis: The dash drops the corpse into the middle of a sentence about composure. Freeman's comedy of manners is doing the work of a ghost story: the body in the house is a parenthesis to the sisters' self-possession.

quotations.text: “That strange shadow on the wall,” replied Mrs. Brigham.
quotations.context: Emma notices the shadow while sewing in the study; her sisters have seen it every night since Edward died.
quotations.analysis: It enters the story as something to remark on, and Caroline will not turn round to look. Freeman lets the reader work out that the shadow is old news to everyone in the room but Emma.

quotations.text: Not a line of its terrible outlines wavered.
quotations.context: Henry, a doctor, moves the study furniture to change the shadow.
quotations.analysis: A shadow that ignores the light is a contradiction stated as an observation. Henry has tested it like a scientist and the test has failed; from here his reasonableness starts to look like fear.

quotations.text: It is well known that the old Manton house is haunted.
quotations.reference: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
quotations.context: The first sentence of Bierce's story.
quotations.analysis: Well known is the phrase of a man who has not checked. Bierce starts in the voice of local consensus so that the story's end can show what the consensus missed.

quotations.text: incredulity is confined to those opinionated persons who will be called “cranks” as soon as the useful word shall have penetrated the intellectual demesne of the Marshall Advance
quotations.reference: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
quotations.context: Continuing the case for the haunting.
quotations.analysis: Bierce mocks the sceptics and the local paper in one sentence, and the joke is aimed at everybody. The reader is invited to side with neither, which is the right position for the ending.

quotations.text: The evidence that the house is haunted is of two kinds; the testimony of disinterested witnesses who have had ocular proof, and that of the house itself.
quotations.reference: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
quotations.context: Setting out the case like a lawyer.
quotations.analysis: The house is called as a witness. The legal parody is funny, and it also tells you exactly how the story will be solved: not by what anyone saw, but by what the house kept.

quotations.text: “The middle toe is missing—it was Gertrude!”
quotations.reference: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
quotations.context: The last line, spoken by Gertrude's brother over the bare footprints in the dust.
quotations.analysis: The detail was planted on the hotel porch, where King admits he once threw over a girl who had lost a toe. It returns as identification. Bierce's method in one line: the supernatural is proved by a physical oddity, and the reader supplies the rest.

quotations.text: It was intolerably unchanged, the dim, dark-toned room.
quotations.context: The first sentence of Dunbar's story, spoken by the dead narrator.
quotations.analysis: Intolerably is the word that tells you who is speaking: only someone who has left could find sameness unbearable. The ghost's first experience is not horror but a housekeeper's discomfort at a room that went on without her.

quotations.text: the very gaps that I myself had left in my bookshelves still stood unfilled
quotations.context: Noticing what has not changed.
quotations.analysis: The dead notice absences. Dunbar gives her ghost an exact, bookish observation — the gaps are hers, and nobody has closed them — so that grief is described from the side of the person grieved for.

quotations.text: my work-basket was in disorder; it was preposterous that so small a thing should hurt me so
quotations.context: One of the first signs that her sister has taken her place.
quotations.analysis: The jealousy of the whole story arrives through a sewing basket. Dunbar makes the smallest domestic change carry the largest loss, and lets the narrator be embarrassed by her own feeling.

quotations.text: I am freed.
quotations.context: The first words of the final section, after she has brought her husband and her sister together.
quotations.analysis: Three words, after pages of possessive watching. The ghost gets out not by being laid to rest by the living but by letting them go, which reverses the usual direction of the form.

quotations.text: Theirs is the fullest joy that the dwellers in the shell of sense can know. Mine is the transcendent joy of the unseen spaces.
quotations.context: The last sentences of the story.
quotations.analysis: The title phrase comes back. Halfway through, Frances used it in a line of verse for the living, pitying them; now it names the happiness she is leaving them to. Dunbar gives her ghost the last word and a larger joy than anyone left in the room.

themes.name: Names, and the right to choose them
Orphans, hired help and respectable farms
Grief, and a future made smaller

quotations.text: not even a brook could run past Mrs. Rachel Lynde’s door without due regard for decency and decorum
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the novel, describing the hollow where Mrs Rachel lives.
quotations.analysis: A brook that is headlong and full of dark secrets in the woods becomes quiet and well-conducted when it reaches a particular window: the village’s disciplinary power is established as a fact of the landscape before any character speaks. The alliteration of ‘decency and decorum’ is Mrs Rachel’s own phrasing, lent to the narrator a paragraph before she is introduced.

quotations.text: I asked her to go into the ladies’ waiting room, but she informed me gravely that she preferred to stay outside. ‘There was more scope for imagination,’ she said. She’s a case, I should say.
quotations.speaker: The station master
quotations.context: Matthew arrives at Bright River to collect a boy and is told what is waiting for him.
quotations.analysis: Anne’s defining phrase reaches the reader at second hand, inside a railwayman’s report, with quotation marks around it as though it were evidence. ‘She’s a case’ is the verdict Avonlea will keep offering for thirty chapters, and the novel’s method is to let her phrase outlive the judgement.

quotations.text: I shall call it⁠—let me see⁠—the Lake of Shining Waters. Yes, that is the right name for it. I know because of the thrill.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: On the drive from Bright River, renaming Barry’s pond.
quotations.analysis: The test she applies is physical rather than aesthetic: a name is right when it produces a thrill, which makes naming a kind of instrument reading. Note that she does this before she knows whether she is allowed to stay — the renaming of the district is done by a child who may be sent back on the morning train.

quotations.text: But if you call me Anne please call me Anne spelled with an e.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: In the Green Gables kitchen, being interrogated by Marilla about the mistake.
quotations.analysis: The sentence concedes and demands in the same breath: she gives up Cordelia and instantly opens a second negotiation. A child with no say over where she sleeps is bargaining over orthography, which is the only territory available to her, and the request is granted — Marilla uses the formula back at her twice in the same scene.

quotations.text: When you hear a name pronounced can’t you always see it in your mind, just as if it was printed out? I can; and A-n-n looks dreadful, but A-n-n-e looks so much more distinguished.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Explaining to Marilla why the letter matters.
quotations.analysis: The explanation is an accurate description of synaesthetic reading, offered by a child to an adult who has never thought about it. It also quietly establishes the difference between the two of them: Marilla hears words, Anne sees them printed, and most of their misunderstandings for the next thirty chapters follow from that.

quotations.text: I can’t. I’m in the depths of despair. Can you eat when you are in the depths of despair?
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Refusing supper on her first evening, having been told she is not wanted.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is borrowed from books and used with complete sincerity, and the question that follows is genuine — she is asking for information. Marilla’s flat reply, that she has never been in the depths of despair, sets the two registers of the novel against each other in three lines of dialogue.

quotations.text: “We might be some good to her,” said Matthew suddenly and unexpectedly.
quotations.speaker: Matthew Cuthbert
quotations.context: Marilla has been listing the reasons the child cannot possibly stay.
quotations.analysis: Seven words that decide the book, and the narrator flags their rarity rather than their content — ‘suddenly and unexpectedly’ is about Matthew speaking at all. The grammar also reverses the household’s assumption: they had applied for a boy who would be some good to them.

quotations.text: Suppose she wasn’t really going to stay here! She would imagine she was. There was scope for imagination here.
quotations.context: Anne’s first morning, kneeling at the east gable window.
quotations.analysis: Free indirect style puts the reader inside a decision being made in real time: the exclamation is Anne’s, and so is the flat sentence that answers it. Imagination is presented here as a deliberate act of management rather than a daydream — she will imagine that she is staying because the alternative is unbearable and no other resource exists.

quotations.text: A bosom friend⁠—an intimate friend, you know⁠—a really kindred spirit to whom I can confide my inmost soul.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Explaining to Marilla what she means when she says she wants a bosom friend.
quotations.analysis: The definition arrives in three stages, each one more literary than the last, and the escalation is the joke. But the sentence also names the novel’s scarcest commodity: Anne has had households, matrons and other people’s twins, and has never once had a person of her own choosing.

quotations.text: It would be so much easier to be good if one’s hair was a handsome auburn, don’t you think?
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: To Mrs Rachel Lynde, immediately after making her apology for the quarrel about her looks.
quotations.analysis: The apology has just been performed with theatrical relish, and this is the sentence that follows it: goodness treated as a matter of appearance, offered to the woman whose remark about her hair caused the quarrel. Montgomery lets Anne win Mrs Rachel over in the same speech in which she reveals she has learned nothing about vanity.

quotations.text: “Carrots! Carrots!”
quotations.speaker: Gilbert Blythe
quotations.context: In the schoolroom, after Gilbert has failed to make Anne look at him.
quotations.analysis: Two words, one line to itself, and five years of plot. The word is an insult about poverty as much as about colour — red hair is the one feature of herself Anne has never been able to reimagine — and it arrives from the only pupil in Avonlea who is her intellectual equal.

quotations.text: “There’s a great deal of difference between being called a crow and being called carrots,” said Anne with dignity. “Gilbert Blythe has hurt my feelings excruciatingly, Diana.”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Diana has pointed out that Charlie Sloane calls her a crow and she does not mind.
quotations.analysis: ‘With dignity’ is the narrator’s small betrayal of a girl who has just broken a slate over a boy’s head, and ‘excruciatingly’ is Anne restoring the scale of the injury by vocabulary alone. The distinction she is defending is real to her and invisible to everyone else, which is the shape of most of her quarrels.

quotations.text: “Marilla, isn’t it nice to think that tomorrow is a new day with no mistakes in it yet?”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: The evening of the liniment cake, after the minister and his wife have gone home.
quotations.analysis: The consolation is offered to Marilla rather than claimed for herself, which is the first sign of the adult Anne. ‘Yet’ is the word that keeps the sentence honest: it concedes that tomorrow will also be filled with mistakes, and proposes only that they have not happened.

quotations.text: “I must do it. My honour is at stake,” said Anne solemnly. “I shall walk that ridgepole, Diana, or perish in the attempt. If I am killed you are to have my pearl bead ring.”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Josie Pye has dared her to walk the ridgepole of the Barrys’ kitchen roof.
quotations.analysis: The language of chivalric romance is applied to a dare from a girl she dislikes, and the will disposing of a pearl bead ring is the exact measure of what Anne owns. The narrator then notes drily that walking ridgepoles is not a thing in which imagination helps you out much — the book’s clearest statement of where the gift stops.

quotations.text: “Yes, it’s green,” moaned Anne. “I thought nothing could be as bad as red hair. But now I know it’s ten times worse to have green hair.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Confessing to Marilla after buying hair dye from a pedlar.
quotations.analysis: The comedy depends on a genuinely painful fact established twenty chapters earlier: the hair is the one thing about herself Anne has never been able to redescribe. Her consolation afterwards — that a wicked act should at least be wicked to some purpose — is the closest the novel comes to a theology of mistakes.

quotations.text: There are so many things in this room and all so splendid that there is no scope for imagination. That is one consolation when you are poor⁠—there are so many more things you can imagine about.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: In Miss Barry’s spare room in Charlottetown, on the visit that follows the hotel concert.
quotations.analysis: The novel’s economics stated in two sentences, and by the person they apply to: imagination is described as a compensation for not having things. It is also a considerable piece of tact, delivered in a velvet-carpeted room belonging to a rich woman who is listening.

quotations.text: I’m not a bit changed⁠—not really. I’m only just pruned down and branched out.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Sitting on Marilla’s lap at Green Gables, home from Queen’s, after Marilla has said she seems grown up and different.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is taken from the orchard outside the window, which is the register Marilla can actually hear — Anne has learned to translate. It also concedes more than it admits: pruning is a loss of growth carried out deliberately, and the last chapters will require exactly that.

quotations.text: “Well now, I’d rather have you than a dozen boys, Anne,” said Matthew patting her hand. “Just mind you that⁠—rather than a dozen boys.
quotations.speaker: Matthew Cuthbert
quotations.context: Walking back with the cows on the last evening of his life, after Anne has said she wishes she had been the boy they sent for.
quotations.analysis: The sentence answers the clerical error of Chapter 1 directly, and Matthew repeats it because he knows he is bad at saying things. Montgomery places it the evening before his death, so that the novel’s one explicit declaration of love is also the last thing he manages to do.

quotations.text: It’s never been easy for me to say things out of my heart, but at times like this it’s easier. I love you as dear as if you were my own flesh and blood and you’ve been my joy and comfort ever since you came to Green Gables.
quotations.speaker: Marilla Cuthbert
quotations.context: The night after Matthew’s funeral, hearing Anne crying in her room.
quotations.analysis: Marilla explains why she can speak before she speaks, which is characteristic: the confession is prefaced by an account of her own reticence. ‘As dear as if’ preserves the fact that Anne is not her flesh and blood, and the novel’s whole argument about who belongs to whom is settled on that conjunction.

quotations.text: When I left Queen’s my future seemed to stretch out before me like a straight road. I thought I could see along it for many a milestone. Now there is a bend in it. I don’t know what lies around the bend, but I’m going to believe that the best does.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Telling Marilla that she has given up the Avery scholarship and will teach at Carmody instead.
quotations.analysis: The image is the opposite of the one she began with: a road she cannot see along is now preferable to a road she can. Note the verb — ‘I’m going to believe’ — which makes optimism an act of will rather than a temperament, and quietly answers everyone who has called her a case.

quotations.text: God’s in his heaven, all’s right with the world,
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: The last line of the novel, whispered at the gable window.
quotations.analysis: The line is Browning’s, sung by a child in a play about a village that is not in fact all right, and Montgomery hands it to a girl whose horizons have just closed in. Quoting rather than asserting is the point: Anne ends the book borrowing somebody else’s certainty and choosing to mean it.

quotations.text: I think some kinds of sewing would be nice; but there’s no scope for imagination in patchwork.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Set to sew red and white diamonds by Marilla, who believes in useful work.
quotations.analysis: The phrase that began as a description of a railway platform has become a general test she applies to everything, from cookery to algebra. It is also a joke about the novel’s own form: a book made of small self-contained episodes stitched into a pattern is complaining about patchwork.

quotations.text: Nay, but this dotage of our general's O'erflows the measure: those his goodly eyes, That o'er the files and musters of the war Have glow'd like plated Mars, now bend, now turn, The office and devotion of their view Upon a tawny front
quotations.speaker: Philo
quotations.context: The opening lines of the play, spoken to a fellow Roman officer just before Antony and Cleopatra walk on.
quotations.analysis: The audience is given the Roman verdict before it is given a single fact, and the verb does the work: measure is the Roman unit of everything, and Antony is accused of exceeding it. Note that the criticism is grammatically a compliment gone wrong — the eyes still glow, they have simply been redirected.

quotations.text: There's beggary in the love that can be reckon'd.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: Answering Cleopatra's opening challenge, 'If it be love indeed, tell me how much.'
quotations.analysis: Her question is a piece of accounting and his answer refuses the ledger, which sets the terms of the whole play. 'Reckon'd' carries both counting and being called to account, so the line quietly declines two different Roman demands in one word.

quotations.text: Let Rome in Tiber melt, and the wide arch Of the ranged empire fall! Here is my space.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: Refusing to hear the messengers from Rome in front of Cleopatra.
quotations.analysis: The first of the play's melting images arrives as bravado and returns in Act IV as diagnosis. 'Here is my space' is three monosyllables after a collapsing empire, and it is spoken by a man standing on a stage — the smallest possible claim, made in the largest possible terms.

quotations.text: he fishes, drinks, and wastes The lamps of night in revel; is not more man-like Than Cleopatra; nor the queen of Ptolemy More womanly than he
quotations.speaker: Octavius Caesar
quotations.context: Reading the dispatches from Alexandria aloud to Lepidus.
quotations.analysis: The charge is not laziness but exchange: Caesar's grievance is that the two of them have swapped a quality he believes is fixed. The sentence is arranged as a balance with Antony and Cleopatra on either side of it, so the syntax performs the crossing it complains of.

quotations.text: This common body, Like to a vagabond flag upon the stream, Goes to and back, lackeying the varying tide, To rot itself with motion.
quotations.speaker: Octavius Caesar
quotations.context: On hearing that Pompey is gaining support among the people.
quotations.analysis: Caesar's one extended image in the play is of the public as pondweed, and it tells you what kind of ruler he will be. 'Lackeying' turns the crowd into a servant running beside a horse, and 'rot itself with motion' denies that popular movement is even alive.

quotations.text: My salad days, When I was green in judgment: cold in blood, To say as I said then!
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: Silencing Charmian, who has reminded her how she once praised Julius Caesar.
quotations.analysis: She rewrites her own past on the spot rather than lose an argument, and the phrase has been so thoroughly borrowed since that its edge is easy to miss: green is unripe, and cold in blood is an accusation of having been insufficiently alive. The revision is the performance.

quotations.text: The barge she sat in, like a burnish'd throne, Burn'd on the water: the poop was beaten gold; Purple the sails, and so perfumed that The winds were love-sick with them
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: In Rome, to Agrippa and Maecenas, minutes after Antony has agreed to marry Octavia.
quotations.analysis: The placing is the argument: the treaty has just been signed and Enobarbus immediately tells the signatories what they have bargained against. Shakespeare keeps much of North's prose almost word for word but breaks it across the verse line, so that the sentence never rests where the metre does.

quotations.text: With divers-colour'd fans, whose wind did seem To glow the delicate cheeks which they did cool, And what they undid did.
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: Continuing the description of Cleopatra on the river Cydnus.
quotations.analysis: Four words at the end of the sentence contradict themselves twice and remain perfectly grammatical. It is the play's whole method in miniature: the fans cool and heat at once, and Cleopatra is not a paradox to be resolved but a description that has to hold both halves.

quotations.text: Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale Her infinite variety: other women cloy The appetites they feed: but she makes hungry Where most she satisfies
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: Answering Maecenas, who has just said that Antony must now leave her for good.
quotations.analysis: The claim is presented as a prediction about Antony's behaviour, not a compliment, which is why the Romans take it seriously. 'Custom' and 'cloy' are both words about repetition wearing things out, and the line's argument is that Cleopatra has found a way of not repeating herself.

quotations.text: Mine honesty and I begin to square.
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: An aside, watching Cleopatra receive Caesar's messenger after Actium.
quotations.analysis: 'Square' means to quarrel, and the line splits a man from his own integrity as though they were two soldiers falling out. Everything Enobarbus says for the rest of the scene is an argument with himself conducted in the third person, and he loses it.

quotations.text: Egypt, thou knew'st too well My heart was to thy rudder tied by the strings, And thou shouldst tow me after
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: In Alexandria after Actium, forgiving Cleopatra for the flight he chose to follow.
quotations.analysis: He calls her by the name of her country, which is what the Romans do, and then describes himself as cargo. The accusation and the excuse are the same sentence: she knew, therefore it is her doing, and he was towed, therefore it is not his.

quotations.text: That which is now a horse, even with a thought The rack dislimns, and makes it indistinct, As water is in water.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: To Eros, watching the evening clouds change shape before his last defeat.
quotations.analysis: 'Dislimns' — unpaints — is rare enough that Shakespeare may have made it, and it treats the sky as a canvas being wiped. The simile then refuses the comfort of a comparison: water in water is not like dissolution, it is the thing itself, and there is nothing left to see it against.

quotations.text: My good knave Eros, now thy captain is Even such a body: here I am Antony: Yet cannot hold this visible shape, my knave.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: Applying the cloud image to himself, moments before asking Eros to kill him.
quotations.analysis: 'Here I am Antony' ought to be the most certain statement a man can make, and the next line takes it back. The name has been public property since the first scene — Philo's, Caesar's, Cleopatra's — and Antony is the last person to lose his grip on it.

quotations.text: But let the world rank me in register A master-leaver and a fugitive
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: Alone in a ditch by Caesar's camp, after Antony has sent his abandoned treasure after him.
quotations.analysis: A man who has spent the play writing other people's reputations asks for his own to be filed under two words. 'Register' is a clerk's word, and the request is for no mitigation at all — he has understood that the record is the only judgement there will be.

quotations.text: I am dying, Egypt, dying: Give me some wine, and let me speak a little.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: Hauled up into the monument, bleeding from his own sword.
quotations.analysis: He has already said the same half-line twenty-seven lines earlier, and repetition is how the scene measures time: the dying takes long enough that he has to announce it twice. The request is for wine and for permission — the most public man in the world asking to be allowed to finish a sentence.

quotations.text: The crown o' the earth doth melt. My lord! O, wither'd is the garland of the war, The soldier's pole is fall'n: young boys and girls Are level now with men; the odds is gone, And there is nothing left remarkable Beneath the visiting moon.
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: The moment Antony dies in her arms at the top of the monument.
quotations.analysis: Grief is expressed as the collapse of every scale of difference: with the pole gone, children and men measure the same. 'The odds is gone' is flat and almost colloquial in the middle of the grandest lament in the play, and it is the line that tells you what she thinks she has lost — not a lover but a standard.

quotations.text: His legs bestrid the ocean: his rear'd arm Crested the world: his voice was propertied As all the tuned spheres
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: Describing her dream of Antony to Dolabella, one of Caesar's officers.
quotations.analysis: She is making a colossus out of a man who died badly two scenes ago, and she asks Dolabella outright whether such a person could have existed. His honest no does not end the exchange: she answers that dreaming him is itself a kind of evidence, which is the play's last defence of the imagination against Roman fact.

quotations.text: He words me, girls, he words me, that I should not Be noble to myself
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: The instant Caesar leaves, having promised her kind treatment.
quotations.analysis: Turning the noun into a verb is the whole judgement: Caesar's courtesy is a technique and she has seen the mechanism. Her word for suicide here is 'noble to myself', which converts a Roman virtue into something a queen can do alone and in private.

quotations.text: the quick comedians Extemporally will stage us, and present Our Alexandrian revels; Antony Shall be brought drunken forth, and I shall see Some squeaking Cleopatra boy my greatness I' the posture of a whore.
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: Explaining to Iras what a Roman triumph would actually involve.
quotations.analysis: The line was first spoken by a boy actor playing Cleopatra, so the theatre is required to admit its own limits at the very moment she rejects them. What she fears is not death or captivity but a bad performance, and the fear is what drives her to write a better final scene.

quotations.text: Give me my robe, put on my crown; I have Immortal longings in me
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: After the clown has delivered the basket of figs and wished her joy o' the worm.
quotations.analysis: She dresses for a coronation rather than a death, and the stage business is deliberate: robe and crown are the properties Caesar intended to parade. The word 'longings' keeps the appetite the Romans accused her of and attaches it to eternity instead of to supper.

quotations.text: I am fire and air; my other elements I give to baser life.
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: Dressed and crowned, a few lines before the asp is applied.
quotations.analysis: Four elements were supposed to make a body; she discards earth and water and keeps the two that rise. It is also a direct answer to Antony's 'kingdoms are clay' in the first scene — the play's opening and closing images of substance are spoken by the two lovers about the same set of things.

quotations.text: Dost thou not see my baby at my breast, That sucks the nurse asleep?
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: With the asp at her breast, as Charmian cries out.
quotations.analysis: The image makes her death an act of feeding, and the venom a child. Cleopatra's own children are barely mentioned in the play; here, at the last possible moment, she becomes a mother to the thing killing her, and asks a question rather than making a claim.

quotations.text: Now boast thee, death, in thy possession lies A lass unparallel'd. Downy windows, close;
quotations.speaker: Charmian
quotations.context: Closing the dead queen's eyes before applying an asp to herself.
quotations.analysis: After five acts of Egypt, empire and infinite variety, the summing-up word is 'lass' — the smallest, plainest, most domestic noun available. Charmian then straightens the crown, which is the only correction anyone in the play manages to make to how Cleopatra will be seen.

quotations.text: She shall be buried by her Antony: No grave upon the earth shall clip in it A pair so famous.
quotations.speaker: Octavius Caesar
quotations.context: The play's closing speech, after the guards find Cleopatra dead.
quotations.analysis: The winner's last act is to arrange the funeral of the people who beat him to it, and 'clip' — embrace — lets the grave do what Caesar prevented. He is already speaking of them as a story worth lamenting, which is exactly the outcome Cleopatra spent the act securing.

themes.name: Pastoral, and the work in it
themes.canonicalName: Pastoral, and the work in it

techniques.name: Prose as a medium of thought
techniques.canonicalName: Prose as a medium of thought

quotations.text: and--in my heart Lie there what hidden woman's fear there will-- We'll have a swashing and a martial outside, As many other mannish cowards have That do outface it with their semblances.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Planning the disguise with Celia, in the hour after her banishment.
quotations.analysis: She describes manhood as a costume other men are also wearing, which turns her disguise into a general observation rather than a deception. 'Outface it with their semblances' is a courtier's phrase about courtiers, and it arrives before she has entered the wood — the play's scepticism about performed identity is in place from the start.

quotations.text: I'll have no worse a name than Jove's own page; And therefore look you call me Ganymede.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Choosing a name for the disguise, immediately after Celia asks what to call her.
quotations.analysis: Ganymede is the boy Jove carried off, and by 1599 the name was ordinary slang for a young male favourite — so Rosalind picks the most charged alias available and the play never explains it. Celia's answering choice, Aliena, simply means the estranged one, which makes the pair a comment on each other.

quotations.text: Sweet are the uses of adversity, Which, like the toad, ugly and venomous, Wears yet a precious jewel in his head;
quotations.speaker: Duke Senior
quotations.context: His first speech, to the lords who have followed him into exile.
quotations.analysis: The toadstone was a piece of folklore that had been doubted for a century, so the consolation rests on an example the audience may not believe. That is characteristic of him: the speech is beautiful, sincere and delivered by a man who will propose killing deer for dinner six lines later.

quotations.text: And this our life exempt from public haunt Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks, Sermons in stones and good in every thing.
quotations.speaker: Duke Senior
quotations.context: The end of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: Each clause puts a court accomplishment into a natural object — speech, learning, preaching — so the forest is praised for being a better version of what he has lost. The last phrase, 'good in every thing', is exactly the kind of generalisation the rest of the play spends five acts testing.

quotations.text: Ay, now am I in Arden; the more fool I; when I was at home, I was in a better place: but travellers must be content.
quotations.speaker: Touchstone
quotations.context: The moment the three exiles arrive in the forest, exhausted.
quotations.analysis: This is the first thing said about Arden by somebody who has just walked there, and it flatly contradicts the speech the audience heard two scenes ago. 'Travellers must be content' is a proverb used as a shrug, and the prose rhythm — three short clauses and a resigned fourth — is the opposite of the duke's expansive verse.

quotations.text: And so, from hour to hour, we ripe and ripe, And then, from hour to hour, we rot and rot; And thereby hangs a tale.
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: Quoting the fool he met in the forest, to the duke and his lords.
quotations.analysis: Jaques is reporting Touchstone, so the play's bleakest formulation reaches us at second hand from a professional joker. The repeated verbs make growth and decay the same mechanical process, and the tag at the end — 'thereby hangs a tale' — refuses to draw any moral at all.

quotations.text: All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players: They have their exits and their entrances; And one man in his time plays many parts, His acts being seven ages.
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: Picking up the duke's remark that their misery is only one scene in a universal theatre.
quotations.analysis: The speech is not Jaques's idea: the duke has just used the theatre image and Jaques takes it off him and runs. 'Merely' means entirely, not slightly, and the seven parts that follow are all masculine and all solitary — there is no scene in his account in which two people are together.

quotations.text: Last scene of all, That ends this strange eventful history, Is second childishness and mere oblivion, Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: The end of the seven ages, as Orlando carries the starving Adam onto the stage.
quotations.analysis: The staging answers the speech: Jaques finishes describing old age as an empty room and an actual old man is carried in and fed. Four repetitions of 'sans' — a French word in an English line — strip the sentence down as they go, and 'everything' arrives where a noun should be.

quotations.text: Blow, blow, thou winter wind. Thou art not so unkind As man's ingratitude; Thy tooth is not so keen, Because thou art not seen, Although thy breath be rude.
quotations.speaker: Amiens
quotations.context: Sung at the duke's table while Orlando and Adam eat.
quotations.analysis: The song makes the argument of the whole forest in six lines: weather is cruel but impersonal, and therefore easier to bear than people. 'Because thou art not seen' is the hinge — the wind has no face to be hurt by, which is precisely what Orlando and Adam have just escaped from at home.

quotations.text: Truly, shepherd, in respect of itself, it is a good life, but in respect that it is a shepherd's life, it is naught. In respect that it is solitary, I like it very well; but in respect that it is private, it is a very vile life.
quotations.speaker: Touchstone
quotations.context: Answering Corin's polite question about how he likes the shepherd's life.
quotations.analysis: Six clauses, each cancelling the last, and the joke is that the form is a parody of scholastic argument aimed at a man who has never been to school. It also happens to be a fair description of pastoral itself — charming in the abstract, poor in the particular.

quotations.text: the property of rain is to wet and fire to burn; that good pasture makes fat sheep, and that a great cause of the night is lack of the sun
quotations.speaker: Corin
quotations.context: Asked by Touchstone whether he has any philosophy in him.
quotations.analysis: Every item is something he has had to know in order to keep animals alive, and the list is funny only if you assume knowledge should look like something else. Touchstone's reply — that a man who has never been at court is damned — is the play's sharpest joke at the expense of the courtly position it keeps testing.

quotations.text: Do you not know I am a woman? when I think, I must speak.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: To Celia, while dressed as Ganymede and desperate for news of Orlando.
quotations.analysis: She is wearing a doublet and hose and claiming a woman's licence to talk, which is the disguise's whole comedy in one sentence. The line is also a conventional joke about women's speech, put in the mouth of the character who has more lines than any other woman Shakespeare wrote.

quotations.text: Love is merely a madness, and, I tell you, deserves as well a dark house and a whip as madmen do: and the reason why they are not so punished and cured is, that the lunacy is so ordinary that the whippers are in love too.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Setting up the offer to cure Orlando of his love.
quotations.analysis: The dark house and the whip were the real treatment for madness in 1599, so the joke has a cold floor under it. The turn comes in the last clause: the reason nobody is treated is that everybody, including the people who would do the whipping, has the disease — which makes love a condition of the whole society rather than a fault in a lover.

quotations.text: Dead Shepherd, now I find thy saw of might, 'Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?'
quotations.speaker: Phebe
quotations.context: Alone with Silvius, after Ganymede has told her to take the offer she has.
quotations.analysis: The quotation is Marlowe's, from Hero and Leander, and the 'dead shepherd' is Marlowe himself, killed six years before — the only such tribute in Shakespeare. Phebe uses a borrowed line to describe a feeling she is convinced is original, which is the play's method for handling love poetry throughout.

quotations.text: it is a melancholy of mine own, compounded of many simples, extracted from many objects, and indeed the sundry's contemplation of my travels
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: Explaining to Rosalind why his sadness is not like anyone else's.
quotations.analysis: The vocabulary is a pharmacist's — simples, compounded, extracted — so he presents his own temperament as a recipe he has made up himself. Rosalind's reply prices it exactly: a traveller who has sold his lands to see other men's has rich eyes and poor hands.

quotations.text: But these are all lies: men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them, but not for love.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Ending a survey of Troilus and Leander, after Orlando has said he will die if refused.
quotations.analysis: She has just spent ten lines rewriting two famous love-deaths as a club to the head and an attack of cramp, and the summary sentence is flat, unornamented and final. The word 'worms' does the work: it puts the plain physical fact where the literature was, and it is spoken by someone who is very much in love.

quotations.text: men are April when they woo, December when they wed: maids are May when they are maids, but the sky changes when they are wives.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Answering Orlando's 'For ever and a day' during the mock marriage.
quotations.analysis: The warning is aimed at both parties, which is what makes it more than a joke about husbands. She then promises to be jealous as a cock-pigeon and to weep for nothing, so the prediction includes herself — she is letting him see the whole marriage before he agrees to it.

quotations.text: And so am I for no woman.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: The fourth voice in a formal round in which Silvius, Phebe and Orlando each declare what love is made of.
quotations.analysis: Three lovers name the person they want and the fourth, who wants somebody present, has to answer with a negative. Repeated three times over twenty lines, the refrain turns the disguise into a liturgy, and Rosalind ends the sequence by comparing the whole performance to Irish wolves howling at the moon.

quotations.text: a poor virgin, sir, an ill-favoured thing, sir, but mine own; a poor humour of mine, sir, to take that that no man else will
quotations.speaker: Touchstone
quotations.context: Presenting Audrey to the duke among the couples about to be married.
quotations.analysis: Four uses of 'poor' in one sentence, and the woman is introduced as a bargain nobody else bid for. It is the only marriage in the last scene described in terms of what it costs, and Shakespeare puts it directly before Hymen arrives to bless the rest.

quotations.text: You to your former honour I bequeath; Your patience and your virtue well deserves it
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: Leaving the wedding party to join the converted Duke Frederick.
quotations.analysis: He distributes futures to each couple in turn, like a man reading a will, and keeps nothing for himself. 'I am for other than for dancing measures,' he says a few lines later, and the play lets him go — a comedy that ends with one guest walking out is making a claim about what its settlement does not cover.

quotations.text: It is not the fashion to see the lady the epilogue; but it is no more unhandsome than to see the lord the prologue. If it be true that good wine needs no bush, 'tis true that a good play needs no epilogue
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Alone on stage after the dance, speaking the epilogue.
quotations.analysis: A bush of ivy was the sign hung outside a tavern, so the proverb means that quality advertises itself — and she is standing there advertising. The epilogue's first move is to point out that a woman is not supposed to be doing this, which prepares the ground for the last joke about what she is underneath.

quotations.text: If I were a woman I would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased me, complexions that liked me and breaths that I defied not
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: The last sentence but one of the play.
quotations.analysis: The conditional is the joke and the point: the actor speaking has been a woman for three hours and a boy all along, and the play chooses its final line to say so out loud. Having spent five acts arguing that identity is something performed, it closes by handing the evidence to the audience.

themes.name: Club, fang and the making of law
themes.canonicalName: Club, fang and the making of law

themes.name: Trace, trail and the day’s haul
Owners, and what a dog is worth
themes.canonicalName: Owners, and what a dog is worth

characters.name: The man in the red sweater

quotations.text: Buck did not read the newspapers, or he would have known that trouble was brewing, not alone for himself, but for every tidewater dog, strong of muscle and with warm, long hair, from Puget Sound to San Diego.
quotations.context: The novel’s opening sentence.
quotations.analysis: The joke about newspapers grants Buck ignorance rather than stupidity, and the sentence then does the reading for him: the danger is a market, described by geography and by coat length. Before the story starts, the reader has been told that what happens to Buck happens to a class of animals, which is why the book keeps count of other dogs.

quotations.text: He was beaten (he knew that); but he was not broken.
quotations.context: After the man in the red sweater has clubbed Buck to the ground for the last time.
quotations.analysis: The bracket is the sentence’s whole method: knowledge is separated from feeling and filed away, which is how Buck will meet everything from here on. Note the passive verbs — things are done to him in this chapter, and the first active thing he does with the lesson is remember it.

quotations.text: That club was a revelation. It was his introduction to the reign of primitive law, and he met the introduction halfway.
quotations.context: Buck, still unable to stand, watching the man who has beaten him.
quotations.analysis: 'Revelation', 'reign' and 'introduction' are the vocabulary of religion and of polite society, applied to a beating with a stick. 'Halfway' is the disturbing word: the novel is claiming that Buck consents to the arrangement, and that the consent is what makes him fit for the North.

quotations.text: They were savages, all of them, who knew no law but the law of club and fang.
quotations.context: Buck’s first day on the Dyea beach.
quotations.analysis: The sentence puts dogs and men in a single category, which is the book’s recurring move and the source of most of the trouble modern readers have with it. It also gives the chapter its title before any incident has proved the point — the proof arrives thirty lines later, when Curly goes down.

quotations.text: It marked, further, the decay or going to pieces of his moral nature, a vain thing and a handicap in the ruthless struggle for existence.
quotations.context: After Buck steals a chunk of bacon from Perrault’s supplies — the first theft of his life.
quotations.analysis: Two appraisals sit in one sentence: 'decay' and 'going to pieces' condemn the change, while 'a vain thing and a handicap' approves of it. The double vocabulary is the naturalist position in miniature, and the novel never resolves it — it simply stops using moral words once Buck has stopped needing them.

quotations.text: Not that Buck reasoned it out. He was fit, that was all, and unconsciously he accommodated himself to the new mode of life.
quotations.context: Immediately after the narrator has explained the theft in the language of Southland law and Northland necessity.
quotations.analysis: The narrator withdraws the argument he has just made from the character who prompted it, which is how London keeps a thinking dog from becoming a talking one. 'Fit' is doing technical work here: it belongs to the vocabulary of natural selection, not of praise.

quotations.text: The dominant primordial beast was strong in Buck, and under the fierce conditions of trail life it grew and grew. Yet it was a secret growth.
quotations.context: The opening of the chapter that ends with Spitz’s death.
quotations.analysis: The grammar makes the beast the subject and Buck the location, which is the book’s way of describing character as something inherited rather than chosen. 'Secret' matters for the plot: Buck spends the chapter avoiding fights precisely because he intends to win the only one that counts.

quotations.text: There is an ecstasy that marks the summit of life, and beyond which life cannot rise.
quotations.context: Buck leading the pack after a snowshoe rabbit in the moonlight.
quotations.analysis: The narrator steps away from the dog entirely here and makes a claim about artists and soldiers before returning to Buck, which is how the hunt is raised to the level of a general law. It is also the closest the novel comes to admitting that the wild is being sold to the reader as a pleasure.

quotations.text: There was no hope for him. Buck was inexorable. Mercy was a thing reserved for gentler climes.
quotations.context: Spitz on three legs, with the circle of huskies waiting to close in.
quotations.analysis: Three short sentences in place of the long periodic ones that surround them: the prose contracts at exactly the moment the killing begins. 'Climes' turns mercy into a matter of latitude rather than character, which excuses Buck and indicts the whole geography instead.

quotations.text: He fought by instinct, but he could fight by head as well.
quotations.context: The decisive moment of the fight with Spitz, as Buck breaks his forelegs one after the other.
quotations.analysis: The novel has spent two chapters arguing that instinct is what survives, and then awards the fight to calculation. Whatever the narrator says about primordial beasts, Buck wins because he does the same feint twice and the other dog cannot adapt.

quotations.text: For the pride of trace and trail was his, and, sick unto death, he could not bear that another dog should do his work.
quotations.context: Dave, dying of an internal injury, fighting to be put back in the harness he has been taken out of to rest.
quotations.analysis: 'Sick unto death' is biblical diction spent on a sled dog, and the effect is to take his preference seriously rather than to make it pathetic. The scene also states the book’s most unexpected proposition: that the harness can be an identity, so that removing it is the injury.

quotations.text: “Undreamed of!” cried Mercedes, throwing up her hands in dainty dismay. “However in the world could I manage without a tent?”
quotations.speaker: Mercedes
quotations.context: A bystander at Dawson has suggested that the party travel without a tent.
quotations.analysis: Her objection is grammatically about management and actually about self-image, and the book lets the word 'dainty' do the damage. The line belongs to the drawing room, which is the point: everything the three newcomers say is imported, and the North charges them freight on it.

quotations.text: And so it went, the inexorable elimination of the superfluous.
quotations.context: Mercedes’s clothes-bags being emptied onto the snow as the load is cut down.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is lifted from evolutionary argument and applied to luggage, and the comedy of that is exact: the same principle will shortly be applied to the dogs and then to the people. London rarely tells the reader a system is at work; here he names one and lets it run through three paragraphs of packing.

quotations.text: Love, genuine passionate love, was his for the first time.
quotations.context: Buck convalescing in John Thornton’s camp after being cut out of Hal’s traces.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is placed after a page of games and roughhousing rather than before it, so the claim is made to rest on evidence. It also quietly disposes of the Santa Clara Valley: the judge’s household gave Buck dignity, partnership and stewardship, and the book counts none of that as love.

quotations.text: “As you love me, Buck. As you love me,” was what he whispered.
quotations.speaker: John Thornton
quotations.context: Before Buck attempts to start a thousand-pound load frozen to the snow at Dawson.
quotations.analysis: Thornton does not give a command, and the repetition turns the wager into a request between equals. The sentence is also a confession that he has staked another creature’s body on a bar-room boast, which the crowd’s cheering afterwards does nothing to settle.

quotations.text: “Pooh! pooh!” said John Thornton; “Buck can start a thousand pounds.”
quotations.speaker: John Thornton
quotations.context: In the Eldorado Saloon, among men arguing about what their dogs can pull.
quotations.analysis: The boast is made in the grammar of the saloon, and the narrative immediately records that Thornton did not know whether it was true and had no money to back it. What follows is the one episode in the novel where Buck’s strength is converted directly into cash, and it is the humans who arrange the sale.

quotations.text: And closely akin to the visions of the hairy man was the call still sounding in the depths of the forest.
quotations.context: In camp during the long summer in the unmapped country east of Dawson.
quotations.analysis: The call is introduced as a relative of the dreams rather than as a voice, which keeps it inside Buck’s nervous system and out of the supernatural. Note that it has no content: London never says what it asks for, only that Buck goes looking for it as though it were a tangible thing.

quotations.text: He was a killer, a thing that preyed, living on the things that lived, unaided, alone, by virtue of his own strength and prowess, surviving triumphantly in a hostile environment where only the strong survived.
quotations.context: After Buck has hunted and killed a great bull moose over four days.
quotations.analysis: The clauses pile up without a main verb after the first, so the sentence performs the swelling pride it describes. 'A thing that preyed' also removes the personal pronoun for a moment: the book’s most individual dog is being described, briefly, as a category of animal.

quotations.text: He had killed man, the noblest game of all, and he had killed in the face of the law of club and fang.
quotations.context: Buck among the bodies of the Yeehats, after Thornton’s death.
quotations.analysis: The phrase 'the law of club and fang' has travelled a long way: it began as a description of what men and dogs on the beach knew, and is now the thing Buck has successfully broken. 'Game' is the cruellest word in the book — it places human beings in the category of animals hunted for sport, exactly reversing the trade that opened the story.

quotations.text: John Thornton was dead. The last tie was broken. Man and the claims of man no longer bound him.
quotations.context: By the pool in the ruined camp, as the wolf pack comes down the valley under a full moon.
quotations.analysis: Three flat statements, the shortest sentences in the chapter, and all of them about other people’s claims rather than Buck’s desires. The novel has been careful never to let him choose the wild over Thornton: the tie is cut by the Yeehats, so the ending is a release rather than a preference.

quotations.text: But more remarkable than this, the Yeehats tell of a Ghost Dog that runs at the head of the pack.
quotations.context: The closing pages, years after the events of the story.
quotations.analysis: The narration hands the ending over to the people Buck has been killing, so that the last account of him is hearsay from his victims. It is also the moment the book stops being naturalism: a dog whose every action has been explained by environment and inheritance leaves the record as a legend.

quotations.text: he may be seen running at the head of the pack through the pale moonlight or glimmering borealis, leaping gigantic above his fellows, his great throat a-bellow as he sings a song of the younger world, which is the song of the pack.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The song was introduced in Chapter 3 as the huskies’ nightly wail, 'the pleading of life' pitched in a minor key; here the same phrase returns with Buck leading it. The tense has also changed to habitual present, which lifts him out of the story’s chronology and into something that keeps happening.

quotations.text: Old longings nomadic leap, Chafing at custom’s chain; Again from its brumal sleep Wakens the ferine strain.
quotations.context: The verse epigraph printed before the first chapter, from John Myers O’Hara’s poem ‘Atavism’.
quotations.analysis: Four lines that give the whole plot away and supply its vocabulary: longing, custom, sleep and strain. 'Brumal' and 'ferine' are dictionary words for winter and wildness, and their stiffness is useful — the book will argue that what wakes in Buck is a technical inheritance rather than a romantic urge.

themes.name: An occult trade with a literature
A defence that needs a battery

techniques.name: A single witness, telling it afterwards

quotations.text: In response to Carnacki's usual card of invitation to have dinner and listen to a story, I arrived promptly at 427, Cheyne Walk
quotations.reference: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
quotations.context: The first sentence of the collection, and of five of the six stories.
quotations.analysis: The word usual is doing the work: before we have met anyone we know this has happened many times and will happen again. Hodgson establishes a routine so that the things inside it can be as irregular as he likes.

quotations.text: Out you go!
quotations.context: Carnacki's dismissal, which ends each case.
quotations.analysis: Three words, genially delivered, immediately after something that ought to keep four grown men talking all night. The formula is a door closing on the subject, and by the third story the reader is waiting for it.

quotations.text: the Electric Pentacle, which is a most marvelous 'Defense'
quotations.reference: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
quotations.context: Introducing his own improvement on the traditional protective circle.
quotations.analysis: Hodgson's single best invention, and the reason these stories still feel unlike anything else: a mediaeval figure of protection rewired with vacuum tubes. The quotation marks around Defense are Carnacki's, and they are the mark of a man using a technical term from an old book.

quotations.text: Theyre must noe lyght come from wythin the barryier.
quotations.reference: No. 2, The House Among the Laurels
quotations.context: Quoted from the Sigsand MS. as he takes the men's pipes away.
quotations.analysis: An invented fourteenth-century sentence used as a safety regulation. The spelling makes it old, the context makes it operational, and the pipes being confiscated makes it real.

quotations.text: I got my tape measure then, and measured out a circle thirty-three feet
quotations.reference: No. 2, The House Among the Laurels
quotations.context: Setting the defences in the great hall.
quotations.analysis: A tape measure, in a haunted house, stated without irony. The whole method is in this clause: the occult is being handled by somebody who would rather be precise than impressive.

quotations.text: this was no piece of silly mumming on my part; but done with a definite intention of erecting a barrier
quotations.reference: No. 2, The House Among the Laurels
quotations.context: Warning the men who will spend the night inside the circle.
quotations.analysis: He anticipates the reader's scepticism and answers it in the tone of a foreman explaining a safety rule. Hodgson keeps making the characters take the ritual seriously as procedure, which is the only way the ritual can frighten anyone.

quotations.text: that feeling of spiritual sickness, as if some delicate, beautiful, inward grace had suffered, which is felt only upon the too near approach of the ab-human
quotations.reference: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
quotations.context: In the pentacle, as the thing in the Grey Room comes close.
quotations.analysis: The damage is moral rather than physical, and Carnacki says it is worse than pain. This is the sentence that separates Hodgson's monsters from the period's ghosts: what they threaten is not the body but something the narrator can only call grace.

quotations.text: the sound of a hoof in the dark billiard room we had just left
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: Just after the rational explanation has begun to look convincing.
quotations.analysis: Hodgson's timing is exact: the noise arrives in the sentence immediately after Carnacki has started listing commonplace possibilities. The detective story is allowed to nearly succeed before the ghost story takes it back.

quotations.text: The clungk clunck, clungk clunck, of the great hoof falls passed right between us
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: Two men flattened against opposite walls of a passage.
quotations.analysis: An invented noise, repeated, with no creature attached to it. The onomatopoeia is faintly ridiculous on the page and works completely in the ear, which is the risk Hodgson takes throughout and usually wins.

quotations.text: the shape of a single enormous hoof
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: In a photograph taken during the haunting, examined afterwards.
quotations.analysis: The evidence is photographic, which for 1910 is the most modern proof available, and it still shows only a shape half-formed out of shadow. Carnacki studies it for a long time without understanding it better, and says so.

quotations.text: there is some inscrutable Protective Force constantly intervening between the human soul
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: Answering Arkright's question about what governs the Unknown Last Line.
quotations.analysis: The nearest thing to consolation in Hodgson, and it arrives as jargon at the end of a story rather than as revelation. Inscrutable is the operative word: something is on our side and nobody knows what it is.

quotations.text: the Outer Monstrosities
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: In the same explanation, naming what the protective force stands between us and.
quotations.analysis: Capitalised, plural, and never described. Hodgson's habit of naming forces he will not show gave later writers a whole vocabulary, and the restraint is why the phrase still carries weight.

quotations.text: the Unknown Last Line of the Saaamaaa Ritual
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: Arkright's question after dinner.
quotations.analysis: A named thing that is defined as unknown, in a ritual with numbered signs and a missing eighth place. The apparatus is elaborate enough to sound like scholarship and vague enough that nothing can be checked — exactly the balance the stories need.

themes.name: Debt, bonds and the price of a life
Doors, dinner and being shut out
Witchcraft, possession and being called mad

quotations.text: Again, if any Syracusian born Come to the bay of Ephesus, he dies, His goods confiscate to the Duke's dispose, Unless a thousand marks be levied To quit the penalty and to ransom him.
quotations.speaker: Duke
quotations.context: The Duke explaining to Egeon why he cannot be spared.
quotations.analysis: A comedy opens with a trade embargo read out in full. The law is not cruel by design but reciprocal — Syracuse does the same to Ephesians — and the sum is what matters: a man's life is quoted at a price, and the rest of the play is spent moving smaller sums of money to the wrong people.

quotations.text: A heavier task could not have been impos'd Than I to speak my griefs unspeakable
quotations.speaker: Egeon
quotations.context: Beginning the account of the shipwreck, at the Duke's request.
quotations.analysis: The line that launches a hundred lines of narrative says the story cannot be told. 'Unspeakable' is doing two jobs: too painful to say, and too large for speech. Nothing else in the play sounds like this, and the register only returns when Egeon does, in the last scene, to a son who does not know his voice.

quotations.text: I to the world am like a drop of water That in the ocean seeks another drop, Who, failing there to find his fellow forth, Unseen, inquisitive, confounds himself.
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Alone on the mart, having sent his servant to the inn.
quotations.analysis: 'Confounds' means both defeats and mingles, so the drop searching the sea is lost in the same motion that dissolves it. He states the play's problem before any error has happened: a man looking for his double risks becoming indistinguishable from what he is looking for. Adriana will take the same image back off him in 2.2 and use it about marriage.

quotations.text: The clock hath strucken twelve upon the bell; My mistress made it one upon my cheek.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: Explaining to the wrong master why dinner is spoiling.
quotations.analysis: Two strokes, two meanings, one word. The joke turns a household bell into a slap and gets a laugh, and it also tells the audience exactly what this servant's day consists of. Shakespeare keeps the pun running: the blows are marks, the marks are money, and the money is what everyone is shouting about.

quotations.text: They say this town is full of cozenage, As nimble jugglers that deceive the eye, Dark-working sorcerers that change the mind, Soul-killing witches that deform the body
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: After his first encounter with the wrong Dromio, who has apparently stolen his gold.
quotations.analysis: Ephesus had this reputation in Acts 19, where converts burn their books of magic, and Shakespeare cashes it in early so that every later mistake has an explanation waiting. The three trades are graded — eye, mind, body — and the play then proceeds to deceive the eye, change the mind and, in Pinch's hands, get at the body.

quotations.text: A man is master of his liberty; Time is their master, and when they see time, They'll go or come.
quotations.speaker: Luciana
quotations.context: Telling her sister not to fret about a husband who has missed dinner.
quotations.analysis: The advice is given by a woman with no husband, and it concedes the argument it means to close: if time is a man's master, the wife waiting at home is mastered by him at one more remove. Adriana spots it immediately and asks the obvious question in the next line.

quotations.text: A wretched soul bruis'd with adversity, We bid be quiet when we hear it cry; But were we burd'ned with like weight of pain, As much, or more, we should ourselves complain
quotations.speaker: Adriana
quotations.context: Answering her sister's recommendation of patience.
quotations.analysis: It is the best reply in the scene and it is about more than marriage: patience is cheap for whoever is not carrying the weight. Adriana ends by telling Luciana that the advice will vanish the day she is wronged herself, and the play proves her right within two acts, when Luciana is the one being courted by a man she thinks is her sister's husband.

quotations.text: Am I so round with you, as you with me, That like a football you do spurn me thus? You spurn me hence, and he will spurn me hither.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: Sent back to the mart by Adriana, after a beating from the master he takes for his own.
quotations.analysis: 'Round' means plain-spoken and also spherical, and the pun holds the whole complaint: he is spoken to bluntly and kicked like a ball between two houses. His next line asks to be cased in leather, which is what a football was made of, so the joke ends with a servant requesting armour.

quotations.text: For know, my love, as easy mayst thou fall A drop of water in the breaking gulf, And take unmingled thence that drop again Without addition or diminishing, As take from me thyself, and not me too.
quotations.speaker: Adriana
quotations.context: Addressing a man she believes is her husband, in the street.
quotations.analysis: She picks up the image her brother-in-law used about himself an hour earlier and makes it a marriage argument: two people mixed like water cannot be separated out by weight. The speech is the most serious thing in the play and it is delivered, without anyone knowing, to the wrong man, which is the cruellest joke Shakespeare plays on anybody here.

quotations.text: Am I in earth, in heaven, or in hell? Sleeping or waking, mad, or well-advis'd? Known unto these, and to myself disguis'd!
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Being led indoors to dine as another woman's husband.
quotations.analysis: 'Known unto these, and to myself disguis'd' is the exact reverse of every other disguise plot on the Elizabethan stage: he is not hiding from them, he is hidden from himself by their certainty. Three lines later he decides to go along with it, which is what keeps the play running — the one man who could stop the errors chooses the dinner.

quotations.text: If the skin were parchment, and the blows you gave were ink, Your own handwriting would tell you what I think.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: Insisting to his master that he really was beaten at the mart earlier that day.
quotations.analysis: The servant offers his body as legal evidence, in a city where documents settle everything. Parchment, ink and handwriting are the instruments of the bonds and bills that drive the middle of the play, and he turns them on his master: the marks are a signed statement, and the signature is his master's.

quotations.text: For slander lives upon succession, For ever hous'd where it gets possession.
quotations.speaker: Balthasar
quotations.context: Persuading Antipholus of Ephesus not to break down his own door.
quotations.analysis: 'Hous'd' and 'possession' are chosen with care by a man standing outside a house he cannot get into. Balthasar's point is practical: force the door and the street will invent a reason. It is also the moment the play turns, because taking the advice sends Antipholus to a courtesan and puts the chain into the wrong hands.

quotations.text: Teach sin the carriage of a holy saint, Be secret-false. What need she be acquainted? What simple thief brags of his own attaint?
quotations.speaker: Luciana
quotations.context: Lecturing the man she takes for her sister's husband on how to conduct an affair.
quotations.analysis: The sister who spent the second act preaching obedience now coaches adultery, and asks the audience to notice that her objection was never to the sin. 'Attaint' is a legal word for being convicted and corrupted at once, which makes her advice a plea to avoid the verdict and keep the offence.

quotations.text: O, train me not, sweet mermaid, with thy note To drown me in thy sister's flood of tears.
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Answering Luciana's advice with a declaration of love.
quotations.analysis: He keeps returning to water: a drop looking for a drop in the first act, and now a mermaid whose song would drown him in another woman's weeping. 'Train' means to lure. The man who came to Ephesus searching has stopped searching, and the play never quite says whether he has found anything or merely stopped caring.

quotations.text: She is spherical, like a globe. I could find out countries in her.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Syracuse
quotations.context: Describing the kitchen maid who has claimed him as her husband.
quotations.analysis: What follows is a tour of Europe conducted over a woman's body — Ireland in the bogs, Spain in her hot breath, America on a nose set with rubies. It is the longest joke in the play and the least comfortable one now, and the man making it is terrified: he is describing someone who knew the moles and warts on his body without being told.

quotations.text: Time is a very bankrupt, and owes more than he's worth to season.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Syracuse
quotations.context: Explaining to Adriana why the clock has struck one after striking two.
quotations.analysis: Everything in Ephesus can be put on account, including the hours. Dromio has just come from watching his master arrested for debt, and the joke is that the afternoon itself has run out of credit and is turning back to avoid the sergeant. It is nonsense, and it is also an exact description of a day in which nothing is paid for on time.

quotations.text: The fellow is distract, and so am I, And here we wander in illusions. Some blessed power deliver us from hence!
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
