quotations.context: After being greeted by name, offered goods and handed a purse of gold all over town.
quotations.analysis: What unnerves him is kindness. He is not being robbed: he is greeted by name, shown silk cut to his measure and handed a purse of gold. A whole city has taken him for somebody, he cannot find out who, and the prayer is the point at which he stops trying to explain it.

quotations.text: I am an ass indeed; you may prove it by my long ears. … When I am cold, he heats me with beating; when I am warm he cools me with beating.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: Beaten for bringing back the rope's end he was sent to buy, by a master who meant to send him for bail.
quotations.analysis: The speech starts as a pun and turns into an account of a whole life, from the hour of his nativity to the day he expects to beg at doors with a limp his master gave him. Both Dromios call themselves asses repeatedly, and this is the point at which the audience is invited to hear the word as a job description.

quotations.text: The venom clamours of a jealous woman Poisons more deadly than a mad dog's tooth.
quotations.speaker: Abbess
quotations.context: Having questioned Adriana about how she treated her husband.
quotations.analysis: The Abbess presses the same point four times — not rough enough, not in private only, not enough — until Adriana boasts of how hard she nagged, then turns the boast into a diagnosis. Luciana protests; Adriana says she was betrayed to her own reproof. Nothing later withdraws the charge, and it is spoken, though nobody on stage yet knows it, by Adriana's own mother-in-law.

quotations.text: Why, what an intricate impeach is this! I think you all have drunk of Circe's cup.
quotations.speaker: Duke
quotations.context: After hearing two sworn accounts of the day that cannot both be true.
quotations.analysis: 'Impeach' is an accusation and 'intricate' means tangled, so the Duke names the problem precisely: this is a legal tangle, not a mystery. Circe turned men into swine, and his guess is that everyone has been transformed. He is wrong about the cause and right about the effect, which is roughly where the audience has been sitting for four acts.

quotations.text: O! grief hath chang'd me since you saw me last, And careful hours with time's deformed hand, Have written strange defeatures in my face.
quotations.speaker: Egeon
quotations.context: Recognising a son who says he has never seen him before.
quotations.analysis: 'Defeatures' means disfigurements, and the writing image returns from Dromio's parchment joke in a register nobody is laughing at. The old man has been condemned, reprieved for a day, and now denied by his own child, who is telling the truth. Shakespeare lets that stand for some fifty lines before the Abbess comes back through the priory gate.

quotations.text: One of these men is genius to the other; And so of these, which is the natural man, And which the spirit? Who deciphers them?
quotations.speaker: Duke
quotations.context: Seeing both pairs of twins together for the first time.
quotations.analysis: A 'genius' was a person's attendant spirit, so the Duke's first thought is that one of each pair must be a spirit and not a man. 'Deciphers' treats the two bodies as a code somebody must read. It is the question the whole play has been asking, put by the one person with the authority to settle it, and he cannot.

quotations.text: Thirty-three years have I but gone in travail Of you, my sons, and till this present hour My heavy burden ne'er delivered.
quotations.speaker: Abbess
quotations.context: Inviting the whole company into the abbey after recognising her husband and sons.
quotations.analysis: 'Travail' is both labour and hardship, and she takes the metaphor the whole distance: the day's confusion has been a delivery, and it has taken thirty-three years. The number does not fit the rest of the play, which points to twenty-five or so, and editors have argued about it since the eighteenth century without agreeing on a fix.

quotations.text: We came into the world like brother and brother, And now let's go hand in hand, not one before another.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: The last two lines of the play, settling which twin should walk first.
quotations.analysis: Shakespeare gives the final couplet to a servant, and uses it to refuse the question the whole play has been about: which of the two is which, and which comes first. The Antipholuses have gone off to a feast with their parents. The Dromios, who own nothing and were bought as infants, decide seniority by walking in together.

themes.name: Hunger and the distribution of grain
themes.canonicalName: Hunger and the distribution of grain

themes.name: The body and the body politic
themes.canonicalName: The body and the body politic

quotations.text: Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.
quotations.speaker: First Citizen
quotations.context: The opening line of the play, spoken by a citizen carrying a club.
quotations.analysis: No Shakespearean tragedy begins with a commoner claiming the floor, and the claim is procedural: he is asking for order before an action, not for pity. The whole play is contained in the request, because the one thing Coriolanus will never grant the citizens is the right to be heard before anything proceeds.

quotations.text: There was a time when all the body's members Rebell'd against the belly, thus accused it: That only like a gulf it did remain I' the midst o' the body, idle and unactive, Still cupboarding the viand, never bearing Like labour with the rest,
quotations.speaker: Menenius
quotations.context: Talking a crowd of hungry men out of a riot over the price of corn.
quotations.analysis: The fable answers a complaint about hoarding by conceding the hoarding and calling it digestion. Its rhetorical trick is the opening 'There was a time', which shifts the argument out of this year's harvest into a fable where the belly's case has already been settled — and the citizens interrupt him twice to say so.

quotations.text: What's the matter, you dissentious rogues, That, rubbing the poor itch of your opinion, Make yourselves scabs?
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: His entrance, immediately after Menenius has spent a hundred lines calming the crowd.
quotations.analysis: His first words undo the fable in three lines: where Menenius made the citizens limbs of a body, he makes them a skin disease on it. 'Opinion' is treated as an itch, which is to say a physical irritation with no content, and that is precisely his view of the vote he will later have to ask for.

quotations.text: He that will give good words to thee will flatter Beneath abhorring.
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: Answering a citizen who says they have always had his good word.
quotations.analysis: He treats courtesy to an inferior as a form of lying, which is consistent and politically fatal in equal measure. The line also explains why he cannot be bought: a man who regards flattery as beneath contempt has no currency to spend in a republic that runs on it.

quotations.text: Marcius, I had rather had eleven die nobly for their country than one voluptuously surfeit out of action.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: In the house, sewing with Virgilia, on the subject of sons.
quotations.analysis: The arithmetic is the shock: eleven is not a figure of speech but a rate of exchange she has evidently worked out. 'Surfeit' plants the play's other appetite — the city outside is rioting over food — so her contempt for a well-fed son runs on the same imagery as the grain crisis.

quotations.text: it more becomes a man Than gilt his trophy: the breasts of Hecuba, When she did suckle Hector, look'd not lovelier Than Hector's forehead when it spit forth blood At Grecian sword, contemning.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Virgilia has just cried out at the thought of her husband's bloody brow.
quotations.analysis: The comparison sets a nursing mother against a wounded son and decides for the wound, which tells us exactly what kind of feeding Volumnia believes in. The verb 'spit' does the work: blood is given an agency and a contempt of its own, as though the forehead were answering the Greek sword back.

quotations.text: O, me alone! make you a sword of me? If these shows be not outward, which of you But is four Volsces?
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: The soldiers take him up in their arms and throw their caps in the air.
quotations.analysis: It is the one moment where a crowd loves him and he is delighted by it, which shows that his difficulty is not with numbers of people but with what those people are entitled to ask. Being made into a weapon is the only public use of his body that he can accept.

quotations.text: Nature teaches beasts to know their friends.
quotations.speaker: Sicinius
quotations.context: Sparring with Menenius in a public place while Rome waits for the victorious army.
quotations.analysis: Menenius answers by asking who the wolf loves, and the exchange turns into a small contest over who gets to use the animal metaphors. It is worth noticing that the tribunes are given the wit to hold their own here: the play does not write them as fools, only as men with an interest.

quotations.text: Bid them wash their faces And keep their teeth clean.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Asked what he shall say to the citizens who are coming to give him their voices.
quotations.analysis: Standing in the gown of humility, he answers a question about political speech with a note about hygiene, and the joke is directed at the audience rather than at anyone on stage. The contempt is specifically for their mouths — the parts that are about to give him what he needs.

quotations.text: Most sweet voices! Better it is to die, better to starve, Than crave the hire which first we do deserve.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Alone in the Forum, between groups of citizens.
quotations.analysis: The sarcasm of the first phrase gives way to a rhymed couplet, and the rhyme makes it a maxim he has clearly held for a long time. 'Starve' is a reckless word to choose in this city in this month, and the citizens who riot over corn in Act I are exactly the men whose hire he is refusing to crave.

quotations.text: What custom wills, in all things should we do't, The dust on antique time would lie unswept, And mountainous error be too highly heapt For truth to o'er-peer.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Still in the Forum, arguing himself out of completing the ceremony.
quotations.analysis: It is a genuinely radical argument — that custom preserves error — and it is being used to avoid asking poor men for their votes. The play repeatedly gives him positions that would be admirable in another mouth, which is what makes him a tragic figure rather than a snob.

quotations.text: For the mutable, rank-scented many, let them Regard me as I do not flatter, and Therein behold themselves:
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: In the street, after being told his election is revoked.
quotations.analysis: He offers his own refusal to flatter as a mirror in which the people may see their own inconstancy, which is an argument and an insult in the same sentence. 'Mutable' is the charge the play half sustains: the citizens do change their minds, and we have just watched two men talk them into it.

quotations.text: What is the city but the people?
quotations.speaker: Sicinius
quotations.context: In the street riot, as the tribunes move to arrest Coriolanus.
quotations.analysis: The citizens answer 'The people are the city', and the echo turns a rhetorical question into something closer to a chant. It is the most quotable line of political theory in the play, and Shakespeare gives it to a man in the middle of organising a lynching — which is not a refutation, only a complication.

quotations.text: Why did you wish me milder? would you have me False to my nature? Rather say I play The man I am.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His mother has just told him he should have dissembled until he had the office.
quotations.analysis: He means 'play' as an accusation and it turns into a confession: the verb concedes that even being oneself is a performance. From this point the play measures him not by whether he acts but by which part he is willing to take, and in 5.3 he will use the language of the theatre again, as a man who has forgotten his lines.

quotations.text: Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant More learned than the ears--waving thy head, Which often, thus, correcting thy stout heart,
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Teaching her son how to stand and what to do with his hands in front of the people.
quotations.analysis: She is giving him a lesson in stagecraft, complete with a demonstration of the gesture, and the phrase 'the eyes of the ignorant' shows she shares his contempt entirely. The difference between mother and son is not principle but competence: she can do the thing they both despise.

quotations.text: You common cry of curs! whose breath I hate As reek o' the rotten fens, whose loves I prize As the dead carcasses of unburied men That do corrupt my air, I banish you;
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Immediately after the tribunes pronounce his banishment in the Forum.
quotations.analysis: Everything he hates is airborne — breath, reek, corrupted air — which is the same sense in which their votes are only noise to him. Reversing the sentence is magnificent and changes nothing: a man can banish a city only from himself, and the city goes on without him for two more acts.

quotations.text: There is a world elsewhere.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His exit line from Rome.
quotations.analysis: Five words to close an act, and the only thing in the speech that turns out to be true: there is a world elsewhere, and it is Antium, and it kills him. The plainness after twenty lines of curses is what makes it land — he stops performing for exactly one line.

quotations.text: Anger's my meat; I sup upon myself, And so shall starve with feeding.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: In the street, having just cursed the tribunes who banished her son.
quotations.analysis: The play's food imagery finally reaches the patrician household: where the citizens wanted corn, she eats her own rage and expects to die of the diet. It is also an exact description of what she does to her son in 5.3, where feeding on him and destroying him are the same act.

quotations.text: One fire drives out one fire; one nail, one nail; Rights by rights falter, strengths by strengths do fail.
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: Alone with his lieutenant, having learned that the Volscian soldiers now prefer Coriolanus.
quotations.analysis: Two proverbs and a rhymed couplet, and the effect is of a man consoling himself with common sense while deciding on a murder. The symmetry of the second line — rights against rights, strengths against strengths — makes assassination sound like a law of physics rather than a choice.

quotations.text: let the Volsces Plough Rome and harrow Italy: I'll never Be such a gosling to obey instinct, but stand, As if a man were author of himself And knew no other kin.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Watching his mother, wife and son approach his tent, and steeling himself.
quotations.analysis: 'As if' gives him away before the sentence ends: he knows the self-authorship is a fiction he is choosing to act out. Four scenes after a mother's teaching failed to make him bow to a crowd, he is using her own vocabulary of performance to try to resist her.

quotations.text: Like a dull actor now, I have forgot my part, and I am out, Even to a full disgrace.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Virgilia has spoken three words to him and he cannot continue.
quotations.analysis: The man who refused to act in the Forum now describes his own collapse as a failure of acting, and 'out' is the technical term for an actor who has dried. His wife does it with a greeting; his mother will need fifty lines and a kneeling child.

quotations.text: Trust to't, thou shalt not--on thy mother's womb, That brought thee to this world.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Telling him he will not reach Rome except over her body.
quotations.analysis: She makes her own body the gate of the city, which completes the play's long argument that Rome is an anatomy. Virgilia and the boy each add a line immediately afterwards, so the threat arrives as a family in sequence rather than as one woman's rhetoric.

quotations.text: O mother, mother! What have you done? Behold, the heavens do ope, The gods look down, and this unnatural scene They laugh at.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Breaking the silence after holding his mother's hand without speaking.
quotations.analysis: The Folio's direction — he holds her by the hand, silent — gives the turn of the tragedy to a pause, and this is what comes out of it: not a decision but a question addressed to the person who made him. 'Unnatural' is the word the play has used for a son marching on his birthplace, and he now applies it to the scene of his surrender.

quotations.text: You have won a happy victory to Rome; But, for your son,--believe it, O, believe it, Most dangerously you have with him prevail'd, If not most mortal to him.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Granting the peace his mother has come to ask for.
quotations.analysis: He states the cost accurately and in the same breath as the concession, which is why the scene is not a redemption. The repeated 'believe it' is the only time in the play he begs anyone to listen, and it is addressed to the one person who has never needed persuading of anything.

quotations.text: There is differency between a grub and a butterfly; yet your butterfly was a grub. This Marcius is grown from man to dragon: he has wings; he's more than a creeping thing.
quotations.speaker: Menenius
quotations.context: Back in Rome, telling Sicinius there is no hope of mercy.
quotations.analysis: Menenius has spent the play making people into parts of a body, and now he makes his friend into a different species altogether. The animal ladder that began with curs and scabs in 1.1 ends with a dragon, and the man himself is by this point absent from every scene that discusses him.

quotations.text: Name not the god, thou boy of tears!
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: In Corioli, in front of the Volscian lords, as Coriolanus swears by Mars.
quotations.analysis: Aufidius has watched him for five acts and knows the one word that will work: not traitor, which is a political charge, but boy, which is a charge about his mother. The insult is accurate, which is why it destroys him — he yielded to a woman and he knows Aufidius watched him do it.

quotations.text: Cut me to pieces, Volsces; men and lads, Stain all your edges on me. Boy! false hound! If you have writ your annals true, 'tis there, That, like an eagle in a dove-cote, I Flutter'd your Volscians in Corioli: Alone I did it. Boy!
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His last speech, to the citizens of the city he sacked.
quotations.analysis: He answers an insult about his mother by reciting the deed that gave him his name, in the city that gave it, to the survivors of it. 'Alone I did it' is the claim the play has been quietly disputing since 1.6, when an entire army picked him up and carried him — and it is the last thing he says before the conspirators move.

quotations.text: My rage is gone; And I am struck with sorrow. Take him up. Help, three o' the chiefest soldiers; I'll be one.
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: Standing over the body, moments after standing on it.
quotations.analysis: The reversal takes four words, and the practical instruction that follows is what makes it convincing: he stops speaking about himself and starts organising a stretcher party. Shakespeare gives the killer the last rites rather than the family, so the play's final act of tenderness comes from the enemy and not from Rome.

themes.name: Clothes, names and who people take you for

quotations.text: It is a manacle of love; I'll place it Upon this fairest prisoner.
quotations.speaker: Posthumus
quotations.context: Clasping the bracelet on Imogen's arm as they part, minutes before her father drives him out of Britain.
quotations.analysis: The love-token is named a fetter and the wife a prisoner in the same breath, and Posthumus means it as gallantry. The play takes him at his word instead: the bracelet is the thing that will be used against her, and the Queen has just called Imogen her prisoner in the scene's opening line.

quotations.text: O blessed that I might not! I chose an eagle, And did avoid a puttock.
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Answering Cymbeline, who has just told her she could have married the Queen's son.
quotations.analysis: A puttock is a kite, the carrion hawk that will not hunt. Imogen answers a king in the middle of a rage with a falconer's joke, and picks the comparison that ranks men the way a court ranks birds. It is the first sign that she will argue rank on its own ground and win.

quotations.text: But I make my wager rather against your confidence than her reputation
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: In Philario's house in Rome, pressing Posthumus towards the bet after he has refused it once.
quotations.analysis: This is the sentence that makes the wager possible. By shifting the target from Imogen to Posthumus's certainty, Iachimo lets him agree without admitting he is putting his wife up as a stake. He has found the exact form of words a proud man can accept, and Philario's attempt to call it off comes one line too late.

quotations.text: Our Tarquin thus Did softly press the rushes ere he waken'd The chastity he wounded.
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: Stepping out of the trunk into Imogen's bedchamber at midnight.
quotations.analysis: He compares himself to a rapist before he has done anything, and the comparison is his own idea. Shakespeare had written Tarquin's approach at length in The Rape of Lucrece, and the echo tells an audience exactly how to feel about a man who will in fact only look. The word our makes Rome the shared ancestor of both crimes.

quotations.text: Here's a voucher Stronger than ever law could make; this secret Will force him think I have pick'd the lock and ta'en The treasure of her honour.
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: Having found the mole under Imogen's breast, deciding he need write nothing else down.
quotations.analysis: A voucher is a document proving a title, and Iachimo knows he has manufactured one out of a birthmark. He says outright that it will force Posthumus to think, which is not the same as showing him anything true. The language of locks, treasure and forfeit runs all through his speech and turns a marriage into a property claim.

quotations.text: She hath been reading late The tale of Tereus; here the leaf's turn'd down Where Philomel gave up.
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: Noticing the book Imogen fell asleep over before he came out of the trunk.
quotations.analysis: Ovid's Philomel is raped by Tereus and has her tongue cut out so she cannot accuse him. Imogen has fallen asleep at the page where the victim stops speaking, and a man is standing over her bed collecting the evidence that will silence her. The detail is offered as one more item in an inventory, which is what makes it cold.

quotations.text: Hark, hark! the lark at heaven's gate sings, And Phœbus 'gins arise,
quotations.speaker: A Musician
quotations.context: The aubade Cloten has hired to be played at Imogen's door at first light.
quotations.analysis: One of the loveliest songs in Shakespeare is paid for by the nastiest man in the play, who has just told the musicians to try whether they can penetrate her with their fingering. The beauty is real and so is the purpose behind it, and the scene gives an audience no way of keeping them apart.

quotations.text: His mean'st garment That ever hath but clipp'd his body, is dearer In my respect, than all the hairs above thee
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Losing patience with Cloten at her chamber door, after he has called Posthumus a beggar bred on scraps.
quotations.analysis: It is the sharpest insult in the play and the most expensive. Cloten repeats the phrase four times in the next twenty lines, and two acts later he is wearing that garment in a Welsh wood, intending to kill its owner in it. Imogen will meet her own sentence again beside a headless body.

quotations.text: Could I find out The woman's part in me! For there's no motion That tends to vice in man but I affirm It is the woman's part.
quotations.speaker: Posthumus
quotations.context: Alone in Rome, immediately after handing Iachimo the ring.
quotations.analysis: Having decided his wife is false, he works outward until every fault in the world belongs to women, including the faults in himself. The speech is a man building a general law out of one bad evening, and its logic is the same as the wager's: a single case is made to stand for all cases. He ends by resolving to write against them.

quotations.text: Britain is a world by itself, and we will nothing pay for wearing our own noses.
quotations.speaker: Cloten
quotations.context: Interrupting the Roman ambassador's demand for the tribute Cassibelan granted.
quotations.analysis: The play gives its most quotable statement of British independence to its greatest fool, and puts it in prose between two speeches of the Queen's ringing verse. The argument is not silly, which is the difficulty: Cymbeline acts on it, goes to war, wins, and then in the last scene quietly pays the money anyway.

quotations.text: How hard it is to hide the sparks of nature!
quotations.speaker: Belarius
quotations.context: Alone outside the cave, having just watched the two boys go up the mountain.
quotations.analysis: Belarius has spent twenty years raising princes as hunters and cannot keep the blood down. He goes on to describe Guiderius flushing and straining at a war story, acting out the feats in his sleep. The play backs him: the boys' courage in the lane wins the battle, and nobody has taught it to them.

quotations.text: 'tis slander, Whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue Outvenoms all the worms of Nile
quotations.speaker: Pisanio
quotations.context: Watching Imogen read the letter that accuses her of adultery and orders her death.
quotations.analysis: Pisanio names the play's real weapon. Nobody in Cymbeline is killed by a lie's author; the lie travels by letter and post-horse from Rome to Wales and does its work at a distance. He has just said the paper cut her throat already, which leaves his sword with nothing to do and makes his disobedience possible.

quotations.text: Poor I am stale, a garment out of fashion, And for I am richer than to hang by th' walls I must be ripp'd.
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Working out why her husband wants her dead, moments after reading the accusation.
quotations.analysis: She reaches for clothing, which is the play's currency for worth, and turns herself into a gown too good to be left hanging and so worth cutting up. The bitterness is in richer: being valuable is the reason for the destruction. Within two hundred lines she will be putting on a boy's doublet to stay alive.

quotations.text: I' th' world's volume Our Britain seems as of it, but not in't; In a great pool a swan's nest.
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Told by Pisanio that if she cannot go back to court she cannot stay in Britain at all.
quotations.analysis: The book and the pool pull in opposite directions: Britain is a page bound into the world's volume but somehow not printed in it, and a nest at the centre of water that could swallow it. Imogen gets the play's most exact image of the island because she is the only character being forced to leave it.

quotations.text: You must forget to be a woman; change Command into obedience
quotations.speaker: Pisanio
quotations.context: Setting out what Imogen will have to do to pass as the page Fidele.
quotations.analysis: The instruction is a list of subtractions, and the first thing to go is the right to give orders. A princess must learn to be spoken to as a servant is spoken to, and Pisanio goes on to add gibes, sauciness and a sunburnt cheek. Imogen cuts him off to say she is almost a man already.

quotations.text: No, nor thy tailor, rascal, Who is thy grandfather; he made those clothes, Which, as it seems, make thee.
quotations.speaker: Guiderius
quotations.context: Answering Cloten, who has demanded whether Guiderius knows him by his clothes.
quotations.analysis: A boy raised in a cave punctures the whole court system of rank in one line, and does it by taking the question literally. Cloten is wearing Posthumus's suit, so the clothes really are making him something he is not. The joke is about to become a beheading, and then a burial that mistakes one man for another.

quotations.text: Our courtiers say all's savage but at court. Experience, O, thou disprov'st report!
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Alone at the mouth of the cave, sick, after the three hunters have gone out for the day.
quotations.analysis: She has been at court all her life and in a cave for two days, and the cave is winning. The couplet sets report against experience, which is the argument the whole play is having: Posthumus took a report over twenty years of experience and ordered a murder on it. Imogen is about to swallow the drug that will bury her.

quotations.text: Fear no more the heat o' th' sun, Nor the furious winter's rages … Golden lads and girls all must, As chimney-sweepers, come to dust.
quotations.speaker: Guiderius
quotations.context: The first stanza of the dirge, spoken and not sung, over a body the brothers believe is the boy Fidele.
quotations.analysis: The most famous lines in the play are spoken over a living woman by her own brothers, who do not know who she is, beside the corpse of the man who meant to rape her. Guiderius says he cannot sing and will word it instead, so the great song of the play arrives stripped of its music, in a flat voice, at a grave dug for nobody.

quotations.text: A headless man? The garments of Posthumus? I know the shape of's leg; this is his hand
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Waking from the drug beside Cloten's body, which is dressed in her husband's suit.
quotations.analysis: She identifies him by the leg, the hand, the thigh, the arms, and every single identification is correct about the clothes and wrong about the man. This is the wager repeated on her: accurate observation assembled into a false conclusion. The one part of the body that would have settled it is the part Guiderius threw in the creek.

quotations.text: The heaviness and guilt within my bosom Takes off my manhood. I have belied a lady, The Princess of this country
quotations.speaker: Iachimo
quotations.context: Beaten and disarmed on the battlefield by a poor soldier he does not recognise as Posthumus.
quotations.analysis: Iachimo explains his own defeat as a physical effect of guilt, which is the only supernatural claim he ever makes. The play lets him be right: he loses to the husband he cheated, without either man knowing. Everything he says here he will say again, at greater length and unprompted, in the tent.

quotations.text: Whom best I love I cross; to make my gift, The more delay'd, delighted.
quotations.speaker: Jupiter
quotations.context: Descending on an eagle to silence the ghosts of the Leonati, who have been complaining about their son's treatment.
quotations.analysis: The god arrives to tell four ghosts that their suffering was never their business. It is the play's only direct statement of how it works, and it is unsatisfying on purpose: a divine plan that explains an ordered murder as a delay in the delivery of happiness. The audience has watched Imogen buried alive and is entitled to be unconvinced.

quotations.text: Kneel not to me. The pow'r that I have on you is to spare you; The malice towards you to forgive you.
quotations.speaker: Posthumus
quotations.context: To Iachimo, who has knelt and offered back the ring and the bracelet.
quotations.analysis: A man who ordered his wife's murder on this man's word declines to take anything from him. The balance of the two lines, power against malice, spare against forgive, is the play's whole fifth act in miniature. Cymbeline immediately takes the cue and extends the pardon to the entire Roman army.

quotations.text: No, my lord; I have got two worlds by't.
quotations.speaker: Imogen
quotations.context: Answering her father, who has just said that finding her brothers has cost her a kingdom.
quotations.analysis: Cymbeline counts in thrones and his daughter counts in brothers, and she has the better arithmetic. She has lost the succession and gained two men she already chose to love in a cave when she had no reason to. The line also quietly disposes of the one grievance that would have made the reunion political.

quotations.text: Although the victor, we submit to Cæsar And to the Roman empire, promising To pay our wonted tribute
quotations.speaker: Cymbeline
quotations.context: The peace settlement, after Britain has won the battle and taken Lucius prisoner.
quotations.analysis: Britain wins the war and pays the money, and the king blames the refusal on his dead wife. No Roman asks for this; it is offered. The play ends its imperial plot the way it ends its marriage plot, by handing back what was taken and calling the result peace, and the last word of the scene is exactly that.

themes.name: Grace, sin and the Reformation argument
Power, service and who commands whom

quotations.text: His waxen wings did mount above his reach, And, melting, heavens conspir'd his overthrow
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Chorus sums up Faustus's career before he has appeared.
quotations.analysis: Icarus was warned, flew too high and fell, which seems a tidy moral until the verb arrives. 'Conspir'd' makes heaven an active party to the overthrow, not a spectator of it, and that one word plants the question the play never settles: whether Faustus falls or is dropped.

quotations.text: Yet art thou still but Faustus, and a man.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus has just listed his medical triumphs, whole cities saved from plague.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is not that medicine fails but that success leaves him what he was. 'But' and 'and a man' treat being human as a rank he has been stuck at. It is the play's first use of his name as a reproach, and the ambition it announces is less for knowledge than for a change of species.

quotations.text: The reward of sin is death: that's hard.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Reading from Jerome's Bible, Faustus translates the Latin he has just quoted.
quotations.analysis: The verse he is reading goes on to say that the gift of God is eternal life. He stops at the half that suits his mood and delivers a verdict on the whole of divinity in two colloquial words. A doctor of theology would know the rest, so the misreading is either wilful or the first sign of a mind already closing.

quotations.text: But his dominion that exceeds in this, Stretcheth as far as doth the mind of man; A sound magician is a mighty god
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus compares the magician's reach with that of emperors and kings, who are obeyed only in their own provinces.
quotations.analysis: The limit he sets on the magician's empire is 'the mind of man', which sounds boundless and is in fact the boundary he has just complained of. 'Sound' is a scholar's word, used of arguments and doctrine, and here it is attached to the one study his university would call unsound.

quotations.text: I'll have them fly to India for gold, Ransack the ocean for orient pearl, And search all corners of the new-found world For pleasant fruits and princely delicates
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: After the Angels leave, Faustus imagines what his spirits will fetch him.
quotations.analysis: The speech begins by promising to resolve 'all ambiguities' and within four lines has become a shopping list. The verbs are a conqueror's, 'ransack' and 'search', but the objects are gold, pearl and fruit. When the play finally shows a spirit sent across the world, it comes back with grapes.

quotations.text: O, Faustus, lay that damned book aside, And gaze not on it, lest it tempt thy soul
quotations.speaker: Good Angel
quotations.context: The Angels' first entrance, while Faustus waits for Valdes and Cornelius.
quotations.analysis: The danger is located in looking. 'Gaze' makes the book a spectacle rather than a text, and the rest of the play bears that out: Faustus is managed by being given things to watch. The line also sets book against book, since the Angel's next words tell him to read the scriptures instead.

quotations.text: For, when we hear one rack the name of God, Abjure the Scriptures and his Saviour Christ, We fly, in hope to get his glorious soul
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Faustus asks whether his conjuring raised Mephistopheles. The answer is that it did so only incidentally.
quotations.analysis: The spell did nothing; the blasphemy did. Faustus has just congratulated himself as 'conjuror laureat', and the devil removes the ground of the boast in three lines without Faustus appearing to notice. 'Glorious' is the striking word: the hunter values the soul more highly than its owner does.

quotations.text: Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Faustus has asked how a damned spirit comes to be standing in Wittenberg, outside hell.
quotations.analysis: Ten monosyllables replace the hell of fire and pitchforks with a state of loss carried everywhere. The line is spoken to a man standing in the same spot, so 'this' takes in Faustus's study too. He has asked for a location and been given a definition, and he responds by changing the subject to his own fortitude.

quotations.text: O, Faustus, leave these frivolous demands, Which strike a terror to my fainting soul!
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Mephistopheles has described being deprived of everlasting bliss.
quotations.analysis: The tempter asks his victim to stop. It is the oddest moment in the scene and the most persuasive warning Faustus ever receives, because it comes from the only witness with direct experience and nothing to gain by it. Faustus's reply is to tell a devil to learn courage from him.

quotations.text: Had I as many souls as there be stars, I'd give them all for Mephistophilis.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Alone after Mephistopheles has gone to carry his offer to Lucifer.
quotations.analysis: The hyperbole works by multiplying the one thing he has only one of. It is also a lover's sentence, given for a person rather than for power, and the play keeps that note: he cuts his arm 'for love of thee'. What he wants from the bargain, at this moment, is company.

quotations.text: he would give his soul to the devil for a shoulder of mutton, though it were blood-raw.
quotations.speaker: Wagner
quotations.context: Wagner sizes up the ragged Clown he intends to hire.
quotations.analysis: The scene follows directly on Faustus's offer, and the Clown's answer sharpens the comparison: at that price he would want it well roasted, with good sauce. A starving man haggles over his soul more carefully than the doctor of divinity has just done, and in prose that makes the terms sound like what they are.

quotations.text: The god thou serv'st is thine own appetite
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Waiting at midnight for Lucifer's answer, Faustus hears a voice telling him to turn to God again, and argues himself out of it.
quotations.analysis: He says it to harden himself, and it is the most accurate sentence he speaks about his own case. The idol is not Lucifer or Belzebub but wanting. The grammar gives him away as well: a man who calls himself 'thou' can diagnose the fault and still treat it as somebody else's.

quotations.text: My blood congeals, and I can write no more.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus has stabbed his arm and begun to write the deed of gift.
quotations.analysis: His body objects before his mind does. The blood that will not flow for Lucifer is answered in the last scene by blood he cannot reach, streaming in the sky. Here the remedy is a pan of coals fetched from below, and he reads the omen correctly for one line before deciding his soul is his own to give.

quotations.text: Consummatum est; this bill is ended, And Faustus hath bequeath'd his soul to Lucifer.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The blood flows again and the deed is finished.
quotations.analysis: 'It is finished' are Christ's last words on the cross in John's gospel, spoken as a debt is paid for others. Faustus uses them to close a sale. The blasphemy is so exact that it is hard to believe a theologian commits it by accident, and the legal diction, 'bill' and 'bequeath'd', belongs to the profession he despised in Scene 1.

quotations.text: Hell hath no limits, nor is circumscrib'd In one self place; for where we are is hell
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Faustus's first question under the new contract: where is hell?
quotations.analysis: Faustus wanted dominion without limits and is told which kingdom actually has none. 'Circumscrib'd' picks up the circle he drew to conjure in: he thought he was enclosing a spirit and has stepped inside something with no edge. His reply is that he thinks hell's a fable, said to a devil in his own study.

quotations.text: My heart's so harden'd, I cannot repent: Scarce can I name salvation, faith, or heaven, But fearful echoes thunder in mine ears
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The Angels have just left; the Evil Angel's last words were that Faustus never shall repent.
quotations.analysis: The hardened heart is Pharaoh's in Exodus, where the text says both that Pharaoh hardened it and that God did. Marlowe leaves the verb passive, so the question of who did the hardening stays open. The speech then shows the mechanism at work: despair offers him knives and halters, and pleasure, in the shape of Homer singing, talks him round.

quotations.text: Never too late, if Faustus can repent.
quotations.speaker: Good Angel
quotations.context: Faustus asks 'Is't not too late?' and the Evil Angel answers first: 'Too late.'
quotations.analysis: The line everyone quotes for its comfort has a condition in the middle of it. Later versions of the play print 'will' here; the 1604 text's 'can' allows that he might not be able to, and turns a promise into a question about grace. The Angel speaks of him in the third person, as he does himself.

quotations.text: Christ cannot save thy soul, for he is just: There's none but I have interest in the same.
quotations.speaker: Lucifer
quotations.context: Faustus has cried out to Christ his Saviour. Lucifer, Belzebub and Mephistopheles enter at once.
quotations.analysis: Lucifer argues from justice and leaves mercy out, exactly as Faustus left out the second half of his verses in Scene 1. 'Interest' is a lender's word: the soul is a property with a claim on it. The fact that Lucifer needs to come in person suggests the prayer was more dangerous to him than he admits.

quotations.text: I cannot read, and therefore wish all books were burnt.
quotations.speaker: Envy
quotations.context: The fourth of the Seven Deadly Sins introduces itself to Faustus.
quotations.analysis: A throwaway joke in the parade that the last line of the tragedy turns serious. The most learned man in Germany will end by offering to burn his books too, and the echo puts him, at the finish, in the position of the sin that hates what it cannot use. Faustus watches the show as a spectator; several of the Sins are portraits.

quotations.text: How! bell, book, and candle,--candle, book, and bell,-- Forward and backward, to curse Faustus to hell!
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: In Rome, invisible, Faustus has boxed the Pope's ear and learns he will be excommunicated.
quotations.analysis: 'Forward and backward' is the phrase he used in Scene 3 for Jehovah's name anagrammatised in his conjuring circle. The ritual of cursing and the ritual of conjuring are made to sound alike, which flatters a Protestant audience and also removes any comfort: he laughs at a curse that the play means literally. The verse has shrunk to a jingle.

quotations.text: But such spirits as can lively resemble Alexander and his paramour shall appear before your grace
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The Emperor has asked to see Alexander the Great. Faustus explains what he can and cannot do.
quotations.analysis: An honest disclaimer, in courtly prose, from the man who was going to raise the dead and be a god. Magic can supply likenesses and nothing more. The Emperor forgets this within a minute and takes the spirits for 'true substantial bodies'; Faustus forgets it three scenes later, when the likeness is Helen and the one deceived is himself.

quotations.text: Tush, Christ did call the thief upon the Cross; Then rest thee, Faustus, quiet in conceit.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Between two halves of the horse-dealer farce, Faustus admits his time is nearly out, and settles down to sleep in his chair.
quotations.analysis: The penitent thief was the standard proof that repentance is possible at the last moment. Faustus uses it as a sedative. 'Tush' and 'quiet in conceit' show him turning a doctrine of mercy into permission to postpone, and the play's cruellest stage direction follows: he sleeps, and a cheated customer pulls his leg off.

quotations.text: I see an angel hovers o'er thy head, And, with a vial full of precious grace, Offers to pour the same into thy soul: Then call for mercy, and avoid despair.
quotations.speaker: Old Man
quotations.context: Mephistopheles has handed Faustus a dagger. The Old Man stops him.
quotations.analysis: The Good Angel has not been seen since Scene 6; now an angel is reported by a human witness and the offer is described as present tense and specific. If the Old Man is to be believed, grace is available in the last act, which makes what follows a refusal. His final clause names the enemy as despair, not the devil.

quotations.text: I do repent; and yet I do despair: Hell strives with grace for conquest in my breast
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The Old Man has left Faustus alone to think about his sins.
quotations.analysis: The line is built as a balance, the same verb form on either side of a semicolon, and that is the trouble with it. Repentance and despair cannot both be true at once in the play's theology, since despair denies what repentance asks for. He describes the contest in his breast as a spectator would, and Mephistopheles settles it with a threat in the next speech.

quotations.text: Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Helen re-enters, brought by Mephistopheles at Faustus's request to drive out thoughts of repentance. The sentence runs on to the burning of Troy.
quotations.analysis: The most famous compliment in English drama is a question, and its measure of beauty is a fleet of warships. 'Was this' carries a faint note of surprise, as if the scholar were checking the legend against the exhibit. He has told the Emperor that such figures are spirits in borrowed shapes, and he greets this one as the woman herself.

quotations.text: Her lips suck forth my soul: see, where it flies!-- Come, Helen, come, give me my soul again.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus has asked Helen to make him immortal with a kiss, and kisses her.
quotations.analysis: The souls of lovers passing in a kiss was an old poetic conceit. Spoken by a man whose soul is contracted to the power that sent this figure, it becomes a literal report, and he delivers it with delight. Asking for the soul back as a game, from a spirit, a few lines after refusing to ask for it from God, is the scene's whole argument.

quotations.text: I will be Paris, and for love of thee, Instead of Troy, shall Wertenberg be sack'd
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus imagines himself as Helen's lover and champion.
quotations.analysis: The scholar casts himself in the story he used to teach, and offers his own university town as the city to be burned. It is said as gallantry. Every comparison in the speech, Paris, Semele, Arethusa, is a mortal ruined by contact with something greater, and the speaker never notices what his examples have in common.

quotations.text: His faith is great; I cannot touch his soul; But what I may afflict his body with I will attempt, which is but little worth.
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Faustus has asked Mephistopheles to torment the Old Man with the greatest torments hell affords.
quotations.analysis: A devil states the limits of his own power, and they are narrow. Against faith he can manage only bodily harm, which he himself rates as worth little. The admission makes nonsense of the threat that has governed Faustus since Scene 6, that repentance will get him torn in pieces, and Faustus is standing there when it is made.

quotations.text: the serpent that tempted Eve may be saved, but not Faustus.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: A scholar has reminded Faustus that God's mercies are infinite.
quotations.analysis: This is pride wearing the clothes of humility. To claim the one sin too large for infinite mercy is to claim, still, to be exceptional, and the man who wanted to be more than a man now insists on being worse than the devil. The scene is in prose, the only time Faustus speaks plainly to friends, and the plainness makes the claim more shocking.

quotations.text: Stand still, you ever-moving spheres of heaven, That time may cease, and midnight never come
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The clock has struck eleven and Faustus is alone.
quotations.analysis: He opens the last speech in the imperative, the mood of a conjuror, and addresses the same spheres he once questioned Mephistopheles about. Nothing obeys. 'Ever-moving' concedes the defeat inside the command. The speech goes on asking for less and less: a year, a month, a week, a natural day.

quotations.text: O, I'll leap up to my God!--Who pulls me down?-- See, see, where Christ's blood streams in the firmament! One drop would save my soul, half a drop: ah, my Christ!
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Midway through the final soliloquy, before the half-hour strikes.
quotations.analysis: The verse breaks into cries and the long second line overruns its metre. His own blood congealed when he tried to sign; this blood streams, and he bargains for it in fractions, a drop and then half a drop, still thinking in prices. 'Who pulls me down?' has no stage direction to answer it, and whether the hand is a devil's or his own is left to the actor.

quotations.text: Ugly hell, gape not! come not, Lucifer! I'll burn my books!--Ah, Mephistophilis!
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Midnight has struck and the devils have entered. These are Faustus's last words.
quotations.analysis: The final offer is the first one the Good Angel asked for, that he lay the book aside, made twenty-four years late and addressed to the wrong party. It is a bargain, not a prayer. The last word is the devil's name, and 'Ah' can be played as terror, reproach or recognition of the only companion he has had.

quotations.text: Cut is the branch that might have grown full straight, And burned is Apollo's laurel-bough, That sometime grew within this learned man.
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Chorus returns after the devils have taken Faustus away.
quotations.analysis: Both main verbs are passive and come first, so the loss is felt before its subject. 'Might have grown' grants that the outcome was not fixed, which sits awkwardly with a Prologue in which the heavens conspired. The laurel is Apollo's, the prize of poets and scholars, and the Chorus mourns the learning even while warning against where it led.

quotations.text: There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all.
quotations.context: From the preface Wilde added in 1891, after the reviews of the magazine version.
quotations.analysis: This is a reply to specific attacks, printed as if it were a general principle. Set it against Chapter XI, where a book poisons the hero, and against Lord Henry’s denial in Chapter XIX that such a thing could happen: the preface and the plot are arguing with each other on the same pages.

quotations.text: All art is at once surface and symbol. Those who go beneath the surface do so at their peril. Those who read the symbol do so at their peril.
quotations.context: The preface’s last substantial pair of statements before the closing line.
quotations.analysis: The two sentences are identical in shape and cancel each other, which leaves a reader with no safe position from which to interpret. It is also a plot summary: this is a book in which a surface and a symbol are separated from each other, and everyone who looks under the cloth comes off badly.

quotations.text: All art is quite useless.
quotations.context: The final line of the preface, standing alone.
quotations.analysis: Useless here means unable to be put to work, which was the aesthetic movement’s defence against a century that wanted everything to improve somebody. The book that follows is about a work of art doing a job — keeping accounts — and destroying the man it belongs to.

quotations.text: I know you will laugh at me,” he replied, “but I really can’t exhibit it. I have put too much of myself into it.
quotations.speaker: Basil Hallward
quotations.context: Basil explaining why the finished portrait will never be shown.
quotations.analysis: He thinks he is confessing to bad art and he is confessing to love. The line also sets the novel’s central proposition before any magic happens: a portrait can contain a person who is not the sitter, which is what makes the later transfer feel less like a spell than a completion.

quotations.text: But beauty, real beauty, ends where an intellectual expression begins.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Lord Henry, in the studio, before he has met Dorian.
quotations.analysis: It is said as a joke about clever men’s faces and it is the rule Dorian will live by: to remain beautiful is to remain unmarked by thought. The novel then arranges for a face that never records a thought and a canvas that records every one, and lets the reader decide which is the man.

quotations.text: I have grown to love secrecy. It seems to be the one thing that can make modern life mysterious or marvellous to us. The commonest thing is delightful if one only hides it.
quotations.speaker: Basil Hallward
quotations.context: Basil explaining why he has never told anyone Dorian’s name.
quotations.analysis: The novel’s great theme is stated in the first chapter by the man who will be murdered for wanting things brought into the open. Concealment is presented here as a refinement of pleasure rather than a moral failure, which is the exact argument Dorian will later use about a locked room at the top of a house.

quotations.text: There is no such thing as a good influence, Mr. Gray. All influence is immoral⁠—immoral from the scientific point of view.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: The opening of the speech in the garden, minutes after being introduced.
quotations.analysis: He is establishing his authority by disclaiming it, which is the oldest move a persuader has. From the scientific point of view is decoration — there is no science in the sentence — and the whole novel is the experiment that follows from a man announcing that influence is impossible and then applying it for an hour.

quotations.text: The aim of life is self-development. To realize one’s nature perfectly⁠—that is what each of us is here for.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: The same speech, a few sentences on.
quotations.analysis: It is genuinely liberating and completely unsupervised: a doctrine with no account at all of other people. Wilde gives it to a man who will never test it, and then hands the testing to somebody with money, beauty and eighteen years, which is as close as the novel comes to an argument against its own best lines.

quotations.text: The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Part of the garden speech, arguing that resistance is what makes desire monstrous.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning around it is medical rather than moral — the body sins once and has done with its sin — and that is the trick. A sentence built to sound like a cure for obsession is in fact a licence, and the novel spends twenty chapters showing that yielding does not get rid of anything.

quotations.text: Nothing can cure the soul but the senses, just as nothing can cure the senses but the soul.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Said quietly, with a hand on Dorian’s shoulder, in the garden.
quotations.analysis: Dorian repeats this line to himself sixteen chapters later on the way to an opium den, and Wilde prints it twice in that scene to make sure the reader hears where it has ended up. A balanced, harmless-sounding chiasmus becomes a man’s excuse for buying oblivion the night after a murder.

quotations.text: If it were I who was to be always young, and the picture that was to grow old! For that⁠—for that⁠—I would give everything! Yes, there is nothing in the whole world I would not give! I would give my soul for that!
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In front of the finished portrait, after Lord Henry’s speech in the garden.
quotations.analysis: There is no devil, no contract and no witness who understands what has happened: the most consequential sentence in the novel is a tantrum in front of a canvas. Wilde keeps the machinery invisible for the rest of the book, so that a reader can never quite decide whether anything supernatural has occurred or whether Dorian is simply right about himself.

quotations.text: It is the real Dorian Gray⁠—that is all.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Dismissing Dorian’s outburst as merely the young man showing his true character.
quotations.analysis: He means it as a shrug about temperament, and it turns out to be a literal description of the object on the easel. This is the novel’s method in one line: a piece of drawing-room cleverness is quietly promoted into a fact, and nobody in the room notices it happen.

quotations.text: Harry! Sibyl Vane is sacred!
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: Answering Lord Henry’s amused questions about when he will be paying for her.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation marks are the only ones Dorian earns in the whole book, and three chapters later he tells the same girl she has killed his love. Sacred belongs to the vocabulary of worship rather than of affection, which is the flaw: he has cast her as a shrine, and shrines are not allowed to have a bad night.

quotations.text: Yes, Dorian, you will always be fond of me. I represent to you all the sins you have never had the courage to commit.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: At dinner, hours before Sibyl’s performance.
quotations.analysis: He is boasting about being a spectator, and he has the relation exactly backwards — Dorian will commit the sins and Lord Henry will hear about them as anecdotes. The line reads as flirtation on the night it is spoken and as an epitaph by Chapter XX, when the one man who acted is dead and the one who talked is unchanged.

quotations.text: you have killed my love. You used to stir my imagination. Now you don’t even stir my curiosity. You simply produce no effect.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In the dressing room, after Sibyl has acted Juliet badly for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The three sentences descend from love to imagination to curiosity to effect, ending in the language of a critic rather than a lover. She has just told him that she can no longer act because she has discovered what love is; he replies by explaining that she was only ever a performance he enjoyed.

quotations.text: It was a poisonous book. The heavy odour of incense seemed to cling about its pages and to trouble the brain.
quotations.context: Dorian reads the yellow-backed French novel Lord Henry has sent him.
quotations.analysis: The narration takes Dorian’s side of the argument the preface has just refused: a book here is an atmosphere you breathe rather than a set of propositions you weigh. Wilde never names the novel, which leaves it as a pure idea of a dangerous book — and keeps the preface’s denial technically intact.

quotations.text: Dorian Gray had been poisoned by a book.
quotations.context: In the middle of a paragraph about Renaissance methods of murder.
quotations.analysis: It arrives at the end of a list of poisoned helmets, gloves and pomanders, so the book is filed as one more elegant instrument. Seven words flatly contradict the preface, and the novel simply lets both stand — which is either Wilde’s carelessness or the point of publishing the preface at all.

quotations.text: It is the face of my soul.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: Holding the lamp up to the portrait for Basil, minutes before the murder.
quotations.analysis: He has been asked to deny the rumours and instead produces a physical exhibit, which is a confession made in the only terms he still understands. Basil’s response is to suggest that they pray, and Dorian’s is to reach for a knife — the novel refuses him the one moment in which saying the true thing might have changed anything.

quotations.text: Each of us has heaven and hell in him, Basil
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In the schoolroom, when Basil urges him to pray.
quotations.analysis: It is said with a wild gesture of despair and it is the most ordinary piece of theology in the novel — the one thing Dorian says that Lord Henry could not have taught him. Within a page he has stabbed the man he said it to, which is the book’s way of showing that knowing the doctrine is not the same as having a conscience.

quotations.text: What was that loathsome red dew that gleamed, wet and glistening, on one of the hands, as though the canvas had sweated blood?
quotations.context: The morning after the murder, looking at the portrait before Alan Campbell arrives.
quotations.analysis: Dew is a word for something clean, and the sentence spends three modifiers being beautiful before it says blood. This is the aestheticist prose doing its usual job of looking away, and the detail it will not name outright is the one that has moved from the body downstairs onto a painted hand.

quotations.text: He himself could not help wondering at the calm of his demeanour, and for a moment felt keenly the terrible pleasure of a double life.
quotations.context: At Lady Narborough’s dinner table, the evening after the body has been destroyed.
quotations.analysis: Terrible pleasure is not remorse; it is connoisseurship applied to his own situation. The novel has him admire his own composure from the outside, which is what the portrait does for him structurally — and it explains why he keeps the thing rather than burning it.

quotations.text: The soul is a terrible reality. It can be bought, and sold, and bartered away. It can be poisoned, or made perfect.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: The last conversation with Lord Henry, who has just called the soul a fashionable myth.
quotations.analysis: The pupil corrects the teacher, using the commercial verbs Lord Henry taught him, and Lord Henry laughs. This is the only time anyone in the novel states the plot as a fact to somebody who could still act on it, and it is received as a good remark and nothing else.

quotations.text: You are the type of what the age is searching for, and what it is afraid it has found.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Praising Dorian for having produced nothing but himself.
quotations.analysis: Afraid it has found is the sharpest thing Lord Henry says, and he says it without noticing. He has spent the novel recommending a life made entirely of sensation, and here he admits that the age which wants such a life is also frightened of the person who actually lives one.

quotations.text: As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work, and all that that meant. It would kill the past, and when that was dead, he would be free.
quotations.context: Picking up the knife in front of the portrait on the last night.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is stated as free indirect thought, so the reader gets Dorian’s logic without a narrator to correct it, and the logic is good — except that he has never worked out which of the two of them is the painting. Kill the past is the wish from Chapter II repeated in the language of a man who has run out of other ideas.

quotations.text: Lying on the floor was a dead man, in evening dress, with a knife in his heart. He was withered, wrinkled, and loathsome of visage. It was not till they had examined the rings that they recognized who it was.
quotations.context: The servants break into the locked room; the last sentences of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book ends with an identification made from jewellery, because the face — the thing everyone in twenty chapters has judged him by — is no longer evidence of anything. Evening dress is the detail that finishes it: the accounts are settled at last, and he is still dressed for dinner.

quotations.text: Welcome to my house! Enter freely and of your own will!
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: The Count greets Harker at the castle door, standing perfectly still.
quotations.analysis: It sounds like hospitality and it is a legal condition: the folklore rule that a vampire must be invited is being satisfied in advance, and Harker signs up to it by walking through the door. The Count makes no move to meet him, which the text notes twice — the crossing has to be the guest’s own act.

quotations.text: Listen to them⁠—the children of the night. What music they make!
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Wolves howling outside the castle during Harker’s first supper.
quotations.analysis: The possessive is doing quiet work — them, not the wolves — and the Count is watching his guest’s face to see whether the phrase registers. What follows is an apology for the tastes of a hunter, which is the second time in a page he has explained himself in terms that only make sense later.

quotations.text: I am all in a sea of wonders. I doubt; I fear; I think strange things, which I dare not confess to my own soul.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: A journal entry written in the castle, before he understands he is a prisoner.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses, each shorter than the last, in a journal that has so far been full of train times and paprika. The diary is the only person he can talk to, and the last clause admits that he is censoring even that — the document the entire novel rests on is being written by a man who dare not write everything down.

quotations.text: We are in Transylvania; and Transylvania is not England. Our ways are not your ways, and there shall be to you many strange things.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Explaining away one of the household’s peculiarities to his guest.
quotations.analysis: He is telling the truth and using it as cover, which is his usual method. The sentence also states the book’s geography as a rule, so that the second half — in which the ways of Transylvania are unloaded at Whitby by a shipping agent — reads as a violation of terms the Count himself set out.

quotations.text: Blood is too precious a thing in these days of dishonourable peace; and the glories of the great races are as a tale that is told.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: The end of the Count’s long account of his family’s wars.
quotations.analysis: He has spent several pages using blood to mean lineage, and here he prices it. The double sense is set up before a single drop is taken, so that every later transfusion carries an argument about descent as well as a medical procedure. A tale that is told is from the Psalms, and he means it as a complaint about being finished.

quotations.text: This man belongs to me! Beware how you meddle with him, or you’ll have to deal with me.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Driving the three women away from Harker in the disused room.
quotations.analysis: Harker has been lying still with his eyes almost shut, waiting, and his own journal admits to a wicked longing. The Count’s intervention is a rescue and a claim of ownership in the same sentence, and the vocabulary is commercial — belongs, deal — which is how he handles everything, including the Essex property.

quotations.text: The last I saw of Count Dracula was his kissing his hand to me; with a red light of triumph in his eyes, and with a smile that Judas in hell might be proud of.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: Harker watches the Count leave the castle, having been made to write letters dated weeks in advance.
quotations.analysis: The triumph is over paperwork: the Count has just obtained three post-dated letters that will keep anyone from looking for Harker until long after he is dead. Stoker gives the villain his most theatrical exit in the novel at the exact moment his weapon is a set of forged dates.

quotations.text: God and the Blessed Virgin and the saints help a poor ignorant soul trying to do his duty.
quotations.speaker: The captain of the Demeter
quotations.context: The last entry in the ship’s log, found lashed to the wheel with the captain’s body.
quotations.analysis: The log is the purest example of the novel’s method: a form designed for positions, weather and watches, kept up by a man whose crew is vanishing one at a time. He records the facts he is permitted to record and can name nothing else, and the empty ship reaches Whitby carrying both its cargo and an official document that proves something happened without being able to say what.

quotations.text: The blood is the life! The blood is the life!
quotations.speaker: R. M. Renfield
quotations.context: Renfield, having cut Seward’s wrist and licked the floor, is taken away by the attendants.
quotations.analysis: He is quoting Deuteronomy, and Seward files it as a symptom. Every element of the diagnosis the doctors need is in this room — an appetite for blood, a servant who responds to a master, a man who knows the neighbouring house is occupied — and it is all written down under the heading of a case note.

quotations.text: There are darknesses in life, and there are lights; you are one of the lights.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Van Helsing to Mina, after reading her transcription of Jonathan’s journal.
quotations.analysis: He says it to the person who has just done the filing, not to anyone who has done anything brave, and it is worth setting beside the decision four chapters later to keep her out of the council. The novel praises Mina in the language of light and then removes her from the room where the work is done.

quotations.text: I shall get my typewriter this very hour and begin transcribing. Then we shall be ready for other eyes if required.
quotations.speaker: Mina Harker
quotations.context: Mina resolves to type out Jonathan’s shorthand journal.
quotations.analysis: This is the sentence on which the second half of the novel turns, and it is about office equipment. Ready for other eyes is the whole problem stated in five words: private records held by separate people cannot be compared, and a hunt that has failed for three hundred pages becomes possible the moment somebody makes copies.

quotations.text: Ah, it is the fault of our science that it wants to explain all; and if it explain not, then it says there is nothing to explain.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Rebuking Seward for refusing to believe what he has seen.
quotations.analysis: The broken grammar makes the argument sound folkloric, but it is a precise objection: a method that treats the unexplained as the non-existent will always return the answer it started with. Stoker gives his most modern characters the newest instruments in the world and then has the oldest man in the room point out that instruments only find what they are built to find.

quotations.text: the consensus of their excuses is that they had been with a “bloofer lady.”
quotations.context: A Westminster Gazette cutting about children going missing on Hampstead Heath.
quotations.analysis: The newspaper reports the phrase as a childish fashion and prints it in inverted commas to keep its distance. Bloofer is a small child’s attempt at beautiful, so the most frightening development in the novel reaches the reader as a piece of quaint local colour in a light news column — which is exactly how it reaches the characters.

quotations.text: She seemed like a nightmare of Lucy as she lay there; the pointed teeth, the bloodstained, voluptuous mouth⁠—which it made one shudder to see⁠—the whole carnal and unspiritual appearance, seeming like a devilish mockery of Lucy’s sweet purity.
quotations.speaker: Dr John Seward
quotations.context: In the Westenra tomb, before Arthur drives the stake.
quotations.analysis: Seward’s vocabulary gives the game away: voluptuous and carnal are not clinical terms, and the man writing is one of the suitors she refused. The novel keeps describing the changed Lucy in the language of unacceptable desire rather than of predation, which is why so much criticism has fixed on this scene.

quotations.text: you would in time, when you had died, have become nosferatu, as they call it in Eastern Europe, and would all time make more of those Un-Deads that so have fill us with horror.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Explaining to Arthur why Lucy’s kiss would have destroyed him.
quotations.analysis: The condition is described as an inheritance that spreads rather than as a curse on an individual, and the reasoning is epidemiological: one case makes more cases, indefinitely. Van Helsing borrows a foreign word to name it because English medicine has none, which is the novel’s argument about the limits of a vocabulary in one sentence.

quotations.text: There are such beings as vampires; some of us have evidence that they exist.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Opening the formal briefing at the asylum, with all the papers in order.
quotations.analysis: He states it as a finding rather than a revelation, and the second clause does the work: not belief, evidence, and some of us, meaning the people in this room who have read the typescript. The supernatural is admitted to the novel by the same procedure a court would use.

quotations.text: We have on our side power of combination⁠—a power denied to the vampire kind; we have sources of science; we are free to act and think; and the hours of the day and the night are ours equally.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Setting out the group’s advantages before the hunt begins.
quotations.analysis: Combination is a late-Victorian word for organised collective action, and it names the thing the novel actually values: not courage but committee work, shared papers and a division of labour. The Count is enormously strong and entirely alone, and the book’s proposition is that the second fact beats the first.

quotations.text: Unclean! Unclean! Even the Almighty shuns my polluted flesh! I must bear this mark of shame upon my forehead until the Judgment Day.
quotations.speaker: Mina Harker
quotations.context: After the communion wafer burns her forehead.
quotations.analysis: The cry is from Leviticus, where it is what a leper is required to shout to warn others off, and Mina applies it to herself before anyone else can. The novel has her take up the vocabulary of ritual pollution for something done to her while she was drugged and held down, and nobody in the room corrects her.

quotations.text: My revenge is just begun! I spread it over centuries, and time is on my side.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Cornered in the Piccadilly house, before escaping through the back.
quotations.analysis: It is the only speech he makes to the whole group, and the boast is about duration rather than strength. Everything the hunters have — telegrams, timetables, a chartered launch — is built for speed, and he answers with centuries. The last four chapters are the novel testing which of the two is right.

quotations.text: Now God be thanked that all has not been in vain! See! the snow is not more stainless than her forehead!
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: At the moment the Count crumbles, with Mina watching.
quotations.analysis: The victory is announced as a fact about a woman’s complexion. Van Helsing checks Mina’s forehead before he checks anything else, and the novel closes its plot by restoring her to a state of visible purity — which tells a reader a good deal about what was thought to have been lost.

quotations.text: We were struck with the fact, that in all the mass of material of which the record is composed, there is hardly one authentic document; nothing but a mass of typewriting
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: Seven years later, taking the papers out of the safe.
quotations.analysis: The book’s last move is to withdraw its own evidence. Mina’s typing saved their lives by making the records comparable, and it destroyed them as proof by leaving no originals — the same act did both. A novel that has spent six hundred pages insisting on documentation ends by admitting it has none.

quotations.text: We want no proofs; we ask none to believe us!
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: The last speech in the novel, with the Harkers’ son on his knee.
quotations.analysis: He turns a fatal evidential weakness into a refusal, and then changes the subject to the boy’s mother. It is a generous ending and an evasive one, and it leaves the reader holding a book that has just declined to argue for its own truth.

quotations.text: I had the story, bit by bit, from various people, and, as generally happens in such cases, each time it was a different story.
quotations.speaker: The narrator
