quotations.context: The opening sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: The first sentence of a tragedy is a warning about evidence. 'Bit by bit' concedes that the pieces arrived separately, and the last clause concedes that they contradicted each other — so everything the reader is about to be shown in close-up third person has been assembled by a man who has just told us his materials do not agree.

quotations.text: He’s looked that way ever since he had his smash-up; and that’s twenty-four years ago come next February
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: The first explanation the narrator is offered for Frome's appearance.
quotations.analysis: The village's word for the event is a word for a cart overturning, and the sentence dates it with the precision people use for a wedding or a death. The whole book is contained in the gap between the mildness of 'smash-up' and the fact that somebody has been counting the Februaries.

quotations.text: He looks as if he was dead and in hell now!
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: Answering his own remark that Frome will probably live to a hundred.
quotations.analysis: Gow has just said the Fromes are tough and will last, and he immediately spoils the compliment. Putting hell in the present tense makes the rest of the book an explanation rather than a mystery: the reader now knows the outcome and is waiting only to be told what it cost.

quotations.text: Guess he’s been in Starkfield too many winters. Most of the smart ones get away.
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: The sentence the narrator says he built all his later inferences around.
quotations.analysis: Two flat statements which between them contain a theory of the whole district: that staying is what does the damage, and that staying is what the less able do. The narrator quotes it twice, and the second quotation is his admission that a reconstruction of twenty-four years has been grown from one man's offhand remark.

quotations.text: it seemed to produce no change except that of retarding still more the sluggish pulse of Starkfield
quotations.speaker: The narrator
quotations.context: The effect of a spell of bright clear cold on the village.
quotations.analysis: The village is given a pulse, which makes the winter a condition rather than a season and the place a patient rather than a location. It is the first of the book's many transfers of medical language away from Zeena, who is the only person in it with a diagnosis.

quotations.text: He seemed a part of the mute melancholy landscape, an incarnation of its frozen woe, with all that was warm and sentient in him fast bound below the surface; but there was nothing unfriendly in his silence.
quotations.speaker: The narrator
quotations.context: After several winter drives to the Junction in Frome's sleigh, in near-silence.
quotations.analysis: The man is absorbed into the scenery and then, in the last clause, quietly handed back his humanity. 'Fast bound below the surface' describes ice over water, and the reconstruction that follows is an attempt to get at what is under it — an attempt the narrator has already told us is guesswork.

quotations.text: We’ll always go on living here together, and some day she’ll lie there beside me.
quotations.speaker: Ethan Frome
quotations.context: Walking Mattie home past the Frome graves, which had always oppressed him.
quotations.analysis: This is the novel's love scene, and it consists of a man imagining a shared grave. The graves that used to stand for everything he could not escape have been converted, in one sentence, into a promise — which tells the reader exactly how narrow the available happiness is.

quotations.text: There was in him a slumbering spark of sociability which the long Starkfield winters had not yet extinguished.
quotations.context: Ethan driving to the village in unusually good spirits, with Zeena away.
quotations.analysis: 'Not yet' is the word that turns a kind sentence into a threatening one. The metaphor is a fire going out slowly in a cold house, and the chapter that contains it is the only one in which Ethan whistles, sings and behaves like a man of twenty-eight.

quotations.text: There the silence had deepened about him year by year.
quotations.context: The history of the farm after his father's accident and his mother's decline.
quotations.analysis: Silence is given a depth and a rate of increase, like snow or debt. The sentence also supplies the motive for the marriage twenty pages before the book states it: Ethan asks Zeena to stay because she has been speaking in a house where nobody spoke.

quotations.text: Sacred to the memory of Ethan Frome and Endurance his wife, who dwelled together in peace for fifty years.
quotations.context: An ancestor's headstone on the knoll, which had interested him as a boy because it bore his name.
quotations.analysis: The wife's name is a virtue and the epitaph is a sentence about duration rather than affection — fifty years, in peace, together. Wharton then has Ethan wonder whether the same words will be written over him and Zeena, and the epilogue answers the question without needing a stone.

quotations.text: backed into the pickle-dish, which fell to the floor with a crash
quotations.context: The cat, startled off the table during the supper Ethan and Mattie have alone.
quotations.analysis: The agent of the disaster is a cat, which lets Wharton destroy the marriage's most valued object without giving anybody the blame or the satisfaction. The dish was a wedding present never used; taking it down for one meal is the only extravagance in the book, and it is punished within the hour.

quotations.text: I’ve got complications
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Reporting the new Bettsbridge doctor's verdict, on her return.
quotations.analysis: Three words, delivered with the air of somebody singled out for a great fate. In a village where everybody has troubles, the word is a promotion, and Wharton has Zeena win the only argument that matters by producing a noun her husband cannot contradict.

quotations.text: To have them was in itself a distinction, though it was also, in most cases, a death-warrant.
quotations.context: The narrator explaining what the word means in that part of the country.
quotations.analysis: The sentence balances social promotion against a death sentence on either side of a comma, and the phrase 'in most cases' quietly leaves room for the ones who live for decades. It is the book's one moment of open irony about Zeena, and it is also the book's refusal to say whether she is ill.

quotations.text: The doctor says it’ll be my death if I go on slaving the way I’ve had to.
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Justifying the hired girl she has already engaged, which means Mattie must go.
quotations.analysis: The medical authority is quoted rather than present, and the word 'slaving' recasts a household in which somebody else does the work. The sentence is unanswerable by design: to argue with it is to be a man who would rather keep a girl than keep his wife alive.

quotations.text: now you’ve took from me the one I cared for most of all
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Holding the pieces of the red glass pickle-dish.
quotations.analysis: She is grieving over crockery, and the phrasing is that of a woman mourning a person — which is the nearest the novel lets her come to saying what she knows about her husband and her cousin. She then stops in a spasm of sobs and hardens again, and the marriage never discusses any of it.

quotations.text: He was a prisoner for life, and now his one ray of light was to be extinguished.
quotations.context: After the failure to raise fifty dollars from Andrew Hale.
quotations.analysis: The sentence arrives immediately after a page of arithmetic — the price of tickets, the mortgage, the three months' credit — so the prison metaphor is being cashed against a ledger rather than a mood. Wharton is precise that the walls are financial, and that the door was shut by a kind man who was also short of money.

quotations.text: Right into the big elm. You said you could. So ’t we’d never have to leave each other any more.
quotations.speaker: Mattie Silver
quotations.context: At the top of the coast, after one run down, her lips against his ear.
quotations.analysis: She proposes it, not him, and she does so by quoting his own boast back at him. The reasoning in the last clause is a child's — this is the only way of not being separated — and the flat construction, with no word for death anywhere in it, is what makes the moment unbearable.

quotations.text: But suddenly his wife’s face, with twisted monstrous lineaments, thrust itself between him and his goal
quotations.context: The second run down the hill, with the elm ahead.
quotations.analysis: Zeena appears at the last possible instant as a hallucination and physically deflects the sled, so the crash that follows is neither a clean death nor a clean escape. Wharton has the marriage intervene in the accident itself, which is why the survivors end up in one kitchen rather than two graves.

quotations.text: A slatternly calico wrapper hung from her shoulders and the wisps of her thin grey hair were drawn away from a high forehead and fastened at the back by a broken comb.
quotations.context: The narrator's first sight of the woman who gets up to prepare the meal in the Frome kitchen.
quotations.analysis: The description is given before the name, so the reader spends a paragraph deciding which of the two women this is and gets it wrong. The broken comb is the detail that does the work: everything in the room has been mended once and is now simply being used broken.

quotations.text: And I say, if she’d ha’ died, Ethan might ha’ lived
quotations.speaker: Mrs Ned Hale
quotations.context: The impulse of complete avowal that seizes her after twenty-four years of reticence.
quotations.analysis: She has already said her minister was shocked by the same sentence, and she repeats it anyway, in dialect, with 'I say' at the front to mark that she knows what she is doing. It converts the accident from a tragedy into a failed mercy, which is a far harder thing for the reader to hold.

quotations.text: I don’t see’s there’s much difference between the Fromes up at the farm and the Fromes down in the graveyard; ’cept that down there they’re all quiet, and the women have got to hold their tongues.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Ned Hale
quotations.context: The last words of the book.
quotations.analysis: The joke is that the dead are quieter, and the sting is in what it concedes about the living: the kitchen is a grave with the arguing left in. Ending a novel about a man who could not speak on a line about women who cannot stop is Wharton's final adjustment to who, in Starkfield, has actually been silenced.

themes.name: Education and what makes a monster
themes.canonicalName: Education and what makes a monster

quotations.text: I shall satiate my ardent curiosity with the sight of a part of the world never before visited, and may tread a land never before imprinted by the foot of man.
quotations.speaker: Robert Walton
quotations.context: Walton writes to his sister from St Petersburgh before the expedition sails.
quotations.analysis: The verbs give the game away: satiate belongs to appetite, not to science, and tread is about leaving a mark rather than finding anything. Walton wants the place to be untouched so that he can be the one who touches it, which is precisely the wish Victor will spend the rest of the book regretting.

quotations.text: I have no friend, Margaret: when I am glowing with the enthusiasm of success, there will be none to participate my joy; if I am assailed by disappointment, no one will endeavour to sustain me in dejection.
quotations.speaker: Robert Walton
quotations.context: From Archangel, waiting for the ice to open.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is addressed to his sister, which means he is telling the one person who loves him that he has nobody. That blindness is the point: Walton defines friendship as an audience for his moods, and within two letters he has found one in a man who will talk for three hundred pages.

quotations.text: One man’s life or death were but a small price to pay for the acquirement of the knowledge which I sought; for the dominion I should acquire and transmit over the elemental foes of our race.
quotations.speaker: Robert Walton
quotations.context: Walton reports what he said to Victor, his rescued passenger, over the first days aboard.
quotations.analysis: He says this to a man who has already paid that price several times over, which is why Victor begins to weep rather than to argue. Note the slide from knowledge to dominion inside one sentence: the enquiry is barely stated before it becomes a claim to rule, and the price is always one man’s and never the speaker’s.

quotations.text: The world was to me a secret which I desired to divine.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Victor contrasts his own childhood curiosity with Clerval’s taste for poetry and adventure.
quotations.analysis: Divine is doing two jobs: to work out, and to do the work of a god. Shelley lets the pun sit there unremarked in a sentence about a small boy, ten chapters before anyone has assembled anything. The world is cast as something withholding information from him, which makes discovery feel like the recovery of a right.

quotations.text: So much has been done, exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein⁠—more, far more, will I achieve: treading in the steps already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and unfold to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Immediately after Waldman’s lecture on the achievements of modern chemistry.
quotations.analysis: He quotes himself in the third person and hands the speech to his soul rather than his mouth, which keeps the boast at arm’s length while still making it. The one moment of real modesty — treading in the steps already marked — is buried between two promises to go further than anyone has gone.

quotations.text: Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge, and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world, than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Victor breaks off his narrative to refuse Walton the secret of animation.
quotations.analysis: The moral is offered as the reason for telling a story that is also, unmistakably, a performance of how far he got. He withholds the method and keeps the glamour, and the alternative he proposes — believing your home town to be the world — is not a life he would accept for himself for an afternoon.

quotations.text: A new species would bless me as its creator and source; many happy and excellent natures would owe their being to me. No father could claim the gratitude of his child so completely as I should deserve theirs.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Working alone through two seasons, imagining what success will mean.
quotations.analysis: Every clause is about what he will receive: blessing, gratitude, a debt so complete that no ordinary father could match it. He imagines fatherhood entirely as a creditor relationship, and the novel then tests the arrangement by giving him exactly one child, who asks him for something.

quotations.text: It was on a dreary night of November, that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the creation scene.
quotations.analysis: Shelley said this was the first sentence she wrote, and the whole chapter is built backwards from it. Beheld makes Victor a spectator at his own experiment, and accomplishment of my toils names the labour rather than the thing produced — the grammar is already looking away from the body on the table.

quotations.text: I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: The moment of animation itself.
quotations.analysis: The most famous event in the novel is reported without a single active verb for Victor: he saw, and then things happened by themselves. There is no lightning, no machinery and no instant of triumph in the text at all, only an eye opening and a man watching. Every screen version has had to invent the scene that Shelley refused to write.

quotations.text: I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation; but now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Moments after the animation, before he runs from the room.
quotations.analysis: Nothing about the creature has changed between the sentence before and the sentence after; what has changed is that Victor has stopped wanting. The horror is described as arriving in him rather than coming from anything, and the novel will hold him to that all the way to the Arctic: the being is made monstrous by a reaction, not by a defect.

quotations.text: Remember, that I am thy creature; I ought to be thy Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: On the Mer de Glace, the first words the creature addresses to Victor at length.
quotations.analysis: He argues in the second person singular that scripture and Milton use for God, and he has picked his precedent with care: Satan fell for a misdeed, and his claim is that he has not committed one. The sentence is a legal submission dressed as a lament, and Victor never answers the argument, only the tone.

quotations.text: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: The end of the creature’s opening appeal on the glacier.
quotations.analysis: Two short clauses containing the novel’s whole theory of character: virtue is a condition, not a substance, and it can be restored by changing the conditions. It is also a threat with the grammar of an offer. The reader has not yet heard the six chapters of evidence that will be produced to support the first half of it.

quotations.text: Of what a strange nature is knowledge! It clings to the mind, when it has once seized on it, like a lichen on the rock.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: After the lessons given to Safie have taught him human history and property.
quotations.analysis: The creature reaches Victor’s subject from the opposite direction and comes to the opposite conclusion: knowledge is not something you go and get, it is something that will not let go of you. He chooses an image from the landscape he actually lives in, which is one of the quiet signs that his education has become his own rather than the De Laceys’.

quotations.text: Accursed creator! Why did you form a monster so hideous that even you turned from me in disgust?
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: Reading Victor’s own laboratory journal, found in the pocket of the clothes he took from the flat.
quotations.analysis: He has learned about his own making from the notes of the man who made him, which is the cruellest use of a document in a novel full of documents. The accusation is not that he was made, but that he was made and then looked at. Even you concedes that everyone else’s disgust was to be expected.

quotations.text: Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I live? Why, in that instant, did I not extinguish the spark of existence which you had so wantonly bestowed?
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: After the De Laceys abandon the cottage and he burns it down.
quotations.analysis: Spark of existence is Victor’s own phrase for what he infused, handed back with wantonly attached to it. This is the hinge of the creature’s narrative: the sentence before it he is grieving, and a few pages later he has met a child in the woods. Shelley puts the turn into a rhetorical question rather than a decision.

quotations.text: You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being. This you alone can do; and I demand it of you as a right which you must not refuse to concede.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: The demand that follows the whole of the creature’s narrative.
quotations.analysis: Six chapters of evidence have been building to the word right, and he uses the vocabulary of contract rather than mercy: demand, concede, must not refuse. Shelley’s father argued in Political Justice that obligations follow from what a being is capable of feeling, and the creature has just spent his narrative proving his capability.

quotations.text: I am malicious because I am miserable. Am I not shunned and hated by all mankind?
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: Replying to Victor’s refusal and threats on the Mer de Glace.
quotations.analysis: The causal because is the most contested word in the novel, and the creature puts it in the present tense rather than the past: not misery made me, but misery is making me, now, and can stop. The question that follows shifts the burden of proof onto everyone who has met him.

quotations.text: You are my creator, but I am your master;⁠—obey!
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: After Victor tears the half-finished female apart in the Orkney hut.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning stops here and does not resume. Six words reverse the relation the whole book has been built on, and the dash before obey marks the exact point at which the creature stops asking. Everything he does afterwards is designed to leave Victor alive and alone, which is the punishment he was given first.

quotations.text: Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: The creature’s last speech before he leaves the island.
quotations.analysis: He has worked out that he cannot be threatened with anything he has not already lost, and states it as a syllogism. Compare Victor, whose power rests entirely on secrets he is afraid to reveal: the two of them are being measured against each other by what they still have to protect.

quotations.text: It is well. I go; but remember, I shall be with you on your wedding night.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: Leaving the Orkneys after the destruction of his companion.
quotations.analysis: Victor reads this as a death sentence on himself and spends three chapters arranging his affairs accordingly. The creature has in fact announced with complete precision what he intends: to take from Victor exactly what Victor took from him, on the night it would be taken. The misreading is entirely Victor’s, and it is made of self-importance.

quotations.text: William, Justine, and Henry⁠—they all died by my hands.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: To his father, refusing the comfort offered after his acquittal in Ireland.
quotations.analysis: It is the one moment in Victor’s narrative where the grammar puts him in the accusative position he has been avoiding for twenty chapters. His father hears it as the raving of a sick man, which lets Victor keep the confession and lose nothing by it — and Elizabeth’s name is not yet on the list only because the wedding has not happened.

quotations.text: I, the miserable and the abandoned, am an abortion, to be spurned at, and kicked, and trampled on.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: Speaking to Walton over Victor’s body in the cabin.
quotations.analysis: He has adopted the vocabulary of the people who drove him off, and the three passive verbs pile up in the order a body would meet them. Shelley gives the creature the last full speech in the novel and lets him convict himself in language he did not invent, which leaves the reader to decide who taught it to him.

quotations.text: Farewell, Walton! Seek happiness in tranquillity, and avoid ambition, even if it be only the apparently innocent one of distinguishing yourself in science and discoveries.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Victor’s last words, on Walton’s ship.
quotations.analysis: This is as close as the novel comes to a moral, and Shelley immediately undercuts it: the next sentence has Victor asking why he should say such a thing, since another man might yet succeed. The warning and its withdrawal are in the same breath, and Walton is left holding both.

quotations.text: He was soon borne away by the waves, and lost in darkness and distance.
quotations.speaker: Robert Walton
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel, as the creature leaves the ship on an ice raft.
quotations.analysis: No body, no pyre and no confirmation: the creature announces his own death and the novel declines to show it. The final verb is passive and the last two nouns are abstractions, so the book closes on a failure of evidence — which is consistent, since every fact in it has reached us through someone else’s letter.

quotations.text: My father’s family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip. So, I called myself Pip, and came to be called Pip.
quotations.context: The opening sentences of the novel.
quotations.analysis: He names himself in the first line, which is the only act of self-creation in the book that works. Everything after this is somebody else's attempt to name him — Handel, my boy, sir, a gentleman — and the final clause, 'came to be called', already concedes that identity is something other people do to you.

quotations.text: My first most vivid and broad impression of the identity of things seems to me to have been gained on a memorable raw afternoon towards evening.
quotations.context: Introducing the churchyard on the marshes.
quotations.analysis: A child's first understanding of the world is dated to the afternoon a man threatened to cut his throat, and the phrase for it is legal and exact rather than emotional. 'The identity of things' is what the rest of the novel systematically takes away from him: nothing turns out to be what it was labelled.

quotations.text: “Hold your noise!” cried a terrible voice, as a man started up from among the graves at the side of the church porch. “Keep still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!”
quotations.speaker: Magwitch
quotations.context: The convict's first appearance, in the churchyard.
quotations.analysis: The man rises out of the family graves, which puts him structurally in the place of Pip's dead parents some four hundred pages before the plot gets there. He is also, at this moment, simply a voice — Dickens gives the sound before the body, so that the marshes seem to produce him.

quotations.text: “You get me a file.” He tilted me again. “And you get me wittles.” He tilted me again. “You bring ’em both to me.”
quotations.speaker: Magwitch
quotations.context: Giving Pip his instructions while holding him upside down.
quotations.analysis: The repeated stage direction between clauses turns a threat into a rhythm, and the two objects demanded — one to eat, one to cut iron — are the whole of what the man needs from the world. Both come back: the file resurfaces in a stranger's hand and then as the weapon used on Pip's sister.

quotations.text: “He calls the knaves Jacks, this boy!” said Estella with disdain, before our first game was out. “And what coarse hands he has! And what thick boots!”
quotations.speaker: Estella
quotations.context: Playing beggar my neighbour at Satis House.
quotations.analysis: Three sentences, three separate grounds of contempt: vocabulary, body and clothing. She never speaks to Pip in this scene, only about him, and the whole novel's machinery of shame is installed here with a card game and a piece of vocabulary Joe taught him.

quotations.text: I took the opportunity of being alone in the courtyard to look at my coarse hands and my common boots. My opinion of those accessories was not favorable. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me now, as vulgar appendages.
quotations.context: Alone in the yard at Satis House, immediately after the card game.
quotations.analysis: He has adopted her adjectives within a page, and the word 'accessories' shows the change happening in his vocabulary before it happens in his conduct. 'They had never troubled me before' is the older narrator marking the exact moment a happy childhood was converted into a grievance.

quotations.text: “There’s one thing you may be sure of, Pip,” said Joe, after some rumination, “namely, that lies is lies. Howsever they come, they didn’t ought to come, and they come from the father of lies, and work round to the same.
quotations.speaker: Joe Gargery
quotations.context: After Pip has invented a coach, a flag and black velvet to describe Satis House.
quotations.analysis: The grammar is wrong in every clause and the reasoning is unanswerable, which is Dickens's standing joke about Joe and also his argument. Joe then adds that Pip is uncommon already, in learning and in size — he refuses the whole category the boy has just started to judge himself by.

quotations.text: Pause you who read this, and think for a moment of the long chain of iron or gold, of thorns or flowers, that would never have bound you, but for the formation of the first link on one memorable day.
quotations.context: Closing the chapter on Pip's first visit to Satis House.
quotations.analysis: The narrator stops the story to address the reader directly, and reaches for a chain — the image already attached to leg-irons, and in Dickens's own earlier Christmas book to a dead man's punishment. Offering iron or gold, thorns or flowers, he declines to say which Pip's turned out to be.

quotations.text: Miss Havisham would embrace her with lavish fondness, murmuring something in her ear that sounded like “Break their hearts my pride and hope, break their hearts and have no mercy!”
quotations.speaker: Miss Havisham
quotations.context: Watching Estella after one of Pip's visits.
quotations.analysis: Pip reports it as something that 'sounded like' the words, so the most damning line in Estella's upbringing reaches the reader through a child who did not quite catch it. The endearments and the instruction are in the same breath: pride and hope are what she calls the girl she is training to be unable to love.

quotations.text: It is a most miserable thing to feel ashamed of home. There may be black ingratitude in the thing, and the punishment may be retributive and well deserved; but that it is a miserable thing, I can testify.
quotations.context: After a year in which the forge has come to look coarse and common to him.
quotations.analysis: The older narrator concedes the charge against the boy in full — ingratitude, deserved punishment — and then insists on the misery anyway, in the language of a witness box. It is the book's characteristic move: guilt admitted so completely that pity becomes possible.

quotations.text: “Mr. Pip,” he replied, with gravity, “Walworth is one place, and this office is another. Much as the Aged is one person, and Mr. Jaggers is another. They must not be confounded together.
quotations.speaker: Wemmick
quotations.context: Pip asks for advice in Little Britain that Wemmick has already given at Walworth.
quotations.analysis: He states as a rule of hygiene what the rest of the novel suffers as a problem: that the person you are at work and the person you are at home are not obliged to agree. Pip has spent the book trying to keep the forge and London apart and calling it shame; Wemmick does the same thing and calls it an address.

quotations.text: he would wash his hands, and wipe them and dry them all over this towel, whenever he came in from a police court or dismissed a client from his room
quotations.context: Describing the closet in Jaggers's room.
quotations.analysis: The ritual is Pilate's, performed several times a day by a man who never states an opinion about guilt. Dickens attaches the smell of the soap to him everywhere he goes, so that the reader is reminded of what is being washed off at exactly the moments Jaggers is at his most impressive.

quotations.text: “Love her, love her, love her! If she favors you, love her. If she wounds you, love her. If she tears your heart to pieces⁠—and as it gets older and stronger it will tear deeper⁠—love her, love her, love her!”
quotations.speaker: Miss Havisham
quotations.context: Holding Pip's head down to hers in the chair at Satis House.
quotations.analysis: Nine imperatives in three sentences, with the conditions arranged so that being hurt and being favoured produce the same instruction. She is not describing love but prescribing a wound, and Pip lies awake that night converting her command into a declaration of his own, which is the point at which the training takes.

quotations.text: “You must know,” said Estella, condescending to me as a brilliant and beautiful woman might, “that I have no heart⁠—if that has anything to do with my memory.”
quotations.speaker: Estella
quotations.context: Explaining to Pip why she does not remember what he remembers.
quotations.analysis: She is answering a question about memory, and the qualification at the end is the sharp part: she suspects that feeling and recollection are the same organ, and that she was denied both at once. Pip hears a coquette's line and misses the diagnosis.

quotations.text: I knew to my sorrow, often and often, if not always, that I loved her against reason, against promise, against peace, against hope, against happiness, against all discouragement that could be.
quotations.context: The narrator interrupting to describe what loving Estella was actually like.
quotations.analysis: Six repetitions of 'against', each one naming something a sensible man would have chosen instead, and the sentence never supplies a reason on the other side. This is the older Pip refusing the conventional account of love as a mistake to be explained, and admitting it as a fact he could not argue with.

quotations.text: “So,” said Estella, “I must be taken as I have been made. The success is not mine, the failure is not mine, but the two together make me.”
quotations.speaker: Estella
quotations.context: Answering Miss Havisham's complaint that she is cold to her.
quotations.analysis: The passive voice is exact and deliberate: she has been made, and she declines both the credit and the blame. It is also an answer to the whole Victorian plot of self-improvement that Pip is living out three streets away — one character is trying to make himself, and the other knows she was manufactured.

quotations.text: “Yes, Pip, dear boy, I’ve made a gentleman on you! It’s me wot has done it! I swore that time, sure as ever I earned a guinea, that guinea should go to you.
quotations.speaker: Magwitch
quotations.context: Revealing himself as Pip's benefactor in the rooms by the river.
quotations.analysis: The grammar Pip has spent three hundred pages learning to be ashamed of is the grammar that paid for the lessons. 'Made a gentleman on you' is a maker's claim over an object, and Pip's horror is not only at the source of the money but at being the thing that was made.

quotations.text: “Look’ee here, Pip. I’m your second father. You’re my son⁠—more to me nor any son. I’ve put away money, only for you to spend.
quotations.speaker: Magwitch
quotations.context: Continuing the revelation, in Pip's chambers at night.
quotations.analysis: He claims a relationship rather than a debt, and the claim is unanswerable because it is true — no one else has spent a life on Pip. 'Second father' also places him behind Joe in the queue, which is the one piece of accounting in the scene that Pip is in no position to dispute.

quotations.text: “Out of my thoughts! You are part of my existence, part of myself. You have been in every line I have ever read since I first came here, the rough common boy whose poor heart you wounded even then.
quotations.speaker: Pip
quotations.context: At Satis House, on learning that Estella will marry Bentley Drummle.
quotations.analysis: He describes her as an editorial presence in everything he has read, which for a man whose education was the whole point of his fortune is a devastating admission about what the education was for. He also calls himself the rough common boy in the same sentence, taking back Estella's word at the one moment he is speaking as an equal.

quotations.text: “O!” she cried, despairingly. “What have I done! What have I done!”
quotations.speaker: Miss Havisham
quotations.context: After Pip's account of his feelings for Estella has shown her what she made.
quotations.analysis: The question repeats twenty and fifty times in a page, and the novel says she never changed the order of the three sentences she was left with by the end. She had asked Pip to forgive her in writing, under her name — the whole scene is a woman trying to get a sentence exactly right, having spent twenty-five years refusing to finish one.

quotations.text: I thought of the two men who went up into the Temple to pray, and I knew there were no better words that I could say beside his bed, than “O Lord, be merciful to him a sinner!”
quotations.context: At Magwitch's death in the prison infirmary.
quotations.analysis: Pip has just told a dying man that his daughter is alive, a lady and loved — the only lie in the novel that costs nobody anything. The prayer he then chooses is the publican's rather than the Pharisee's, which quietly settles the question of who in this book has been standing at the front of the temple.

quotations.text: “Lookee here, old chap,” said Joe, bending over me. “Ever the best of friends; ain’t us, Pip?”
quotations.speaker: Joe Gargery
quotations.context: Nursing Pip through the fever, having paid his debts.
quotations.analysis: The same sentence he used in Chapter 7 to comfort a crying child, produced again fifty chapters later without a word of reproach in between. Joe's vocabulary has not moved at all while Pip's has been expensively remade, and the novel's judgement is contained in which of the two turns out to have needed changing.

quotations.text: I have been bent and broken, but⁠—I hope⁠—into a better shape.
quotations.speaker: Estella
quotations.context: In the ruined garden of Satis House, eleven years later.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor belongs to the forge: iron is bent and broken into shape by heat and hammering, and the woman raised in a brewer's house finishes the novel speaking Joe's trade. The hesitation marked by the dashes is the only uncertainty she has ever expressed.

quotations.text: as the morning mists had risen long ago when I first left the forge, so the evening mists were rising now, and in all the broad expanse of tranquil light they showed to me, I saw no shadow of another parting from her.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel, as published.
quotations.analysis: The sentence closes a loop opened in Chapter 19, where mists rose as Pip walked away from the forge towards London. What it does not do is say they marry: 'no shadow of another parting' is a negative, seen in mist, by a narrator who has been wrong about every prospect he has ever surveyed.

quotations.text: I do, in the next place, complain of my own great want of judgment, in being prevailed upon by the entreaties and false reasoning of you and some others, very much against my own opinion, to suffer my travels to be published.
quotations.reference: A Letter from Captain Gulliver to His Cousin Sympson
quotations.context: The prefatory letter added for Faulkner’s edition, written years after the voyages.
quotations.analysis: The book opens by regretting its own publication. Swift builds a paratext that quarrels with itself — a publisher vouching for the text, an author disowning it — so that a reader who wants to know what is authoritative here has nowhere to stand before the first voyage begins.

quotations.text: they shouted for joy, and danced upon my breast, repeating several times as they did at first, “Hekinah degul.”
quotations.context: After Gulliver has drunk two hogsheads of Lilliputian wine while pegged to the ground.
quotations.analysis: The foreign words are left untranslated, so the reader is put exactly where Gulliver is: watching a ceremony and guessing at its meaning. Swift also gets the scale into the verb — they dance on his chest — which makes the wonder physical before it is political.

quotations.text: we conjecture it is either some unknown animal, or the god that he worships; but we are more inclined to the latter opinion
quotations.context: From the official inventory two Lilliputian officers make of Gulliver’s pockets.
quotations.analysis: The officers reason correctly from what they can observe: the object is consulted before every action, so it governs him. Swift’s joke about a nation that worships the clock is delivered entirely inside a customs document, and the form of the passage — a numbered search of a man’s body — is as pointed as its content.

quotations.text: It is allowed on all hands, that the primitive way of breaking eggs, before we eat them, was upon the larger end
quotations.context: Reldresal explaining the origin of the war with Blefuscu.
quotations.analysis: The phrase ‘allowed on all hands’ is the vocabulary of settled doctrine applied to breakfast. Swift then supplies casualty figures — eleven thousand deaths rather than submit — so the scene works by keeping the cause trivial while the consequences stay at full historical size.

quotations.text: his majesty has determined to make use only of low heels in the administration of the government
quotations.context: The same conversation, on the two parties of the empire.
quotations.analysis: Party is reduced to footwear and the reduction changes nothing about how the politics behaves: patronage follows the heel height, and the heir hedges by wearing one of each and walking with a hobble. The satire is not that the difference is small but that a small difference is enough.

quotations.text: They look upon fraud as a greater crime than theft, and therefore seldom fail to punish it with death
quotations.context: Gulliver’s account of Lilliputian laws, which he reports with approval.
quotations.analysis: This chapter is the one place where Lilliput is used as a model rather than a joke, and the reasoning given is commercial: honesty has no defence against fraud, so credit collapses without it. Swift puts his own convictions into the mouth of a ridiculous state, which stops the book being read as simple contempt.

quotations.text: I cannot but conclude the bulk of your natives to be the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth.”
quotations.context: The king’s conclusion after several audiences on the history and constitution of England.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built to sound judicial: he has recapitulated, compared question with answer, and only then delivers. Swift makes the verdict physically intimate — the king is stroking Gulliver as he says it — so that contempt and gentleness arrive in the same gesture.

quotations.text: The king was struck with horror at the description I had given of those terrible engines, and the proposal I had made.
quotations.context: After Gulliver has offered the king the secret of gunpowder as a proof of his usefulness.
quotations.analysis: The reversal is complete and Gulliver misses it entirely: he files the refusal under the king’s narrow principles and nice scruples. Swift lets the reader hold two readings of the same scene at once, and the gap between them is where the satire lives.

quotations.text: whoever could make two ears of corn, or two blades of grass, to grow upon a spot of ground where only one grew before, would deserve better of mankind, and do more essential service to his country, than the whole race of politicians put together.”
quotations.context: Gulliver reporting the king’s opinion of what constitutes useful knowledge.
quotations.analysis: The standard offered here is the one the whole book measures learning against, and it is agricultural rather than philosophical: does it feed anybody? Part III is built to fail this test, which is why the Academy of Lagado is placed a hundred pages after this sentence rather than before it.

quotations.text: he proceeds to the last remedy, by letting the island drop directly upon their heads, which makes a universal destruction both of houses and men.
quotations.context: The means by which the king of Laputa suppresses a rebellious town below.
quotations.analysis: The flying island is a machine for occupation: it blocks the sun and rain first, and only crushes as a last resort. Swift gives the tactic a bureaucratic sequence of escalating measures, and the chapter then explains why the king hesitates — his own estates are down there, and the island’s bottom might crack.

quotations.text: He has been eight years upon a project for extracting sunbeams out of cucumbers, which were to be put in phials hermetically sealed, and let out to warm the air in raw inclement summers.
quotations.context: The first projector Gulliver meets in the grand academy of Lagado.
quotations.analysis: The project is not absurd in principle — it is a scheme to store summer heat — and that is what makes it dangerous: the man is eight years in and asking for funds. Swift attacks not curiosity but the institution that pays for eight years of it while the country outside has stopped growing food.

quotations.text: Perjury, oppression, subornation, fraud, pandarism, and the like infirmities, were among the most excusable arts they had to mention; and for these I gave, as it was reasonable, great allowance.
quotations.context: In Glubbdubdrib, where the governor can summon the dead and question them.
quotations.analysis: The list is arranged as a descent and then stopped short, so the reader waits for what could possibly be worse. Swift’s device here is historiographical rather than fantastic: the dead are called up not for spectacle but to correct the record that the living have written about them.

quotations.text: “Happy nation, where every child hath at least a chance for being immortal! Happy people, who enjoy so many living examples of ancient virtue, and have masters ready to instruct them in the wisdom of all former ages!
quotations.context: Gulliver’s reaction on first hearing that some Luggnaggians never die, before he has met one.
quotations.analysis: Swift makes him deliver the whole eloquent programme — wealth, learning, a record of the ages — and only then takes him to see the Struldbrugs. The chapter separates two things the wish for immortality usually keeps welded together, and Gulliver has already committed himself in public before the distinction arrives.

quotations.text: They were the most mortifying sight I ever beheld; and the women more horrible than the men.
quotations.context: Meeting five or six Struldbrugs of various ages at Luggnagg.
quotations.analysis: The correction is flat and brief after the rapture, and the second clause — that the women are worse — is the period’s ordinary misogyny surfacing in a passage about the horror of not dying. Swift’s satire and Swift’s prejudices are in the same sentence, and an honest reading has to hold both.

quotations.text: “that the use of speech was to make us understand one another, and to receive information of facts; now, if anyone said the thing which was not, these ends were defeated, because I cannot properly be said to understand him
quotations.context: The Houyhnhnm master working out what Gulliver can mean by a lie.
quotations.analysis: The argument is a definition rather than a moral: if speech exists to convey facts, a false sentence is not wicked but void, and leaves the hearer worse informed than silence. It takes the master some difficulty to grasp the concept at all, and Gulliver needs it before he can explain a single English institution.

quotations.text: in recounting the numbers of those who have been killed in battle, I cannot but think you have said the thing which is not.”
quotations.context: The master’s response to Gulliver’s account of European wars and their casualties.
quotations.analysis: The Houyhnhnm phrase for lying is used, for once, against Gulliver, and it is used because the truth is too large to be credible. Swift gets the sharpest effect available to satire here: the honest report of Europe is indistinguishable, to a reasonable listener, from an invention.

quotations.text: I enjoyed perfect health of body, and tranquillity of mind; I did not feel the treachery or inconstancy of a friend, nor the injuries of a secret or open enemy.
quotations.context: Gulliver’s account of his settled life among the Houyhnhnms.
quotations.analysis: The happiness is described entirely by subtraction — no treachery, no enemy, no bribes, no informers — so the paragraph is a catalogue of England with the sign reversed. He is at his most contented exactly where he has nobody of his own kind to be content with.

quotations.text: wherein I have not been so studious of ornament as of truth.
quotations.context: The opening of the last chapter, addressed to the reader.
quotations.analysis: The claim to plainness is the oldest guarantee in travel writing and Swift has spent four voyages making it worthless. Gulliver closes the account with the same promise Sympson opened it with, and by now the reader has seen what his plain reporting can be made to carry.

quotations.text: principal design was to inform, and not to amuse thee.
quotations.context: The same paragraph, on his purpose in publishing.
quotations.analysis: Six words that a great many readers have ignored for three centuries, since the book’s afterlife has been mostly in nurseries. Set beside the letter to Sympson, where Gulliver complains that nobody has reformed in six months, the sentence is already an admission of failure.

quotations.text: when I behold a lump of deformity and diseases, both in body and mind, smitten with pride, it immediately breaks all the measures of my patience
quotations.context: The final paragraph of the book, on what he can and cannot tolerate in his own species.
quotations.analysis: He will forgive humanity its natural vices and not its pride, which is precisely the vice he is displaying while he says so, and Swift has him admit as much a few lines earlier. The book ends by catching its narrator in the fault the book exists to attack.

quotations.text: Seems, madam! nay it is; I know not 'seems.'
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: His first extended speech, answering Gertrude's question about why his grief looks so particular.
quotations.analysis: He objects to a verb, which tells you what kind of hero this is going to be. The irony is scheduled three scenes later, when he decides to put on an appearance deliberately, and the play never lets him have the word back.

quotations.text: O, that this too too solid flesh would melt Thaw and resolve itself into a dew!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The first soliloquy, immediately after the court has left the stage.
quotations.analysis: Three verbs of dissolving in a row, each one weaker than the last, so the wish loses force as it is spoken. Nothing here is about revenge or a ghost: the speech happens before he knows anything, which means the despair is prior to the plot rather than caused by it.

quotations.text: Frailty, thy name is woman!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: In the same soliloquy, on his mother's remarriage.
quotations.analysis: He generalises from one woman to half the species in five words, and the grammar does the work: an abstract noun is addressed directly, then given a name. The line is quoted as if it were the play's verdict, but it is spoken by a man who has just told us he cannot bear to think about it.

quotations.text: This above all: to thine ownself be true, And it must follow, as the night the day, Thou canst not then be false to any man.
quotations.speaker: Lord Polonius
quotations.context: The end of a long farewell lecture to Laertes, who is trying to catch a ship.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted piece of wisdom in the play belongs to its most tiresome speaker, and he contradicts it within a scene by sending Reynaldo to lie about Laertes abroad. Read in context it is advice about self-interest rather than integrity, which is why the court repeats it and nobody follows it.

quotations.text: Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
quotations.speaker: Marcellus
quotations.context: Watching Hamlet follow the Ghost away along the platform.
quotations.analysis: It is given to a minor soldier, not to the prince, which matters: the corruption is visible from the guard post before anyone at court admits it. 'Something' is doing a great deal of work — nobody on stage yet knows what, and the audience has not been told either.

quotations.text: My tables,--meet it is I set it down, That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain;
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Alone, minutes after the Ghost has gone.
quotations.analysis: He has just been told his uncle is a murderer and his response is to reach for a notebook. Writing it down converts unbearable testimony into a manageable proposition, and the stage direction that follows — he actually writes — makes the intellectual habit physical.

quotations.text: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, Than are dreamt of in your philosophy.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Horatio, who has just been asked to swear on the sword while the Ghost calls from under the stage.
quotations.analysis: It is usually quoted as mysticism; in position it is an argument with a sceptic who has already seen the ghost and is still reasoning. Note the address: Hamlet uses his friend's name to make the rebuke personal, and the line's authority depends on a spirit shouting from beneath the floorboards.

quotations.text: How strange or odd soe'er I bear myself, As I perchance hereafter shall think meet To put an antic disposition on,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Swearing his friends to secrecy about anything they may see him do.
quotations.analysis: The madness is announced in advance, under oath, as a wardrobe decision — 'put on' is the verb used for clothes. That advance notice is what keeps the question alive for four acts: everything strange Hamlet does afterwards has been pre-authorised, so nothing he does can settle the matter.

quotations.text: Though this be madness, yet there is method in 't.
quotations.speaker: Lord Polonius
quotations.context: An aside during the conversation about words, words, words.
quotations.analysis: Polonius is right and cannot use it. He detects the design under the nonsense and then draws the wrong conclusion about what the design is for, which is the court's characteristic failure: good observation, bad inference. The line is spoken aside, so the audience is invited to grade his reading against theirs.

quotations.text: Denmark's a prison.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, moments after working out that they were sent for.
quotations.analysis: Three words of prose, offered as a flat statement of fact to two men who have just been hired as warders without quite realising it. The exchange that follows turns it into a philosophical game about thinking making it so, which is exactly how Hamlet avoids being pinned down by people fishing for symptoms.

quotations.text: What a piece of work is a man! how noble in reason! how infinite in faculty!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Explaining to the schoolfellows why he has lost all his mirth.
quotations.analysis: A textbook humanist celebration of mankind, delivered in prose to two informers, and finished a few lines later with dust. He is performing an orthodoxy in order to demonstrate that he no longer holds it — the praise is a set-up for the dismissal.

quotations.text: O, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Alone after the First Player's speech about Hecuba.
quotations.analysis: The trigger is not the murder but a professional actor crying about a woman dead for centuries. Hamlet's self-disgust is comparative and aesthetic: somebody else produced a convincing performance of grief and he has not, which is a strange thing to punish yourself for and a precise clue to what he thinks feeling is.

quotations.text: the play 's the thing Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The couplet that ends Act II, having just admitted the Ghost may be a devil.
quotations.analysis: It is the only plan in the play arrived at by argument, and it is a piece of experimental design: a stimulus, a subject, an observer. The rhyme gives it the confidence of a conclusion, and the flaw is buried in the verb — a conscience caught is a reaction, not a confession.

quotations.text: To be, or not to be, that is the question, Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, Or to take arms against a sea of troubles, And by opposing end them?
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Spoken while Claudius and Polonius are hidden, having placed Ophelia in his path.
quotations.analysis: The speech contains no first-person pronoun and names nobody: it is written as a general problem in ethics, not a private confession. That is worth noticing because two men are listening for symptoms and hear philosophy instead — the most intimate speech in the play is also the most carefully depersonalised.

quotations.text: Thus conscience does make cowards of us all; And thus the native hue of resolution Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The close of the same soliloquy, before he sees Ophelia.
quotations.analysis: 'Conscience' here means consciousness as much as moral scruple, and the metaphor is a complexion: thought spreads over resolve like an illness over a face. It is the play's own diagnosis of its hero, offered by the hero, which is one reason the diagnosis has never quite been improved on.

quotations.text: O, what a noble mind is here o'erthrown!
quotations.speaker: Ophelia
quotations.context: Alone on stage after Hamlet's exit, before the watchers come out.
quotations.analysis: She is the only character who mourns Hamlet as a loss rather than assessing him as a problem, and she does it in a formal lament built from three-part lists — eye, tongue, sword. The speech also establishes what he was like before the play began, information the audience has no other way of getting.

quotations.text: The lady protests too much, methinks.
quotations.speaker: Queen Gertrude
quotations.context: Watching the Player Queen swear she will never remarry.
quotations.analysis: Asked to judge a play about a widow's promise, Gertrude gives a critic's verdict on the acting rather than a wife's answer to the charge. Whether that is composure or blindness is the closest the play comes to telling us what she knows, and it declines to decide.

quotations.text: O, my offence is rank it smells to heaven;
quotations.speaker: King Claudius
quotations.context: Alone, trying to pray, immediately after the play has broken up.
quotations.analysis: This is the moment the audience stops needing the Ghost: the confession comes from the murderer, unprompted, with nobody listening. Shakespeare gives the proof to the theatre and withholds it from Hamlet, who walks in forty lines later and sees only a man at his devotions.

quotations.text: My words fly up, my thoughts remain below: Words without thoughts never to heaven go.
quotations.speaker: King Claudius
quotations.context: Rising from his knees, seconds after Hamlet has left without killing him.
quotations.analysis: The couplet is a joke at Hamlet's expense that Hamlet never hears: he spared a man whose prayer was not working. The chiastic arrangement of words and thoughts — up, below, words, thoughts — makes the failure sound like a law of physics rather than a moral judgement.

quotations.text: How all occasions do inform against me, And spur my dull revenge!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: On a plain in Denmark, watching Fortinbras's army march towards Poland.
quotations.analysis: 'Inform against' is legal language for turning informer, so Hamlet describes the world as a witness giving evidence against him. It is his last soliloquy, and the resolution it reaches is immediately undercut by the fact that he is being escorted onto a ship to England as he speaks it.

quotations.text: Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio: a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent fancy:
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: In the churchyard, holding a skull the gravedigger has identified.
quotations.analysis: It is the first death in the play he can speak about without a theory, and the reason is that he has a name and a memory to attach to the bone. The scene is in prose, and the joking goes on around him: the play's most affecting moment about mortality is set in a workplace where corpses are routine.

quotations.text: There's a divinity that shapes our ends, Rough-hew them how we will,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Telling Horatio how he found and rewrote the sealed commission on board ship.
quotations.analysis: He credits providence in the middle of an account of his own forgery, seal and all. The Hamlet of Act V explains his actions after he has taken them rather than before, and the change in tense is the change in the man: less deliberation, more report.

quotations.text: the readiness is all: since no man has aught of what he leaves, what is't to leave betimes?
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Horatio, who has offered to call off the fencing match.
quotations.analysis: Set this against 'To be, or not to be': the same question about dying, answered now in prose, in one sentence, with no metaphors. He has stopped arguing, and the calm is not peace but a kind of exhaustion that the plot immediately exploits.

quotations.text: Which have solicited. The rest is silence.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Dying, having given his vote for the succession and told Horatio to report the circumstances.
quotations.analysis: His last act is administrative: a vote, a request for an accurate account, and then nothing. 'The rest' means both what remains to be said and what remains of him, and the man who could not stop talking hands the talking over and stops.

themes.name: Legitimacy and the cost of a crown

quotations.text: So shaken as we are, so wan with care, Find we a time for frighted peace to pant, And breathe short-winded accents of new broils To be commenced in strands afar remote.
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: The opening lines of the play, announcing a crusade to Jerusalem.
quotations.analysis: The kingdom is described as a body out of breath, and the sentence itself is short-winded, breaking into clauses that never quite reach the main proposal. By the end of the scene the crusade has been cancelled, so the play's first policy is abandoned inside fifty lines.

quotations.text: I know you all, and will awhile uphold The unyoked humour of your idleness: Yet herein will I imitate the sun, Who doth permit the base contagious clouds To smother up his beauty from the world,
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Alone, immediately after agreeing to the Gadshill robbery.
quotations.analysis: The tense does the damage: 'will uphold' means he is choosing to keep company he has already judged. Placing this soliloquy in the first tavern scene means an audience watches every later joke knowing it is being kept for a purpose, which is why the play can be very funny and never quite comfortable.

quotations.text: If all the year were playing holidays, To sport would be as tedious as to work; But when they seldom come, they wish'd for come, And nothing pleaseth but rare accidents.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: The middle of the same soliloquy.
quotations.analysis: Pleasure is explained as a matter of scarcity management, which is the theory of kingship his father will set out in 3.2 applied to a tavern. The couplet-like balance of 'playing holidays' against 'work' also quietly concedes that Hal finds Eastcheap laborious, which nothing in his behaviour there suggests.

quotations.text: So honour cross it from the north to south, And let them grapple: O, the blood more stirs To rouse a lion than to start a hare!
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Interrupting his uncle's careful explanation of the conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: Worcester is trying to lay out a plan and Hotspur answers with hunting. The two animals are the whole of his politics: he cannot imagine an opponent worth less than a lion, and the play will kill him partly because he refuses to notice the hares around him — an absent father, an unarrived ally.

quotations.text: By heaven, methinks it were an easy leap, To pluck bright honour from the pale-faced moon, Or dive into the bottom of the deep, Where fathom-line could never touch the ground, And pluck up drowned honour by the locks;
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Still ignoring Worcester, in the same speech.
quotations.analysis: Honour is treated as an object with a physical location, and both locations are unreachable by design — the moon and a depth past any sounding line. Dragging a drowned thing up by the hair is a grim image for a young man's ideal, and it is the closest the play comes to predicting how he will look at Shrewsbury.

quotations.text: A plague of all cowards, I say, and a vengeance too! marry, and amen! Give me a cup of sack, boy.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Arriving at the Boar's-Head after running away at Gadshill.
quotations.analysis: He comes through the door with an accusation already in flight, which is the technique of his whole defence: attack first and let the details arrive later. The order for sack in the same breath sets the rhythm of the scene — moral outrage and refreshment, alternating, for three hundred lines.

quotations.text: O monstrous! eleven buckram men grown out of two!
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Keeping count while Falstaff describes the robbery.
quotations.analysis: Hal supplies the arithmetic the audience has been doing silently, which is why the line always gets its laugh. It also shows the pattern of their friendship: Falstaff invents and Hal audits, and every one of their scenes ends with the accounts being read back to him.

quotations.text: banish plump Jack, and banish all the world.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Playing Hal in the improvised interview, pleading his own case in the prince's voice.
quotations.analysis: He has manoeuvred himself into speaking the prince's lines so that the plea for his own life comes out of Hal's mouth by proxy. 'All the world' is not vanity but an accurate description of what the tavern scenes contain — carriers, drawers, hostesses, thieves — none of which survives into the reign that follows.

quotations.text: I do, I will.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Answering, in the king's part, Falstaff's plea not to be banished.
quotations.analysis: Four words, two tenses, and the whole of Part 2 in the second one. The present tense keeps it inside the game, the future steps outside it, and the knocking at the door arrives immediately afterwards so that nobody on stage has to decide which he meant.

quotations.text: Why, so can I, or so can any man; But will they come when you do call for them?
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Answering Glendower's claim that he can call spirits from the vasty deep.
quotations.analysis: The reply does not deny magic; it asks for evidence of attendance, which is a joke about rebellion as much as about sorcery. The two men are at this moment allies who have between them neither Northumberland's army nor Glendower's, so the question lands on the alliance itself.

quotations.text: O, while you live, tell truth and shame the devil!
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Ending the argument with Glendower over the map at Bangor.
quotations.analysis: It is a proverb, delivered as if newly minted, by a man who cannot hear a boast without correcting it. The line is worth setting beside Falstaff at the Boar's-Head: this play's two most attractive characters are the one who cannot stop lying and the one who cannot stop calling it out.

quotations.text: Had I so lavish of my presence been, So common-hackney'd in the eyes of men, So stale and cheap to vulgar company, Opinion, that did help me to the crown, Had still kept loyal to possession
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: Lecturing Hal on why Richard II lost the throne.
quotations.analysis: The king's theory of power is entirely about supply: appear rarely and you are valued, appear often and you are spent. He also lets slip the true basis of his title in a single word — 'Opinion' helped him to the crown, not God or law — which is the most honest sentence he speaks in either part.

quotations.text: Percy is but my factor, good my lord, To engross up glorious deeds on my behalf; And I will call him to so strict account, That he shall render every glory up,
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Promising his father that he will take Hotspur's reputation.
quotations.analysis: A factor is an agent who buys goods for someone else, so Hal casts his rival as an employee who has been accumulating stock on his account. Honour is not fought for here but audited, and the vocabulary is the tavern's — reckonings, accounts, rendering up — applied to a battlefield.

quotations.text: The land is burning; Percy stands on high; And either we or they must lower lie.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: The last words of the tavern scene in Act III, spoken to Falstaff before leaving for the wars.
quotations.analysis: Hal drops into rhyme to exit, and Falstaff's first response is to call it rare words and order breakfast. The couplet marks the point where the prince starts speaking in the register of the campaign and the knight declines to follow him into it.

quotations.text: Tut, tut; good enough to toss; food for powder, food for powder; they'll fill a pit as well as better: tush, man, mortal men, mortal men.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Westmoreland has just remarked how wretched Falstaff's recruits look.
quotations.analysis: The repetitions are the sound of a man who has already settled the question and is now only soothing an objection. He has taken bribes from the men who could pay and marched the ones who could not, and 'mortal men' converts an admission of fraud into a piece of philosophy about death in general.

quotations.text: The Prince of Wales doth join with all the world In praise of Henry Percy: by my hopes, This present enterprise set off his head, I do not think a braver gentleman, More active-valiant or more valiant-young, More daring or more bold, is now alive
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Offering, before the king and the rebel envoy, to fight Hotspur in single combat.
quotations.analysis: The praise is public, generous and tactically perfect: it makes the challenge impossible to refuse without loss. Vernon repeats it to Hotspur in the next act, and the report of it moves Hotspur more than the pardon that Worcester has just suppressed.

quotations.text: Why, thou owest God a death.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Falstaff has just asked Hal to stand over him if he falls in the battle.
quotations.analysis: The commonplace is delivered as a piece of bookkeeping — a death is a debt, and debts are what this friendship runs on. Falstaff's reply, that it is not due yet and he would be loath to pay before the day, turns mortality into a bill he intends to dispute, and leads straight into the catechism on honour.

quotations.text: Honour hath no skill in surgery, then? no. What is honour? a word. What is in that word honour? what is that honour? air. A trim reckoning! Who hath it? he that died o' Wednesday.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Alone on stage before the battle, in the speech he calls his catechism.
quotations.analysis: He conducts it as a catechism, question and answer, which is the form used to teach children the articles of faith — so the demolition of honour is carried out in the shape of a lesson in belief. 'He that died o' Wednesday' gives the abstraction a day of the week, and that is what finishes it off.

quotations.text: O gentlemen, the time of life is short!
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: His last speech to his men before the charge at Shrewsbury.
quotations.analysis: It is the only moment where Hotspur sounds as if he has understood something rather than merely felt it, and it arrives twenty lines after Worcester has withheld the pardon that would have made the charge unnecessary. The play lets him have his finest line on the strength of a lie he does not know he has been told.

quotations.text: Two stars keep not their motion in one sphere; Nor can one England brook a double reign, Of Harry Percy and the Prince of Wales.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Meeting Hotspur face to face for the first and only time.
quotations.analysis: They have never shared a scene until this moment, and the play has been arranging the comparison for four acts without letting them meet. The astronomy is courteous — two stars, not a star and a candle — and the shared first name in the last line makes the duel look briefly like a man fighting himself.

quotations.text: But thought's the slave of life, and life time's fool; And time, that takes survey of all the world, Must have a stop. O, I could prophesy, But that the earthy and cold hand of death Lies on my tongue: no, Percy, thou art dust And food for--
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Dying at Hal's feet on the field at Shrewsbury.
quotations.analysis: The man who could not finish listening to anybody now cannot finish his own sentence, and Hal completes it for him with the word 'worms'. Having spent the play chasing a future, he dies mid-prophecy, and the broken line is the most eloquent piece of punctuation in the play.

quotations.text: The better part of valour is discretion; in the which better part I have saved my life.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Getting up off the battlefield after playing dead to escape Douglas.
quotations.analysis: The proverb is normally the other way round, and reversing it turns a maxim about courage into a defence of cowardice without changing a word's meaning. It follows a short argument that a corpse is the counterfeit and a living man who fakes death is the true image of life, which is as close to a philosophy as he ever gets.

quotations.text: No, that's certain; I am not a double man: but if I be not Jack Falstaff, then am I a Jack. There is Percy:
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Carrying Hotspur's body on his back, in front of a prince who saw him lying dead.
quotations.analysis: 'Double' means both a phantom and a man carrying a second body, so the denial is also a description of what the audience is looking at. Hal lets the claim stand and offers to gild the lie, which tells us more about the prince's politics than about his affection.

quotations.text: O for a Muse of fire, that would ascend The brightest heaven of invention, A kingdom for a stage, princes to act And monarchs to behold the swelling scene!
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The opening lines of the play.
quotations.analysis: The play begins by wishing it were a different play, performed by actual kings in an actual kingdom. 'A kingdom for a stage' reverses Richard III's famous bargain, and the wish is impossible by design: everything the Chorus asks for is precisely what the theatre cannot supply, which is how the audience gets recruited.

quotations.text: can this cockpit hold The vasty fields of France? or may we cram Within this wooden O the very casques That did affright the air at Agincourt?
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Prologue, apologising for the theatre.
quotations.analysis: The question is rhetorical and the answer is no, which is the point: the play will do it anyway, and the audience will have agreed to let it. 'Wooden O' describes the playhouse the first spectators were standing in, and the word for helmets, casques, is doing the work of an entire army.

quotations.text: And let us, ciphers to this great accompt, On your imaginary forces work.
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: Asking the audience to supply what the stage cannot.
quotations.analysis: A cipher is a zero, worth nothing alone and everything in the right column, and the actors are cheerfully calling themselves nothings. 'Forces' is the play's first use of a military word, and it is applied to the audience — the invasion of France begins with the people watching being conscripted.

quotations.text: May I with right and conscience make this claim?
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: After Canterbury's long genealogical argument for the French crown.
quotations.analysis: It is the right question, asked of the one man in England with a financial interest in the answer. Canterbury does not say yes: he says 'The sin upon my head, dread sovereign', which offers to take the blame rather than to remove it — and Henry accepts the offer without pressing further.

quotations.text: for many a thousand widows Shall this his mock mock out of their dear husbands; Mock mothers from their sons, mock castles down;
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: Replying to the Dauphin's present of tennis balls.
quotations.analysis: He is answering an insult, and he answers it by itemising the dead in advance: widows, then mothers, then buildings, in descending order of grief. 'Mock' is used five times in three lines, so a joke about tennis turns into the word for the whole war — and the responsibility is carefully assigned to the man who made the joke.

quotations.text: for his nose was as sharp as a pen, and a' babbled of green fields.
quotations.speaker: Hostess
quotations.context: Describing Falstaff's death to Pistol, Bardolph and Nym.
quotations.analysis: The greatest comic character in English drama dies offstage, between scenes, in a hostess's muddled prose, and is given one unforgettable image by a woman who is not trying to be eloquent. Eastcheap is being closed down: within forty lines the survivors are on their way to France to steal what they can.

quotations.text: Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more; Or close the wall up with our English dead.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: At Harfleur, rallying an assault that has already failed once.
