quotations.analysis: Turn sonnet, as a man might turn Turk or turn soldier: love converts him into a literary form. Armado gets there three acts before the lords do, and his letter to Jaquenetta arrives in the Princess’s hands in Act IV while Berowne’s reaches a schoolmaster. The subplot is not imitating the main plot; it is ahead of it.

quotations.text: Beauty is bought by judgement of the eye, Not uttered by base sale of chapmen’s tongues.
quotations.speaker: Princess of France
quotations.context: Her first speech, cutting off Boyet’s compliment.
quotations.analysis: She refuses the currency the play runs on before she has been on stage twenty lines, and she does it in the language of trade: beauty is not stock to be talked up by a pedlar. Everything the men do afterwards, from sonnets to the Muscovite masque, is base sale of chapmen’s tongues, and she has already declined to buy.

quotations.text: ’Tis deadly sin to keep that oath, my lord, And sin to break it.
quotations.speaker: Princess of France
quotations.context: Standing outside the gates, told she cannot come in because of the vow.
quotations.analysis: She puts the men in a position they never work out of: the oath is wrong either way, so nothing they do about it can be virtuous. Berowne spends a hundred lines in Act IV arguing that breaking it is a religious duty, which is only half of what she said here, and she never grants him the other half.

quotations.text: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?
quotations.speaker: Rosaline
quotations.context: Answering Berowne, who has just asked her the same question word for word.
quotations.analysis: She gives him his own sentence back unaltered, and it is the first thing she says to him. The tactic sets the pattern for every exchange they have: he supplies the material and she returns it with the ownership changed. It also tells the audience they have met before, so the courtship the men think they are starting is already several years old.

quotations.text: Why, all his behaviours did make their retire To the court of his eye, peeping thorough desire.
quotations.speaker: Boyet
quotations.context: Telling the Princess that Navarre has fallen for her.
quotations.analysis: Boyet reads a face the way the lords read books, and he is right. The pun on court does the work: the King’s whole household has withdrawn into one organ, so the academy has already shrunk to the size of a man looking at a woman. Berowne will build his Act IV defence of love out of eyes, and Boyet has got there first.

quotations.text: “Remuneration”! O, that’s the Latin word for three farthings.
quotations.speaker: Costard
quotations.context: Alone, after Armado has paid him for carrying a letter.
quotations.analysis: He works out the exchange rate of a word by what it bought, which is the only honest method anyone in the play uses. Berowne pays him a guerdon eighty lines later and Costard prices that too, at elevenpence farthing better. Set beside Holofernes hoarding Latin for its own sake, the countryman’s accounting looks like the sane position.

quotations.text: This wimpled, whining, purblind, wayward boy, This Signior Junior, giant-dwarf, Dan Cupid
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: Alone, admitting he is in love and furious about it.
quotations.analysis: Four adjectives and then a title that contradicts itself twice over, junior and signior, giant and dwarf. Berowne abuses Cupid in the most elaborate style he has, which is the joke: the man complaining about love-rhymes is composing one. The speech ends with him agreeing to love, write, sigh, pray, sue and groan, in that order.

quotations.text: Glory grows guilty of detested crimes, When, for fame’s sake, for praise, an outward part, We bend to that the working of the heart
quotations.speaker: Princess of France
quotations.context: About to shoot a deer she does not want to kill.
quotations.analysis: She is describing herself: she will shoot for the credit of shooting well. The lines put a name to what the King did in the play’s first speech, hunting fame and bending the heart to it, and they come from the only character who admits to doing it. Four scenes later the deer is dead and Holofernes has written a poem about it.

quotations.text: The preyful Princess pierced and pricked a pretty pleasing pricket
quotations.speaker: Holofernes
quotations.context: Improvising an epitaph on the deer for Sir Nathaniel.
quotations.analysis: Six words beginning with p, which Holofernes calls affecting the letter and says argues facility. It is a complete school exercise, executed correctly and for nothing. He follows it with a poem that gets fifty sores out of one by adding the letter L, and he is genuinely pleased. The scene is funny and also the clearest picture in the play of learning with no object.

quotations.text: From women’s eyes this doctrine I derive. They sparkle still the right Promethean fire; They are the books, the arts, the academes, That show, contain, and nourish, all the world
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: All four men are now exposed, and Berowne has been asked to prove their loving lawful.
quotations.analysis: The academy is not abandoned but relocated, with women installed where the library used to be. It is a magnificent argument and it keeps the men exactly where they started, treating women as the means to something else. The Princess answers it in Act V by asking for a year, and none of these hundred lines is any use to Berowne then.

quotations.text: Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves, Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths.
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: The end of the speech that releases all four men from the statute.
quotations.analysis: The couplet turns on one verb used twice, and the balance is so neat that nobody on stage looks for the hole in it. Berowne is arguing that a promise you regret was never binding, which is what he told the King in Act I as a joke. The women’s reply is to give the four men a promise with a year attached.

quotations.text: They have been at a great feast of languages and stolen the scraps.
quotations.speaker: Moth
quotations.context: Aside to Costard, watching Armado and Holofernes greet each other in Latin.
quotations.analysis: A page says in one sentence what the play takes five acts to demonstrate. The insult is precise: the scraps are real food, taken from a real feast, but nobody at this table cooked anything. Costard extends it at once, saying they have lived long on the almsbasket of words, which makes the learned men beggars living on other people’s leftovers.

quotations.text: That he should be my fool, and I his fate.
quotations.speaker: Rosaline
quotations.context: Telling the other women what she would do to Berowne if she had him in her power.
quotations.analysis: Said as a fantasy of revenge, and by the end of the scene it has come true in a form she has not imagined: she does become his fate, and the sentence she passes is a year among the dying. The line is worth setting beside her last speech, where the same wit that plans this torture is used to explain what a jest costs.

quotations.text: Henceforth my wooing mind shall be expressed In russet yeas and honest kersey noes.
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: After the Muscovite masque has been exposed, renouncing taffeta phrases.
quotations.analysis: Russet and kersey are cheap cloth, set against the taffeta and three-piled hyperboles he has just forsworn, so the renunciation is still a figure of speech. Rosaline catches it two lines later when he says sans crack or flaw and she asks him to drop the sans. He admits he has a trick of the old rage and will leave it by degrees.

quotations.text: I am sorry, madam, for the news I bring Is heavy in my tongue. The King your father—
quotations.speaker: Marcadé
quotations.context: Entering in the middle of the Nine Worthies, as Armado and Costard square up to fight.
quotations.analysis: He never finishes the sentence; the Princess does it for him. Two and a half lines of plain statement stop a scene that has run nearly seven hundred, and Berowne’s response is the stage direction in words: worthies away, the scene begins to cloud. Nothing said after this has the same footing as anything said before it.

quotations.text: A time, methinks, too short To make a world-without-end bargain in.
quotations.speaker: Princess of France
quotations.context: The King has asked, at the latest minute of the hour, for her love.
quotations.analysis: World-without-end comes from the prayer book, and she uses it to measure marriage against the few hours the courtship has actually lasted. This is the answer to everything Berowne argued in Act IV, and it is not a refusal: she sets a hermitage and a year, and says come challenge me by these deserts. The terms are the point.

quotations.text: A jest’s prosperity lies in the ear Of him that hears it, never in the tongue Of him that makes it.
quotations.speaker: Rosaline
quotations.context: Explaining why Berowne must spend a year making the sick laugh.
quotations.analysis: The whole play is tested against this sentence. Every wit in it has assumed the credit belongs to the speaker, and Rosaline moves it to the listener. It also justifies her sentence exactly: if the dying will laugh at his jokes he may keep them, and if they will not, the fault was never in their ears.

quotations.text: Our wooing doth not end like an old play. Jack hath not Jill.
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: After all four women have set their terms and are leaving.
quotations.analysis: He names the genre the audience expected and says it has not arrived, and the King answers that it wants a twelvemonth and a day, to which Berowne replies that is too long for a play. Two characters stand inside the story and discuss its shape, and the ending they describe is the one they are in.

quotations.text: When icicles hang by the wall, And Dick the shepherd blows his nail
quotations.speaker: Winter
quotations.context: The second of the two songs that close the play, sung by the pageant players.
quotations.analysis: Dick, Tom, Marian and greasy Joan are the first people in the play with ordinary names and ordinary jobs, and they arrive in the last ninety seconds. The song has no wit in it at all, only frozen milk, a red nose and a staring owl, and it is the plainest and best-liked writing in the whole comedy.

books.title: Lyrical Ballads
books.author: William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge

themes.name: The language really used by men
Five years, and the mind checking itself

techniques.name: Speaking to someone in the poem

quotations.text: The majority of the following poems are to be considered as experiments.
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the unsigned note that introduces the 1798 volume.
quotations.analysis: A word borrowed from the laboratory, at a moment when poetry was still expected to be an art of finish. It sets up the reader to judge by results rather than by decorum, and it is the first sign that the book intends an argument as well as a collection.

quotations.text: It is an ancyent Marinere, And he stoppeth one of three.
quotations.reference: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere, 1-2
quotations.context: The first lines of the book.
quotations.analysis: Archaic spelling, ballad metre and a man seizing a stranger, all in fourteen words. Coleridge is announcing an old form on purpose; the volume that claims to use ordinary speech opens in a language nobody had spoken for two hundred years.

quotations.text: With my cross bow I shot the Albatross.
quotations.reference: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
quotations.context: The end of the first part, after the bird has followed the ship for nine days.
quotations.analysis: The crime is reported in a single line with no motive attached, and the poem never supplies one. Everything that follows is disproportionate to it, which is the point: the Marinere's world runs on a scale of consequence that no explanation will fit.

quotations.text: Water, water, every where, Ne any drop to drink.
quotations.reference: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
quotations.context: The becalmed ship on a rotting sea.
quotations.analysis: The 1798 spelling keeps the archaic 'ne', which later editions dropped, and the line is better for the awkwardness: the ballad is pretending to be older than it is. The image survives in ordinary speech, usually misquoted, which is a fair measure of the poem's reach.

quotations.text: Oh! what’s the matter? what’s the matter?
quotations.context: The opening of the poem about a farmer who catches an old woman taking sticks.
quotations.analysis: A poem that begins with a question a neighbour would ask over a wall. Wordsworth took the incident from a medical book and put it in ballad metre, and the effect is a case study told in the voice of village gossip.

quotations.text: I’ve measured it from side to side: ’Tis three feet long, and two feet wide.
quotations.context: The narrator describing the pond beside the thorn.
quotations.analysis: The most mocked couplet of the age, and entirely deliberate: a man who cannot tell a story reaches for the only certainty he has, a tape measure. Wordsworth cut the lines in 1820 under pressure, which is the clearest evidence of how far the experiment had gone.

quotations.text: The cocks did crow to-whoo, to-whoo, And the sun did shine so cold.
quotations.context: Johnny's entire account of his night, given at the end of the poem.
quotations.analysis: Four hundred lines of a mother's terror resolve into two lines of synaesthesia from the boy everyone in the poem has been worrying about. It is the volume's boldest claim: the imagination it has been arguing for turns up in the character the reader was invited to pity.

quotations.text: A simple child, dear brother Jim
quotations.context: The first line of the poem, in its 1798 form.
quotations.analysis: The address to 'brother Jim' was dropped from later editions, and with it the sense of a poem begun in the middle of a conversation. Keeping the 1798 reading shows how casual the opening was meant to sound before the argument starts.

quotations.text: Nay, we are seven!
quotations.context: The last line of the poem, after the adult has explained twice that two of the children are dead.
quotations.analysis: The poem ends with the child unmoved and the adult out of arguments, and Wordsworth gives her the final word rather than a moral. What looks like a poem about a child's confusion is a poem about an adult's certainty failing in the open.

quotations.text: Why William, on that old grey stone
quotations.context: Matthew opening the argument, finding the poet sitting and doing nothing.
quotations.analysis: The objection is given first and given a name. By letting the sensible position speak in its own voice, the poem earns the reply it is about to make, and the pair becomes a debate rather than a lecture.

quotations.text: Think you, mid all this mighty sum Of things for ever speaking, That nothing of itself will come, But we must still be seeking?
quotations.context: The poet's answer to Matthew.
quotations.analysis: The case for what he calls a wise passiveness, put as a question rather than a claim. 'Things for ever speaking' gives the world the active part and the mind the receptive one, which reverses the usual account of attention.

quotations.text: Up! up! my friend, and clear your looks
quotations.context: The reply poem, ordering Matthew away from his books.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation marks do real work: the poem's argument is about energy, and it starts by sounding like someone pulling a friend out of a chair. The doctrine that follows is only tolerable because it arrives in this voice.

quotations.text: One impulse from a vernal wood May teach you more of man, Of moral evil and of good, Than all the sages can.
quotations.context: The middle of the poem, at its most provocative.
quotations.analysis: The claim is deliberately excessive — more than all the sages — and that excess has been quoted against Wordsworth ever since. Read in the argument it belongs to, it is a move in a debate, not a position paper.

quotations.text: We murder to dissect.
quotations.context: The end of the stanza about science and art.
quotations.analysis: Four words that have outlived their poem. The charge is not against knowledge but against a method that takes a living thing apart to describe it, and the volume's own practice — watching people closely without explaining them — is the alternative on offer.

quotations.text: Five years have passed; five summers, with the length Of five long winters!
quotations.context: The opening of the last poem in the volume.
quotations.analysis: The same span counted three ways, each slower than the last, so that the line performs the passage it reports. After twenty-two ballads the ear notices at once that the rhyme has gone and the sentences have stopped stopping every fourth line.

quotations.text: sensations sweet, Felt in the blood, and felt along the heart
quotations.context: Describing what the remembered landscape has done for him in the years away.
quotations.analysis: The claim is physiological, not sentimental: a memory of a place is described as something circulating in the body. It is the volume's clearest statement that feeling is a kind of evidence.

quotations.text: The still, sad music of humanity
quotations.context: Accounting for what maturity has given him in place of youth's raw pleasure.
quotations.analysis: The compensation is other people's suffering, heard rather than witnessed. The phrase quietly justifies the rest of the book: the vagrants, huntsmen and mothers of the preceding poems are the music he means.

quotations.text: a sense sublime Of something far more deeply interfused
quotations.context: The poem's central and most careful passage.
quotations.analysis: Everything here is held at arm's length — a sense, something, far more deeply — because naming it would commit him to a doctrine. The vagueness is exact: this is a man describing an experience he trusts and cannot define.

quotations.text: Nature never did betray The heart that loved her
quotations.context: Turning to his sister, and telling her what will hold when the rest does not.
quotations.analysis: A promise made to somebody else, at the point where the poet has stopped trusting his own future. Read beside the Marinere's voyage at the other end of the book, the assurance looks less like a doctrine than a hope stated out loud.

books.title: M. R. James: Collected Ghost Stories
books.author: M. R. James

themes.name: Documents, and what they let out

quotations.text: St Bertrand de Comminges is a decayed town on the spurs of the Pyrenees, not very far from Toulouse, and still nearer to Bagnères-de-Luchon.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the first story in the first volume.
quotations.analysis: A guidebook sentence: a real town, two real reference points, a distance. James begins in the register of somebody who has been there, and the whole method of the collection is in that choice.

quotations.text: As for the fragments of ostensible erudition which are scattered about my pages, hardly anything in them is not pure invention
quotations.context: James accounting for the scholarship in his own stories.
quotations.analysis: A cataloguer of medieval manuscripts admitting that his learned apparatus is fiction — and the double negative keeps a scholar's caution even here. The admission matters because the erudition is what persuades a reader to accept everything else.

quotations.text: there never was, naturally, any such book as that which I quote in “The Treasure of Abbot Thomas”
quotations.context: In the same paragraph, on the sources he cites.
quotations.analysis: The word naturally is doing the work: he expects you to have believed in the book, and finds it obvious that you should not have. It is the closest thing in the preface to a conjuror explaining a trick.

quotations.text: in “Oh, Whistle, and I’ll Come to You” I had Felixstowe in mind
quotations.context: Identifying the settings that are real.
quotations.analysis: He names the seaside town, and the story's terror is thereby attached to a place with a railway station and a hotel. James understood that a reader frightened at the right coordinates stays frightened on holiday.

quotations.text: most of which were read to friends at Christmas-time at King’s College, Cambridge
quotations.context: How the stories first reached an audience.
quotations.analysis: These were written to be spoken, in a room, at night, to people who knew the author. The sentence explains the shape of every story in the book: short, spoken-paced, and building to one moment a listener could react to aloud.

quotations.text: coarse black hairs, longer than ever grew on a human hand; nails rising from the ends of the fingers and curving sharply down and forward, grey, horny and wrinkled
quotations.context: What Dennistoun sees beside him at the table, having first seen it in a drawing.
quotations.analysis: Every detail is one a naturalist could record — length, colour, curvature, texture — and the horror is that the list is so competent. James frightens by cataloguing, which is what he did for a living.

quotations.text: the nails were fearfully long and that the light shone through them
quotations.context: Stephen watching the two children on the lawn in the moonlight.
quotations.analysis: One physical impossibility, stated in a subordinate clause: light passing through a fingernail. James gets his effect by making the whole sentence ordinary except for a single fact that cannot be true.

quotations.text: Mr Wraxall compares it to the tentacle of a devil-fish
quotations.context: Describing the shape emerging from the hooded figure on an engraving.
quotations.analysis: The horror is reported at two removes — a comparison, inside a quotation, from a dead man's notebook — and the reader is left to do the seeing. The sentence is also the model for the whole collection's tact.

quotations.text: It ought to mean, ‘Who is this who is coming?’ Well, the best way to find out is evidently to whistle for him.
quotations.reference: “Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad”
quotations.context: Parkins translating the Latin on the whistle he has just dug up.
quotations.analysis: He reads the warning correctly and treats it as a research question. That single sentence is James's whole argument about scholarship: the translation is right, the inference is professional, and it is the worst decision in the book.

quotations.text: a horrible, an intensely horrible, face of crumpled linen
quotations.reference: “Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad”
quotations.context: The figure that rises from the spare bed in a hotel room at Burnstow.
quotations.analysis: The most famous phrase James wrote, and it names a material rather than a creature. He then declines to say what expression was on it, which leaves the reader to supply the one thing the sentence has carefully withheld.

quotations.text: Fair is foul, and foul is fair: Hover through the fog and filthy air.
quotations.speaker: The Witches
quotations.context: The closing couplet of the first scene, spoken by all three witches together.
quotations.analysis: Twelve lines into the play, the audience is handed its instructions: nothing here will be safely readable. The chiasmus turns two opposed words into a closed loop, and the shift into rhymed trochaic tetrameter sets the witches apart from every other voice in the play before they have done anything at all.

quotations.text: All hail, Macbeth, thou shalt be king hereafter!
quotations.speaker: Third Witch
quotations.context: The third of three greetings on the heath, after Glamis and Cawdor.
quotations.analysis: The sentence does not contain an instruction, a condition or a route. It is the flat future tense that does the damage: Macbeth is told what will be, and spends the play converting a prediction into a plan while believing he is only keeping an appointment.

quotations.text: It is too full o' the milk of human kindness To catch the nearest way.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Reading Macbeth's letter about the prophecy, alone.
quotations.analysis: She diagnoses him in a single image, and the image is not an insult — it grants him a nature she considers a practical obstacle. 'The nearest way' is the whole murder rendered as a route on a map, which is exactly the kind of euphemism the couple will need for the next two acts.

quotations.text: Come, you spirits That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here, And fill me from the crown to the toe top-full Of direst cruelty!
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone, after learning that Duncan will arrive that night.
quotations.analysis: The cruelty she wants has to be sent for, which tells the audience she does not already possess it. 'Crown to the toe' puts the crown on her body as well as on Duncan's head, and the request to be unsexed treats womanhood as a set of feelings — pity, remorse, the milk she later names — that would get in the way.

quotations.text: Look like the innocent flower, But be the serpent under't.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Instructing Macbeth as Duncan approaches the castle.
quotations.analysis: The advice is a compressed piece of stage direction: a face to wear and a thing to be. It also answers Duncan's complaint sixty lines earlier that there is no art to find the mind's construction in the face — the play has just supplied the art, and given it to the other side.

quotations.text: If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well It were done quickly.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone, leaving the banquet at which Duncan is his guest.
quotations.analysis: Four uses of 'done' in twelve words, and not one of them names the act. The line is thinking in circles because the speaker will not let the word 'murder' into it, and the soliloquy goes on to reject the plan entirely on grounds of consequence rather than conscience.

quotations.text: I have no spur To prick the sides of my intent, but only Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself And falls on the other.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: The end of the soliloquy in which he decides not to kill Duncan.
quotations.analysis: He can find no reason for the murder except the wanting of it, and he says so as though that settled the matter. The rider who over-leaps the saddle is a comic image for a catastrophic one, and the sentence breaks off before it lands — the falling is left to the rest of the play.

quotations.text: Is this a dagger which I see before me, The handle toward my hand?
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone at night, moving towards Duncan's chamber.
quotations.analysis: The dagger is offered to him handle first, as a servant would offer it — the hallucination is helpfully arranging the murder. He asks a question rather than making a claim, and keeps asking: the speech is a man conducting an experiment on his own mind and losing.

quotations.text: Methought I heard a voice cry 'Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep'.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Immediately after the murder, still holding the daggers.
quotations.analysis: He reports the sentence rather than owning it, and the voice uses his name as though he were already a story being told about someone else. Sleep is the first of the ordinary things the murder takes away, and the play keeps the receipt: Lady Macbeth will be walking in her sleep three acts later.

quotations.text: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather The multitudinous seas in incarnadine, Making the green one red.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Looking at his hands after Duncan's murder.
quotations.analysis: The scale inverts inside four lines: an ocean cannot clean one hand, so the hand stains the ocean. 'Incarnadine' and 'multitudinous' are Latinate and enormous; 'making the green one red' is four monosyllables and a colour. Shakespeare gives the man the grand version and then the plain one, and the plain one is worse.

quotations.text: O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Speaking to Lady Macbeth while concealing the plan to kill Banquo.
quotations.analysis: The endearment and the scorpions arrive in the same breath, and he tells her about the state of his mind precisely in order to avoid telling her its contents. This is the scene where the marriage stops being a partnership: from here he acts and she is informed afterwards, if at all.

quotations.text: It will have blood; they say, blood will have blood.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: After the guests have been sent away from the ruined banquet.
quotations.analysis: He quotes a proverb, which is the closest he now comes to a moral framework: murder is described as a creature with an appetite of its own. The grammar has no agent in it anywhere, and that is the point — by Act III he has stopped experiencing his killings as things he decides to do.

quotations.text: Macbeth shall never vanquish'd be until Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill Shall come against him.
quotations.speaker: Third Apparition
quotations.context: The third apparition, a crowned child holding a tree.
quotations.analysis: The prophecy hands him an impossibility and he accepts the gift without examining the wrapping — a child holding a branch has already shown him how the wood will move. Equivocation works here not by lying but by offering a picture the listener would rather keep.

quotations.text: Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak Whispers the o'er-fraught heart and bids it break.
quotations.speaker: Malcolm
quotations.context: To Macduff, on hearing that his wife and children are dead.
quotations.analysis: The one piece of straightforwardly good advice in the play, and it is about language. Set it against Macbeth, who has spent four acts refusing to name what he is doing; the play's cure for grief is the opposite of the habit that produced it.

quotations.text: Out, damned spot! out, I say!
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Sleepwalking, watched by a doctor and her gentlewoman.
quotations.analysis: She told her husband in 2.2 that a little water clears us of this deed, and she is now scrubbing a hand that has nothing on it. The speech is in prose, which for a queen at this point in a tragedy is itself a diagnosis, and it is broken into fragments that move between all three murders at once.

quotations.text: My way of life Is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf; And that which should accompany old age, As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends, I must not look to have.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone at Dunsinane as the English army approaches.
quotations.analysis: He itemises exactly what he has lost, in order, and the list is entirely made of relationships. It is the most accurate self-assessment anyone makes in the play, and it changes nothing — a few lines later he is shouting at a servant about the colour of his face.

quotations.text: To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow, Creeps in this petty pace from day to day To the last syllable of recorded time.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: On being told that the queen is dead.
quotations.analysis: Asked to feel something about his wife's death, he produces a theory of time instead. The repetition flattens the future into a queue, and 'syllable' quietly turns all of history into something merely said aloud — which sets up the walking shadow and the poor player five lines later.

quotations.text: Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player That struts and frets his hour upon the stage And then is heard no more.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: The continuation of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is aimed at the actor saying it, in a theatre, to people who will go home in an hour. It is the bleakest thing in the play and also the most theatrically self-aware: the man who wanted to be remembered as king describes existence as a performance nobody will recall.

quotations.text: Macduff was from his mother's womb Untimely ripp'd.
quotations.speaker: Macduff
quotations.context: In single combat with Macbeth, answering the claim that no man of woman born can harm him.
quotations.analysis: The last guarantee fails on a technicality, and the technicality is a birth. Macbeth's response — that the word has 'cow'd my better part of man' — admits the whole trick: he had been fighting on the strength of a sentence rather than an army.

quotations.text: Our fears do make us traitors.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macduff
quotations.context: To Ross, on learning that her husband has fled to England.
quotations.analysis: Six words that convict Macduff of the thing the whole play is about — acting on fear and calling it strategy. She is defending nobody, least of all herself, and the scene that follows makes her the only character permitted to be simply right.

quotations.text: More needs she the divine than the physician.
quotations.speaker: Doctor
quotations.context: After watching Lady Macbeth sleepwalk.
quotations.analysis: Medicine hands the case over: what is wrong with her is not a condition. The line pairs with Macbeth's demand two scenes later that the same doctor pluck a rooted sorrow from the memory, and with Scotland itself, repeatedly described as a patient nobody can treat.

quotations.text: Stars, hide your fires; Let not light see my black and deep desires.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Aside, immediately after Duncan names Malcolm his heir.
quotations.analysis: The first thing he does after the obstacle appears is ask the universe to look away. Light and dark run through the whole play as a moral lighting rig, and here Macbeth is operating it himself — he wants not to be seen, including by himself.

themes.name: Desire and the law made against it

quotations.text: Spirits are not finely touch'd But to fine issues, nor Nature never lends The smallest scruple of her excellence But, like a thrifty goddess, she determines Herself the glory of a creditor,
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Handing the commission to Angelo in the first scene.
quotations.analysis: Virtue is described as a loan advanced on interest, and the metaphor governs the rest of the play: nothing in Vienna is given, everything is lent, weighed or repaid. The Duke is also, in the same breath, telling Angelo that a reputation which is never spent is worthless — advice he is about to enforce experimentally.

quotations.text: Mortality and mercy in Vienna Live in thy tongue and heart: old Escalus, Though first in question, is thy secondary.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: The formal transfer of power, with Escalus standing by.
quotations.analysis: Two abstractions are located in two organs, and the split is exact: death is something Angelo will say and mercy something he would have to feel. The last clause is the quiet cruelty — the older and better judge is demoted in the same sentence that gives the younger man the power of life.

quotations.text: so our decrees, Dead to infliction, to themselves are dead; And liberty plucks justice by the nose; The baby beats the nurse, and quite athwart Goes all decorum.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Explaining to Friar Thomas why he has let the laws lapse and why he will not enforce them himself.
quotations.analysis: This is the Duke's own confession of negligence, and it is made to a priest rather than to the city. The two images are of insolence rather than crime — a nose pulled, a nurse slapped — which suggests the danger he fears is to the dignity of the law rather than to anybody's safety.

quotations.text: a man whose blood Is very snow-broth; one who never feels The wanton stings and motions of the sense, But doth rebate and blunt his natural edge With profits of the mind, study and fast.
quotations.speaker: Lucio
quotations.context: Lucio describing the new deputy to Isabella at the nunnery.
quotations.analysis: Melted snow is water that was once solid, so even the insult concedes that something has been made cold rather than being cold by nature. Lucio is usually unreliable; here he is exactly right about the diagnosis and exactly wrong about the prognosis, which is the play's method with him throughout.

quotations.text: Our doubts are traitors And make us lose the good we oft might win By fearing to attempt.
quotations.speaker: Lucio
quotations.context: Pushing a reluctant Isabella to go and plead for her brother.
quotations.analysis: The line is quoted as encouragement so often that its context is worth keeping: it is a rake persuading a novice to leave her convent and go and bargain with a man for a life. 'Attempt' carried a sexual sense in this period, and the play will make that second meaning explicit within one act.

quotations.text: We must not make a scarecrow of the law, Setting it up to fear the birds of prey, And let it keep one shape, till custom make it Their perch and not their terror.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: The first words of his administration, refusing Escalus's plea for Claudio.
quotations.analysis: It is the best defence of enforcement anybody makes, and it is made with an image of birds settling comfortably on the thing meant to frighten them. Notice that Angelo's argument is about the law's appearance rather than its justice: he is worried about being laughed at, which is the same anxiety the Duke admitted in 1.3.

quotations.text: Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall: Some run from brakes of ice, and answer none: And some condemned for a fault alone.
quotations.speaker: Escalus
quotations.context: Alone, after failing to save Claudio.
quotations.analysis: Three lines of rhyme dropped into a prose-heavy scene, marking a moment of private judgement in a public office. The chiasmus balances rising and falling so evenly that it refuses to blame anyone, which is precisely the temper Angelo has just overruled.

quotations.text: Condemn the fault and not the actor of it? Why, every fault's condemn'd ere it be done: Mine were the very cipher of a function, To fine the faults whose fine stands in record, And let go by the actor.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Answering Isabella's opening argument in the first interview.
quotations.analysis: He is right, and the rightness is the problem: a law that punishes acts and not persons is not a law at all. 'Cipher' means a zero, so he pictures his own office as a nothing — and by the end of the scene he will have become exactly the actor he refuses to distinguish from the fault.

quotations.text: And mercy then will breathe within your lips, Like man new made.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: The climax of her first appeal: if he were in Claudio's place and Claudio in his.
quotations.analysis: The image is of God breathing life into Adam, so showing mercy is presented not as a kindness but as the moment a man becomes human at all. It is also the most physical thing she has said to him, and the speech that follows it is the one in which he begins to notice her voice.

quotations.text: O, it is excellent To have a giant's strength; but it is tyrannous To use it like a giant.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Pressing the argument after Angelo tells her that her brother dies tomorrow.
quotations.analysis: The sentence concedes the power before objecting to its use, which is why it works on a man who will not hear his authority questioned. It also states the play's political thesis in fifteen words: nothing here is wrong with the law itself, only with the scale at which a person chooses to apply it.

quotations.text: but man, proud man, Drest in a little brief authority, Most ignorant of what he's most assured, His glassy essence, like an angry ape, Plays such fantastic tricks before high heaven As make the angels weep;
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Contrasting divine thunder with the noise a magistrate makes.
quotations.analysis: 'Glassy essence' means both mirror-like and breakable, so the soul is at once a reflecting surface and something easily smashed. She is describing authority in general and has no idea she is describing the man in front of her; the audience, having heard him for a scene and a half, does.

quotations.text: What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine? The tempter or the tempted, who sins most? Ha! Not she: nor doth she tempt: but it is I
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Alone on stage the moment Isabella leaves.
quotations.analysis: The question is asked and answered inside four lines, and he gets it right: she does not tempt, and the fault is his. The play never lets him plead ignorance afterwards, which is why what he does in 2.4 is a decision rather than a fall.

quotations.text: Thieves for their robbery have authority When judges steal themselves.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Still alone, working out what his desire will cost the city.
quotations.analysis: He sees the whole constitutional consequence before he commits the offence: a corrupt bench licenses every crime beneath it. The line is also the play's answer to its own title, since a judge who steals has set the measure by which he must be measured.

quotations.text: Blood, thou art blood: Let's write good angel on the devil's horn: 'Tis not the devil's crest.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Waiting for Isabella's second visit, having found he cannot pray.
quotations.analysis: The tautology is the point: after a scene of argument he arrives at a fact that admits no argument. The heraldic image turns his own name into a label that can be written on the wrong animal, and 'good angel' is one letter away from the name he signs on warrants.

quotations.text: I do arrest your words. Be that you are, That is, a woman; if you be more, you're none; If you be one, as you are well express'd By all external warrants, show it now, By putting on the destined livery.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Isabella has just said that women are frail; Angelo takes the admission literally.
quotations.analysis: He uses the vocabulary of his office to conduct a seduction — arrest, warrants, livery — so the extortion is phrased entirely in legal terms. The trap is grammatical: she conceded a general frailty, and he converts it into a personal obligation with the word 'now'.

quotations.text: Who will believe thee, Isabel? My unsoil'd name, the austereness of my life, My vouch against you, and my place i' the state, Will so your accusation overweigh, That you shall stifle in your own report
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Isabella threatens to tell the world what he is.
quotations.analysis: He does not deny that she could prove it; he explains that proof is not what decides such cases. 'Overweigh' returns the play to its scales, and in Act V the Duke will stage a hearing designed to demonstrate, at length and in public, that Angelo's calculation was accurate.

quotations.text: Then, Isabel, live chaste, and, brother, die: More than our brother is our chastity.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act II, having refused Angelo's terms.
quotations.analysis: The decision is taken in a rhymed couplet, the form Shakespeare uses to close a scene and settle a question, so the verse itself insists that there is nothing left to discuss. She addresses herself and her absent brother in the same line, which is as close as the play comes to showing her weigh the two.

quotations.text: Be absolute for death; either death or life Shall thereby be the sweeter. Reason thus with life: If I do lose thee, I do lose a thing That none but fools would keep:
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: The disguised Duke preparing Claudio for execution.
quotations.analysis: It is a consolation built entirely out of contempt for living, and it persuades Claudio for about a hundred lines. The Duke knows at this point that he intends to save him, which makes the whole speech an exercise conducted on a man under sentence for the benefit of the man delivering it.

quotations.text: Ay, but to die, and go we know not where; To lie in cold obstruction and to rot; This sensible warm motion to become A kneaded clod; and the delighted spirit To bathe in fiery floods, or to reside
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Two words after agreeing that death is a fearful thing and shamed life a hateful one.
quotations.analysis: The fear is entirely physical until the fourth line, and the shift from 'warm motion' to 'kneaded clod' is the whole argument: what terrifies him is not punishment but the loss of temperature and movement. The speech begins with 'Ay, but' — a man conceding the philosophy and then finding it does not reach.

quotations.text: Sweet sister, let me live: What sin you do to save a brother's life, Nature dispenses with the deed so far That it becomes a virtue.
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Asking Isabella to accept Angelo's bargain.
quotations.analysis: He does not ask her to sin for him; he argues that in these circumstances it would not be a sin, which is exactly the reasoning Angelo used on her an act earlier. Hearing her brother speak in the deputy's voice is what produces the violence of her reply.

quotations.text: O you beast! O faithless coward! O dishonest wretch! Wilt thou be made a man out of my vice? Is't not a kind of incest, to take life From thine own sister's shame?
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Her immediate answer to Claudio's plea.
quotations.analysis: Three vocatives in a line and a half, each one shorter in patience than the last, and then a legal-sounding question that is not really a question. 'Made a man' is the cruellest phrase: she tells him that buying his life at this price would cost him his manhood as surely as it would cost her her chastity.

quotations.text: O, what may man within him hide, Though angel on the outward side!
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act III, in rhymed tetrameter.
quotations.analysis: The metre changes to the short, chanting line Shakespeare gives to choruses and spirits, which lifts the Duke out of the action and into the position of a commentator on it. The pun on Angelo's name has been waiting since the first scene, and it is sprung only once the plot to trap him is already in motion.

quotations.text: Take, O, take those lips away, That so sweetly were forsworn; And those eyes, the break of day, Lights that do mislead the morn:
quotations.speaker: A boy, singing
quotations.context: The song at Mariana's moated grange, which she breaks off when the friar arrives.
quotations.analysis: The only song in the play is given to the one character with nothing to do but wait, and she apologises for it immediately. Its subject is a broken oath, which is Angelo's offence against her five years before the plot begins, so the scene of the bed trick opens by reminding us who was wronged first.

quotations.text: I swear I will not die to-day for any man's persuasion.
quotations.speaker: Barnardine
quotations.context: Dragged out of his cell to be executed so that his head can be sent to Angelo.
quotations.analysis: A guilty man defeats the entire apparatus of the plot by declining to co-operate with it, and the Duke has no answer except to look for a different corpse. It is the one point in the play where authority, disguised or not, is simply told no and has to go away.

quotations.text: 'An Angelo for Claudio, death for death!' Haste still pays haste, and leisure answers leisure; Like doth quit like, and MEASURE still FOR MEASURE.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Sentencing Angelo at the city gate, after the marriage to Mariana.
quotations.analysis: The title arrives as a judicial formula in the mouth of a judge who has already prevented the death he is avenging. Everything in the line is balanced — haste against haste, like against like — and the balance is a performance, since Claudio is alive behind the scenes and the Duke knows it.

quotations.text: Let him not die. My brother had but justice, In that he did the thing for which he died: For Angelo, His act did not o'ertake his bad intent, And must be buried but as an intent
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Kneeling beside Mariana to beg for the life of the man she believes killed her brother.
quotations.analysis: She saves Angelo on a technicality of intention, not on a plea for mercy — the argument is that nothing actually happened, which she believes to be true. It is also the first time she concedes that Claudio's sentence was lawful, so her forgiveness of Angelo is bought at the price of agreeing that her brother deserved to die.

quotations.text: If he be like your brother, for his sake Is he pardon'd; and, for your lovely sake, Give me your hand and say you will be mine.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Claudio has just been unmuffled and restored; the proposal follows within three lines.
quotations.analysis: A pardon and a proposal are delivered in the same sentence, with the grammar making the second conditional on the goodwill created by the first. The Folio gives Isabella no reply here or at the second asking forty lines later, and every production has to decide what a woman does with a hand held out in front of a crowd.

quotations.text: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago⁠—never mind how long precisely⁠—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.
quotations.context: The opening of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The imperative does not give a name, it proposes one, and the difference matters in a book where Ahab's name is a judgement and the whale's is a trade nickname. The dashes then bury the only concrete facts — no money, nothing to do — inside an aside, so that the voyage arrives sounding like a whim rather than the last resort it turns out to be.

quotations.text: Who ain’t a slave? Tell me that.
quotations.context: Explaining why he ships before the mast rather than as a passenger or an officer.
quotations.analysis: The question is a joke about taking orders, and in a book published in 1851 by a New York house it is also not a joke. Ishmael's cheerful universalising — everybody is somebody's servant, so the thump goes round — is the exact argument the novel dismantles later, when Chapter 89 puts real people under the law of loose-fish.

quotations.text: Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.
quotations.context: Getting into bed at the Spouter-Inn beside a stranger he has spent the evening dreading.
quotations.analysis: The sentence works by putting the two adjectives where the two nouns expect to be judged: it is sobriety and drunkenness that decide, not heathen and Christian. Ishmael has reasoned his way out of a terror in about four lines, and the speed of the reversal sets the pattern for a narrator who revises his categories whenever the evidence asks him to.

quotations.text: Delight is to him⁠—a far, far upward, and inward delight⁠—who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, ever stands forth his own inexorable self.
quotations.speaker: Father Mapple
quotations.context: The close of the sermon on Jonah, preached to a congregation of whalemen about to sail.
quotations.analysis: Mapple's sermon has spent twenty minutes on the duty of obedience and ends by blessing the man who stands against every authority on earth. Ahab will take the second half of that lesson and leave the first, which is why the sermon has to come before he appears: the book gives him his theology in a church, from a pulpit shaped like the bow of a ship.

quotations.text: No more my splintered heart and maddened hand were turned against the wolfish world. This soothing savage had redeemed it.
quotations.context: Sitting by the fire with Queequeg the morning after their first night in the same bed.
quotations.analysis: The cure for the November in his soul turns out to be one specific person rather than the sea at all, which quietly undoes the whole rationale of Chapter 1. Note that redemption is credited to a man Ishmael was ready to call a devil the night before, and that the verb is in the past perfect — it has already happened, before the narrator noticed.

quotations.text: But as in landlessness alone resides highest truth, shoreless, indefinite as God⁠—so, better is it to perish in that howling infinite, than be ingloriously dashed upon the lee, even if that were safety!
quotations.context: A six-paragraph chapter about a sailor named Bulkington, who is never mentioned again.
quotations.analysis: The shortest chapter in the book states the ethic the rest of it will test to destruction, and then deletes the character it was attached to. Bulkington exists to make the argument and disappear, which is Melville telling the reader early that this book will introduce people for the length of an idea.

quotations.text: “I will have no man in my boat,” said Starbuck, “who is not afraid of a whale.”
quotations.speaker: Starbuck
quotations.context: Ishmael's introduction of the first mate, before Ahab has appeared on deck.
quotations.analysis: Fear is being described as a professional qualification: the man who feels none has no instrument for measuring the danger. Placed ten chapters before the quarter-deck scene, the line also tells the reader exactly what will be wrong with Ahab's command, and exactly why Starbuck will lose the argument — his courage is a calculation, and calculations can be shouted down.

quotations.text: “Vengeance on a dumb brute!” cried Starbuck, “that simply smote thee from blindest instinct! Madness! To be enraged with a dumb thing, Captain Ahab, seems blasphemous.”
quotations.speaker: Starbuck
quotations.context: The one objection raised on deck after Ahab names the voyage's real purpose.
quotations.analysis: Starbuck's case is that the whale cannot be guilty because it cannot intend, and the word he reaches for is theological rather than commercial. That choice loses him the argument: by admitting the question is about God, he lets Ahab answer on the same ground, and the reply about striking the sun follows immediately.

quotations.text: All visible objects, man, are but as pasteboard masks. But in each event⁠—in the living act, the undoubted deed⁠—there, some unknown but still reasoning thing puts forth the mouldings of its features from behind the unreasoning mask. If man will strike, strike through the mask!
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: Answering Starbuck's objection in front of the assembled crew.
quotations.analysis: Ahab's metaphysics is stated as stage property: the world is scenery, and something is standing behind it. The argument only works if there is a face under the mask, and he concedes two sentences later that there may be nothing at all — then says it does not matter. That concession, made aloud and immediately abandoned, is the clearest evidence in the book that he knows what he is doing.

quotations.text: Talk not to me of blasphemy, man; I’d strike the sun if it insulted me.
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: The same speech, in reply to Starbuck's word for the voyage.
quotations.analysis: The conditional is the whole trick: he does not claim to be equal to the sun, only to be willing. Ahab consistently wins arguments by shifting them from what is possible to what he is prepared to do, and a crew that has just been given grog and a gold coin is in no state to notice the substitution.

quotations.text: The path to my fixed purpose is laid with iron rails, whereon my soul is grooved to run.
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: Alone in the cabin immediately after the quarter-deck scene, in a soliloquy printed with a stage direction.
quotations.analysis: He chooses the most modern image available in 1851 — a railway — to describe a fate he insists is his own. The metaphor concedes more than he means: rails are laid by somebody, and the thing that runs on them has no say in the route. Ninety chapters later he will ask outright who laid them.

quotations.text: All that most maddens and torments; all that stirs up the lees of things; all truth with malice in it; all that cracks the sinews and cakes the brain; all the subtle demonisms of life and thought; all evil, to crazy Ahab, were visibly personified, and made practically assailable in Moby Dick.
quotations.context: The narrator's account of how Ahab's injury became a metaphysics.
quotations.analysis: Six clauses beginning with 'all' pile up before the sentence will name its subject, so the reader feels the accumulation before learning where it is going. The operative word is 'assailable': the appeal of the whale is not that it is evil but that it can be reached with a harpoon, which is what abstract grievances cannot.

quotations.text: It was the whiteness of the whale that above all things appalled me.
quotations.context: The opening admission of the chapter Ishmael gives to a colour.
quotations.analysis: 'Appalled' still carried its root sense of being made pale, so the sentence quietly turns the reader white as it reports the whiteness. Ishmael also separates himself from Ahab here: the captain is frightened by malice, the narrator by a colour, and it is the narrator's fear that the book then spends a whole chapter failing to explain.

quotations.text: is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows⁠—a colourless, all-colour of atheism from which we shrink?
quotations.context: Near the end of the chapter on whiteness, after a long list of white things that are and are not terrible.
quotations.analysis: 'Blankness, full of meaning' is a contradiction stated as a fact, and it describes the novel's method as much as its subject. The whole chapter is built out of questions rather than assertions; Ishmael cannot get the colour to signify, and by refusing to force it he shows exactly what Ahab does when he decides the whale is an argument.

quotations.text: God help thee, old man, thy thoughts have created a creature in thee; and he whose intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus; a vulture feeds upon that heart forever; that vulture the very creature he creates.
quotations.context: After a description of Ahab bursting from his cabin at night, driven out of his hammock by his own dreams.
quotations.analysis: The purpose has become a separate organism living inside the man who made it, which is a more precise account of obsession than any diagnosis of madness. Melville folds the Prometheus story in on itself: the punishment is not sent by the gods but manufactured by the sufferer, so the vulture and the thing it feeds on have the same author.

quotations.text: The sea had jeeringly kept his finite body up, but drowned the infinite of his soul.
quotations.context: After Pip is left alone in the open Pacific and eventually picked up by the ship.
quotations.analysis: The chiasmus of finite body and infinite soul turns a rescue into a drowning, and the adverb does the moral work: the sea is not indifferent here but mocking. Melville has made the one survival in the middle of the book a disaster, which is worth holding against the Epilogue, where survival is presented as the plainest of facts.

quotations.text: So man’s insanity is heaven’s sense; and wandering from all mortal reason, man comes at last to that celestial thought, which, to reason, is absurd and frantic; and weal or woe, feels then uncompromised, indifferent as his God.
quotations.context: Explaining what the crew mean when they call Pip mad.
quotations.analysis: The sentence reverses the crew's verdict without contradicting it: Pip is exactly what they say he is, and that is the qualification. What he has acquired is indifference, the same quality the novel has just attributed to God, which makes his madness a kind of promotion and the ship's diagnosis a failure of rank rather than of medicine.

quotations.text: Come; let us squeeze hands all round; nay, let us all squeeze ourselves into each other; let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness.
quotations.context: Working congealed spermaceti back into liquid with the rest of the crew.
quotations.analysis: The verb is repeated until it stops being industrial and becomes affectionate, which is the whole movement of the chapter: a task performed for the oil market produces the book's frankest declaration of love. The sentence also rewrites a phrase of Lady Macbeth's about the milk of human kindness, replacing an accusation of softness with a recommendation.

quotations.text: Look not too long in the face of the fire, O man! Never dream with thy hand on the helm! Turn not thy back to the compass; accept the first hint of the hitching tiller; believe not the artificial fire, when its redness makes all things look ghastly.
quotations.context: After Ishmael, steering at night, falls asleep facing the try-works and nearly capsizes the ship.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives about steering are also three imperatives about reading, and the near-disaster is the only time the narrator endangers the Pequod himself. Set the advice beside Ahab, who has spent the voyage looking at nothing else: the novel offers the corrective just two chapters before the doubloon proves how little good corrections do.

quotations.text: And some certain significance lurks in all things, else all things are little worth, and the round world itself but an empty cipher, except to sell by the cartload, as they do hills about Boston, to fill up some morass in the Milky Way.
quotations.context: Ahab pausing at the doubloon nailed to the mainmast.
quotations.analysis: This is the case for symbolism stated by its most compromised witness, and the alternative he offers is commerce: either things mean, or they are gravel to be carted away. The chapter then has six other characters read the same coin, which demonstrates the opposite of what Ahab needs — that significance lurks everywhere and therefore settles nowhere.

quotations.text: Close! stand close to me, Starbuck; let me look into a human eye; it is better than to gaze into sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God.
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: On a calm morning three days before the chase, talking to his first mate about forty years at sea.
quotations.analysis: After a hundred chapters of addressing the sun, the lightning and a severed whale's head, he asks to look at a person, and finds his own wife and child reflected there. The reversal lasts about a page: the same speech ends by ordering Starbuck to stay aboard, so the one moment of contact is spent buying the mate's absence.

quotations.text: Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm?
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: The same conversation, a few sentences later.
quotations.analysis: The first question puts a name on both sides of the verb and gets no answer, which is what the punctuation is for — the comma keeps the two Ahabs from resolving into one. Ninety-five chapters after declaring his soul grooved to run, he asks who laid the rails, and the arm he cannot account for is the one that will throw the harpoon.

quotations.text: Towards thee I roll, thou all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with thee; from hell’s heart I stab at thee; for hate’s sake I spit my last breath at thee.
quotations.speaker: Ahab
quotations.context: His last words, thrown at the whale as the Pequod goes down behind him.
quotations.analysis: 'All-destroying but unconquering' is an accurate summary of the situation and a defeat dressed as a distinction: the whale wins and is granted no victory. Ahab keeps the second person throughout, so the final speech of the book is addressed to an animal, and the harpoon line he throws with it catches him round the neck and takes him under.

quotations.text: Now small fowls flew screaming over the yet yawning gulf; a sullen white surf beat against its steep sides; then all collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it rolled five thousand years ago.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the narrative proper, after the ship has gone down.
quotations.analysis: The sea is given a burial cloth and then denied any interest in the burial; five thousand years is the biblical age of the world, so the closing measure is one the Pequod's Quaker owners would recognise. Every noun in the sentence is doing the same work — the surf is sullen, the gulf yawns — and none of them is mourning.

quotations.text: It was the devious-cruising Rachel, that in her retracing search after her missing children, only found another orphan.
quotations.context: The final sentence of the book, describing the ship that picks Ishmael up.
quotations.analysis: The rescue is written as a disappointment: the Rachel is looking for her own children and finds a stranger. Melville has already had Ahab refuse this captain a day's search in Chapter 128, so the last act of the novel is the ship he wronged saving the only man left, and the last word is a category rather than a name.

themes.name: The war that has not ended
themes.canonicalName: The war that has not ended

techniques.name: Digging out the past behind a character
techniques.canonicalName: Digging out the past behind a character

quotations.text: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: It is reported speech with no speech marks, so the reader arrives in the middle of a household conversation already under way. The name is the formal one, husband's surname and all, and the last word is the only assertion of a self in the sentence — a woman defined by a title choosing to do one small thing alone.

quotations.text: What a lark! What a plunge!
quotations.context: The June air at the front door recalling a window at Bourton.
quotations.analysis: Two exclamations with no attribution and no verb: the prose has slipped into Clarissa's own idiom within three sentences of the start. 'Plunge' is the word that matters, since it carries both diving into the morning and going under, and the novel will use water for both all day.

quotations.text: In people’s eyes, in the swing, tramp, and trudge; in the bellow and the uproar; the carriages, motorcars, omnibuses, vans, sandwich men shuffling and swinging; brass bands; barrel organs; in the triumph and the jingle and the strange high singing of some aeroplane overhead was what she loved; life; London; this moment of June.
quotations.context: Crossing Victoria Street on the way to the flower shop.
quotations.analysis: The sentence withholds its verb for forty words, so the noise accumulates before anything is said about it, and then the last three items are stripped to bare nouns separated by semicolons. 'This moment of June' is the smallest of the three and the one that will be gone by the evening.

quotations.text: The leaden circles dissolved in the air.
quotations.context: Big Ben striking, early in the day.
quotations.analysis: The clock is not described as a sound but as a shape with weight, spreading and vanishing, which makes the passing of an hour something the reader can watch disappear. The sentence returns unchanged several times, and by the last occurrence it arrives just after a death, which is how a refrain acquires a meaning it did not start with.

quotations.text: She had a perpetual sense, as she watched the taxi cabs, of being out, out, far out to sea and alone; she always had the feeling that it was very, very dangerous to live even one day.
quotations.context: Clarissa on her own habit of standing apart from what she is in the middle of.
quotations.analysis: The image arrives while she is looking at traffic, which is the point: nothing has happened. Both halves double a word — out, out; very, very — so the sentence sounds like someone insisting on something they cannot get anyone to take seriously, and the novel will spend the day proving that one day can indeed be fatal.

quotations.text: Fear no more the heat o’ the sun Nor the furious winter’s rages.
quotations.context: Read off an open book in a Hatchards window.
quotations.analysis: The lines are from the funeral song in Cymbeline, and Clarissa picks them up as consolation without dwelling on the fact that they are sung over a body. Septimus will arrive at the same words independently, which is the first evidence that the two plots are running on one text.

quotations.text: She had the oddest sense of being herself invisible; unseen; unknown
quotations.context: On being, at fifty-two, Mrs Richard Dalloway and nothing else.
quotations.analysis: Three words for the same condition, each a shade further from company, separated by semicolons so that they read as a slow settling rather than a list. The sense is presented as odd rather than distressing, which is more unsettling than a complaint would be.

quotations.text: The world has raised its whip; where will it descend?
quotations.reference: The motor car and the aeroplane
quotations.context: Septimus's first appearance, held up in the crowd around the stopped car.
quotations.analysis: It is printed as a separate paragraph, unattributed and in the present tense, so it reads as a general statement before the reader realises it is a symptom. The crowd around him is speculating about royalty; he is the only person there who has been where the whip already fell.

quotations.text: I am alone; I am alone!
quotations.speaker: Lucrezia Warren Smith
quotations.context: By the fountain, having left Septimus on the seat.
quotations.analysis: The repetition is not emphasis but the sound of somebody with nobody to say it to, and the sentence has no listener inside the novel at all. Woolf places it in the middle of the most public space in the book, a park full of people, and the paragraph around it widens to Roman roads and ancient marshland — loneliness given geological scale.

quotations.text: He woke with extreme suddenness, saying to himself, “The death of the soul.”
quotations.context: Peter waking from a doze on a seat in Regent's Park.
quotations.analysis: The phrase arrives before its object does; only afterwards does he attach it to a scene at Bourton where Clarissa was rude about a neighbour's affair. Woolf shows a judgement forming as a sensation first and an argument second, which is how most of the novel's opinions about people are made.

quotations.text: The compensation of growing old, Peter Walsh thought, coming out of Regent’s Park, and holding his hat in hand, was simply this; that the passions remain as strong as ever
quotations.context: Leaving the park in the early afternoon.
quotations.analysis: He is fifty-three, in love with a married woman he refuses to admit he is in love with, and calls the persistence of feeling a compensation. The novel lets the claim stand and then follows him through an entire day of proving its second half — that age brings the power to handle what one feels — false.

quotations.text: He had gone through the whole show, friendship, European War, death, had won promotion, was still under thirty and was bound to survive.
quotations.context: Septimus's history: the volunteer who congratulated himself on feeling nothing.
quotations.analysis: Four years are itemised as a list with commas, in which a friendship, a continental war and a death carry equal weight and none carries any. 'The whole show' is the language soldiers used, and here it is doing exactly the work it was invented for — making an experience small enough to carry.

quotations.text: He had not cared when Evans was killed; that was worst
quotations.context: The charge Septimus brings against himself in the small hours.
quotations.analysis: The crime he cannot forgive is an absence, not an act, and the two-word verdict at the end is delivered in his own voice without any narrator softening it. The whole medical apparatus of the novel is engaged in treating a man for a failure of feeling that he has already identified more accurately than either doctor.

quotations.text: Once you fall, Septimus repeated to himself, human nature is on you. Holmes and Bradshaw are on you.
quotations.context: After Sir William has decided on a home in the country.
quotations.analysis: The two doctors are named in the same breath as human nature and given the same grammar — something that is 'on you', like weather or a pack. Woolf has made the medical profession into a hunting metaphor, and the sentence explains why, an hour later, a man will prefer a window to a waiting room.

quotations.text: Proportion, divine proportion, Sir William’s goddess
quotations.context: The narrator stepping aside to describe what Bradshaw actually worships.
quotations.analysis: The novel abandons any single consciousness here and speaks in its own voice, capitalising an abstraction into a deity with a biography — hospitals walked, salmon caught, a son begotten in Harley Street. Making a medical principle into a goddess lets Woolf treat a professional opinion as a religion with converts and casualties.

quotations.text: Conversion is her name and she feasts on the wills of the weakly, loving to impress, to impose, adoring her own features stamped on the face of the populace.
quotations.context: Proportion's less presentable sister, named a page later.
quotations.analysis: The verbs escalate from impress to impose, and the last image — a face stamped on a population like a head on a coin — puts missionary work, empire and psychiatric care in a single frame. This is the most openly political sentence in the novel, and it is aimed at a doctor with excellent manners.

quotations.text: order rest in bed; rest in solitude; silence and rest; rest without friends, without books, without messages
quotations.context: Sir William's prescription, described by the narrator in his own idiom.
quotations.analysis: The word 'rest' appears four times in a single clause and each repetition takes something else away, so that a comfort is converted into a deprivation by accumulation alone. Read the list as a description of a room rather than a treatment and it is a cell — which is the reading the sentence is engineered to produce.

quotations.text: (But he could not bring himself to say he loved her; not in so many words.)
quotations.context: Richard arriving home with roses he has carried across London for that purpose.
quotations.analysis: Woolf puts the most important fact of the marriage inside brackets, which is exactly the status it has in the marriage. The reader knows what the flowers were rehearsed to say and Clarissa does not, and the novel treats that ordinary failure with the same seriousness it gives to a death.

quotations.text: love and religion would destroy that, whatever it was, the privacy of the soul
quotations.reference: Miss Kilman, Elizabeth and the Strand
quotations.context: Clarissa at the window, watching the old woman in the house opposite.
quotations.analysis: The two forces usually credited with saving people are here named as the two most likely to invade them, and the grammar hesitates — 'whatever it was' — because she cannot define the thing she is defending. It is the nearest Clarissa comes to a creed, and she arrives at it while looking through a window at a stranger going to bed.

quotations.text: here was one room; there another. Did religion solve that, or love?
quotations.reference: Miss Kilman, Elizabeth and the Strand
quotations.context: The same passage, stating the problem the old woman opposite represents.
quotations.analysis: The supreme mystery is reduced to a matter of architecture: two rooms, and no way through the wall. Posing it as a question with two candidate answers and no verdict is characteristic — the novel prefers to leave the problem standing and let a party be the provisional reply.

quotations.text: Holmes was coming upstairs. Holmes would burst open the door.
quotations.context: The last minute of Septimus's life, alone in the sitting room.
quotations.analysis: Two short sentences beginning with the same name, one in the past continuous and one in the conditional: the doctor is both already here and about to arrive. Septimus then considers a bread knife, the gas and a razor before the window, so the death is not an impulse but the last item on a list of doors that are shut.

quotations.text: Death was defiance. Death was an attempt to communicate; people feeling the impossibility of reaching the centre which, mystically, evaded them; closeness drew apart
quotations.context: Clarissa alone in a small room, having been told of the young man's suicide.
quotations.analysis: She reaches an interpretation of a stranger's death by way of her own life, and the sentence turns from statement to explanation without a break. The clause about closeness drawing apart is her marriage, her lost friendship with Sally and her own party all at once, and she does not notice that she has changed subject.

quotations.text: She felt glad that he had done it; thrown it away while they went on living.
quotations.context: The same scene, a moment before she returns to her guests.
quotations.analysis: 'Glad' is the word the novel risks everything on, and the semicolon does the work: the act is named only as 'it', twice, and never as death. Setting his throwing away against their going on living makes survival, not suicide, the thing that requires justifying.

quotations.text: It is Clarissa, he said. For there she was.
quotations.context: The last two sentences of the novel, in Peter Walsh's mind.
quotations.analysis: After a day of remembering her the answer turns out to be presence rather than memory, and the novel ends on the verb 'was' — past tense at the exact moment of arrival. There is no dialogue, no meeting and no resolution: a man identifies the source of his own terror and ecstasy, and the book stops.

themes.name: Men, women and what manhood licenses
Repair, and what it cannot mend

quotations.text: There is a kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick and her: they never meet but there's a skirmish of wit between them.
quotations.speaker: Leonato
quotations.context: Explaining Beatrice to the messenger, who has just heard her insult a man she claims not to care about.
quotations.analysis: The phrase frames the relationship as a spectacle the household enjoys, which is exactly why the two of them cannot drop it: an audience is watching. Note that it is the uncle who supplies the label, before either of them is on stage together — their love is a matter of public commentary before it is a matter of feeling.

quotations.text: What, my dear Lady Disdain! are you yet living?
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: His first words to Beatrice in the play, after she has interrupted him.
quotations.analysis: He greets her with an allegorical title, as though she were a figure in a morality play rather than a person, and she takes the personification off him in her reply and feeds it.
