Neither of them uses the other's name in this whole exchange, which is the shape of the defence they have both agreed to.

quotations.text: I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Agreeing, competitively, with Benedick's claim that he loves no woman.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is precise: both are noise made by a creature that does not mean anything by it. She says this in front of her uncle and a room of guests, which makes it a position she will have to be seen to abandon — and the friends who trick her know it.

quotations.text: Can the world buy such a jewel?
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Asking Benedick what he thinks of Hero, minutes after arriving in Messina.
quotations.analysis: Benedick has just asked whether he means to buy her, and Claudio's answer accepts the vocabulary without noticing it. He values Hero as a possession whose worth is set by general agreement, which is why a general agreement that she is worthless can destroy her in one scene.

quotations.text: it must not be denied but I am a plain-dealing villain. I am trusted with a muzzle and enfranchised with a clog;
quotations.speaker: Don John
quotations.context: To Conrade, who has advised him to look more cheerful now that he is reconciled to his brother.
quotations.analysis: He claims the one virtue available to him — not pretending — and describes his pardon as a muzzle and a chained block. The imagery is of a dangerous animal on a lead, and it is his own; the play gives him no motive beyond the position his birth has left him in.

quotations.text: Sigh no more, ladies, sigh no more, Men were deceivers ever, One foot in sea and one on shore, To one thing constant never:
quotations.speaker: Balthasar
quotations.context: The song sung in Leonato's orchard while Benedick hides in the arbour.
quotations.analysis: The song tells women to stop grieving over men who are unreliable by nature, and it is performed as cover for three men about to tell an elaborate lie. Its advice is also the play's plot in advance: Claudio will be exactly the deceiver described, and the ladies will be told to let him go.

quotations.text: No, the world must be peopled. When I said I would die a bachelor, I did not think I should live till I were married.
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Alone in the orchard, immediately after the gulling.
quotations.analysis: He reverses a public vow in two sentences and gives a reason of cosmic scale for a decision of purely private appetite. The joke in the second sentence is a genuine piece of self-knowledge dressed as a quibble: he did not expect to live long enough to be caught out, and he has been.

quotations.text: Contempt, farewell! and maiden pride, adieu! No glory lives behind the back of such. And, Benedick, love on; I will requite thee, Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand:
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Coming forward after overhearing Hero and Ursula discuss her pride.
quotations.analysis: She surrenders in rhymed verse, the only time she speaks it, and the metrical shift does the work a soliloquy would do elsewhere. The falconry image — a wild bird taken to the hand — is one she chooses herself, and it concedes rather more than the trick actually asked for.

quotations.text: Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.
quotations.speaker: Hero
quotations.context: The closing line of the scene in which she and Ursula trap Beatrice.
quotations.analysis: Hero, who is usually spoken about rather than speaking, gets the couplet that names the play's method. A trap is not an arrow: it requires planning, bait and a victim who walks in, and every match in Messina is made that way, including the one that goes wrong.

quotations.text: Comparisons are odorous: palabras, neighbour Verges.
quotations.speaker: Dogberry
quotations.context: Trying to tell Leonato what his watch has arrested, on the morning of the wedding.
quotations.analysis: He means odious, and the mistake is funnier than the word he wanted; but the scene is also the play's most painful piece of timing, because Leonato is in a hurry and sends him away. The catastrophe of Act IV is entirely preventable, and it is prevented by nobody because of who is speaking.

quotations.text: O, what men dare do! what men may do! what men daily
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: In the church, beginning the accusation, having so far refused to say the word 'marry'.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation is about men, not about Hero, and it is the nearest the scene comes to self-knowledge: what men dare do is precisely what Claudio is about to do to a girl in front of her father. The line breaks off mid-sentence, and the completed thought never arrives.

quotations.text: Give not this rotten orange to your friend; She's but the sign and semblance of her honour.
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Handing Hero back to Leonato at the altar.
quotations.analysis: The image is of fruit that looks sound and is spoiled inside, and it turns a person into damaged goods being returned to a supplier. 'Sign and semblance' is the play's own subject stated by its worst reader of signs: Claudio has believed a semblance, and he is accusing her of being one.

quotations.text: But fare thee well, most foul, most fair! farewell, Thou pure impiety and impious purity!
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: His last words to Hero before she faints.
quotations.analysis: Two lines of perfectly balanced antithesis produced by a man in what he presents as uncontrollable grief — the rhetoric is far too neat for the emotion it claims. Shakespeare gives him the figure twice over, with the nouns and adjectives swapped in the second half, so that the speech sounds composed in advance, because it was.

quotations.text: I do love nothing in the world so well as you: is not that strange?
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Alone with Beatrice in the empty church after Hero has been carried out.
quotations.analysis: The declaration arrives in the wreckage of somebody else's wedding, and he ends it with a question because he cannot say it without a shrug. 'Nothing' is the title word, and here it is doing honest work for once: he loves nothing so well, in a play where nothing has been the cause of all the trouble.

quotations.text: Kill Claudio.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Her answer when Benedick tells her to bid him do anything for her.
quotations.analysis: Two words, immediately after a page of elaborate prose, and the shortest speech either of them makes in the play. It is the point where the comedy's machinery — a lover offering extravagant service — is taken literally, and the audience's laughter, which almost always comes, is part of what the scene is testing.

quotations.text: O God, that I were a man! I would eat his heart in the market-place.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Explaining to Benedick why Claudio is her enemy.
quotations.analysis: She says it three times in twenty lines, which is a measure of how completely her wit has failed her. 'In the market-place' is the detail that matters: Hero was destroyed in public, so the revenge Beatrice imagines is public too, and it has to be carried out by a man because the law and the sword both belong to men.

quotations.text: But manhood is melted into courtesies, valour into compliment, and men are only turned into tongue, and trim ones too
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Continuing the same speech, on the men of Messina.
quotations.analysis: It is a complaint about talk from the play's best talker, and it convicts her own weapon: wit is what the men have instead of action. The verbs are all of liquefaction and exchange — melted, turned — as though a substance had been swapped for a currency.

quotations.text: O that he were here to write me down an ass! But, masters, remember that I am an ass; though it be not written down, yet forget not that I am an ass.
quotations.speaker: Dogberry
quotations.context: In the prison, having been called an ass by Conrade during the examination.
quotations.analysis: His grievance is that the insult has not been entered in the record, and the joke is that he insists on the record being complete even when it damns him. Messina has just ruined a girl on unwritten testimony; the constable is the only person in the play who believes that what is said should be written down.

quotations.text: For there was never yet philosopher That could endure the toothache patiently,
quotations.speaker: Leonato
quotations.context: Refusing his brother's advice to bear his daughter's disgrace calmly.
quotations.analysis: He answers moral consolation with dentistry, and the deflation is the point: the men who counsel patience have not been in the chair. It is the best serious writing in the play and it is given to the man who, one scene earlier, wished his daughter dead rather than shamed.

quotations.text: Done to death by slanderous tongues Was the Hero that here lies:
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Reading the epitaph at Leonato's monument, believing Hero dead.
quotations.analysis: The penance is a poem, hung on a tomb containing nobody, read by the man whose tongue did most of the slandering — and the epitaph does not name him. Shakespeare gives the scene formal rhymed stanzas and a ritual, which is either the repair Messina needs or an exact measure of how cheap its rituals are.

quotations.text: for man is a giddy thing, and this is my conclusion.
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Explaining why nobody should mock him for marrying after swearing he never would.
quotations.analysis: He does not defend the reversal; he generalises it into a fact about the species and calls that a conclusion. It is the play's answer to its own machinery — people are talked into things, and the sensible response is to marry, dance, and not examine it too closely.

books.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
books.author: Frederick Douglass

quotations.text: Mr. Douglass has very properly chosen to write his own Narrative, in his own style, and according to the best of his ability, rather than to employ someone else. It is, therefore, entirely his own production
quotations.speaker: William Lloyd Garrison
quotations.context: In the preface, before the reader reaches Douglass's first sentence.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a defence, which means it tells you what the accusation was. Garrison has to certify the authorship of a book whose author is standing beside him, and the very act of certifying reproduces the assumption it answers — the reader is being asked to trust a white man about a black man's prose.

quotations.text: I have no accurate knowledge of my age, never having seen any authentic record containing it.
quotations.context: The second sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: An autobiography conventionally opens with a date, and this one opens with the absence of one. The words are the language of evidence — accurate, authentic, record — so the first thing Douglass establishes is not a feeling but a documentary gap, and the rest of the chapter shows that the gap was arranged.

quotations.text: slaveholders have ordained, and by law established, that the children of slave women shall in all cases follow the condition of their mothers
quotations.context: Immediately after reporting the rumour that his owner was his father.
quotations.analysis: He does not pursue the rumour; he cites the statute instead, and the shift from gossip to legislation is the whole method of the book in one move. Naming the law also names the incentive: a rule that makes a man's children his property turns a private crime into an investment.

quotations.text: It was the bloodstained gate, the entrance to the hell of slavery, through which I was about to pass.
quotations.context: On witnessing the whipping of his aunt, as a small child.
quotations.analysis: The image is architectural rather than emotional: a gate is something you go through on the way somewhere, so the beating is presented as an initiation into a place that he had been living in all along without seeing it. The tense does the work — he is about to pass through a door he has already been carried across.

quotations.text: No words, no tears, no prayers, from his gory victim, seemed to move his iron heart from its bloody purpose.
quotations.context: Describing the whipping of his aunt in the kitchen at daybreak.
quotations.analysis: Three refusals in a row, each shorter than a clause needs to be, and then the sentence stops. The triple negative registers a system rather than a temper: appeals of every kind have been tried and none of them is a working part of this arrangement.

quotations.text: This they would sing, as a chorus, to words which to many would seem unmeaning jargon, but which, nevertheless, were full of meaning to themselves.
quotations.context: On the songs sung by people walking to the great house farm.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built as a correction: a first clause in the voice of the overhearing stranger, then a hinge on 'nevertheless', then the truth. Douglass is describing a coded literature that his readers have been in the presence of without noticing, and he is describing his own book at the same time.

quotations.text: Slaves sing most when they are most unhappy. The songs of the slave represent the sorrows of his heart; and he is relieved by them, only as an aching heart is relieved by its tears.
quotations.context: Answering northerners who cite the singing as evidence of contentment.
quotations.analysis: This is the book acting as an expert witness on a disputed piece of evidence, and it wins by explaining the mechanism rather than by protesting. The comparison with weeping is exact: relief is admitted, and the admission is what makes the correction hard to dismiss.

quotations.text: It would forever unfit him to be a slave. He would at once become unmanageable, and of no value to his master.
quotations.speaker: Hugh Auld
quotations.context: Forbidding his wife to continue teaching Douglass to read, with Douglass in the room.
quotations.analysis: The argument against literacy is put in the language of property maintenance — fitness, manageability, value — and it is the most accurate sentence any enslaver speaks in the book. Auld believes he is protecting an asset, and he is in fact reading out the instructions.

quotations.text: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
quotations.context: Immediately after overhearing Hugh Auld's prohibition.
quotations.analysis: The verb is 'understood', not 'decided': what he has been handed is a map rather than a motive, and he had the motive already. The short declarative closes the scene like a door, and the next seven years of the narrative are spent walking the route it names.

quotations.text: That cheerful eye, under the influence of slavery, soon became red with rage; that voice, made all of sweet accord, changed to one of harsh and horrid discord; and that angelic face gave place to that of a demon.
quotations.context: On the change in Sophia Auld after her husband stops the lessons.
quotations.analysis: Three parallel clauses, each pairing a feature with its ruin, so that a woman is described by the same method Douglass uses for a plantation economy. The agent named in the sentence is not Sophia Auld but slavery, which is the book's consistent claim: ownership damages the owner as reliably as it damages anybody else.

quotations.text: I would at times feel that learning to read had been a curse rather than a blessing. It had given me a view of my wretched condition, without the remedy. It opened my eyes to the horrible pit, but to no ladder upon which to get out.
quotations.context: After reading The Columbian Orator and abolitionist speeches, aged about twelve.
quotations.analysis: The second and third sentences say the same thing twice, once abstractly and once as an image, and the repetition enacts the state it describes: a mind going round something it cannot leave. It also refuses the comfortable version of the story, in which education arrives as deliverance.

quotations.text: The silver trump of freedom had roused my soul to eternal wakefulness.
quotations.context: Describing the period after he could read, when the thought of his condition would not leave him.
quotations.analysis: The trumpet is the one from the resurrection, which makes wakefulness a permanent condition rather than a morning. Read beside the sentences around it — he wishes himself a beast, he envies the stupidity of others — the grandeur of the image is the problem, not the consolation.

quotations.text: Thus ended our little Sabbath school in the pious town of St. Michael’s.
quotations.context: After class leaders broke up a Sunday reading class with sticks and missiles.
quotations.analysis: One flat sentence, and the whole weight rests on the word 'pious', which is doing the work a page of argument would otherwise do. Douglass rarely raises his voice at moments like this; he lets the adjective sit next to the facts and leaves the reader to make the collision.

quotations.text: You are loosed from your moorings, and are free; I am fast in my chains, and am a slave!
quotations.context: Alone on the banks of the Chesapeake, speaking aloud to the sails on the bay.
quotations.analysis: The clause structure is a pair of balanced opposites, and the man speaking it has nobody to hear him but the ships. It is the first speech Douglass ever reports himself making, and it is already built like a platform address — the future lecturer is audible in it years before he has an audience.

quotations.text: I was broken in body, soul, and spirit.
quotations.context: After six months under Edward Covey.
quotations.analysis: Three nouns, no qualification, and the passive voice admitting that it worked. Douglass gives the defeat its own paragraph before he gives the fight one, and the ordering matters: the recovery in August only counts because he has let the reader see the man who had stopped wanting to read.

quotations.text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
quotations.context: Introducing the fight with Covey, halfway through the longest chapter in the book.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a chiasmus, and it turns on its axis exactly where the book does. Note that both halves are passive: a man is made, and then made again, so even the recovery is described as something done to him — the agency arrives in the next paragraph, with his hands.

quotations.text: This battle with Mr. Covey was the turning-point in my career as a slave. It rekindled the few expiring embers of freedom, and revived within me a sense of my own manhood.
quotations.context: Immediately after the two-hour fight in the stable yard.
quotations.analysis: 'Career' is a startling word to apply to being owned, and it is chosen: it insists that the years had a shape and that he can analyse them. Both verbs — rekindled, revived — describe the return of something that existed before Covey, which is how Douglass avoids making freedom a thing granted to him by an event.

quotations.text: It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom.
quotations.context: Describing what the fight with Covey did to him.
quotations.analysis: He takes the central image of the religion his enslavers profess and applies it to an act of physical violence against one of them. That is the argument of the appendix made in a single phrase, four chapters early, and it is why the book cannot be read as a quarrel with Christianity.

quotations.text: In coming to a fixed determination to run away, we did more than Patrick Henry, when he resolved upon liberty or death. With us it was a doubtful liberty at most, and almost certain death if we failed.
quotations.context: On the six men who planned to take a canoe up the Chesapeake in 1836.
quotations.analysis: He does not ask to be compared to a founding patriot; he asserts that the comparison undersells him, and then supplies the arithmetic. Addressed to American readers who kept Patrick Henry's sentence on their walls, the claim converts a national slogan into a test its owners have failed.

quotations.text: They came because they wished to learn. Their minds had been starved by their cruel masters. They had been shut up in mental darkness.
quotations.context: On the Sabbath school he kept at William Freeland's, which grew to over forty scholars.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is deliberately physical — starved, shut up — and it matches the accounting of pork and meal earlier in the book, so that a withheld education is placed in the same ledger as a withheld ration. Every one of those scholars risked thirty-nine lashes to attend, which Douglass mentions without adjective.

quotations.text: I have never approved of the very public manner in which some of our western friends have conducted what they call the underground railroad
quotations.context: Opening the final chapter, explaining why he will not describe his escape.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is tactical, not moral: he goes on to honour the courage of the people he is criticising. What the sentence establishes is that the author has a professional judgement about what may be printed, which quietly rebuts the idea that a witness owes the reader everything he knows.

quotations.text: I felt like one who had escaped a den of hungry lions.
quotations.context: Quoting a letter he wrote to a friend on reaching New York in September 1838.
quotations.analysis: He quotes his own younger self rather than describing the feeling directly, and then immediately undercuts it: the elation subsides within a paragraph into insecurity and loneliness among thousands of strangers. The structure refuses the ending that the escape narrative is expected to supply.

quotations.text: I must hold on to that, to preserve a sense of my identity.
quotations.context: Letting Nathan Johnson choose him a surname in New Bedford, on condition that the first name stays.
quotations.analysis: He has been Bailey, Stanley and Johnson within a fortnight, and the surname that reaches the title page is picked out of Walter Scott by a man he has just met. Against all that, the retained forename is the whole of the continuity he has, and he says so in the vocabulary of ownership: hold on, preserve.

quotations.text: I love the pure, peaceable, and impartial Christianity of Christ: I therefore hate the corrupt, slaveholding, women-whipping, cradle-plundering, partial and hypocritical Christianity of this land.
quotations.context: Opening the appendix, written to forestall the charge that he is an enemy of religion.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built as a balance with a hinge — 'I therefore hate' — so that the hatred is presented as a consequence of the love rather than an alternative to it. The second half runs to six adjectives against the first half's three, and the compounds are all crimes, so the prose is weighted the way the argument is.

quotations.text: I follow him to serve my turn upon him:
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Explaining to Roderigo, in the street at night, why he still works for Othello.
quotations.analysis: 'Follow' and 'serve' are the vocabulary of loyal service, and he uses both against their meaning in a single line. The plan is announced in the play's first fifty lines, so nothing Iago does later is a surprise to anyone except the people on stage.

quotations.text: But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve For daws to peck at: I am not what I am.
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: The end of his account of the two kinds of servant.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a flat contradiction that cannot be unpacked into sense, which is exactly its function: he tells the truth about himself in a form that guarantees nothing follows from it. It also inverts the formula God gives Moses, and the audience is left holding a confession no character has heard.

quotations.text: Even now, now, very now, an old black ram Is topping your white ewe.
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Shouted up at Brabantio's window in the dark, before Othello has appeared.
quotations.analysis: The audience is given the marriage as an image of livestock before it meets either partner, and the colour contrast is doing the work of an argument. Iago is anonymous in the dark here, which lets the play introduce the prejudice as a voice from the street rather than the view of a named character.

quotations.text: Rude am I in my speech, And little bless'd with the soft phrase of peace:
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Beginning his defence before the Duke and the senators.
quotations.analysis: A claim to be a poor speaker, made in perfectly balanced verse at the opening of the most persuasive speech in the play. The modesty is a rhetorical device with a long pedigree, and its success in this scene is what makes Act III so painful: he can handle a senate but not an insinuation.

quotations.text: She loved me for the dangers I had pass'd, And I loved her that she did pity them.
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Ending his account of how the courtship happened, over dinners at her father's house.
quotations.analysis: The couplet balances two lines and two verbs and quietly reveals an asymmetry: she loves a story, he loves being listened to. That is a real marriage and a fragile one, and Iago's whole campaign consists of offering Othello a different story about himself.

quotations.text: I do perceive here a divided duty: To you I am bound for life and education;
quotations.speaker: Desdemona
quotations.context: Asked by her father, in front of the Senate, where she owes most obedience.
quotations.analysis: She answers a question about love with an analysis of obligation, and the structure of the speech — father first, husband second, precedent from her own mother — is legal rather than romantic. It is the most politically skilful thing anyone says in the scene, and she is about twenty.

quotations.text: Look to her, Moor, if thou hast eyes to see: She has deceived her father, and may thee.
quotations.speaker: Brabantio
quotations.context: His parting shot as the Senate breaks up.
quotations.analysis: A father's last piece of spite, delivered in a rhyming couplet so that it sticks. Iago never has to make this argument himself: it has already been said in public by a senator, and Othello recalls it in the middle of Act III as though it were evidence.

quotations.text: The Moor is of a free and open nature, That thinks men honest that but seem to be so, And will as tenderly be led by the nose As asses are.
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act I, working out his plan.
quotations.analysis: It is an accurate character reference and a plan of attack in the same sentence: the quality he names is generosity, and he treats it as an exploit. The animal simile arrives at the end of the thought rather than the beginning, so the insult lands after the compliment has been accepted.

quotations.text: Reputation, reputation, reputation! O, I have lost my reputation! I have lost the immortal part of myself, and what remains is bestial.
quotations.speaker: Cassio
quotations.context: Drunk and disgraced, moments after the brawl that costs him his lieutenancy.
quotations.analysis: Five uses of the word in three lines, in prose, from a man too drunk to vary his vocabulary — and the content is theologically serious. Iago answers by calling reputation an idle imposition, then tells Othello the opposite in 3.3, which is the clearest evidence that he believes neither.

quotations.text: Excellent wretch! Perdition catch my soul, But I do love thee! and when I love thee not, Chaos is come again.
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: As Desdemona leaves the garden, seconds before Iago begins.
quotations.analysis: He phrases his love as a condition on which the order of the world depends, and does it minutes before the world is dismantled. The construction is a hostage to fortune and the play collects: within four hundred lines he will love her not, and the noun he chose is the one that arrives.

quotations.text: Good name in man and woman, dear my lord, Is the immediate jewel of their souls: Who steals my purse steals trash;
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Refusing, at length, to say what he is thinking.
quotations.analysis: He argues for the sanctity of reputation as a reason not to speak, which makes the withholding look like scruple rather than technique. The same man told Cassio in 2.3 that reputation was an idle imposition; the contradiction is never noticed on stage because each speech is exactly what its hearer needs.

quotations.text: O, beware, my lord, of jealousy; It is the green-eyed monster which doth mock The meat it feeds on;
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Warning Othello against a feeling he has not yet described.
quotations.analysis: A warning that functions as an instruction: the word is placed in Othello's mind under cover of protecting him from it. The image is of something that plays with its food rather than eating it, which is a fair description of what Iago is doing for the rest of the scene.

quotations.text: Trifles light as air Are to the jealous confirmations strong As proofs of holy writ:
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Alone, having just taken the handkerchief from Emilia.
quotations.analysis: He states his epistemology out loud and it is correct: once a man is jealous, weight of evidence stops mattering and any object will do. The comparison with scripture is precise — proof that cannot be questioned because questioning it is already the offence.

quotations.text: Farewell the tranquil mind! farewell content! Farewell the plumed troop, and the big wars, That make ambition virtue!
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Rounding on Iago, having accepted that his wife is unfaithful.
quotations.analysis: Told that his marriage is over, he says goodbye to his career. The list is entirely military — troops, banners, drums — because his occupation and his sense of himself are the same thing, and Iago has just removed the domestic foundation the whole structure stood on.

quotations.text: Villain, be sure thou prove my love a whore, Be sure of it; give me the ocular proof:
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Seizing Iago by the throat in the middle of the garden scene.
quotations.analysis: The demand sounds rigorous and is already a defeat: he has accepted the charge and is asking only to be shown it. Note the word order — 'my love a whore' assumes the conclusion inside the request — and note that what he is eventually given to see is a conversation about another woman.

quotations.text: Like to the Pontic sea, Whose icy current and compulsive course Ne'er feels retiring ebb, but keeps due on
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Rejecting Iago's suggestion that he may change his mind.
quotations.analysis: He describes his own resolve as a current that cannot turn, using a geographical fact about the Black Sea to make a psychological claim. The passage appears in the Folio and not in the 1622 quarto, so some early readers met an Othello who never said it.

quotations.text: But I do think it is their husbands' faults If wives do fall: say that they slack their duties, And pour our treasures into foreign laps,
quotations.speaker: Emilia
quotations.context: Undressing Desdemona for bed, after a conversation about whether any woman would betray her husband.
quotations.analysis: The argument is causal rather than moral: she is not defending adultery but explaining it as a response. Coming at the end of an act in which Desdemona has been struck and called a whore, it is the play's only sustained analysis of marriage from inside one, and it is spoken by the woman who lost the handkerchief.

quotations.text: It is the cause, it is the cause, my soul,-- Let me not name it to you, you chaste stars!-- It is the cause.
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Entering the bedchamber with a light, Desdemona asleep.
quotations.analysis: Three statements and no object: he cannot say what the cause is, and the refusal is addressed to the stars rather than to himself. 'Cause' is a legal word, and he uses it to convert a murder into a sentence — the speech is the machinery by which he becomes, in his own account, a judge.

quotations.text: Put out the light, and then put out the light:
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Standing over the bed with a taper in his hand.
quotations.analysis: The same six words twice, meaning a candle and then a life, and the difference between them is the whole of the following seven lines: the lamp can be relit, she cannot. He is working out the metaphor while holding the object, which is why the line can only be understood in performance.

quotations.text: Nobody; I myself. Farewell Commend me to my kind lord: O, farewell!
quotations.speaker: Desdemona
quotations.context: Asked by Emilia who has done this deed.
quotations.analysis: Her last act is to lie to protect the man who has just killed her, and the adjective she chooses for him is 'kind'. Whether this is love, self-abnegation or a final failure of the play to let her speak for herself has been argued for four centuries, and the text supplies no stage direction to settle it.

quotations.text: O, the more angel she, And you the blacker devil!
quotations.speaker: Emilia
quotations.context: Hearing Othello admit that he killed Desdemona, and that she died denying it.
quotations.analysis: She reaches for the colour vocabulary the play has been circling since the first scene, and turns it on Othello at the moment he is least able to answer. It is also the first time anyone in Cyprus contradicts him to his face, and the whole exposure of Iago follows from a servant refusing to be quiet.

quotations.text: Demand me nothing: what you know, you know: From this time forth I never will speak word.
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Asked why he has ensnared Othello's soul and body.
quotations.analysis: The one thing an audience wants at the end of this play is an explanation, and he withholds it deliberately, in a couplet, having talked more than anyone else for five acts. The silence is his last piece of control: no motive can now be checked against the deeds.

quotations.text: Speak of me as I am; nothing extenuate, Nor set down aught in malice: then must you speak Of one that loved not wisely but too well;
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: His last speech, before the concealed dagger.
quotations.analysis: He commissions his own obituary and then dictates it, which is not quite the same as accepting judgement. The phrase 'loved not wisely but too well' is a considerable piece of editing by a man who smothered his wife on the word of an ensign, and the play lets him have it without endorsing it.

themes.name: Loss, exile and what can be carried out

quotations.text: Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit Of that forbidden Tree, whose mortal taste Brought death into the world, and all our woe, With loss of Eden, till one greater Man Restore us, and regain the blissful seat
quotations.context: The opening of the poem, before the invocation names its muse.
quotations.analysis: The sentence withholds its verb for sixteen lines: everything here is object, and the reader is left holding disobedience, fruit, death, woe and Eden with nothing yet to do with them. Placing the remedy inside the first sentence, before the crime has been narrated, also tells you the poem is not a suspense plot.

quotations.text: That to the highth of this great argument I may assert the Eternal Providence, And justify the ways of God to men.
quotations.context: The close of the invocation to the heavenly muse.
quotations.analysis: 'Argument' means both the poem's subject and a case put to a court, and Milton takes the second sense seriously enough to have God testify in Book III. 'Justify' is a legal verb: he is not proposing to praise God but to answer a charge, which is a startling thing to promise in a poem's first thirty lines.

quotations.text: yet from those flames No light, but rather darkness visible Served only to discover sights of woe
quotations.context: Satan's first sight of Hell, as far as angels can see.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is a contradiction that works as a description: flames that illuminate nothing except how much there is to dread. Milton needs light in Hell so that the fallen can see each other and their situation, and needs it to be useless, so he invents a category of darkness that performs the office of light.

quotations.text: What though the field be lost? All is not lost; the unconquerable will, And study of revenge, immortal hate, And courage never to submit or yield:
quotations.context: Satan's first speech to Beelzebub on the burning lake.
quotations.analysis: Read the list rather than the tone: an unconquerable will, a course of study in revenge, and hate described as immortal. Three of the four items are heroic virtues and one is simply a refusal to stop, and the speech works on the reader exactly as it works on the legions — by sounding like resolve before it can be inspected as a programme.

quotations.text: The mind is its own place, and in itself Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.
quotations.context: Satan taking possession of Hell on landing.
quotations.analysis: The claim is refuted by the speaker himself three books later, when he finds that the mind being its own place is precisely the trouble. The symmetry of the line invites agreement before the sense has been checked: it is the kind of sentence that survives detached from its speaker, which is how it usually travels.

quotations.text: Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven.
quotations.context: The conclusion of Satan's speech on first surveying his new kingdom.
quotations.analysis: The line presents a choice that was never on offer — nobody asked him to choose between ruling and serving — and its balance disguises the fact that one half is imaginary. It also sets the terms the rest of the poem will dismantle, since service in Heaven is shown to involve conversation, work and food, and reigning in Hell turns out to mean addressing an audience with nowhere else to go.

quotations.text: Awake, arise, or be for ever fallen!
quotations.context: Satan rousing the legions lying stunned on the lake.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives and a threat, all in one line of monosyllables after hundreds of lines of elaborate syntax — the sudden plainness is the point. 'Fallen' does double work as a military disgrace and as their actual physical position, and the whole sentence can be shouted, which is what it is for.

quotations.text: Long is the way And hard, that out of Hell leads up to light;
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: Satan addressing the assembly before volunteering for the journey alone.
quotations.analysis: He is describing a route through Chaos and stating, without noticing, the moral condition of everyone listening. The line is also a piece of management: by making the errand sound impossible he ensures nobody else offers to share it, and the sole risk becomes sole credit.

quotations.text: The one seemed woman to the waist, and fair, But ended foul in many a scaly fold Voluminous and vast, a serpent armed With mortal sting.
quotations.context: The first description of Sin, seated at the gates of Hell.
quotations.analysis: Milton gives the allegory a joint: fair above, foul below, with the change of substance happening at the waist. The serpent's shape arrives here, long before Eden, so that when Satan enters a real snake in Book IX he is putting on something already in the family.

quotations.text: Chaos umpire sits, And by decision more embroils the fray By which he reigns; next him, high arbiter, Chance governs all.
quotations.context: The description of the abyss Satan must cross.
quotations.analysis: Both officials named here are supposed to settle disputes, and both make them worse: the umpire's rulings increase the brawl he presides over. Milton is describing a region without providence, and he does it by borrowing the vocabulary of courts and games and showing it failing.

quotations.text: Hail, holy Light, offspring of Heaven first-born!
quotations.context: The invocation opening Book III, as the poem leaves Hell for Heaven.
quotations.analysis: A blind man greets the one thing he cannot have, and the greeting is a formal salutation rather than a lament. The passage that follows turns the poem's structure into biography: he has just come up out of darkness in the narrative, and has not come up out of it at all.

quotations.text: I made him just and right, Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall.
quotations.speaker: God the Father
quotations.context: God, seeing Satan approach the new world, states in advance where the fault will lie.
quotations.analysis: The whole defence is balanced on one line, and on the difference between 'sufficient' and 'certain'. Had man been made unable to fall, the standing would have been mechanical; the poem's God would rather be accused of cruelty than build a creature whose obedience proves nothing.

quotations.text: Freely they stood who stood, and fell who fell.
quotations.speaker: God the Father
quotations.context: Extending the same argument from man to the angels.
quotations.analysis: Nine words, eight of them monosyllables, and the same adverb governing both halves — the freedom is identical on either side of the outcome. The chiasmus makes standing and falling grammatically equal, which is exactly the claim: nothing in the arrangement favoured one result over the other.

quotations.text: Which way I fly is Hell; myself am Hell; And, in the lowest deep, a lower deep Still threatening to devour me opens wide,
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: Alone on Mount Niphates, in sight of Eden, before entering the garden.
quotations.analysis: This is the answer to his own boast in Book I: the mind being its own place is the trap, not the escape. The geometry is the frightening part — a lowest deep that keeps opening a lower one means there is no floor, and Milton gives the idea in four monosyllables before the sentence stops.

quotations.text: So farewell hope, and with hope farewell fear, Farewell remorse! All good to me is lost; Evil, be thou my good:
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: The conclusion of the soliloquy on Niphates, where he considers repentance and rejects it.
quotations.analysis: He gives up fear in the same breath as hope, which is an accurate account of what despair buys. The last clause is an address, not a statement: he is conscripting evil the way a poet conscripts a muse, and the sentence has the shape of a prayer with the object swapped.

quotations.text: For contemplation he and valour formed, For softness she and sweet attractive grace; He for God only, she for God in him.
quotations.context: The narrator's first description of Adam and Eve, seen through Satan's eyes.
quotations.analysis: The doctrine is stated in the most memorable line available, with the parallel structure doing the work of proof. It is worth noticing who is looking: the description is placed inside Satan's field of view, and the poem's own drama spends five more books quietly declining to behave as the line prescribes.

quotations.text: My author and disposer, what thou bidd’st Unargued I obey; so God ordains: God is thy law, thou mine: to know no more Is woman’s happiest knowledge, and her praise.
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve answering Adam at the end of their first day in the poem.
quotations.analysis: She states the hierarchy more absolutely than Adam ever does, and she states it in an argument — the speech is fluent, ordered and rhetorically confident, which is not what unargued obedience sounds like. Five books later she will open a debate on exactly this question and win it.

quotations.text: With thee conversing I forget all time, All seasons and their change: all please alike.
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve to Adam in the garden at evening.
quotations.analysis: The love poem she then speaks is built as a list of everything she likes and a repeat of the same list with the word 'without' inserted, so that the structure itself performs the point. Here at its head, 'conversing' carries its older sense of living with as well as talking to, and it is talk that the Fall will first spoil.

quotations.text: Abashed the Devil stood, And felt how awful goodness is, and saw Virtue in her shape how lovely
quotations.context: Satan, discovered in the garden, faced down by the young angel Zephon.
quotations.analysis: The verb comes first and the subject second, so the shame arrives before the person it belongs to. 'Awful' still means awe-producing here, and the moment matters because it is the one place where Satan is shown recognising good as attractive rather than as an obstacle — and then walking on.

quotations.text: So spake the Seraph Abdiel, faithful found; Among the faithless, faithful only he;
quotations.context: After Abdiel has answered Satan's argument in front of the assembled rebel host.
quotations.analysis: The repetition works like a count: faithful, faithless, faithful, with the tally narrowing to 'only he'. Milton, writing after the Restoration had made his own politics unspeakable, gives his invented character the one action available to a defeated dissenter — to say so out loud and then leave.

quotations.text: ‘Let there be light!’ said God; and forthwith light Ethereal, first of things, quintessence pure, Sprung from the Deep
quotations.speaker: Raphael
quotations.context: Raphael's account of the first day of creation.
quotations.analysis: The quoted command takes half a line and the consequence begins in the same line, so the syntax enacts the speed of the thing described. Milton then cannot leave it alone and spends three clauses classifying the light, which is the characteristic movement of this book: a scriptural sentence followed by a poet unable to stop looking at it.

quotations.text: Heaven is for thee too high To know what passes there; be lowly wise; Think only what concerns thee and thy being;
quotations.speaker: Raphael
quotations.context: Raphael closing down Adam's questions about the motion of the heavens.
quotations.analysis: 'Lowly wise' is not an instruction to be ignorant but to be wise about the right things, and the test of it is that the angel has just spent three books answering questions. The serpent will offer Adam's wife the exact opposite bargain — knowledge as promotion — and the phrasing of this warning is what makes the offer recognisable.

quotations.text: And what is faith, love, virtue, unassayed Alone, without exterior help sustained?
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve arguing that she and Adam should work in separate parts of the garden.
quotations.analysis: This is Milton's own position, put in the mouth of the character about to be ruined by acting on it: he had argued in print that a virtue never exposed to its opposite is worth nothing. The poem does not refute her. It simply lets the argument be correct and the morning be a disaster.

quotations.text: Go; for thy stay, not free, absents thee more; Go in thy native innocence, rely On what thou hast of virtue, summon all; For God towards thee hath done his part; do thine.
quotations.speaker: Adam
quotations.context: Adam conceding the argument and letting Eve go alone.
quotations.analysis: He gives way on the same principle he is worried about: keeping her by command would make her presence worthless. The last four words are the whole theology of the poem compressed into a domestic exchange, and they are said by a man who has just lost an argument he was right to be having.

quotations.text: So saying, her rash hand in evil hour Forth reaching to the fruit, she plucked, she eat. Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat, Sighing through all her works, gave signs of woe
quotations.context: The Fall itself, at the end of the serpent's argument.
quotations.analysis: Two monosyllabic verbs, side by side without a conjunction, take up less room than the adjective attached to her hand — the act is smaller than everything around it. Then the sentence widens instantly to the whole planet, and the disproportion between the gesture and the consequence is the effect Milton has been building for nine books.

quotations.text: he scrupled not to eat, Against his better knowledge, not deceived, But fondly overcome with female charm.
quotations.context: Adam eating the fruit Eve brings him.
quotations.analysis: The clauses are arranged to remove every excuse in turn: not ignorant, not tricked, simply unwilling to be left. 'Fondly' means foolishly, and the line is the poem's coldest, because it denies Adam the dignity of a mistake and gives him a motive most readers recognise.

quotations.text: Nor love thy life, nor hate; but what thou livest Live well; how long or short, permit to Heaven.
quotations.speaker: Michael
quotations.context: Michael answering Adam, after the vision of the lazar-house of diseases.
quotations.analysis: Adam has just asked how to meet death and been shown every way it arrives. The answer refuses both available postures, clinging and despair, and puts the emphasis on an adverb: the question is not the length of the life but the manner of it, which is the first piece of advice in the poem that applies to a reader.

quotations.text: then wilt thou not be loth To leave this Paradise, but shalt possess A Paradise within thee, happier far.
quotations.speaker: Michael
quotations.context: Michael's summary of what Adam is to add to his knowledge before leaving.
quotations.analysis: The offer is comparative — happier far — which is a startling thing to say to a man being evicted from the best place there has ever been. The list that leads up to it is all practice rather than information: faith, virtue, patience, temperance, love. Paradise becomes something done, not somewhere lived.

quotations.text: The world was all before them, where to choose Their place of rest, and Providence their guide. They, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, Through Eden took their solitary way.
quotations.context: The last four lines of the poem.
quotations.analysis: Every phrase pulls two ways at once: a whole world to choose from and nowhere in particular to go; guided, and wandering; hand in hand, and solitary. Milton refuses either a triumph or a lament, and the final rhythm — slow, with a caesura in each of the last two lines — makes the reader walk out at their pace.

quotations.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The sentence claims to report a consensus and names nobody who holds it; the passive construction hides the mothers who are the actual subject. Read strictly it is also false in the book that follows, where the single men are in want of nothing and the women are in want of an income.

quotations.text: You mistake me, my dear. I have a high respect for your nerves. They are my old friends. I have heard you mention them with consideration these twenty years at least.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Answering his wife’s complaint that he has no compassion on her nerves.
quotations.analysis: The joke depends on treating an ailment as an acquaintance, and it establishes the marriage in a line: he has been amusing himself at her expense for two decades and has changed nothing. Twenty years is also the age of the eldest daughter, which quietly dates the arrangement.

quotations.text: She is tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt me; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: At the Meryton assembly, refusing Bingley’s suggestion that he dance with Elizabeth, who is sitting close enough to hear.
quotations.analysis: Eight words decide the first half of the book. The grammar is the insult: she is graded, then found insufficient for a purpose, with no verb that admits she is a person in the room. Elizabeth’s response is to repeat it as a comic story, which is how a wound is kept fresh.

quotations.text: I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Discussing Darcy’s behaviour at the assembly with Charlotte Lucas and her family.
quotations.analysis: She names the mechanism of her own prejudice and does not notice she has done it. The two pronouns are balanced against each other across the comma, which is the shape the whole novel will take: two kinds of pride meeting and neither able to see the other’s.

quotations.text: Vanity and pride are different things, though the words are often used synonymously. A person may be proud without being vain. Pride relates more to our opinion of ourselves, vanity to what we would have others think of us.
quotations.speaker: Mary Bennet
quotations.context: Mary offering the company the benefit of her reading.
quotations.analysis: The distinction is sound and the novel uses it: Darcy is proud and Wickham is vain, and the difference is exactly the one Mary draws. Austen’s joke is that the book’s dullest speaker supplies its most useful definition, and nobody in the room listens.

quotations.text: My good opinion once lost is lost forever.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: At Netherfield, admitting to a resentful temper during an evening of sparring with Elizabeth.
quotations.analysis: He says this as a confession of a fault and plainly regards it as a standard. The novel then spends fifty chapters disproving it about him, since his good opinion of Elizabeth survives her refusal and her family; the line is a self-portrait that has stopped being accurate.

quotations.text: That will do extremely well, child. You have delighted us long enough. Let the other young ladies have time to exhibit.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Stopping Mary’s second song at the Netherfield ball.
quotations.analysis: A father humiliates a daughter in public and the sentence is constructed so that the cruelty travels inside a compliment. It is the clearest instance of the habit Elizabeth will later have to judge: her father’s wit is aimed at his own children and costs him nothing.

quotations.text: My reasons for marrying are, first, that I think it a right thing for every clergyman in easy circumstances (like myself) to set the example of matrimony in his parish.
quotations.speaker: Mr Collins
quotations.context: Proposing to Elizabeth, having secured her mother’s permission but not her attention.
quotations.analysis: He begins a proposal with an enumerated list and the first item is professional example. The woman is not in the sentence at all; she appears later, as the third reason, on the recommendation of somebody else. Austen lets the syntax do the whole characterisation.

quotations.text: An unhappy alternative is before you, Elizabeth. From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents. Your mother will never see you again if you do not marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again if you do.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Called in by Mrs Bennet to force Elizabeth to accept Collins.
quotations.analysis: He supports his daughter by pretending not to, which lets him defeat his wife and stay amusing at the same time. The sentence is perfectly balanced around the two parents, and the balance is the point: Elizabeth’s rescue arrives as a joke, and the same detachment will let Lydia go to Brighton.

quotations.text: I am not romantic you know. I never was. I ask only a comfortable home; and considering Mr. Collins’s character, connections, and situation in life, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as fair, as most people can boast on entering the marriage state.
quotations.speaker: Charlotte Lucas
quotations.context: Telling Elizabeth that she has accepted Mr Collins.
quotations.analysis: She asks only for a house and states her odds like an actuary, and the novel never corrects her arithmetic. Set against the first sentence of the book, this is the same proposition with the irony taken out, spoken by the person whom the marriage market has priced most accurately.

quotations.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: The first proposal, at the Hunsford parsonage, while Elizabeth is re-reading Jane’s letters.
quotations.analysis: Four short sentences, three of them about his own resistance, and the declaration arrives only in the fourth. ‘Struggled’ and ‘repressed’ treat his feeling as an enemy position, so that by the time he reaches ‘admire and love’ he has already told her what the offer costs him.

quotations.text: I had not known you a month before I felt that you were the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Refusing Darcy, after he has asked why he is rejected with so little civility.
quotations.analysis: The superlative is a hostage to fortune and Austen collects on it twenty-six chapters later. Note the precision of ‘a month’: she dates her verdict exactly, which is what makes it possible for the novel to show her the evidence she had not yet seen.

quotations.text: Be not alarmed, Madam, on receiving this letter, by the apprehension of its containing any repetition of those sentiments, or renewal of those offers, which were last night so disgusting to you.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: The opening of the letter handed to Elizabeth in the park at Rosings.
quotations.analysis: He hands over the one form of speech she cannot interrupt, and opens by disclaiming any renewal of the offer, which is how he makes the document readable. From here the novel’s evidence arrives in writing, and its turning point involves no event at all — only a second reading.

quotations.text: But vanity, not love, has been my folly. Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted prepossession and ignorance, and driven reason away, where either were concerned. Till this moment, I never knew myself.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Alone, having read Darcy’s letter twice and reconstructed everything Wickham told her.
quotations.analysis: She does not accuse herself of loving the wrong man but of a fault in method: she was pleased by one and slighted by the other, and let that do her thinking. ‘Vanity, not love, has been my folly’ applies Mary’s distinction from Chapter 5 to herself, thirty chapters after it was laughed at.

quotations.text: I have never had a cross word from him in my life, and I have known him ever since he was four years old.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Reynolds
quotations.context: The Pemberley housekeeper showing the house to Elizabeth and the Gardiners.
quotations.analysis: The testimony that changes Elizabeth’s mind comes from a servant with twenty years of observation and no reason to flatter a stranger. Austen makes the evidence economic rather than romantic: landlord and master are job titles, and Darcy is being assessed on how he treats people who cannot answer back.

quotations.text: In what an amiable light does this place him!
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Standing in the Pemberley gallery, hearing the housekeeper describe Darcy’s care of his sister.
quotations.analysis: ‘This place’ is doing double duty: the phrase means this circumstance, and she is standing in the house itself. The estate is functioning as evidence — grounds, portraits, accounts of conduct over years — where conversation had produced only impressions.

quotations.text: Unhappy as the event must be for Lydia, we may draw from it this useful lesson; that loss of virtue in a female is irretrievable⁠—that one false step involves her in endless ruin⁠—that her reputation is no less brittle than it is beautiful⁠—and that she cannot be too much guarded in her behaviour towards the undeserving of the other sex.
quotations.speaker: Mary Bennet
quotations.context: To Elizabeth, while the family waits for news of Lydia.
quotations.analysis: The consolation is monstrous and the description is correct, which is the difficulty the novel will not dissolve. ‘Brittle’ and ‘beautiful’ are yoked by alliteration into a single property that a woman owns and can break, and nothing in the plot disproves the account — only Darcy’s money limits the damage.

quotations.text: Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?
quotations.speaker: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
quotations.context: In the Longbourn shrubbery, demanding that Elizabeth promise never to accept Darcy.
quotations.analysis: The objection has left the realm of income and become almost sacramental: a house has shades, and a marriage would defile them. It is the class argument in its purest and least answerable form, and the novel answers it by having the interview itself convince Darcy to propose again.

quotations.text: I am only resolved to act in that manner which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you, or to any person so wholly unconnected with me.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Refusing Lady Catherine the promise she has come for.
quotations.analysis: She claims the right to define her own happiness and denies her interrogator any standing at all, and she does it in the flattest, least witty sentence she speaks in the book. The wit is dropped because this is not a duel; it is a jurisdictional claim.

quotations.text: For what do we live but to make sport for our neighbours, and laugh at them in our turn?
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Reading Mr Collins’s letter aloud to Elizabeth, who cannot enjoy it.
quotations.analysis: It is the closest thing he has to a philosophy, and the novel has just finished showing what it costs: the daughter he did not watch has been retrieved with somebody else’s money. The rhetorical question assumes an answer that the last hundred pages have withdrawn.

quotations.text: I have been a selfish being all my life, in practice, though not in principle. As a child I was taught what was right, but I was not taught to correct my temper.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: Walking with Elizabeth after the second proposal has been accepted.
quotations.analysis: The distinction between practice and principle is the same one Elizabeth reached in Chapter 36, and Austen gives the two confessions a matching shape so that the marriage is founded on a shared diagnosis. He blames an upbringing and does not use it as an excuse, which is the difference between him and Wickham.

quotations.text: I am the happiest creature in the world. Perhaps other people have said so before, but not one with such justice. I am happier even than Jane; she only smiles, I laugh.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Writing to Mrs Gardiner, who had been at Pemberley with her.
quotations.analysis: She claims a superlative and then immediately audits it, which is exactly how she has argued all book. The comparison with Jane is not vanity but accuracy about temperament: the sister who thinks well of everyone smiles, and the one who has had to revise her judgements laughs.

themes.name: A fraction, and what it decides
The code of the first families
Debt, allowance and a town's opinion
A joke that lasts twenty years

techniques.name: Pairs that cannot be told apart
Glass strips and an Indian knife

quotations.text: I wish I owned half of that dog.
quotations.context: David Wilson, newly arrived, listening to an invisible dog bark.
quotations.analysis: The joke needs its second half — he would kill his half — and the town cannot supply it. A man's whole career is decided in the four seconds it takes them to fail at a syllogism, which is the same failure that will let them accept a changed baby.

quotations.text: Because I would kill my half.
quotations.context: Wilson's answer when somebody asks why.
quotations.analysis: A logician's joke about indivisible property, offered to a town whose entire economy rests on dividing people into parts. Twain sets the terms of the book in a throwaway line: a fraction of a living thing cannot be owned separately, and the law says otherwise.

quotations.text: You ought to be sold down the river.
quotations.context: Percy Driscoll, having decided to sell his four thieving slaves locally instead.
quotations.analysis: The sentence that starts the plot. It is spoken as mercy, received as mercy, and written down that night in his diary as a humane day's work — and it is what sends Roxy to the cradle three chapters later.

quotations.text: To all intents and purposes Roxy was as white as anybody, but the one sixteenth of her which was black outvoted the other fifteen parts and made her a negro.
quotations.context: The narrator, introducing Roxy.
quotations.analysis: 'Outvoted' is the whole argument in one word: the classification is a procedure, not a fact, and a minority of the arithmetic wins because the rules were written that way. Twain states it without heat, in the voice of a man reading out a regulation.

quotations.text: Her child was thirty-one parts white, and he, too, was a slave, and by a fiction of law and custom a negro.
quotations.context: The same passage, moving from mother to son.
quotations.analysis: A fiction is what lawyers call a thing everyone agrees to treat as true. Twain uses the technical sense and the ordinary one at once, and the sentence quietly tells the reader that the machinery about to run for twenty-three years is made of paper.

quotations.text: Adam was but human—this explains it all. He did not want the apple for the apple’s sake, he wanted it only because it was forbidden.
quotations.context: The motto at the head of the chapter in which Driscoll's slaves steal.
quotations.analysis: Placed above a theft, the aphorism refuses the moral the chapter seems to offer. The people who stole are not wicked; they are human beings in a house where everything is forbidden them, and the calendar says so before the narrative does.

quotations.text: Whoever has lived long enough to find out what life is, knows how deep a debt of gratitude we owe to Adam, the first great benefactor of our race. He brought death into the world.
quotations.context: The motto over the chapter in which Roxy contemplates drowning herself and her child.
quotations.analysis: The bleakest joke in the calendar, standing over the chapter where a mother works out that death is better than the auction block. The aphorism arrives as wit and is then taken literally by the plot beneath it.

quotations.text: Dey sha’n’t, oh, dey
quotations.context: Roxy at the cradle in the night, after learning her child can be sold.
quotations.analysis: The sentence breaks before it finishes. Everything Roxy does for the rest of the novel — the switch, the blackmail, the escape from Arkansas — is contained in a half-spoken refusal muttered over a cot at two in the morning.

quotations.text: It ain’t no lie, nuther. It’s jes de truth, en nothin’ but de truth, so he’p me. Yassir—you’s my son—
quotations.context: Roxy telling Tom what she did in 1830.
quotations.analysis: She swears it in the language of a courtroom oath, thirteen chapters before the courtroom. The revelation is also a transfer of power: from this line on the woman he has just refused a dollar can hang him with a sentence, and both of them know it.

quotations.text: If you pick up a starving dog and make him prosperous, he will not bite you. This is the principal difference between a dog and a man.
quotations.context: The motto over the chapter called Sold Down the River.
quotations.analysis: The chapter beneath it has a son selling his mother to a cotton planter after she has saved him twice. The calendar's dog returns from chapter one, and the joke that once cost Wilson his practice now measures Tom exactly.

quotations.text: April 1. This is the day upon which we are reminded of what we are on the other three hundred and sixty-four.
quotations.context: The motto over the chapter of the trial.
quotations.analysis: Over a courtroom, the joke becomes a verdict on everybody in it: a town that has been fooled for twenty-three years is about to be told so, and the man who wrote the line is the one doing the telling.

quotations.text: These marks are his signature, his physiological autograph, so to speak, and this autograph can not be counterfeited
quotations.context: Wilson explaining finger-prints to a court that has never heard of them.
quotations.analysis: A signature nobody can forge, in a book where every other kind of identity — a name, a will, a family, a race — turns out to be forgeable. The science arrives as a relief and settles the wrong question, which is Twain's joke on the ending.

quotations.text: Upon this haft stands the assassin’s natal autograph, written in the blood of that helpless and unoffending old man who loved you and whom you all loved.
quotations.context: Wilson, holding the knife in front of the jury.
quotations.analysis: The rhetoric is pure theatre — the pause, the raised eyes, the clock — and it works because the town has spent twenty years underestimating the man performing it. Twain gives his outsider the one scene in which a Dawson's Landing audience listens.

quotations.text: make upon the window the finger-prints that will hang you!
quotations.context: The end of Wilson's demonstration, addressed across the courtroom.
quotations.analysis: The order is to produce the evidence himself, in public, and he obeys by fainting. Two secrets are settled in one sentence: who killed the Judge, and who has been living in the Driscoll house since 1830.

quotations.text: The poor fellow could not endure the terrors of the white man’s parlor, and felt at home and at peace nowhere but in the kitchen.
quotations.context: What becomes of the real heir once he has his name and his money back.
quotations.analysis: The restoration is a formality. Twenty-three years of training cannot be reversed by a verdict, and the novel's coldest sentence shows a free man with an estate who is comfortable only where he used to be sent.

quotations.text: the spirit in her eye was quenched
quotations.context: Roxy after the trial.
quotations.analysis: The most vital character in the book is dismissed in half a line. Twain gives her the courage, the plan and the nerve for twenty-one chapters and then records, without ceremony, that the ending has taken all of it away.

quotations.text: As soon as the Governor understood the case, he pardoned Tom at once, and the creditors sold him down the river.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: A murderer is pardoned because imprisoning him would waste an asset, and the estate's creditors take him instead. The threat from chapter two arrives as the final clause of the book, and the law that has just performed a miracle of detection hands a man over as goods.

quotations.text: Tell the truth or trump--but get the trick.
quotations.context: The first motto in the book, above the chapter that names Wilson.
quotations.analysis: A card-player's morality, and the working rule of nearly everyone in Dawson's Landing. It also describes the trial: Wilson tells the truth and takes the trick, and the town cannot tell the two apart.

themes.name: The story he tells about himself

quotations.text: The cold passed reluctantly from the earth, and the retiring fogs revealed an army stretched out on the hills, resting.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The two active verbs belong to the weather, and the army is merely revealed by it, lying still. Before a single man has spoken, the grammar has established the arrangement the book will keep: the natural world does things, and the soldiers are things it does them to.

quotations.text: He had grown to regard himself merely as a part of a vast blue demonstration.
quotations.context: After months of drill and no fighting.
quotations.analysis: A war is reduced to a colour and a gesture, as though the Union army were a piece of political theatre he has been hired to stand in. 'Merely' is Henry's word, not Crane's, and it registers the disappointment of a boy who enlisted for something with names in it.

quotations.text: He was a mental outcast.
quotations.context: After failing to find any other man visibly wrestling with the same fear.
quotations.analysis: Four words on their own, and the isolation is entirely self-generated: he has been reading other men's faces and finding nothing, which proves only that they are doing the same thing he is. The novel's first joke is that everyone in the regiment believes himself the only coward in it.

quotations.text: And there were iron laws of tradition and law on four sides. He was in a moving box.
quotations.context: On realising that he cannot simply leave the regiment on the march.
quotations.analysis: The image turns a body of comrades into a container with walls, and the repetition of 'law' inside one clause makes the enclosure sound legal rather than social. It also sets up the chapters ahead: when he does escape the box, he finds that there is nowhere outside it to be.

quotations.text: He suddenly lost concern for himself, and forgot to look at a menacing fate. He became not a man but a member.
quotations.context: During the first assault, firing with the rest of the line.
quotations.analysis: Courage arrives here as a loss rather than an achievement — of self-consciousness, and then of separate selfhood. The pun on 'member' is doing real work: he is briefly a limb of something larger, which is exactly the condition he cannot reproduce when he is alone in Chapter VI.

quotations.text: He felt that he was a fine fellow. He saw himself even with those ideals which he had considered as far beyond him.
quotations.context: Immediately after surviving the first charge, and minutes before the second.
quotations.analysis: The verbs are all of perception — felt, saw — because nothing has been established except a sensation. Crane places this self-congratulation directly before the flight so that the reader watches an identity get assembled and demolished inside a single short chapter.

quotations.text: To the youth it was an onslaught of redoubtable dragons.
quotations.context: As the second attack comes on and the men around him begin to break.
quotations.analysis: The phrase 'to the youth' is the hinge: Crane marks the image as Henry's own, so the dragons are a boy's reading matter arriving on a battlefield. He will use the same creatures later to congratulate himself on having met them, which is how the novel measures what he has learned.

quotations.text: He had fled, he told himself, because annihilation approached.
quotations.context: Alone in the woods, constructing a defence of his flight.
quotations.analysis: 'He told himself' is the whole technique in three words: the sentence reports a proposition without adopting it. The Latinate 'annihilation' is several registers above anything Henry says out loud, which marks the reasoning as a performance for an audience of one.

quotations.text: There was the law, he said. Nature had given him a sign.
quotations.context: After throwing a pine cone at a squirrel, which runs away.
quotations.analysis: He has conducted an experiment designed to produce the result he wanted and calls the result a law. Crane lets the reasoning stand for a page and then walks him into a dead man's face, which is nature's other sign and is not addressed to him at all.

quotations.text: It was the religion of peace. It would die if its timid eyes were compelled to see blood. He conceived Nature to be a woman with a deep aversion to tragedy.
quotations.context: Walking deeper into the woods, away from the sound of the guns.
quotations.analysis: 'He conceived' marks the whole proposition as Henry's invention, and the gendering of Nature as a squeamish woman is the sentimental nineteenth-century picture the book exists to dismantle. Three sentences later he pushes aside the green boughs and finds the corpse.

quotations.text: The corpse was dressed in a uniform that had once been blue, but was now faded to a melancholy shade of green.
quotations.context: In the clearing of pine boughs that Henry has just described as a chapel.
quotations.analysis: A Union uniform has decayed into the colour of the forest, so the man has been absorbed by the landscape rather than commemorated by it. Crane spends the rest of the paragraph on ants moving across the face: the detail is clinical, and the only emotion in the sentence has been transferred onto a colour.

quotations.text: Where yeh hit, ol’ boy?
quotations.speaker: The tattered soldier
quotations.context: In the column of wounded men, asked in what Crane calls a brotherly tone.
quotations.analysis: It is the friendliest sentence in the novel and the one Henry cannot bear, because among these men the wound is the credential and he has none. The question is asked twice more in the next chapters, and it is what finally drives him to leave a badly hurt man alone in a field.

quotations.text: He wished that he, too, had a wound, a red badge of courage.
quotations.context: Walking among men whose injuries he has begun to envy.
quotations.analysis: The title phrase appears once, in Henry's mind, as a wish — which makes the whole book the story of a metaphor he goes looking for and then receives by accident. A badge is worn to be read by others, so what he wants is not courage but the sign of it.

quotations.text: The red sun was pasted in the sky like a wafer.
quotations.context: The final sentence of the chapter, immediately after Jim Conklin's death.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is flat, domestic and slightly absurd, and it stands alone as a paragraph where a novel of 1895 would normally place a reflection. Whether the wafer is a communion host or a seal on an envelope has been argued for a century; either way the sky is doing nothing, and the refusal to say more is the point.

quotations.text: He felt that he was regarding a procession of chosen beings.
quotations.context: Watching a column of troops move up towards the fighting.
quotations.analysis: Men marching into danger become a religious procession because he is looking at them from outside, and the novel is careful that this is a matter of position rather than of merit. A few pages later he privately hopes the army will be beaten, so that his flight will look like foresight.

quotations.text: He adroitly and fiercely swung his rifle. It crushed upon the youth’s head. The man ran on.
quotations.context: In a retreating crowd, after Henry grabs at a man to ask what has happened.
