quotations.analysis: Three short sentences, no adjective of feeling, and the assailant is gone before the second one ends. This is the wound the regiment will read as evidence of courage, delivered by a panicking Union soldier to a man who has run away — the novel's central irony arrives in nineteen words and is never commented on.

quotations.text: He had been out among the dragons, he said, and he assured himself that they were not so hideous as he had imagined them.
quotations.context: The morning after his return to the regiment, with his head bandaged.
quotations.analysis: Two verbs of self-address in one sentence — he said, he assured himself — and the dragons are the same ones he ran from in Chapter VI. The revision is complete: an experience he did not have is now a qualification, and the reader is shown the machinery rather than told about it.

quotations.text: It was not well to drive men into final corners; at those moments they could all develop teeth and claws.
quotations.context: Henry's state of mind before the fighting in which the regiment is told to hold.
quotations.analysis: The proposition is offered as general wisdom and is in fact a threat made by a frightened man to nobody in particular. Crane has been describing armies as animals since Chapter II, and here the imagery finally arrives inside Henry's own account of himself.

quotations.text: they now looked upon him as a war devil.
quotations.context: After Henry keeps firing at an enemy that has already withdrawn.
quotations.analysis: The reputation is made by men watching him rather than by anything he decided, and the thing they watched was him failing to notice that the fighting had stopped. Courage in this novel is consistently a reading made by other people of behaviour that had some quite different cause.

quotations.text: They fight like a lot ’a mule drivers. I can spare them best of any.
quotations.speaker: An officer
quotations.context: Two officers on horseback, discussing which regiment to send in, within hearing of Henry and Wilson.
quotations.analysis: The regiment's finest hour is arranged in a sentence about expendability, and the two men who overhear it go back and say nothing. Everything Henry does in the last six chapters is fuelled by an insult, which means the novel's climax of courage has an entirely petty engine.

quotations.text: It was a woman, red and white, hating and loving, that called him with the voice of his hopes.
quotations.context: As Henry takes the regimental colours from a dying sergeant.
quotations.analysis: The flag is given the only romantic attachment in the novel, and it is granted invulnerability precisely because Henry needs something in the field that cannot be killed. Note that the colours are described by their colours: the book's whole palette turns up in one object a man can carry.

quotations.text: He found that he could look back upon the brass and bombast of his earlier gospels and see them truly.
quotations.context: Marching away from the field in the rain, reviewing everything that has happened.
quotations.analysis: He congratulates himself on having seen through his own self-congratulation, which is the same operation one level up. The novel's difficulty is concentrated here: nothing in the sentence is false, and nothing in it is evidence, since the man assessing the account is the man who wrote it.

quotations.text: He had been to touch the great death, and found that, after all, it was but the great death. He was a man.
quotations.context: The settled conclusion of his review of himself.
quotations.analysis: The repetition of 'the great death' drains the phrase between its first appearance and its second, which is either maturity or the deflation of a boy's word. Then four monosyllables award him the title he wanted in Chapter I, and the book declines to say whether the award is deserved.

quotations.text: Over the river a golden ray of sun came through the hosts of leaden rain clouds.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: It is the shape of a consoling ending without the content of one: a ray of sun, a river, and no statement about what any of it means. 'Hosts' is the only word carrying any military weight, and it belongs to the clouds — the weather keeps the vocabulary of armies, and the armies have marched off the page.

themes.name: Divine right and the anointed body
themes.canonicalName: Divine right and the anointed body

themes.name: Inheritance and the law of succession
Words, names and what they can do
England as a garden and an estate
themes.canonicalName: England as a garden and an estate

quotations.text: How long a time lies in one little word! Four lagging winters and four wanton springs End in a word: such is the breath of kings.
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke
quotations.context: Richard has just cut Bolingbroke's banishment from ten years to six.
quotations.analysis: Four years are measured in seasons rather than numbers, so the mercy is felt as weather before it is understood as arithmetic. The couplet closes on 'breath', which makes royal authority a matter of air moving — a definition Bolingbroke will spend the play quietly disproving by using armies instead.

quotations.text: The language I have learn'd these forty years, My native English, now I must forego: And now my tongue's use is to me no more Than an unstringed viol or a harp,
quotations.speaker: Mowbray
quotations.context: Sentenced to perpetual banishment, before he leaves for Italy.
quotations.analysis: Exile is described as a speech impediment rather than a loss of land, which sets the play's terms early: to be removed from England is to be removed from English. The instrument images are all of things still intact and simply unusable, and Richard will reach for the same idea when his own name is taken away.

quotations.text: Teach thy necessity to reason thus; There is no virtue like necessity.
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: Gaunt tries to console his banished son at the gate.
quotations.analysis: The advice is to argue backwards from what cannot be changed until it looks like a choice, and Bolingbroke refuses it outright in the lines that follow. It is worth noticing that Richard adopts precisely this habit of mind from Act III onwards, at which point Gaunt's consolation reads as a description of political defeat.

quotations.text: Methinks I am a prophet new inspired And thus expiring do foretell of him: His rash fierce blaze of riot cannot last, For violent fires soon burn out themselves;
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: Dying at Ely House, waiting for the king to arrive.
quotations.analysis: 'Expiring' does double duty: it means dying and it means breathing out, so the prophecy and the last breath are the same event. Gaunt claims authority not from office but from proximity to death, which is the only position from which anyone in this play tells Richard the truth to his face.

quotations.text: This royal throne of kings, this scepter'd isle, This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars, This other Eden, demi-paradise, This fortress built by Nature for herself Against infection and the hand of war,
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The opening of Gaunt's speech on England, still waiting for Richard.
quotations.analysis: The famous passage is a single sentence that does not reach its main verb for more than twenty lines, and when it arrives the verb is 'Is now leased out'. Quoted on its own the speech sounds like praise; read to the end of its grammar it is a complaint about a property transaction, and the delay is the point.

quotations.text: That England, that was wont to conquer others, Hath made a shameful conquest of itself.
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The close of the England speech, moments before Richard enters.
quotations.analysis: The couplet turns a war verb inwards, so that the country becomes both army and territory. It is also the play's structural thesis in two lines: nobody invades England here, and every wound in the next four acts is administered by an Englishman to another Englishman's title.

quotations.text: Landlord of England art thou now, not king: Thy state of law is bondslave to the law; And thou--
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The quarrel with Richard at the bedside, cut off by the king.
quotations.analysis: Gaunt swaps one title for another and the whole indictment is done. A landlord holds property for income; a king holds a country in trust, and the difference is the lease Richard has just signed. The dash marks the sentence Richard interrupts, and it is the last time anyone at court speaks to him like this.

quotations.text: The ripest fruit first falls, and so doth he; His time is spent, our pilgrimage must be. So much for that. Now for our Irish wars:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Richard's response to the news that Gaunt is dead.
quotations.analysis: Two lines of decorous condolence, then 'So much for that', and the tone drops from elegy to agenda inside a single verse line. The switch is the seizure of the Lancastrian estate happening at the level of style, several seconds before Richard says the word 'seize'.

quotations.text: The caterpillars of the commonwealth, Which I have sworn to weed and pluck away.
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke
quotations.context: Explaining to York, on the road in Gloucestershire, why he has come back armed.
quotations.analysis: Bolingbroke gives his invasion a horticultural justification: he is not raising an army, he is doing the weeding the owner has neglected. The gardener in 3.4 will use exactly this vocabulary without knowing it has already been used as a war aim, and the repetition is how the play checks Bolingbroke's claim against a disinterested witness.

quotations.text: Not all the water in the rough rude sea Can wash the balm off from an anointed king; The breath of worldly men cannot depose The deputy elected by the Lord:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Newly landed from Ireland, before the bad news begins to arrive.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the language of chemistry — oil that water cannot lift — and it is answered within fifty lines not by an argument but by a series of reports. Note that the sentence concedes more than it means to: if worldly breath cannot depose a king, the play then shows a king deposed by worldly hands instead.

quotations.text: For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground And tell sad stories of the death of kings; How some have been deposed; some slain in war, Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: After hearing that his Welsh army has dispersed and his favourites are dead.
quotations.analysis: Richard proposes the one activity no king can afford, which is sitting down, and he does it in the first person plural, recruiting the stage and the audience into an audience of his own. The list that follows is a catalogue of history-play plots, so he is effectively asking to be read rather than obeyed.

quotations.text: All murder'd: for within the hollow crown That rounds the mortal temples of a king Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits, Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: The middle of the same speech on the coast of Wales.
quotations.analysis: The crown stops being an ornament and becomes an architectural space with a tenant in it, and the tenant is a jester. 'Hollow' is doing two jobs at once — the shape of the metal, and the emptiness of the office — and the word will still be working in 4.1 when Richard hands the thing over and finds nothing inside it.

quotations.text: I live with bread like you, feel want, Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus, How can you say to me, I am a king?
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Rebuking his followers for trying to comfort him.
quotations.analysis: 'Subjected' is the key word: it means made into a subject and also made liable to, and Richard hears both meanings at once. Having spent a hundred lines insisting that a king is a different order of being, he now proves the opposite from the evidence of his own appetite.

quotations.text: What must the king do now? must he submit? The king shall do it: must he be deposed? The king shall be contented: must he lose The name of king? o' God's name, let it go:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: On the walls at Flint Castle, after Northumberland brings Bolingbroke's demands.
quotations.analysis: Richard refers to himself in the third person throughout, as though reading the part of a king from a script someone else is writing. The questions are rhetorical but the answers are real concessions, so the speech gives away the kingdom in the grammar while the surface sounds like defiance.

quotations.text: Down, down I come; like glistering Phaethon, Wanting the manage of unruly jades. In the base court? Base court, where kings grow base, To come at traitors' calls and do them grace.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Descending from the castle wall to meet Bolingbroke in the lower courtyard.
quotations.analysis: Richard narrates his own stage movement, turning a walk downstairs into the fall of a boy who could not hold his father's horses. The pun on 'base' — the name of the yard, and a moral judgement — lets him lose the high ground physically while claiming it verbally, which is the whole tactic of his last three acts.

quotations.text: When our sea-walled garden, the whole land, Is full of weeds, her fairest flowers choked up, Her fruit-trees all upturned, her hedges ruin'd, Her knots disorder'd and her wholesome herbs Swarming with caterpillars?
quotations.speaker: A gardener's man
quotations.context: In the Duke of York's garden at Langley, while the Queen listens unseen.
quotations.analysis: A servant asks why he should tend one garden when the larger one is ruined, and in doing so repeats Gaunt's sea-wall and Bolingbroke's caterpillars from a position with nothing to gain. The play's political analysis is given to people with no rank at all, and delivered as a question about work.

quotations.text: And if you crown him, let me prophesy: The blood of English shall manure the ground, And future ages groan for this foul act; Peace shall go sleep with Turks and infidels,
quotations.speaker: Bishop of Carlisle
quotations.context: Interrupting the deposition in Westminster Hall; he is arrested for treason immediately afterwards.
quotations.analysis: 'Manure' is an agricultural word placed in a cathedral register, and it keeps the garden imagery running into the political climax. The prophecy is unusual in Shakespeare for being entirely accurate and entirely useless: the audience already knows the Wars of the Roses happened, and the men on stage crown Bolingbroke anyway.

quotations.text: God save the king! Will no man say amen? Am I both priest and clerk? well then, amen.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Brought into Westminster Hall to surrender the crown in public.
quotations.analysis: He offers the loyal shout and then has to supply the response himself, playing both halves of a church service to an audience that will not join in. The line measures the deposition better than any argument in the scene: the form still exists, and nobody is willing to take part in it.

quotations.text: Now is this golden crown like a deep well That owes two buckets, filling one another, The emptier ever dancing in the air, The other down, unseen and full of water:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Holding one side of the crown while Bolingbroke holds the other.
quotations.analysis: Two men gripping a single object become a mechanism in which neither can rise without the other falling. The conceit also quietly insults the winner: the bucket that goes up is the empty one, and it is 'dancing in the air' while the full one sits unseen at the bottom.

quotations.text: Ay, no; no, ay; for I must nothing be; Therefore no no, for I resign to thee. Now mark me, how I will undo myself;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Asked directly whether he is content to resign the crown.
quotations.analysis: The line will not settle into an answer: 'Ay' and 'I' sounded alike, so 'Ay, no' is also 'I, no', a man agreeing and cancelling himself in the same breath. It is the shortest statement in the play of what deposition does to a person whose identity was an office.

quotations.text: Was this the face that faced so many follies, And was at last out-faced by Bolingbroke? A brittle glory shineth in this face: As brittle as the glory is the face;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Looking into the mirror he has demanded, immediately before smashing it.
quotations.analysis: 'Face' is used as noun and verb within one line, so the word for a countenance becomes the word for bluffing, and the pun diagnoses his reign. Breaking the glass is meant to prove that grief has changed him; Bolingbroke's reply, that he has only destroyed the shadow of his face, is the coldest line in the play.

quotations.text: I have been studying how I may compare This prison where I live unto the world: And for because the world is populous And here is not a creature but myself, I cannot do it; yet I'll hammer it out.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Alone in the cell at Pomfret Castle.
quotations.analysis: This is the only soliloquy Richard has, and it opens by admitting that the comparison he wants to make does not work. 'Hammer it out' is a smith's phrase for beating metal into shape, so the thinking is presented as manual labour — the first honest work the play lets him do.

quotations.text: I wasted time, and now doth time waste me; For now hath time made me his numbering clock: My thoughts are minutes; and with sighs they jar Their watches on unto mine eyes, the outward watch,
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Hearing music played badly in time, in the cell at Pomfret.
quotations.analysis: The chiasmus puts the same two words on either side of the verb and swaps who is doing what, which is the play's plot in nine syllables. What follows is not self-pity but mechanism: a man itemising his own body as clockwork, down to the finger wiping tears off a dial.

quotations.text: 'Have I no friend will rid me of this living fear?' Was it not so?
quotations.speaker: Exton
quotations.context: Exton repeating to a servant what he heard the new king say.
quotations.analysis: The murder is commissioned by a question left hanging in a room, and the play stages the moment of interpretation rather than the moment of ordering. Because Exton has to check the wording twice with a servant, Bolingbroke keeps the deniability that lets him banish the killer in the last scene.

quotations.text: I'll make a voyage to the Holy Land, To wash this blood off from my guilty hand:
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke, now King Henry IV
quotations.context: The last lines of the play, spoken over Richard's coffin.
quotations.analysis: The new reign opens with a promise of expiation that the two parts of Henry IV never allow him to keep; he is still planning the same crusade, and still failing to leave, in the play that follows. Washing also picks up Richard's claim that no water could remove the balm of kingship, and applies the image to a stain instead of a blessing.

quotations.text: Now is the winter of our discontent Made glorious summer by this sun of York; And all the clouds that lour'd upon our house In the deep bosom of the ocean buried.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The first lines of the play, spoken alone on an empty stage.
quotations.analysis: The famous first clause is only half a sentence, and the half that follows reverses it: the winter is over. 'Sun of York' is a pun on son and on Edward's badge, and the whole passage is a victory speech delivered by the one man in the family who has no use for victory.

quotations.text: Why, I, in this weak piping time of peace, Have no delight to pass away the time, Unless to spy my shadow in the sun And descant on mine own deformity
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The middle of the opening soliloquy, explaining what peace leaves him to do.
quotations.analysis: 'Descant' is a musical term for improvising above a fixed melody, so his deformity is presented as a theme he performs variations on rather than a fact he suffers. The whole speech is his own account of his motives, which is exactly the reason to treat it with care.

quotations.text: And therefore, since I cannot prove a lover, To entertain these fair well-spoken days, I am determined to prove a villain And hate the idle pleasures of these days.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The turn of the opening soliloquy, immediately before Clarence is led across the stage under guard.
quotations.analysis: 'Determined' carries both senses at once — resolved, and settled in advance by something outside him — and the play never chooses between them. Note also that the reasoning is theatrical rather than moral: he cannot get the lover's part, so he takes the other one.

quotations.text: Never hung poison on a fouler toad. Out of my sight! thou dost infect my eyes.
quotations.speaker: Lady Anne
quotations.context: Beside the coffin of Henry VI, answering Richard's compliment on her spitting.
quotations.analysis: She wins this exchange and every other one in the scene, which is what makes the ending of it so hard to explain away. Her images are all of contagion — poison, infection, basilisks — and by the end of the scene she has accepted a ring from the source.

quotations.text: Take up the sword again, or take up me.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Kneeling with his breast bared, after Anne has let the sword fall.
quotations.analysis: One line, one repeated verb, two incompatible offers — and the staging does the arguing, since she must physically choose. He has converted a confession of murder into a proposal by making the only alternative another killing, which she has just refused to perform.

quotations.text: Was ever woman in this humour woo'd? Was ever woman in this humour won? I'll have her; but I will not keep her long.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Alone, the moment Anne has left the stage.
quotations.analysis: Two rhetorical questions to us, and then the third line disposes of her in eleven words. The rhyme of woo'd and won makes the whole seduction sound like a completed piece of business, and the audience is being invited to applaud a performance whose victim has only just walked off.

quotations.text: Shine out, fair sun, till I have bought a glass, That I may see my shadow as I pass.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The couplet that closes the wooing scene.
quotations.analysis: The shadow he could only 'descant on' in the first scene is now something he wants to look at, and he intends to buy a mirror to do it. Success has not altered how he sees his body; it has simply made him curious about the man who could pull this off.

quotations.text: Thou elvish-mark'd, abortive, rooting hog! Thou that wast seal'd in thy nativity The slave of nature and the son of hell!
quotations.speaker: Queen Margaret
quotations.context: Cursing Richard in front of the whole Yorkist court, which has been trying to ignore her.
quotations.analysis: 'Rooting hog' is his own badge, the white boar, turned into an insult, and 'seal'd in thy nativity' claims that his body was a signature written at birth. Richard's answer is to wait for her to finish and then substitute her name for his at the end of the curse — the only way anyone in the play ever interrupts her.

quotations.text: Why strew'st thou sugar on that bottled spider, Whose deadly web ensnareth thee about? Fool, fool! thou whet'st a knife to kill thyself.
quotations.speaker: Queen Margaret
quotations.context: To Queen Elizabeth, who has just tried to make peace in the quarrel.
quotations.analysis: Margaret is right about everything and heard by nobody, which is her function until Act IV, when Elizabeth comes to her to be taught this vocabulary. The same 'bottled spider' returns from Elizabeth's own mouth in 4.4, quoted almost exactly — the play keeps a record of who was listening.

quotations.text: And thus I clothe my naked villany With old odd ends stolen out of holy writ; And seem a saint, when most I play the devil.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Alone after the quarrel scene, explaining his method to the audience.
quotations.analysis: He describes piety as a costume made of offcuts, and the verb 'play' places the whole performance in a theatre. This is a confession no other character will ever hear, and it arrives fifty lines after he has publicly forgiven his enemies for the injuries he invented.

quotations.text: Thus, like the formal vice, Iniquity, I moralize two meanings in one word.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: An aside, after telling the young prince that fame lives long without characters.
quotations.analysis: He names his own theatrical ancestry: the Vice of the morality plays, who joked with the audience while damning the hero. 'Moralize' means to draw out a meaning, and he is boasting that he can do it twice at once — one meaning for the boy, the other for us.

quotations.text: Off with his head! Now, by Saint Paul I swear, I will not dine until I see the same.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: At the council table, moments after asking the Bishop of Ely for strawberries.
quotations.analysis: The domestic detail is the horror: an execution is fitted into the gap before lunch, and the oath is sworn on a saint. Hastings has spoken one cautious conditional — 'if they have done this thing' — and the word 'if' is treated as the treason.

quotations.text: O momentary grace of mortal men, Which we more hunt for than the grace of God! Who builds his hopes in air of your good looks, Lives like a drunken sailor on a mast, Ready, with every nod, to tumble down Into the fatal bowels of the deep.
quotations.speaker: Hastings
quotations.context: On the way to the block, an hour after gloating over the executions at Pomfret.
quotations.analysis: The image is exact about what he got wrong: a sailor high on a mast can see further than anybody on deck and is still the first to fall. 'Nod' does double work — the roll of the ship and the small movement of a great man's head — so favour and shipwreck become the same gesture.

quotations.text: Tut, I can counterfeit the deep tragedian; Speak and look back, and pry on every side, Tremble and start at wagging of a straw, Intending deep suspicion
quotations.speaker: Buckingham
quotations.context: Answering Richard's question about whether he can act frightened, just before the mayor arrives.
quotations.analysis: Two men openly rehearse a piece of political theatre in front of the audience, and then perform it badly on purpose so that the citizens will believe it. 'Intending' here means stretching or pretending, and the vocabulary throughout is an actor's: counterfeit, tragedian, offices, stratagems.

quotations.text: I am not in the giving vein to-day.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Cutting off Buckingham, who has asked for the earldom he was promised.
quotations.analysis: One flat line of prose rhythm inside the verse ends a partnership that has run since Act I. 'Vein' is a mood and also a blood vessel, and the joke is that Buckingham has just declined to spill any; the alliance ends not in a quarrel but in a change of subject.

quotations.text: 'Lo, thus' quoth Dighton, 'lay those tender babes:' 'Thus, thus,' quoth Forrest, 'girdling one another Within their innocent alabaster arms: Their lips were four red roses on a stalk, Which in their summer beauty kiss'd each other.
quotations.speaker: Tyrrel
quotations.context: Reporting the murder of the princes, which he arranged but did not watch.
quotations.analysis: The play's most terrible act is reported at two removes, by a man quoting the murderers quoting each other, and the language is the prettiest in the play. 'Four red roses on a stalk' puts the Lancastrian emblem on two Yorkist children, which is the civil war reduced to the size of two sleeping boys.

quotations.text: Bloody thou art, bloody will be thy end; Shame serves thy life and doth thy death attend.
quotations.speaker: Duchess of York
quotations.context: The last words Richard's mother speaks to him, as he marches out to meet Richmond.
quotations.analysis: A rhymed couplet from a mother is a formal withdrawal of blessing, and the chiasmus of blood at either end of the first line makes his beginning and his end the same substance. He has had the drums sounded through her speech, so the audience hears it over noise he ordered.

quotations.text: Is the chair empty? is the sword unsway'd? Is the king dead? the empire unpossess'd? What heir of York is there alive but we?
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: On being told that Richmond is at sea, coming to claim the crown.
quotations.analysis: Four questions in two lines, all of them rhetorical, all of them asked by a man who took the chair by proving it was empty when it was not. He has become the legitimacy he used to dismantle, and the argument he now makes is the one his victims could have made against him.

quotations.text: What do I fear? myself? there's none else by: Richard loves Richard; that is, I am I. Is there a murderer here? No. Yes, I am: Then fly. What, from myself?
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Waking in his tent at midnight after the ghosts have visited.
quotations.analysis: The soliloquy that was always a performance for us becomes a quarrel with no audience at all, and the syntax splits into question and answer as though two people were speaking. 'I am I' should be the most secure sentence in the language; here it is the last thing he can get to hold still.

quotations.text: My conscience hath a thousand several tongues, And every tongue brings in a several tale, And every tale condemns me for a villain.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: The same speech, a few lines later.
quotations.analysis: The word he chose for himself in the first scene is now the verdict returned against him, and by a court made entirely of voices. Repetition of 'every' turns conscience into a crowd, which is the first time in the play that Richard is outnumbered in a room.

quotations.text: Conscience is but a word that cowards use, Devised at first to keep the strong in awe: Our strong arms be our conscience, swords our law.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Addressing his officers on the morning of Bosworth, a hundred lines after the nightmare.
quotations.analysis: He is arguing with the speech he made in the night, in public, in front of men who did not hear it. The claim that conscience was invented to control the powerful is a political theory, and he advances it a few hours before dying on a field where every ghost has voted the other way.

quotations.text: A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Unhorsed in the field, hunting for Richmond among the decoys.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted line in the play is an offer to trade everything he has killed for back for a single animal, and it is spoken twice within seven lines, so the second time it is not rhetoric. Catesby offers to fetch a horse and Richard refuses, because what he wants is not escape but Richmond.

quotations.text: We will unite the white rose and the red: Smile heaven upon this fair conjunction, That long have frown'd upon their enmity!
quotations.speaker: Richmond
quotations.context: The closing speech, with the crown newly taken from Richard's body.
quotations.analysis: The settlement is announced rather than shown: the bride is a woman who never appears on stage and the peace is described in the future tense throughout. After five acts of a man who told the audience the truth and lied to everyone else, the play ends with a public statement nobody is invited to examine.

quotations.text: England hath long been mad, and scarr'd herself; The brother blindly shed the brother's blood, The father rashly slaughter'd his own son, The son, compell'd, been butcher to the sire
quotations.speaker: Richmond
quotations.context: Summing up the wars, a few lines before the play ends.
quotations.analysis: The lines summarise not just this play but the three Henry VI plays before it, and the father-and-son image is lifted almost directly from a scene in the last of them. The country is given a body that has been wounding itself, which is the only diagnosis the tetralogy offers for civil war.

quotations.text: I was born in the year 1632, in the city of York, of a good family, though not of that country, my father being a foreigner of Bremen
quotations.context: The first sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: Year, city, family standing and the father’s country of origin, in that order: the opening is the form a deposition or a parish record takes, not the form a story takes. Defoe buys credit with it before a single event has happened, and many first readers spent it on believing the book was true.

quotations.text: the middle station of life was calculated for all kind of virtue and all kind of enjoyments; that peace and plenty were the handmaids of a middle fortune
quotations.context: Crusoe’s father arguing against a life at sea, in the one long speech he is given.
quotations.analysis: The father does not moralise; he makes an actuarial case, listing the distempers and vicissitudes that fall on the ranks above and below. The word ‘calculated’ gives the game away — virtue here is a matter of exposure and risk, and Crusoe spends the rest of the book proving his father’s figures right.

quotations.text: But my ill fate pushed me on now with an obstinacy that nothing could resist; and though I had several times loud calls from my reason and my more composed judgment to go home, yet I had no power to do it.
quotations.context: After the wreck off Yarmouth, going on to London by land rather than home to York.
quotations.analysis: He describes a compulsion and simultaneously reports that his reason was calling him home, so the sentence holds both explanations — fate, and a man choosing. Defoe uses that doubleness throughout: Crusoe is never so determined by Providence that he is not also answerable.

quotations.text: He offered me also sixty pieces of eight more for my boy Xury, which I was loth to take; not that I was unwilling to let the captain have him, but I was very loth to sell the poor boy’s liberty, who had assisted me so
quotations.context: The Portuguese captain’s offer, after the boy has spent weeks keeping watch on the African coast.
quotations.analysis: The reluctance and the price are in the same sentence, and the price wins. Crusoe records that he was loth to sell the boy’s liberty, which shows he knows exactly what is being sold; the transaction is entered in the narrative with the same care as the eighty pieces of eight for the boat.

quotations.text: he would give the boy an obligation to set him free in ten years, if he turned Christian: upon this, and Xury saying he was willing to go to him, I let the captain have him.
quotations.context: The terms on which Crusoe agrees to let the captain have Xury.
quotations.analysis: Conversion is made a condition of freedom, and the deal satisfies Crusoe’s conscience completely. Read this beside Friday, who is taught to say Master before he is taught yes and no: the book uses the same settlement twice and calls it kindness both times.

quotations.text: I stated very impartially, like debtor and creditor, the comforts I enjoyed against the miseries I suffered
quotations.context: Setting out his situation in two columns after the first weeks ashore.
quotations.analysis: The simile is not decorative: what follows is literally ruled into evil and good, item against item, cast off wretched against alive when the rest drowned. A merchant’s habit is applied to the state of a soul, and the comfort Crusoe draws from it comes from the form rather than from anything in the entries.

quotations.text: September 30, 1659⁠—I, poor miserable Robinson Crusoe, being shipwrecked during a dreadful storm in the offing, came on shore on this dismal, unfortunate island, which I called “The Island of Despair”; all the rest of the ship’s company being drowned, and myself almost dead.
quotations.context: The opening entry of the journal, written up later but dated to the day of the wreck.
quotations.analysis: The entry is dated to a day on which he had neither ink nor the heart to write, so the journal is a reconstruction pretending to be immediate. Naming the place is the first act of possession in the book, and the name he gives it will be quietly dropped as the island becomes an estate.

quotations.text: I began to suggest that God had miraculously caused His grain to grow without any help of seed sown, and that it was so directed purely for my sustenance on that wild, miserable place.
quotations.context: Finding green barley stalks growing near his fortification.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is careful — no seed was sown, therefore the cause is supernatural, therefore it is directed at him — and every step of it is sound except the first. Defoe shows a man deriving personal providence from an incomplete inventory of his own actions.

quotations.text: At last it occurred to my thoughts that I shook a bag of chickens’ meat out in that place; and then the wonder began to cease; and I must confess my religious thankfulness to God’s providence began to abate, too
quotations.context: Remembering, a little later, what he emptied out at that spot.
quotations.analysis: The correction is the most interesting sentence in the religious argument of the book, and Defoe lets Crusoe admit that his thankfulness abated with the wonder. Nothing is retracted — he goes on to say the hand of Providence was in it anyway — but the reader has now watched the machinery of a miracle being dismantled and rebuilt.

quotations.text: “Call on Me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify Me.”
quotations.context: The verse he lights on when he opens a Bible during the fever.
quotations.analysis: He opens the book casually, as he says, and the method is the one Betteredge uses with Robinson Crusoe itself in The Moonstone a century and a half later. Crusoe dates his deliverance from this reading rather than from any rescue, so the turning point of the novel is an act of interpretation.

quotations.text: I was king and lord of all this country indefensibly, and had a right of possession; and if I could convey it, I might have it in inheritance as completely as any lord of a manor in England.
quotations.context: Surveying the fertile side of the island for the first time.
quotations.analysis: Title, possession and inheritance arrive in one breath, and the legal vocabulary is exact: indefeasible right, conveyance, a manor in England. Crusoe cannot convey it to anybody and says so, which makes the claim a piece of pure form — ownership asserted because there is nobody present to dispute it.

quotations.text: how much more happy this life I now led was, with all its miserable circumstances, than the wicked, cursed, abominable life I led all the past part of my days
quotations.context: Reviewing his condition after the conversion, with the calendar and the Sabbath restored.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is between two lives and not two places, and it is the argument the whole island section rests on: solitude with belief is preferable to society without it. Defoe needs this settled before the footprint arrives, because everything after Chapter XI tests it.

quotations.text: I was lord of the whole manor; or, if I pleased, I might call myself king or emperor over the whole country which I had possession of: there were no rivals; I had no competitor, none to dispute sovereignty or command with me
quotations.context: Reflecting on how little his stores of corn and goats actually mean to him.
quotations.analysis: The passage climbs from manor to king to emperor and then collapses, because sovereignty with no rivals is indistinguishable from having nothing. Defoe puts the emptiness and the grandeur in the same sentence, and the reflection that follows — that he had nothing to covet — is the nearest the novel comes to contentment.

quotations.text: I was exceedingly surprised with the print of a man’s naked foot on the shore, which was very plain to be seen on the sand. I stood like one thunderstruck, or as if I had seen an apparition.
quotations.context: Walking towards his boat about noon, fifteen years into his stay.
quotations.analysis: Everything hangs on the singular: one print, and no others, which is why it cannot be explained and cannot be ignored. Defoe surrounds it with sober detail — about noon, very plain to be seen — and the effect of that plainness is the most frightening moment in eighteenth-century English fiction.

quotations.text: they were national, and I ought to leave them to the justice of God, who is the Governor of nations, and knows how, by national punishments, to make a just retribution for national offences
quotations.context: Arguing himself out of a plan to ambush and kill the cannibals.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is jurisdictional: these are national crimes, so they belong to a court he is not sitting in. It is the best moral thinking Crusoe does in the book, and it should be set against Chapter III, where the same faculty found no difficulty whatever in selling a boy.

quotations.text: I have been, in all my circumstances, a memento to those who are touched with the general plague of mankind, whence, for aught I know, one half of their miseries flow
quotations.context: Looking back over the whole course of his life from the settled island.
quotations.analysis: He offers himself as an exhibit, which is what a providential autobiography is supposed to do, and names the disease as discontent with one’s station. The claim sits oddly beside a narrator who is at that moment fortifying an island he has declared his own property.

quotations.text: kissed the ground, and laid his head upon the ground, and taking me by the foot, set my foot upon his head; this, it seems, was in token of swearing to be my slave forever.
quotations.context: On the shore, immediately after the rescue.
quotations.analysis: Crusoe reports the gesture and supplies its meaning in the same breath — ‘this, it seems’ — although he has no language in common with the man making it. The relationship is therefore interpreted into existence by the person it benefits, before a single word has been exchanged.

quotations.text: I let him know his name should be Friday, which was the day I saved his life; I called him so for the memory of the time. I likewise taught him to say “Master”; and then let him know that was to be my name
quotations.context: The first lesson, on the way back to the fortification.
quotations.analysis: A man is named after a date in Crusoe’s calendar, and the second word he is taught is the name of his owner; yes and no come afterwards. The order of instruction is the whole relationship, and Defoe sets it down without a syllable of comment.

quotations.text: if God much stronger, much might as the wicked devil, why God no kill the devil, so make him no more do wicked?”
quotations.context: Friday’s reply during a lesson on the devil and temptation.
quotations.analysis: The question is the oldest difficulty in Christian apologetics, put by a man who has been learning English for a few months, and Crusoe admits he was strangely surprised and ill qualified to answer. It is the only argument in the book that the narrator loses.

quotations.text: My island was now peopled, and I thought myself very rich in subjects; and it was a merry reflection, which I frequently made, how like a king I looked. First of all, the whole country was my own property, so that I had an undoubted right of dominion. Secondly, my people were perfectly subjected⁠—I was absolutely lord and lawgiver⁠—they all owed their lives to me, and were ready to lay down their lives, if there had been occasion for it, for me. It was remarkable, too, I had but three subjects, and they were of three different religions⁠—my man Friday was a Protestant, his father was a Pagan and a cannibal, and the Spaniard was a Papist. However, I allowed liberty of conscience throughout my dominions.
quotations.context: With Friday, Friday’s father and the Spaniard all on the island.
quotations.analysis: Three men become dominion, property and a constitutional settlement, complete with liberty of conscience granted from above to a Protestant, a pagan and a Catholic. The passage is offered as a merry reflection, and it is also a precise short description of how a colony describes itself.

quotations.text: And thus I left the island, the 19th of December, as I found by the ship’s account, in the year 1686, after I had been upon it eight-and-twenty years, two months, and nineteen days
quotations.context: Sailing at last, twenty-eight years after the wreck.
quotations.analysis: The great release of the book is given as an arithmetic result to the day, checked against the ship’s account rather than his own post. After a lifetime of counting, the final figure is the only celebration Crusoe permits himself.

quotations.text: From forth the fatal loins of these two foes A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life;
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Prologue, spoken before any character appears.
quotations.analysis: 'Take their life' means both to be born and to kill themselves, so the sentence contains the whole plot in three words. Shakespeare gives away the ending on purpose: the audience is not being asked what happens but how long it takes, which is the question the rest of the play answers in days and hours.

quotations.text: What, drawn, and talk of peace! I hate the word, As I hate hell, all Montagues, and thee
quotations.speaker: Tybalt
quotations.context: To Benvolio, who has drawn his sword only to separate the fighting servants.
quotations.analysis: He hates a word, not a person — the grammar puts 'peace', 'hell', 'all Montagues' and 'thee' into the same list, as though they were the same kind of thing. It is the clearest statement in the play that the feud is not about a grievance but about an identity somebody would have to give up.

quotations.text: My child is yet a stranger in the world; She hath not seen the change of fourteen years, Let two more summers wither in their pride, Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride.
quotations.speaker: Capulet
quotations.context: Refusing, for the moment, Paris's request for Juliet's hand.
quotations.analysis: This is the same man who in Act III gives his daughter four days to marry or be turned out of doors, and he has not changed his opinion of her in between — only been contradicted. The play plants his reasonableness early so that the later scene registers as something other than a bad temper.

quotations.text: O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright! It seems she hangs upon the cheek of night Like a rich jewel in an Ethiope's ear; Beauty too rich for use, for earth too dear!
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: Seeing Juliet for the first time, across the Capulets' hall.
quotations.analysis: He does not know her name and is already making her a light source in a room full of torches. The imagery of brightness set in darkness runs from here to the tomb, where Romeo will call a burial vault a lantern; the play's love scenes are all lit against black.

quotations.text: If I profane with my unworthiest hand This holy shrine, the gentle fine is this: My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready stand To smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: The opening quatrain of the sonnet the lovers make between them at the feast.
quotations.analysis: Romeo offers a quatrain and Juliet answers with one in the same rhyme scheme, which means she has recognised the form and chosen to complete it. Two strangers producing a single sonnet is the most economical way Shakespeare ever found to show people discovering they think alike, and it happens before either knows the other's surname.

quotations.text: My only love sprung from my only hate! Too early seen unknown, and known too late!
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: On being told by the Nurse that the young man is a Montague.
quotations.analysis: The line is balanced on the word 'only', which does duty twice and means something different each time: sole love, sole hatred. 'Too early' and 'too late' inside one line is the play's own clock complaining, four scenes before there is anything to be late for.

quotations.text: It is the east, and Juliet is the sun.
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: In the Capulet orchard, seeing a light at the window above.
quotations.analysis: Nine monosyllables and one name, which is unusually plain for a man who has spent Act I in elaborate paradoxes. The metaphor also quietly reverses the scene's conditions: it is the middle of the night, and he is describing a sunrise.

quotations.text: O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo? Deny thy father and refuse thy name; Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love, And I'll no longer be a Capulet.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Alone at her window, unaware that Romeo is below.
quotations.analysis: 'Wherefore' means why, not where: she is asking why he has to be that particular man, and she answers her own question in the next three lines by offering to change her name instead. Within a minute of her first private speech she has proposed the practical solution the adults spend five acts failing to find.

quotations.text: What's in a name? that which we call a rose By any other name would smell as sweet;
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Continuing the same speech, arguing with the word 'Montague'.
quotations.analysis: The argument is philosophically sound and turns out to be false in Verona, where names cost lives. Juliet is testing whether language can be separated from the world, and the rest of the play is the experiment failing: a name gets Mercutio killed and a letter that never arrives kills the rest.

quotations.text: It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden; Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be Ere one can say 'It lightens.'
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Refusing to exchange vows on the spot, in the middle of the orchard scene.
quotations.analysis: Four uses of 'too' in two lines, and the simile is chosen for its speed: lightning is over before the word for it can be said. She sees the danger of haste more clearly than the Friar does, and proposes marriage thirty lines later anyway.

quotations.text: My bounty is as boundless as the sea, My love as deep; the more I give to thee, The more I have, for both are infinite.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Called away by the Nurse, returning to the window for the third time.
quotations.analysis: Verona runs on exchange — dowries, bonds of kinship, favours owed — and this is the one economy in the play that does not work by subtraction. The rhyme of 'sea' and 'thee' ties the scale of the image to the person it is addressed to, which is why the hyperbole does not sound like boasting.

quotations.text: Good night, good night! parting is such sweet sorrow, That I shall say good night till it be morrow.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: The end of the orchard scene, after three false exits.
quotations.analysis: The couplet is a joke about its own form: she says good night twice and then promises to keep saying it until morning, which is exactly what the preceding hundred lines have been doing. The oxymoron is conventional, but the staging makes it literal — she cannot leave, and the scene keeps restarting.

quotations.text: Virtue itself turns vice, being misapplied; And vice sometimes by action dignified.
quotations.speaker: Friar Laurence
quotations.context: Gathering herbs at dawn, before Romeo arrives to ask for a wedding.
quotations.analysis: He is talking about plants, and he has just said that the same flower cheers when smelt and kills when tasted. The couplet is also his own defence in advance: everything he does from here is a good thing misapplied, and he will use one of those flowers to fake a death.

quotations.text: Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.
quotations.speaker: Friar Laurence
quotations.context: The last line of the scene, as Romeo hurries him towards the wedding.
quotations.analysis: It is the exit line of a scene in which the Friar has just agreed to marry two teenagers who met the previous night. The advice is sound, the speaker ignores it, and the play stages the consequence twice over — a messenger who does not arrive and a friar who arrives half a minute late.

quotations.text: These violent delights have violent ends And in their triumph die, like fire and powder, Which as they kiss consume
quotations.speaker: Friar Laurence
quotations.context: Waiting for Juliet at the cell, immediately before he marries them.
quotations.analysis: The image is gunpowder meeting a flame, and the verb for their meeting is 'kiss'. He is warning against the wedding he is about to perform, which is the pattern of his whole part: accurate diagnosis followed immediately by the opposite action.

quotations.text: A plague o' both your houses! I am sped.
quotations.speaker: Mercutio
quotations.context: Stabbed under Romeo's arm as Romeo tries to part the fighters.
quotations.analysis: He curses both families, which is his right: he belongs to neither and is dying for a quarrel he has only ever mocked. He says it three times in twenty lines, and the play takes the curse literally — the next four deaths are Capulets and Montagues.

quotations.text: O, I am fortune's fool!
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: Standing over Tybalt's body, told to run before the Prince arrives.
quotations.analysis: Five words, and every one of them shifts the agency away from the man who has just done the killing. It is the play's habit in miniature: the characters keep describing as fate a sequence of things they have chosen, and the audience has watched Romeo choose this one.

quotations.text: And you be not, hang, beg, starve, die in the streets, For, by my soul, I'll ne'er acknowledge thee,
quotations.speaker: Capulet
quotations.context: To Juliet, who has said she will not marry Paris.
quotations.analysis: Four verbs with nothing between them, each one a worse outcome than the last, from a man who two acts earlier wanted her consent before anything was agreed. Neither her mother nor her nurse contradicts him, and the scene ends with Juliet alone on stage for the first time since the orchard.

quotations.text: Go, counsellor; Thou and my bosom henceforth shall be twain.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Alone, after the Nurse has advised her to marry Paris and forget Romeo.
quotations.analysis: She ends fourteen years of intimacy in a line and a half, and she does it in verse to a woman who has just spoken prose. 'Twain' is a marriage word turned inside out: the one relationship in the play that predates the action is dissolved just as the Nurse becomes useless to her.

quotations.text: I have a faint cold fear thrills through my veins, That almost freezes up the heat of life
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Alone in her chamber with the Friar's vial, having sent the Nurse away.
quotations.analysis: She describes the drug's effect before she has taken it, which is the point of the speech: she has already imagined waking among her ancestors' bones and is going through with it anyway. It is the longest she is left alone on stage, and she uses the time to test the plan for flaws rather than to hesitate.

quotations.text: Is it even so? then I defy you, stars!
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: In Mantua, on hearing from Balthasar that Juliet lies dead in the Capulet vault.
quotations.analysis: The Prologue called him star-cross'd; here he answers the Prologue directly, and the defiance takes the form of doing exactly what the stars were said to have arranged. He is acting on news that is fifteen minutes out of date, which is the only thing wrong with the whole plan.

quotations.text: O true apothecary! Thy drugs are quick. Thus with a kiss I die.
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: In the tomb, having drunk the poison beside Juliet's body.
quotations.analysis: He praises the tradesman for the quality of the goods, which is a startling thing to do in the middle of a suicide, and the compliment is about speed. The last words turn the poison into the kiss, so that the drug and the marriage meet in one action.

quotations.text: Yea, noise? then I'll be brief. O happy dagger! This is thy sheath; there rust, and let me die.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: In the tomb, hearing the watch approach after the Friar has fled.
quotations.analysis: 'I'll be brief' is the shortest deathbed intention in Shakespeare, and she keeps to it: no lament, no speech to the body, twelve words and a stab. Calling her own body the dagger's sheath makes the suicide a consummation, and it is the only wedding night the play allows to finish.

quotations.text: For never was a story of more woe Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.
quotations.speaker: Prince
quotations.context: The last two lines of the play, over the bodies and the reconciled fathers.
quotations.analysis: The Prince calls it a story, not a crime, which is how Verona will be able to live with it: the fathers have just agreed to put up gold statues. Her name comes first and his is possessive — 'her Romeo' — the one moment the play's title order is reversed, and it is the closing rhyme.

quotations.text: possessed a strength of understanding, and coolness of judgment, which qualified her, though only nineteen, to be the counsellor of her mother
quotations.context: The narrator’s first account of the eldest Dashwood sister.
quotations.analysis: A nineteen-year-old is described as her mother’s counsellor, which characterises the mother as much as the daughter. The nouns are all about control — strength, coolness, judgment — and the clause that follows insists she also has strong feelings, so the novel cannot later be read as praising numbness.

quotations.text: She was sensible and clever; but eager in everything: her sorrows, her joys, could have no moderation. She was generous, amiable, interesting: she was everything but prudent.
quotations.context: The narrator introducing Marianne, immediately after the account of Elinor.
quotations.analysis: Three compliments and then the single withheld word. ‘Everything but prudent’ concedes that she lacks only one quality and structures the whole plot around its absence, and the list of generous, amiable, interesting is exactly what Willoughby will find useful.

quotations.text: people always live forever when there is an annuity to be paid them; and she is very stout and healthy, and hardly forty. An annuity is a very serious business; it comes over and over every year, and there is no getting rid of it.
quotations.speaker: Fanny Dashwood
quotations.context: Persuading her husband out of the last version of his promise to his dying father.
quotations.analysis: The objection to an annuity is that the recipients will be so inconsiderate as to survive. Notice the shift from a moral question to a bookkeeping one: ‘a very serious business’ and ‘no getting rid of it’ are the phrases of a woman describing a liability, and nobody in the room corrects her.

quotations.text: I think very highly of him⁠—that I greatly esteem, that I like him.
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Answering her mother and sister about her feelings for Edward Ferrars.
quotations.analysis: Three verbs in ascending order, each hedged, and none of them the one she means. It is not coldness but accuracy: she has no engagement and no declaration, so she claims only what she can defend — and her sister immediately treats the precision as an insult to love itself.

quotations.text: Esteem him! Like him! Cold-hearted Elinor! Oh! worse than cold-hearted! Ashamed of being otherwise. Use those words again, and I will leave the room this moment.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Bursting out at Elinor’s careful account of her feelings for Edward.
quotations.analysis: She repeats her sister’s two verbs as though quoting evidence at a trial, and the charge is not that Elinor feels nothing but that she is ashamed to say so. Forty chapters later Marianne will use the same word about her own conduct, and mean the opposite by it.

quotations.text: Oh! happy house, could you know what I suffer in now viewing you from this spot, from whence perhaps I may view you no more!⁠—And you, ye well-known trees!⁠—but you will continue the same.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Walking alone in front of the house on the family’s last evening at Norland.
quotations.analysis: She addresses a house and then a stand of trees, and both refuse to answer, which she takes personally. The apostrophe is her method in miniature: feeling counts as real only when it is performed aloud, and the complaint that the trees will continue the same is a complaint that grief has no witness.

quotations.text: with me a flannel waistcoat is invariably connected with aches, cramps, rheumatisms, and every species of ailment that can afflict the old and the feeble.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Rejecting Mrs Jennings’s suggestion that Colonel Brandon admires her.
quotations.analysis: A whole character is dismissed on the evidence of one garment, which is precisely the reasoning Marianne uses in the other direction about Willoughby. The novel remembers the joke: the last paragraph about her marriage returns to the flannel waistcoat, and by then the garment has stopped being funny.

quotations.text: with what transporting sensation have I formerly seen them fall! How have I delighted, as I walked, to see them driven in showers about me by the wind! What feelings have they, the season, the air altogether inspired! Now there is no one to regard them. They are seen only as a nuisance, swept hastily off, and driven as much as possible from the sight.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Told by Elinor that the walks at Norland are thick with dead leaves.
quotations.analysis: Three exclamations about her own past sensations, and then a grievance: the leaves are now swept up by people who do not feel them. Elinor’s one-line reply, that not everyone shares her passion for dead leaves, is the driest thing she says in the book, and it lands because Marianne has just claimed a monopoly on noticing.

quotations.text: What have wealth or grandeur to do with happiness?
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Objecting to Elinor’s remark about the uses of money.
quotations.analysis: A rhetorical question that the plot spends the next thirty chapters answering in detail. Within ten lines Marianne has priced her own competence at about two thousand a year, which is roughly the income of the man she is rejecting as too old.

quotations.text: Your competence and my wealth are very much alike, I dare say; and without them, as the world goes now, we shall both agree that every kind of external comfort must be wanting. Your ideas are only more noble than mine. Come, what is your competence?
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Turning her sister’s objection about money into a question with a number in it.
quotations.analysis: The trick is to let Marianne keep the nobler word and then ask her to define it. Austen’s characters argue about income the way other novels’ characters argue about virtue, and the scene ends with a figure rather than a principle.

quotations.text: We have been engaged these four years.
quotations.speaker: Lucy Steele
quotations.context: Telling Elinor about her engagement to Edward Ferrars, in a conversation Lucy has carefully arranged.
quotations.analysis: Six words, placed after a long approach designed to make Elinor ask for them. The disclosure is an act of aggression disguised as intimacy: once Elinor holds the secret as a confidence, she is the one person in England who cannot use it.

quotations.text: to be as solemnly engaged to him, as if the strictest legal covenant had bound us to each other.
quotations.speaker: Lucy Steele
quotations.context: Marianne, quoting her own understanding of her position with Willoughby after his letter arrives.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is to a legal instrument, which is exactly what she does not have. A private understanding, however sincere, leaves no document and no claim; Lucy Steele’s four-year engagement is equally unwritten and she treats it as property, which is why she wins.

quotations.text: For four months, Marianne, I have had all this hanging on my mind, without being at liberty to speak of it to a single creature; knowing that it would make you and my mother most unhappy whenever it were explained to you
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Telling Marianne, for the first time, how long she has known about Lucy’s engagement.
quotations.analysis: The unit is time, not feeling: four months, without liberty to speak, while being told repeatedly that she does not feel enough. The sentence also explains the novel’s structure — the reader has been kept inside Elinor’s silence too, and only now learns what it weighed.

quotations.text: I acknowledge that her situation and her character ought to have been respected by me. I do not mean to justify myself, but at the same time cannot leave you to suppose that I have nothing to urge⁠—that because she was injured she was irreproachable, and because I was a libertine, she must be a saint.
quotations.speaker: John Willoughby
quotations.context: At Cleveland, at midnight, while Marianne lies dangerously ill upstairs.
quotations.analysis: He concedes the charge and then immediately reopens it, which is the pattern of the whole confession: an apology with a defence folded inside it. ‘Because I was a libertine, she must be a saint’ is a real argument about evidence, offered by a man who needs it not to be true.

quotations.text: I felt that she was infinitely dearer to me than any other woman
quotations.speaker: John Willoughby
quotations.context: Describing the effect of Marianne’s note, received in London after he had decided to marry Miss Grey.
quotations.analysis: The comparative is the problem: she is dearer than other women, and he has already worked out what she is worth against an income. Austen allows the feeling to be genuine precisely so that the novel cannot be read as saying that charming men are simply insincere.

quotations.text: My illness has made me think. It has given me leisure and calmness for serious recollection. Long before I was enough recovered to talk, I was perfectly able to reflect. I considered the past: I saw in my own behaviour, since the beginning of our acquaintance with him last autumn, nothing but a series of imprudence towards myself, and want of kindness to others.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Convalescent at Barton, setting out her own conduct to Elinor.
quotations.analysis: The self-examination is conducted in the vocabulary of accounting — a series, a beginning, a survey of behaviour since last autumn — which is how her sister thinks, not how she does. Note that she blames imprudence and unkindness to others, never the strength of her feelings.

quotations.text: I compare it with what it ought to have been; I compare it with yours.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Refusing Elinor’s attempt to excuse her conduct by comparing it with other people’s.
quotations.analysis: Two clauses, the second shorter and harder than the first. She adopts an absolute standard and then names a person as its measure, which is the precise reversal of Chapter 4, where the same sister’s behaviour was evidence of a cold heart.

quotations.text: I will be calm⁠—I will be mistress of myself.
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Watching from the window as a horseman she takes to be Edward dismounts at the gate.
quotations.analysis: She states self-command as an intention rather than a fact, which is the closest the novel comes to admitting what it has cost her. Two chapters of evidence follow: when Edward’s news finally arrives she leaves the room and cries until she thinks she will never stop.

quotations.text: Marianne Dashwood was born to an extraordinary fate. She was born to discover the falsehood of her own opinions, and to counteract, by her conduct, her most favourite maxims. She was born to overcome an affection formed so late in life as at seventeen, and with no sentiment superior to strong esteem and lively friendship, voluntarily to give her hand to another!
quotations.context: The narrator summing up Marianne’s marriage to Colonel Brandon.
quotations.analysis: The mock-heroic opening promises a destiny and delivers a list of maxims disproved. ‘Born to discover the falsehood of her own opinions’ makes the second marriage a correction rather than a reward, and readers have argued ever since about whether the joke is affectionate or a shrug.

quotations.text: among the merits and the happiness of Elinor and Marianne, let it not be ranked as the least considerable, that though sisters, and living almost within sight of each other, they could live without disagreement between themselves, or producing coolness between their husbands.
quotations.context: The final sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book closes not on either marriage but on the relation between the sisters, and phrases their achievement in the negative — no disagreement, no coolness. After a plot driven by what one sister could not tell the other, the last thing the novel counts as happiness is two women living within sight of each other and still speaking.

themes.name: What a poem can be made to do
Love as a claim and a risk
A face that unsettles the categories

quotations.text: From fairest creatures we desire increase, That thereby beauty’s rose might never die
quotations.context: The opening lines of the sequence, before any person has been addressed.
quotations.analysis: The sequence begins with a general law, not a person: we want beautiful things to continue. 'Increase' is a farming and a banking word before it is a human one, which sets the terms for the next sixteen poems — the young man is treated as capital that is not being put to work.

quotations.text: When I do count the clock that tells the time
quotations.context: The opening of the first poem in the sequence to make time itself the subject.
quotations.analysis: Ten monosyllables and a ticking rhythm. Counting the clock is a pointless activity — the clock is already counting — and the poem's argument grows out of that helplessness rather than out of any fact about the young man.

quotations.text: And all in war with Time for love of you, As he takes from you, I engraft you new.
quotations.context: The couplet that ends the last of the poems arguing for a child.
quotations.analysis: The turn the whole sequence rests on. Up to here the answer to time was a son; from here it is the poem. 'Engraft' keeps the gardening language of the earlier argument, so the substitution sounds like the same plan rather than a new one.

quotations.text: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate
quotations.context: The opening of the best-known poem in the sequence, immediately after the procreation group ends.
quotations.analysis: The question is rhetorical and the answer is no: the poem spends its quatrains explaining why summer is the weaker term. What looks like the most conventional compliment in English is in fact a refusal of the comparison it offers.

quotations.text: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
quotations.context: The couplet of sonnet 18.
quotations.analysis: 'This' is the poem, named twice and never described. The claim is a contract with the reader: the young man survives only as long as someone is doing what you are doing now, which is why the line still works.

quotations.text: Devouring Time, blunt thou the lion’s paws
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that follows the immortality claim of 18.
quotations.analysis: Having promised to defeat time, the speaker spends a poem giving it permission to destroy everything else. The bargaining is comic in scale — lions, tigers, the phoenix — and the single exception at the end is the point of it.

quotations.text: A woman’s face with nature’s own hand painted, Hast thou the master mistress of my passion
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that describes the young man's beauty directly.
quotations.analysis: Two categories in one phrase, and no punctuation in 1609 to separate them. The compliment works by taking the language kept for women and handing it to a man, and the poem's feminine rhymes keep the doubleness audible through all fourteen lines.

quotations.text: O! learn to read what silent love hath writ:
quotations.context: The couplet of a poem comparing the speaker to an actor who forgets his part.
quotations.analysis: The instruction is to the young man and to us. A poet who cannot speak in person asks to be read instead, which makes writing a second-best — the first time the sequence admits that the page is a substitute for presence.

quotations.text: When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes, I all alone beweep my outcast state
quotations.context: The opening of the sequence's clearest poem about status and envy.
quotations.analysis: Public judgement and private misery in two lines. 'All alone' is doing the work: the shame is social, the weeping is not, and the poem's recovery will also be private — a thought, not a change in circumstances.

quotations.text: Haply I think on thee, and then my state, Like to the lark at break of day arising
quotations.context: The turn of sonnet 29, after eight lines of envy.
quotations.analysis: 'Haply' means by chance: the rescue is accidental, which is why it is believable. The line lifts on 'arising' and the verse follows it, the one place in the sequence where a change of mood is audible as a change of rhythm.

quotations.text: When to the sessions of sweet silent thought I summon up remembrance of things past
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that follows 29, again turning private feeling into public procedure.
quotations.analysis: A court is convened inside a head: sessions, summon, and later cancelled debts and accounts paid. Grief is conducted as legal business until the couplet dismisses the court by remembering one person.

quotations.text: Full many a glorious morning have I seen Flatter the mountain tops with sovereign eye
quotations.context: The first of the three poems that respond to an injury the sequence never specifies.
quotations.analysis: The excuse is built before the accusation. By making the young man the sun, the poem forgives him for behaving like weather, and 'flatter' quietly admits that the light was never sincere in the first place.

quotations.text: Roses have thorns, and silver fountains mud
quotations.context: The second line of the poem in which the speaker argues the young man's case for him.
quotations.analysis: A proverb offered as comfort, and it is the beginning of a defence that goes so far the speaker calls himself an accessory to the crime. Consolation and self-disgust arrive in the same poem, which is the sequence's characteristic move.

quotations.text: Not marble, nor the gilded monuments Of princes shall outlive this powerful rhyme
quotations.context: The opening of the most confident of the immortality poems.
quotations.analysis: Horace made the claim first, and every Elizabethan reader knew it. What Shakespeare adds is the demolition: statues smeared, masonry overturned, war's fire — the monument wins by being the only thing with nothing physical to destroy.

quotations.text: Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore, So do our minutes hasten to their end
quotations.context: The opening of the poem placed, in the 1609 order, at the number of minutes in an hour.
quotations.analysis: The simile does two things at once: it gives time a sound, and it makes each minute replace the one before rather than follow it. 'Pebbled' is the detail that stops it being a figure of speech — it is a real beach, and the poem is about being on it.

quotations.text: How with this rage shall beauty hold a plea, Whose action is no stronger than a flower?
quotations.context: Early in the poem that follows the ruin of sonnet 64.
quotations.analysis: Law again: a plea, an action, a case that cannot be won. Time is not argued with here but litigated against, and beauty's counsel has nothing to file. The answer, when it comes, is a miracle in black ink — the weakest possible defence, named as such.

quotations.text: That time of year thou mayst in me behold When yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang
quotations.context: The opening of the poem in which the speaker describes his own ageing.
quotations.analysis: 'Or none, or few' corrects itself mid-line, as though the speaker is looking while he writes. The second quatrain gives him a day, the third an hour of embers: each image covers less time than the last, so the poem shortens as it goes.

quotations.text: Bare ruin’d choirs, where late the sweet birds sang.
quotations.context: The fourth line of the autumn poem, completing its first image.
quotations.analysis: Branches, a gutted monastery and an empty choir stall in one phrase, written within living memory of the dissolution. The birds were singers in a building that no longer sings, which makes a private poem about age carry a national ruin inside it.

quotations.text: Farewell! thou art too dear for my possessing
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that ends the affair with the young man.
quotations.analysis: 'Dear' means beloved and expensive in the same breath, and the rest of the poem is conducted in contract law — estimate, charter, patent, bonds. A love affair is dissolved as though the deeds had been faulty from the start, which is both dignified and a way of not saying goodbye.

quotations.text: They that have power to hurt, and will do none
quotations.context: The opening of the sequence's coldest and most argued-over poem.
quotations.analysis: Praise with no warmth in it: the admired people are stone, unmoved, slow to temptation. Whether the poem approves of them has been argued for two centuries, and the case for irony rests entirely on the last line.

quotations.text: Lilies that fester smell far worse than weeds.
quotations.context: The final line of the poem praising those who do not act.
