quotations.analysis: Thirteen lines of cool admiration, then a smell. The line is a proverb Shakespeare also gave to a king in Edward III, and placed here it retracts the compliment without withdrawing it: the higher the beauty, the worse the rot.

quotations.text: When in the chronicle of wasted time
quotations.context: The opening of the poem that reads old poetry as prophecy.
quotations.analysis: 'Wasted' means used up rather than squandered. The poem turns literary history into a compliment — every medieval praise of a beautiful face was an attempt at this one — and then admits that present beauty leaves its admirers without the words to praise it.

quotations.text: Let me not to the marriage of true minds Admit impediments
quotations.context: The opening of the poem most often read at weddings.
quotations.analysis: The words come from the marriage service, where the congregation is asked to declare impediments. The poem borrows the ceremony's authority for a love that has no ceremony, and then defines that love entirely by what it refuses to do.

quotations.text: Love’s not Time’s fool, though rosy lips and cheeks Within his bending sickle’s compass come
quotations.context: The third quatrain of the definition poem.
quotations.analysis: A fool is a servant kept for entertainment, so the denial is specific: love is not on time's payroll. The concession in the next line is equally specific — lips and cheeks are inside the blade's reach — which leaves love defended everywhere except the body.

quotations.text: O thou, my lovely boy, who in thy power Dost hold Time’s fickle glass, his fickle hour
quotations.context: The opening of the twelve-line poem that closes the young man's part of the sequence.
quotations.analysis: The last address to him is the first to call him a boy. He holds time's hourglass rather than escaping it, and the poem's six couplets — no quatrains, no turn — read like an account being settled. In 1609 the missing couplet is printed as empty brackets.

quotations.text: In the old age black was not counted fair
quotations.context: The first line of the group addressed to the woman.
quotations.analysis: The subject changes and so does the method: instead of praising, the poem argues about taste. 'Fair' means pale, beautiful and just at once, and the sequence spends its last twenty-five poems pulling those meanings apart.

quotations.text: The expense of spirit in a waste of shame Is lust in action
quotations.context: The opening of the one poem in the sequence that addresses nobody.
quotations.analysis: No 'I', no 'thou', until the couplet says 'none knows well'. Lust is described in its three tenses at once — sought, had, hated — and the absence of a speaker is the point: this is a trap the poem says everybody is in.

quotations.text: My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun
quotations.context: The opening of the anti-blazon.
quotations.analysis: Every comparison the sonnet tradition had worn out is named and refused — sun, coral, snow, roses, perfume, music — and the couplet then claims that the refusal is the compliment. It works because the poem never actually describes her, only what she is not.

quotations.text: Whoever hath her wish, thou hast thy ‘Will,’
quotations.context: The opening of the first of the two poems built on the speaker's own name.
quotations.analysis: Will is desire, a man called William, and a sexual pun, and the poem uses all three about a dozen times. The joke is not only bawdy: a name that means 'wanting' cannot secure anything, and the poem's speaker is asking to be one of many.

quotations.text: When my love swears that she is made of truth, I do believe her though I know she lies
quotations.context: The opening of a poem printed in an earlier version in The Passionate Pilgrim in 1599.
quotations.analysis: Both people are lying, both know, and the arrangement holds. 'Lies' arrives at the end of the second line carrying its other meaning, and the couplet's flattery is mutual — which makes this the sequence's most companionable poem and its least romantic.

quotations.text: Two loves I have of comfort and despair, Which like two spirits do suggest me still
quotations.context: The poem that states the triangle directly; also printed in 1599.
quotations.analysis: The morality play is borrowed whole — a good angel and a bad one arguing over a soul — and then spoiled, because the speaker cannot tell which has won and does not expect to. The couplet's 'fire out' is the crudest line in the sequence and the most honest about what he is waiting to learn.

quotations.text: My love is as a fever longing still For that which longer nurseth the disease
quotations.context: Late in the group, after the poems of disgust.
quotations.analysis: Desire as an illness that feeds on its own cure. The medical language lets the speaker describe himself as a patient who has sacked his doctor — reason — and the last couplet turns the diagnosis on her, swearing she is fair while calling her black as hell.

quotations.text: For I have sworn thee fair; more perjured I, To swear against the truth so foul a lie.
quotations.context: The last couplet of the last poem addressed to the woman.
quotations.analysis: He has spent the group accusing her of breaking oaths and ends by declaring himself the worse perjurer. It is the closing position of the whole sequence: not forgiveness, not blame, but an admission that the praise itself was the lie.

themes.name: Empire, loot and what comes home
London, its suburbs and its river

characters.name: Mahomet Singh, Abdullah Khan and Dost Akbar

quotations.text: “It is cocaine,” he said,—“a seven-per-cent. solution. Would you care to try it?”
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Watson has at last asked which it is today, morphine or cocaine.
quotations.analysis: The offer is the shock. Holmes does not hide the habit or defend it; he states the concentration like a chemist and passes the case across as he might a cigar. Doyle, a practising doctor writing in 1889, gives Watson the medical objection and gives Holmes the better lines, and the drug was legal. The scene sets the terms of the book: a mind that treats its own body as apparatus.

quotations.text: “My mind,” he said, “rebels at stagnation. Give me problems, give me work, give me the most abstruse cryptogram or the most intricate analysis, and I am in my own proper atmosphere.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: His answer to Watson’s warning about what the drug will do to him.
quotations.analysis: Give me, three times: the grammar is a craving. Holmes describes work and cocaine as substitutes for one another, which makes crime a kind of supply. The client who knocks a few pages later is welcome for the reason the syringe was, and the last sentence of the novel will confirm that the case was only ever an interval between doses.

quotations.text: Detection is, or ought to be, an exact science, and should be treated in the same cold and unemotional manner.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes reviewing Watson’s pamphlet on the Jefferson Hope case, which he thinks was spoiled by romance.
quotations.analysis: Is, or ought to be: the correction concedes that it is not yet. Holmes goes on to compare Watson’s book to an elopement worked into a proposition of Euclid, and the novel that follows is exactly that — a love story run through a problem. Doyle lets his detective condemn the form of the book he is in, and then writes it anyway.

quotations.text: Was ever such a dreary, dismal, unprofitable world? See how the yellow fog swirls down the street and drifts across the dun-coloured houses.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: At the window, just before the landlady brings up Mary Morstan’s card.
quotations.analysis: Unprofitable is Hamlet’s word for the uses of this world, and Holmes borrows the pose with it. The fog is doing two jobs. It is the London the case will be conducted in, and it is the inside of his head without a problem: yellow, dun, nothing with an edge. A reader is being shown that the great reasoner’s complaint is closer to melancholy than to logic.

quotations.text: “You really are an automaton,—a calculating-machine!” I cried. “There is something positively inhuman in you at times.”
quotations.speaker: Dr John Watson
quotations.context: Watson has remarked on how attractive the client is; Holmes says he did not observe it.
quotations.analysis: Watson is stung on Mary’s behalf, within minutes of meeting her. Holmes answers that the most winning woman he ever knew was hanged for poisoning three children, so the exchange sets feeling against statistics, and the book will need both: Watson’s attention keeps Mary a person, and Holmes’s keeps her a case. The word inhuman will come back, far less playfully, when Watson looks at Tonga.

quotations.text: In an experience of women which extends over many nations and three separate continents, I have never looked upon a face which gave a clearer promise of a refined and sensitive nature.
quotations.context: Watson’s first description of Mary Morstan as she sits down in Baker Street.
quotations.analysis: The boast is comic and Doyle surely knows it, but the method is serious: Watson reads character straight off a face and treats the reading as a promise. He is right about Mary. He will use the identical procedure on the launch in chapter X and find bestiality, and the novel never suggests that a technique which works on a governess might fail on a stranger from the Andamans.

quotations.text: There was something strangely incongruous in this Oriental figure framed in the commonplace doorway of a third-rate suburban dwelling-house.
quotations.context: A servant in a yellow turban opens Thaddeus Sholto’s front door.
quotations.analysis: Watson finds the man incongruous; the plot says he is nothing of the kind. A suburb like this is where Indian money was spent, and the servant is in the doorway because a major came home rich. The sentence frames him like a picture, which is how the book treats almost every Indian it shows in London: as décor that came back with the furniture.

quotations.text: An oasis of art in the howling desert of South London.
quotations.speaker: Thaddeus Sholto
quotations.context: Thaddeus showing his guests into a room of tapestries, tiger-skins and a hookah.
quotations.analysis: Doyle had dined with Oscar Wilde the evening this novel was commissioned, and Thaddeus is an aesthete drawn for laughs. The joke has a point he cannot see. His oasis is furnished from a murdered man’s jewel-box, and the desert he despises is the ordinary England his father’s money let him withdraw from. Taste, in this room, is what plunder looks like a generation on.

quotations.text: The cursed greed which has been my besetting sin through life has withheld from her the treasure, half at least of which should have been hers.
quotations.speaker: Major John Sholto
quotations.context: The Major’s deathbed confession to his sons, as Thaddeus reports it.
quotations.analysis: Half at least should have been hers — and the rest? The dying man reckons only with the English claim on the jewels, his dead friend’s daughter. The four convicts whose secret he bought with an oath, and the rajah before them, do not enter the account. He adds that he made no use of the treasure; possession was the whole pleasure. It is a miser’s confession and it is also, on a small scale, a colonial one.

quotations.text: Surely it was the place of a loyal friend to rejoice at such news; yet I am ashamed to say that selfishness took me by the soul, and that my heart turned as heavy as lead within me.
quotations.context: Thaddeus has put the value of the treasure at not less than half a million sterling.
quotations.analysis: Watson is honest about a feeling that does him no credit, and that honesty is what keeps him likeable through the book. It also gives the narrator a private stake in the outcome. From here the man telling the story of the hunt for the treasure wants it lost, and the reader should hold that in mind when he reports his relief in chapter XI as if it were simple.

quotations.text: How often have I said to you that when you have eliminated the impossible whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth?
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: In the locked room, asking Watson how the second intruder got in.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted rule in detective fiction, and here it is doing modest work: not the door, not the window, not the chimney, so the hole in the roof. As logic it is sound only if the list of possibilities is complete, and Holmes never shows that it is. What the sentence really supplies is tone. It turns a guess that happens to be right into a law, and how often makes Watson, and the reader, the slow pupil.

quotations.text: I could not but think what a terrible criminal he would have made had he turned his energy and sagacity against the law, instead of exerting them in its defence.
quotations.context: Watson watching Holmes go over the floor on his knees with a lens and a tape measure.
quotations.analysis: The sentence before this compares Holmes to a trained blood-hound and gives him beady eyes like a bird’s, so the detective is drawn in animal terms chapters before the Islander is. Watson means a compliment. But the book has already shown a Holmes who works for stimulation rather than for justice, and the thought that his side of the law is a matter of temperament is left sitting in the reader’s mind.

quotations.text: Facts are better than mere theories, after all.
quotations.speaker: Athelney Jones
quotations.context: Jones coming down from the garret, having found the trap-door Holmes had already shown Watson.
quotations.analysis: He is quoting Holmes’s creed back at him and has it upside down. Jones found one fact and hung a prepared theory on it — the brother did it, for the money — while the footprint, the thorn and the wooden stump are all in the room and fit none of it. Doyle makes the official detective the theorist and the amateur the empiricist, and the joke costs Thaddeus Sholto a night in the cells.

quotations.text: It was soothing to catch even that passing glimpse of a tranquil English home in the midst of the wild, dark business which had absorbed us.
quotations.context: Watson leaving Mary at Mrs Forrester’s door at two in the morning: hall-light, stained glass, barometer, stair-rods.
quotations.analysis: English home on one side, wild and dark on the other: Watson sorts the night into domestic and foreign. The case will not let the division stand. The wild business is an English major’s fraud carried out from an English villa, and the income that built such halls came, often enough, from where the treasure did. The glimpse soothes him because it lets him forget that.

quotations.text: They are naturally hideous, having large, misshapen heads, small, fierce eyes, and distorted features.
quotations.context: Holmes reading aloud from the first volume of a new gazetteer, under Andaman Islands.
quotations.analysis: Holmes, who never guesses, takes this on trust because it is in print. The entry goes on to put the people’s height below four feet and to end every shipwreck with a cannibal feast; none of it is true of the Andamanese, who were not cannibals and did not use blowpipes either. Naturally is the word to watch. It turns a judgement about looks into a fact of nature, and the chapter treats a book of colonial hearsay as the same kind of evidence as a footprint.

quotations.text: An injured lady, half a million in treasure, a black cannibal, and a wooden-legged ruffian. They take the place of the conventional dragon or wicked earl.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Cecil Forrester
quotations.context: Mary’s employer, hearing Watson’s account of the case over tea.
quotations.analysis: Doyle lets a character name the genre. Mrs Forrester hears a list of stock parts, and she is right: a man has been cast as the dragon. The remark is light, and it is the most self-aware line in the book, since it admits that the black cannibal is a role the story required rather than a person it met. Mary’s reply, that she cares nothing for the money, quietly declines the role written for her as well.

quotations.text: Never have I seen features so deeply marked with all bestiality and cruelty.
quotations.context: The searchlight falls on the second figure on the Aurora’s deck, seconds before the shooting.
quotations.analysis: This is the only look the novel takes at Tonga alive, and it is a verdict. Watson has been told what to expect by the gazetteer and sees it: the paragraph calls him a creature, gives him half animal fury, and has both men draw revolvers at the sight of him before he moves. A doctor who prides himself on reading faces reads this one as not human, and the narrative then shoots him. The sentence should be quoted as evidence about Watson and his sources, not about the Andamanese.

quotations.text: Somewhere in the dark ooze at the bottom of the Thames lie the bones of that strange visitor to our shores.
quotations.context: The police launch sweeps the water with its light and finds no body.
quotations.analysis: After creature and savage, visitor is almost courteous, and our shores makes the death a matter of geography: he was not from here. The present tense is the detail to notice. Watson, writing later, leaves the bones in the river beside the jewels, as though the two foreign things the Thames swallowed that night were of a kind. There is no inquest, and nobody asks whether firing was necessary.

quotations.text: To him it brought murder, to Major Sholto it brought fear and guilt, to me it has meant slavery for life.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small in the launch’s cabin, facing the iron box, before his full story.
quotations.analysis: The cursed Indian jewel was a familiar device by 1890, and it is a convenient one: a curse puts the harm in the stones rather than in the men who stole them. Small’s own sentence undoes the superstition. Murder, fear, guilt and penal labour are what theft and the law produce without supernatural help. Note also who is missing from his list of victims: the rajah who owned it, and Tonga, who has just died for it.

quotations.text: Whoever had lost a treasure, I knew that night that I had gained one.
quotations.context: Mary has accepted Watson beside the empty chest.
quotations.analysis: The pun closes the love story and gives away its logic. Mary takes the place of the jewels in Watson’s sentence, something gained as the other thing is lost, and whoever waves off the question of whose loss it was. It was hers, in law. The line is meant as tenderness and largely is, but it also completes a plot in which the woman’s fortune had to be destroyed before the man could speak.

quotations.text: Whose loot is this, if it is not ours? Where is the justice that I should give it up to those who have never earned it?
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Athelney Jones has told him that he has thwarted justice by sinking the jewels.
quotations.analysis: Loot came into English from Hindi, and Small uses it without embarrassment: he does not claim the treasure was clean, only that nobody in the room has a better title. Earned is a grotesque word for murder followed by twenty years in a swamp, yet the challenge stands. The Sholtos’ claim rests on fraud and the Crown’s on conquest. Doyle gives the argument to a convict in handcuffs and lets no one reply.

quotations.text: One month India lay as still and peaceful, to all appearance, as Surrey or Kent; the next there were two hundred thousand black devils let loose, and the country was a perfect hell.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small, an overseer on an indigo plantation near Muttra, describing the outbreak of 1857.
quotations.analysis: This is how the rebellion was told in Britain for a generation: a sleeping county, then fiends, with no cause in between. To all appearance is the phrase that lets daylight in, since a country that only looked like Surrey had reasons of its own. The voice is Small’s, a half-educated soldier’s, and Doyle may be characterising him; but nothing in the novel contradicts him, and his Indian partners are the only Indians it allows a motive.

quotations.text: We only ask you to do that which your countrymen come to this land for. We ask you to be rich.
quotations.speaker: Abdullah Khan
quotations.context: At the fort gate in Agra, with a knife at Small’s throat, proposing the murder of the merchant Achmet.
quotations.analysis: The clearest statement about empire in the book, and Doyle gives it to an Indian conspirator by way of an English convict. It removes any difference between what the four are about to do at a side-gate and what the East India Company did at large: both are people coming to this land to be rich. Small does not dispute it. He asks for three minutes and takes the oath, and the sign of the four is, from that moment, a joint venture.

quotations.text: He was stanch and true, was little Tonga. No man ever had a more faithful mate.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small describing the escape from the Andamans in Tonga’s canoe.
quotations.analysis: Set this beside Watson’s bestiality and cruelty: the only man who knew Tonga calls him faithful, and means it. But the praise is a master’s. Little, mate and, elsewhere, hell-hound, imp and poor Tonga are the words for a dog or a child, and the same speaker beat him with a rope’s end. The book offers two accounts of the Islander, a monster and a pet, and no third in which he might have had reasons of his own.

quotations.text: We earned a living at this time by my exhibiting poor Tonga at fairs and other such places as the black cannibal. He would eat raw meat and dance his war-dance: so we always had a hatful of pennies after a day’s work.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: How the two of them lived in England while Small watched Pondicherry Lodge.
quotations.analysis: Here the novel shows, almost by accident, how its own monster was made. The black cannibal is an act, put on for an English crowd that pays to be frightened, and Small knows it is an act; the raw meat is a turn. Mrs Forrester used the same phrase over tea in chapter IX. Doyle sees the fairground trick clearly enough to describe it and does not notice that the gazetteer, and chapter X, are selling the same show.

quotations.text: But love is an emotional thing, and whatever is emotional is opposed to that true cold reason which I place above all things.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes declining to congratulate Watson on his engagement.
quotations.analysis: He has just praised Mary’s genius for the work, in keeping the Agra plan out of all her father’s papers, so the objection is not to her. It is a creed, and the book has tested it. Cold reason found two men and lost half a million pounds; it took a night and a dog to do what a confession then made unnecessary. Holmes places reason above all things in the same breath as he admits to feeling limp as a rag.

quotations.text: “For me,” said Sherlock Holmes, “there still remains the cocaine-bottle.” And he stretched his long white hand up for it.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: The last lines. Watson has observed that he gets a wife and Jones the credit, and asked what is left for Holmes.
quotations.analysis: The novel ends on the gesture it began with, the long white hand and the bottle on the mantelpiece, so the whole case is enclosed between two doses. It is an oddly bleak finish for an adventure story. Everyone else is paid in the ordinary coin of plots, marriage, promotion, the gallows; the hero’s reward is the return of his boredom. Doyle had not yet decided that Holmes would be a series, and he closes him here as a character study of a man who cannot bear to be unoccupied.

books.title: Sleepy Hollow and Other American Halloween Stories
books.author: Washington Irving, Edgar Allan Poe and others

themes.name: Money, land and who gets the farm

techniques.name: The teller who gives himself away

characters.name: The narrator of The Yellow Wall-Paper

quotations.text: this sequestered glen has long been known by the name of SLEEPY HOLLOW, and its rustic lads are called the Sleepy Hollow Boys throughout all the neighboring country
quotations.context: Introducing the valley, before any character appears.
quotations.analysis: The place is named by its reputation rather than on a map, and the capitals give it the air of something quoted from local speech. Irving establishes that everything in the story is what people say about the place.

quotations.text: A drowsy, dreamy influence seems to hang over the land, and to pervade the very atmosphere.
quotations.context: The next sentence, explaining the valley's character.
quotations.analysis: Two adjectives that mean nearly the same thing, and a verb that will not commit — seems. Irving builds the supernatural out of climate and hearsay, so that nothing in the story ever has to be true.

quotations.text: the apparition of a figure on horseback without a head
quotations.context: The dominant spirit of the place, as the neighbourhood describes it.
quotations.analysis: The most famous image in American folklore is introduced as a piece of village reputation, at second hand, several thousand words before anything rides. Irving lets the community invent the ghost, and then sends Ichabod out to meet what it invented.

quotations.text: He was tall, but exceedingly lank, with narrow shoulders, long arms and legs, hands that dangled a mile out of his sleeves
quotations.context: The first description of Ichabod Crane.
quotations.analysis: Comic exaggeration done with exact parts — shoulders, arms, sleeves — so that the reader can see him before the sentence ends. Irving is teaching American prose how to do caricature without cruelty, and the technique passes straight into Twain.

quotations.text: Spare the rod and spoil the child
quotations.context: Ichabod's professional motto, quoted approvingly by the narrator.
quotations.analysis: A proverb from Proverbs, used to license a schoolmaster's caning and reported with a perfectly straight face. It is the first sign that this narrator will tell you what people believe without ever telling you what he believes.

quotations.text: his appetite for the marvellous, and his powers of digesting it, were equally extraordinary
quotations.context: On Ichabod's reading, which includes Cotton Mather's history of New England witchcraft.
quotations.analysis: The eating metaphor runs through the whole portrait — the man who can out-eat anybody also swallows every story he is told. Irving makes credulity a form of greed, which sets up the ride home exactly.

quotations.text: a huge feeder, and, though lank, had the dilating powers of an anaconda
quotations.context: At the Van Tassel table.
quotations.analysis: A schoolmaster compared to a snake swallowing something whole, in a sentence that is entirely affectionate. The joke also tells you what he wants from the farm, which is everything on it.

quotations.text: was found the hat of the unfortunate Ichabod, and close beside it a shattered pumpkin
quotations.context: What the search party finds by the brook in the morning.
quotations.analysis: The evidence is laid out and not interpreted: a hat, a pumpkin, hoof-prints at furious speed. Irving gives the reader everything needed to solve it and then spends his last pages letting the village prefer the ghost.

quotations.text: Ye are a baggage: the Slys are no rogues; look in the chronicles; we came in with Richard Conqueror.
quotations.speaker: Sly
quotations.context: Outside the alehouse, refusing to pay for the glasses he has broken.
quotations.analysis: He defends his family's standing by appealing to a history book he has never read and getting the Conqueror's name wrong. The play's first words are therefore a man insisting on an identity he cannot support — which is exactly the trick the lord is about to play on him from the other direction.

quotations.text: Come, madam wife, sit by my side and let the world slip: we shall ne'er be younger.
quotations.speaker: Sly
quotations.context: The last thing Sly says before the Padua play begins.
quotations.analysis: He has accepted the lordship, the wife who is a page in a dress, and the play about to be performed for him, all within a scene. These are almost his final words in the text: the character who has just learned to let the world slip is himself allowed to slip out of the comedy without explanation.

quotations.text: To see fair Padua, nursery of arts
quotations.speaker: Lucentio
quotations.context: Arriving in the city to study.
quotations.analysis: The play he has walked into is not about arts but about prices, and he will abandon the university within forty lines for a disguise and a marriage. Padua's reputation is set up in the second line of the main plot precisely so that everything that follows can ignore it.

quotations.text: Her eldest sister is so curst and shrewd That till the father rid his hands of her, Master, your love must live a maid at home;
quotations.speaker: Tranio
quotations.context: Explaining the household's rules to Lucentio.
quotations.analysis: Katherina is introduced to the audience as a problem of logistics: a thing the father must be rid of before the real business can proceed. 'Curst' and 'shrewd' are both technical terms of abuse for women rather than descriptions, and they are applied by a servant who has seen her once.

quotations.text: I come to wive it wealthily in Padua; If wealthily, then happily in Padua.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Telling Hortensio what kind of wife he is looking for.
quotations.analysis: The couplet makes wealth the condition of happiness in so many words, and the repetition of 'in Padua' turns the city into a marketplace with a location. Nothing later in the play retracts this; the love, if it is there, arrives after the terms have been agreed.

quotations.text: What, will you not suffer me? Nay, now I see She is your treasure, she must have a husband; I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day And for your love to her lead apes in hell.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: To her father, who has just sent Bianca out of the room after Katherina struck her.
quotations.analysis: The violence of the scene is real and so is the grievance underneath it: she is describing, accurately, a household in which one daughter is the treasure and the other the obstacle. Dancing barefoot at a younger sister's wedding and leading apes in hell were both proverbial fates of the unmarried, so she is naming the future arranged for her.

quotations.text: Asses are made to bear, and so are you.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: In the middle of the wit duel, after Petruchio invites her to sit on him.
quotations.analysis: She takes his innuendo and returns it as an insult in the same number of syllables, which is what the whole scene consists of. His reply — 'Women are made to bear, and so are you' — changes bearing weight into bearing children, and the exchange shows the two of them evenly matched at the only game either of them is playing.

quotations.text: Thus in plain terms: your father hath consented That you shall be my wife; your dowry 'greed on; And, Will you, nill you, I will marry you.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Ending the wooing scene, before her father returns.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses, and her consent is not among them: the father has agreed, the money has been agreed, and the remaining matter is announced rather than asked. 'Will you, nill you' — whether you are willing or not — is the plainest sentence in the play about how the marriage is made.

quotations.text: For I am he am born to tame you Kate, And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate Conformable as other household Kates.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Immediately before Baptista comes back to hear how the wooing went.
quotations.analysis: The pun runs through wild cat, Kate and cates, which were delicacies laid on a table — three meanings of a name she has already told him she does not use. Renaming is the first move of the taming, and it is done here in front of her while she is being told what she will become.

quotations.text: Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong, To strive for that which resteth in my choice: I am no breeching scholar in the schools; I'll not be tied to hours nor 'pointed times, But learn my lessons as I please myself.
quotations.speaker: Bianca
quotations.context: To her two disguised suitors, who are arguing about who teaches her first.
quotations.analysis: The obedient daughter, alone with two men and out of her father's hearing, says that the choice rests with her and sets the timetable herself. A breeching scholar is a schoolboy still young enough to be whipped, and she is refusing the position the whole household has assigned her.

quotations.text: To me she's married, not unto my clothes:
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Refusing to change out of the ridiculous outfit he has worn to his wedding.
quotations.analysis: It is a good argument, and it is made by a man who has spent the morning proving the opposite: the clothes are the entire point of the performance, as the Induction has already demonstrated on a tinker. He will use the same principle in reverse in 4.3, when a cap and a gown become grounds for ruining a tailor.

quotations.text: I see a woman may be made a fool, If she had not a spirit to resist.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: At the wedding, being told she will not be staying for the dinner.
quotations.analysis: It is the clearest statement of her position in the play, and it is made in public at her own wedding feast. The conditional is doing the work: she is not saying she has resisted successfully, only that resistance is the one thing standing between her and being made ridiculous — and four lines later she is carried out of the door.

quotations.text: I will be master of what is mine own: She is my goods, my chattels; she is my house, My household stuff, my field, my barn, My horse, my ox, my ass, my any thing;
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Removing Katherina from her own wedding feast, pretending to defend her from thieves.
quotations.analysis: The list descends from buildings to livestock to 'my any thing', and the legal terms are accurate: a wife's goods did pass to her husband. What makes the speech theatre rather than doctrine is the pantomime around it — he draws a weapon on an imaginary gang in order to carry her off as a rescue.

quotations.text: My falcon now is sharp and passing empty; And till she stoop she must not be full-gorged, For then she never looks upon her lure.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Alone on stage at the country house, after the food has been thrown away.
quotations.analysis: Every word is technical: a sharp hawk is hungry, stooping is the dive to the lure, full-gorged is fed. The audience is being handed a working method rather than a metaphor, and the calm of the vocabulary is what makes the speech disturbing — this is a man describing standard practice.

quotations.text: This is a way to kill a wife with kindness; And thus I'll curb her mad and headstrong humour. He that knows better how to tame a shrew, Now let him speak: 'tis charity to show.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: The end of the same soliloquy.
quotations.analysis: The phrase now used to mean overwhelming someone with affection is invented here to describe starvation and enforced sleeplessness carried out in the name of care. The closing invitation to the audience is the sharpest thing in the play: he asks a theatre full of husbands whether anyone has a better method, and waits.

quotations.text: Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak; And speak I will; I am no child, no babe: Your betters have endured me say my mind, And if you cannot, best you stop your ears.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: When the cap she has asked for is taken away from her.
quotations.analysis: She claims the right to speak rather than the cap, and the argument she makes is about who has authority over her tongue. Her next lines say that if her heart conceals its anger it will break — a physiological claim, not a rhetorical one, and the strongest case in the play for reading the last speech as something other than a change of mind.

quotations.text: Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun: But sun it is not, when you say it is not; And the moon changes even as your mind.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: On the road to Padua, after agreeing that the sun is the moon and being contradicted again.
quotations.analysis: She gives him the answer he wants and then explains the rule she has worked out: truth is whatever he last said. The third line is not obedience but a description of his behaviour, and productions that play the scene as a shared joke and productions that play it as defeat are both working from the same words.

quotations.text: Marry, peace it bodes, and love and quiet life, And awful rule and right supremacy; And, to be short, what not, that's sweet and happy?
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: When Katherina goes to fetch the other two wives.
quotations.analysis: Peace, love and quiet life are listed in the same breath as awful rule and right supremacy, as though they were the same thing rather than its price. 'Awful' here means awe-inspiring, which makes the sentence a definition of the household he thinks he has built.

quotations.text: The wager thou hast won; and I will add Unto their losses twenty thousand crowns; Another dowry to another daughter, For she is changed, as she had never been.
quotations.speaker: Baptista
quotations.context: After Katherina comes when sent for.
quotations.analysis: A father watches his daughter obey and responds by paying out: the transformation is priced at twenty thousand crowns and described as producing a different daughter altogether. It is the last word of the marriage market that opened the play, and it makes the obedience speech that follows a piece of after-sales demonstration.

quotations.text: Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper, Thy head, thy sovereign; one that cares for thee, And for thy maintenance commits his body To painful labour both by sea and land,
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: Instructing Bianca and the Widow on a wife's duty.
quotations.analysis: The argument is contractual: he labours by sea and land, she keeps warm at home, and obedience is the payment due. It is also a description of a marriage that is not hers — Petruchio has been at no sea, and the man who earned his wife by refusing her food is standing in the room while she says it.

quotations.text: My mind hath been as big as one of yours, My heart as great, my reason haply more, To bandy word for word and frown for frown; But now I see our lances are but straws,
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: Near the end of the obedience speech.
quotations.analysis: The past tense is doing something the rest of the speech does not: she tells the other women that she was their equal in mind and their superior in reason, and then says the weapons were never real. 'Bandy word for word' is an exact description of what she did to Petruchio in 2.1, so the speech remembers the wit duel even as it disowns it.

quotations.text: Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot, And place your hands below your husband's foot: In token of which duty, if he please, My hand is ready; may it do him ease.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: The last lines of the speech, and almost her last in the play.
quotations.analysis: Everything hangs on 'if he please' and on what the actor does with a hand that is offered rather than placed. The gesture is conditional, the token is symbolic, and Petruchio's reply is not thanks but a summons to bed — after which Katherina says nothing at all for the remaining eleven lines of the play.

quotations.text: Then what might your meaning be in calling me ‘Sir John’ these different times, when I be plain Jack Durbeyfield, the haggler?
quotations.speaker: John Durbeyfield
quotations.context: On the road to Marlott, to Parson Tringham, who has greeted him by a title.
quotations.analysis: He states his own name and trade accurately and in dialect, and it is the last time in the book anyone does so without embarrassment. The sentence is the hinge of the whole plot: a man asks for an explanation of a courtesy, and is given an ancestry he cannot afford.

quotations.text: ’Tis because we be on a blighted star, and not a sound one, isn’t it, Tess?
quotations.speaker: Abraham Durbeyfield
quotations.context: In the cart on the road to Casterbridge, after Tess has explained the stars to him, and before the mail-cart kills the horse.
quotations.analysis: A child converts an astronomy lesson into a theory of his family’s luck, and the novel lets it stand as the best available explanation. The image is agricultural rather than cosmic — the blighted apple on the stubbard-tree — so the cosmology is made out of the only materials the Durbeyfields have.

quotations.text: might some say, where was Tess’s guardian angel? where was the providence of her simple faith? Perhaps, like that other god of whom the ironical Tishbite spoke, he was talking, or he was pursuing, or he was in a journey, or he was sleeping and not to be awaked.
quotations.context: In The Chase, at the moment the narrative declines to describe.
quotations.analysis: The question is put into the mouth of an imagined objector — ‘might some say’ — so that the narrator can ask it without quite owning it. The answer comes from Elijah mocking the priests of Baal, which turns a plea for providence into a joke about a god who is out of the office.

quotations.text: Why it was that upon this beautiful feminine tissue, sensitive as gossamer, and practically blank as snow as yet, there should have been traced such a coarse pattern as it was doomed to receive; why so often the coarse appropriates the finer thus, the wrong man the woman, the wrong woman the man, many thousand years of analytical philosophy have failed to explain to our sense of order.
quotations.context: Immediately after the assault, in the narrator’s own voice.
quotations.analysis: Tess is described as fabric and the assault as a pattern traced on it, which keeps the violence entirely out of the grammar: there is no assailant in the sentence, only a coarseness that appropriates a fineness. The evasion has been read both as Hardy’s delicacy and as his failure of nerve.

quotations.text: An immeasurable social chasm was to divide our heroine’s personality thereafter from that previous self of hers who stepped from her mother’s door to try her fortune at Trantridge poultry-farm.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the first phase.
quotations.analysis: The damage is described as social rather than personal: what has changed is not Tess but the distance between two versions of her, and the chasm is measured from her mother’s door to a poultry farm. Hardy ends the phase on a job title, which is where the novel always puts its weight.

quotations.text: How could I be expected to know? I was a child when I left this house four months ago. Why didn’t you tell me there was danger in menfolk? Why didn’t you warn me? Ladies know what to fend hands against, because they read novels that tell them of these tricks; but I never had the chance o’ learning in that way, and you did not help me!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: Back at Marlott, answering her mother’s complaint that she has not managed to get Alec to marry her.
quotations.analysis: The accusation is about information, not morality: ladies read novels and therefore know, and Tess had no access to the warning. It is the only moment in the book where she names the mechanism of her own ruin, and she names it as a class fact.

quotations.text: But all the while she was making a distinction where there was no difference. Feeling herself in antagonism, she was quite in accord. She had been made to break an accepted social law, but no law known to the environment in which she fancied herself such an anomaly.
quotations.context: Walking at night after her return, believing herself a figure of guilt among innocent birds and hedges.
quotations.analysis: The sentence performs a small legal argument: there is an accepted social law and there is the law of the environment, and only the first has been broken. ‘Feeling herself in antagonism, she was quite in accord’ inverts her self-accusation without arguing with it, which is Hardy’s usual method of defence.

quotations.text: Sorrow, I baptize thee in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: In the bedroom at Marlott, at one in the morning, her father having locked the door against the parson.
quotations.analysis: She uses the exact liturgical formula, which is why the vicar afterwards cannot say the rite was invalid — only that it will not buy a place in the churchyard. The child’s name is a common noun, so the sentence baptises an emotion, and the form of words is the one piece of institutional authority Tess is able to take for herself.

quotations.text: So passed away Sorrow the Undesired⁠—that intrusive creature, that bastard gift of shameless Nature, who respects not the social law
quotations.context: After the burial in the corner of the churchyard reserved for the unbaptised and the suicides.
quotations.analysis: Three epithets in one clause, each in a different voice: the mother’s, the parish’s and the narrator’s. ‘Shameless Nature, who respects not the social law’ sets the two jurisdictions of the whole novel against each other in eight words, and leaves no doubt which one Hardy thinks is real.

quotations.text: The world was drawn to a larger pattern here. The enclosures numbered fifty acres instead of ten
quotations.context: Tess’s first sight of the Var valley from the ridge, on the way to Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: The change of scene is registered as a change of measurement: fields, herds and horizons all get bigger, and so does the room she has to move in. Hardy is careful to make the relief agricultural — this is better land, and better land means steadier work.

quotations.text: What a fresh and virginal daughter of Nature that milkmaid is!
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: Angel identifying the new milkmaid, to himself, at Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: Every word of it is a category rather than a person, and two of them will be used against her within a year. He is not lying and he is not looking: the sentence is a piece of pastoral criticism applied to a colleague, and the novel records that he said it to himself.

quotations.text: There was hardly a touch of earth in her love for Clare. To her sublime trustfulness he was all that goodness could be⁠—knew all that a guide, philosopher, and friend should know. She thought every line in the contour of his person the perfection of masculine beauty, his soul the soul of a saint, his intellect that of a seer.
quotations.context: During the engagement at Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: Her love is described as having no earth in it, in a book where earth is the one thing that can be relied on. The triple structure — guide, philosopher and friend, then saint and seer — makes her devotion sound liturgical, and prepares the exact ground on which he will later refuse her.

quotations.text: under the edge of the carpet she discerned the faint white margin of the envelope containing her letter to him, which he obviously had never seen, owing to her having in her haste thrust it beneath the carpet as well as beneath the door.
quotations.context: The morning of the wedding, in the room where Angel has been sleeping.
quotations.analysis: The disaster is a matter of half an inch of floor covering, and Hardy makes the reader watch her find it rather than reporting it afterwards. Note that the sentence assigns the error to her haste, not to malice or fate: the novel’s catastrophes are almost always this small and this domestic.

quotations.text: I repeat, the woman I have been loving is not you.
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: At the old d’Urberville farmhouse, hours after his own confession has been forgiven.
quotations.analysis: ‘I repeat’ tells us he has already said it once, which is the cruellest word in the sentence. He does not accuse her of anything; he unmakes her, replacing a person with a category error, and the novel has spent a whole phase showing that the category was his invention.

quotations.text: How can we live together while that man lives?⁠—he being your husband in nature, and not I.
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: Refusing Tess’s plea to be allowed to stay with him as a servant if not as a wife.
quotations.analysis: He converts an assault into a marriage and then reasons from it: the man who forced her is ‘your husband in nature’. The argument is legal in shape and biological in content, and it is the clearest statement in the book of the belief the subtitle was written to attack.

quotations.text: Close under the eaves of the stack, and as yet barely visible, was the red tyrant that the women had come to serve⁠—a timber-framed construction, with straps and wheels appertaining⁠—the threshing-machine which, whilst it was going, kept up a despotic demand upon the endurance of their muscles and nerves.
quotations.context: Dawn at Flintcomb-Ash, as the threshing gang assembles.
quotations.analysis: The machine is given a colour, a title and a household of servants before it is given a technical description. ‘Despotic demand’ converts a wage relationship into a political one, and the women are the last link in it: the engine sets the speed, and Tess cannot step off the platform while it runs.

quotations.text: Whip me, crush me; you need not mind those people under the rick! I shall not cry out. Once victim, always victim⁠—that’s the law!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: On the threshing rick, after striking Alec across the mouth with her leather glove.
quotations.analysis: She invites the punishment and states the principle in the same breath, and the word she chooses is ‘law’. It is the same word the narrator used in Phase the Second about the accepted social law she had broken, and here Tess speaks it as if it were physics.

quotations.text: Remember, my lady, I was your master once! I will be your master again. If you are any man’s wife you are mine!
quotations.speaker: Alec d’Urberville
quotations.context: Holding her by the shoulders on the rick, after she has refused his offer to keep her family.
quotations.analysis: Three sentences, three tenses: was, will be, are. The vocabulary is of ownership throughout, and ‘my lady’ is a sneer at the ancestry that brought her to him in the first place. The threat is also a prediction, and the novel lets it come true.

quotations.text: I must cry to you in my trouble⁠—I have no one else! I am so exposed to temptation, Angel. I fear to say who it is, and I do not like to write about it at all. But I cling to you in a way you cannot think! Can you not come to me now, at once, before anything terrible happens?
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: The letter written at Flintcomb-Ash and sent to Angel’s parents to be forwarded to Brazil.
quotations.analysis: She will not name the danger even in a private letter, which is exactly the reticence that has cost her twice already. The phrase ‘before anything terrible happens’ is the novel’s only piece of accurate forecasting, and the distance to Brazil guarantees that it arrives too late to be one.

quotations.text: Angel, I am almost glad⁠—yes, glad! This happiness could not have lasted. It was too much. I have had enough; and now I shall not live for you to despise me!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: Waking on the stone at Stonehenge as the police close in at dawn.
quotations.analysis: Her last argument is about time rather than justice: the happiness was too much, so it could not have lasted, so ending it now is a form of thrift. ‘I shall not live for you to despise me’ shows that the wedding night is still the governing event of her life, five years and two men later.

quotations.text: the President of the Immortals, in Aeschylean phrase, had ended his sport with Tess.
quotations.context: As the black flag rises over Wintoncester gaol and Angel and Liza-Lu watch from the hill.
quotations.analysis: Hardy puts ‘Justice’ in quotation marks and then hands the credit to a figure out of Aeschylus, which lets him blame a god he does not believe in for a sentence passed by an English court. The evasion is deliberate: no judge, no juror and no clergyman is named, and the reader is left to supply them.

themes.name: Play, work and the difference between them
themes.canonicalName: Play, work and the difference between them

quotations.text: Most of the adventures recorded in this book really occurred; one or two were experiences of my own, the rest those of boys who were schoolmates of mine.
quotations.context: The opening of Twain’s preface, signed before the story begins.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the flat voice of a deposition, and it is doing two jobs: it licenses the book’s cruelties as reportage and it warns the reader not to look for a moral design. Twain goes on to say that Tom is a composite of three boys and therefore belongs to the composite order of architecture — a joke that quietly admits how much arranging has been done.

quotations.text: He was not the Model Boy of the village. He knew the model boy very well though⁠—and loathed him.
quotations.context: Introducing Tom, after the first chase round the house.
quotations.analysis: The capital letters make the Model Boy an office rather than a person, and the drop to lower case in the second sentence quietly demotes him. ‘Loathed’ is much stronger than the joke requires, and it sets the book’s position early: the village’s system of rewards is not being satirised from outside but hated from within.

quotations.text: Every time I let him off, my conscience does hurt me so, and every time I hit him my old heart most breaks.
quotations.speaker: Aunt Polly
quotations.context: Alone in the kitchen, after Tom has escaped over the fence.
quotations.analysis: Her dilemma is stated as a perfect trap with no third option, and the balanced grammar — every time, every time — is the sound of an argument she has had with herself for years. It tells the reader before Chapter 2 that punishment in this book is a ritual nobody expects to work.

quotations.text: “Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”
quotations.speaker: Tom Sawyer
quotations.context: Answering Ben Rogers, who has come to jeer at him for working on a Saturday.
quotations.analysis: The rhetorical question does all the work: scarcity is invented out of nothing, and Ben is converted in four lines. Tom never claims the job is pleasant — he claims it is rare, which is the distinction the next paragraph turns into a law of human action.

quotations.text: He had discovered a great law of human action, without knowing it⁠—namely, that in order to make a man or a boy covet a thing, it is only necessary to make the thing difficult to attain.
quotations.context: After the fence has been whitewashed three times over by other boys who paid for the privilege.
quotations.analysis: The narrator takes a boy’s trick and restates it as economics, and the phrase ‘without knowing it’ opens the distance between the adult telling and the child acting that the whole book runs on. It is also a rare instance of Twain giving the reader the moral of an episode outright, and he immediately undercuts it with a joke about the wise philosopher who wrote the book.

quotations.text: Work consists of whatever a body is obliged to do, and that Play consists of whatever a body is not obliged to do.
quotations.context: The narrator continuing his commentary on the whitewashing.
quotations.analysis: Both definitions turn on obligation rather than effort, which is why the book can put pirates, treasure-hunting and a three-day ordeal in a cave on the same side of the line as a game. The examples that follow — treadmills against Mont Blanc — make the point that the difference is in who is making you do it.

quotations.text: Huckleberry was cordially hated and dreaded by all the mothers of the town, because he was idle and lawless and vulgar and bad⁠—and because all their children admired him so, and delighted in his forbidden society, and wished they dared to be like him.
quotations.context: Tom meets the juvenile pariah of the village on his way to school.
quotations.analysis: The sentence gives the official reason and the real one in the same breath, joined by an ‘and’ that pretends they are the same kind of thing. Note the order of the adjectives — idle first, bad last — which is the town’s scale of values rather than a moral one.

quotations.text: “Say⁠—what is dead cats good for, Huck?”
quotations.speaker: Tom Sawyer
quotations.context: Tom has just noticed what Huck is swinging by the tail.
quotations.analysis: The question is asked in the tone of one specialist consulting another, and the discussion that follows — spunk-water, bean-burying, the exact words to say — has the structure of a technical seminar. It is also the hinge of the plot: this conversation is what takes two children into a graveyard at midnight.

quotations.text: “Tom, we got to keep mum. You know that. That Injun devil wouldn’t make any more of drownding us than a couple of cats, if we was to squeak ’bout this and they didn’t hang him.
quotations.speaker: Huckleberry Finn
quotations.context: The two boys in the old tannery, an hour after the murder.
quotations.analysis: Huck’s reasoning is entirely practical and entirely correct, and it is the practical argument, not the oath, that binds them. The simile about cats returns the reader to the dead cat that took them to the graveyard, which is Twain’s habit of letting the comic props reappear as threats.

quotations.text: “Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swears they will keep mum about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.”
quotations.context: The oath written on a pine shingle in red keel and signed in blood.
quotations.analysis: The capital letters are the boys’ idea of what a legal document looks like, copied from nothing they have ever read properly. The document is a game and a binding contract at once — this is the point in the novel where play stops being separable from consequence, and a man goes to trial because two children have signed a shingle.

quotations.text: Tom’s fearful secret and gnawing conscience disturbed his sleep for as much as a week after this
quotations.context: The days following Muff Potter’s arrest.
quotations.analysis: ‘For as much as a week’ is the sentence’s sting: the narrator measures a child’s remorse against an adult’s and finds it short. Twain neither excuses Tom nor makes him a monster — he simply records the duration, and then lets the guilt come back every time the schoolboys hold another inquest on a dead cat.

quotations.text: The pipe dropped from the fingers of the Red-Handed, and he slept the sleep of the conscience-free and the weary.
quotations.context: The first night on Jackson’s Island, in the pirate camp.
quotations.analysis: The boys’ chosen titles are used straight-faced by the narrator, so that ‘the Red-Handed’ and ‘conscience-free’ sit in the same clause. The joke has an edge: Huck, who has no conscience to trouble him about running away, is the one of the three with a murder on his mind and can still sleep.

quotations.text: the congregation rose and stared while the three dead boys came marching up the aisle
quotations.context: In the middle of the funeral sermon preached over Tom, Joe and Huck.
quotations.analysis: The narration keeps calling them dead after they have walked in, which is exactly how the congregation sees them for the length of a held breath. Tom has engineered the best entrance available to a human being, and the novel notes a few lines later that Huck, who has no family in the church, gets no share of the welcome.

quotations.text: “Speak out, my boy⁠—don’t be diffident. The truth is always respectable. What did you take there?”
quotations.context: Counsel for the defence examining Tom in the murder trial.
quotations.analysis: The lawyer’s maxim collides immediately with the answer — a dead cat — and the court laughs. Twain places the book’s most solemn statement about truth one line before its silliest object, which is his standard method for keeping a moral from hardening into a lesson.

quotations.text: Tom began⁠—hesitatingly at first, but as he warmed to his subject his words flowed more and more easily; in a little while every sound ceased but his own voice; every eye fixed itself upon him
quotations.context: Tom breaking the oath in open court, with Injun Joe sitting in the room.
quotations.analysis: The act of conscience is described in exactly the vocabulary the book uses for his performances — warming to his subject, every eye on him — so that the bravest thing Tom does is also his best entrance. Twain does not let the reader separate the two, and the chapter ends with the witness terrified for months afterwards.

quotations.text: There were some that believed he would be President, yet, if he escaped hanging.
quotations.context: St Petersburg’s verdict on Tom after the trial.
quotations.analysis: The village’s two available futures for a remarkable boy are the highest office in the country and the gallows, and it cannot tell which is coming. The sentence also dates the book precisely: this is a river town’s idea of how far a bright, unmanageable child might go, and the joke was old enough by 1876 to be affectionate.

quotations.text: “Tom, Tom, we’re lost! we’re lost! We never can get out of this awful place! Oh, why did we ever leave the others!”
quotations.speaker: Becky Thatcher
quotations.context: In McDougal’s cave, after the candles have shown them an unfamiliar passage.
quotations.analysis: Becky is given the plain statement of the situation while Tom is still constructing reassurances, which reverses the usual distribution of realism in the novel. The exclamation marks and the repetition are the only hysteria the book allows anybody, and it is immediately followed by Tom keeping his voice cheerful — a performance, and the thing that gets them out.

quotations.text: Injun Joe’s bowie-knife lay close by, its blade broken in two. The great foundation-beam of the door had been chipped and hacked through, with tedious labor; useless labor, too, it was, for the native rock formed a sill outside it
quotations.context: When the cave door is opened, a fortnight after the town sealed it.
quotations.analysis: The passage is written as a forensic reconstruction — knife, beam, sill, the hollow worn in stone by dripping water — and the repetition of ‘labor’ makes the dying man’s work sound like the whitewashing chapter turned inside out. Twain then has the town hold a picnic at the cave mouth for the funeral, which is the harshest judgement in the book and is delivered without comment.

quotations.text: “Don’t talk about it, Tom. I’ve tried it, and it don’t work; it don’t work, Tom. It ain’t for me; I ain’t used to it.
quotations.speaker: Huckleberry Finn
quotations.context: Found in an empty hogshead after three weeks in the Widow Douglas’s house.
quotations.analysis: The repetition is not rhetoric but exhaustion, and the complaint that follows is entirely about the body: washing, combing, clothes that let no air through, meals by the clock. Huck makes the only sustained case in the novel against what the town calls kindness, and Tom defeats it with an argument about club membership.

quotations.text: So endeth this chronicle. It being strictly a history of a boy, it must stop here; the story could not go much further without becoming the history of a man.
quotations.context: The first sentences of the Conclusion, after the last chapter.
quotations.analysis: The archaism of ‘So endeth’ borrows the cadence of a lesson read in church, and is then used to explain a purely technical decision about where a book stops. The remark about novels of grown people ending with a marriage also tells you what Twain thinks he has avoided — and Huckleberry Finn, nine years later, is the history of a boy who does not stop.

themes.name: The sea as voice and limit
themes.canonicalName: The sea as voice and limit

quotations.text: looking at his wife as one looks at a valuable piece of personal property which has suffered some damage
quotations.context: Léonce, having told Edna she is burnt beyond recognition, on her return from the beach.
quotations.analysis: The simile is the narrator's, not Léonce's, and it is dropped into an otherwise placid domestic paragraph without comment. Two sentences later Edna is holding out her hands to be given back her rings, which the novel lets the reader connect on their own.

quotations.text: An indescribable oppression, which seemed to generate in some unfamiliar part of her consciousness, filled her whole being with a vague anguish.
quotations.context: Alone on the porch at night, after Léonce has scolded her for neglecting the children and gone to sleep.
quotations.analysis: Every term in the sentence is an admission of ignorance — indescribable, unfamiliar, vague — and the vagueness is precise rather than lazy. Chopin will not let Edna have a word for her own condition at the moment she first feels it, which is what distinguishes this book from a novel of grievance.

quotations.text: In short, Mrs. Pontellier was not a mother-woman.
quotations.context: After an account of how the Grand Isle mothers idolise their children.
quotations.analysis: 'In short' pretends that the sentence is a summary of the preceding paragraph, when in fact it is the introduction of a category that did not exist before Chopin coined it. The hyphen is doing the work: motherhood is being described as a type of person rather than a relationship, which is the first step in separating the two.

quotations.text: A certain light was beginning to dawn dimly within her
quotations.context: At the start of the short chapter that stands back from the story to explain what is happening to Edna.
quotations.analysis: The clause is completed in the corpus by a phrase that takes the promise straight back: the light shows the way and forbids it. Chopin puts her heroine's whole predicament into one image before the plot has moved at all, and the novel spends thirty-three chapters demonstrating that the prohibition was accurate.

quotations.text: In short, Mrs. Pontellier was beginning to realize her position in the universe as a human being, and to recognize her relations as an individual to the world within and about her.
quotations.context: The narrator's summary of the change taking place over the summer.
quotations.analysis: The phrasing is that of a philosophical treatise, and it is applied to a woman on a holiday gallery who has done nothing more remarkable than agree to a swim. Chopin repeats the formula 'In short, Mrs. Pontellier' from two chapters earlier, so that the negative definition is now answered by a positive one.

quotations.text: The voice of the sea is seductive; never ceasing, whispering, clamoring, murmuring, inviting the soul to wander for a spell in abysses of solitude; to lose itself in mazes of inward contemplation.
quotations.context: The end of the short chapter that explains the summer's effect on Edna.
quotations.analysis: The tense is present and general — this is what the sea does, not what it did that evening — which lifts the sentence out of the narrative and lets it be used again. Note that the invitation is to solitude rather than to freedom, and that the novel takes the offer literally in its last chapter.

quotations.text: But the very passions themselves were aroused within her soul, swaying it, lashing it, as the waves daily beat upon her splendid body.
quotations.context: Listening to Mademoiselle Reisz play, in a room of holidaymakers who applaud politely.
quotations.analysis: Edna had expected music to produce pictures — solitude, hope, longing — and gets the emotions themselves with no images attached. The comparison to the surf is the book's first link between the piano and the Gulf, and it makes the effect of art physical in a novel that is about to make the body the whole question.

quotations.text: A feeling of exultation overtook her, as if some power of significant import had been given her to control the working of her body and her soul.
quotations.context: The night she finally swims, after a whole summer of failing to.
quotations.analysis: The achievement is small — she has crossed a few yards of shallow water — and the language is that of investiture, because what she has actually acquired is the experience of directing herself. 'Body and soul' is the formula Chopin will hand back to her at the end of the novel, when she refuses to let anyone else possess either.

quotations.text: She grew daring and reckless, overestimating her strength. She wanted to swim far out, where no woman had swum before.
quotations.context: Minutes into her first successful swim.
quotations.analysis: The narrator supplies the judgement — overestimating — before Edna has come to any harm, so the reader is warned in the same breath as being exhilarated. 'Where no woman had swum before' is exploration language applied to a stretch of Gulf that men crossed every day, and the qualification is the whole point.

quotations.text: I would give up the unessential; I would give my money, I would give my life for my children; but I wouldn’t give myself.
quotations.speaker: Edna Pontellier
quotations.context: Arguing with Adèle Ratignolle on the beach after Robert's departure.
quotations.analysis: She is drawing a distinction her friend cannot follow, and she knows it — the next sentence admits she is only beginning to understand it herself. Putting life in the middle of the list and self at the end inverts the usual scale of sacrifice, and the novel's ending turns on whether that inversion can be sustained.

quotations.text: Once she stopped, and taking off her wedding ring, flung it upon the carpet. When she saw it lying there, she stamped her heel upon it, striving to crush it.
quotations.context: Alone in the house after quarrelling with Léonce about her abandoned reception day.
quotations.analysis: The gesture fails: the boot heel does not mark the ring, and she puts it back on within the paragraph. Chopin gives her heroine one melodramatic act and then shows the object surviving it undamaged, which is a fair summary of what the institution will do to her rebellion.

quotations.text: It was not a condition of life which fitted her, and she could see in it but an appalling and hopeless ennui.
quotations.context: Leaving the Ratignolles' apartment after an evening of perfect domestic harmony.
quotations.analysis: The scene she has just watched is genuinely happy, and the novel does not undercut it: the failure is one of fit rather than of value. Chopin's refusal to make the alternative life contemptible is what stops the book being a tract, and it is also what leaves Edna with nowhere to go.

quotations.text: She began to do as she liked and to feel as she liked.
quotations.context: After deciding that stamping on a ring was childish, and abandoning her Tuesdays at home.
quotations.analysis: One flat sentence, two verbs, no adverb of approval or alarm, and it describes what would have been a scandal in most novels of the period. The second half is the more radical: she stops performing feelings as well as duties, and the household's whole machinery of visits and callers falls over as a result.

quotations.text: The bird that would soar above the level plain of tradition and prejudice must have strong wings. It is a sad spectacle to see the weaklings bruised, exhausted, fluttering back to earth.
quotations.speaker: Mademoiselle Reisz
quotations.context: Reported by Edna to Arobin, after Reisz felt her shoulder blades to see whether her wings were strong.
quotations.analysis: It reaches the reader at second hand, quoted by a woman repeating a warning she has decided to treat as a joke. Chopin then plants the image where it will be needed: the last chapter opens with a bird with a broken wing coming down to the water, and offers no gloss on it at all.

quotations.text: The pigeon house pleased her. It at once assumed the intimate character of a home
quotations.context: Having moved out of her husband's house into a small rented one around the corner.
quotations.analysis: The name is a servant's joke about the size of the place, and Edna adopts it without embarrassment. The passage goes on to describe a sense of having gone down in the social scale and risen in the spiritual one, which is the novel's most explicit statement that independence here is also a reduction.

quotations.text: I am no longer one of Mr. Pontellier’s possessions to dispose of or not. I give myself where I choose.
quotations.speaker: Edna Pontellier
quotations.context: To Robert, who has just explained that he had dreamed of Léonce setting her free.
quotations.analysis: She answers the offer by rejecting its grammar: the question of who may dispose of her does not arise. It is the clearest thing she says in the book, it is addressed to the man she loves, and he is unable to hear it — the next time she is in the room he has gone, leaving a note about loving her enough to leave.

quotations.text: Think of the children, Edna. Oh think of the children! Remember them!
quotations.speaker: Adèle Ratignolle
quotations.context: Whispered, in an exhausted voice, immediately after Adèle's confinement.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives from a woman who has just given birth, addressed to the one person in the room who did not want to be there. Chopin gives the novel's decisive sentence to the sweetest character in it, and makes it an appeal rather than an argument — which is exactly why Edna cannot dispose of it.

quotations.text: perhaps it is better to wake up after all, even to suffer, rather than to remain a dupe to illusions all one’s life
quotations.speaker: Edna Pontellier
quotations.context: Walking home with Doctor Mandelet from Adèle's bedside.
quotations.analysis: It is the only assessment of her own awakening that Edna offers anybody, and it is hedged twice — 'perhaps', 'after all' — as though she were still working it out on the pavement. The doctor has just described the illusions as a trap set by nature to secure mothers for the race, so her reply is an answer to a theory as well as a statement about herself.

quotations.text: A bird with a broken wing was beating the air above, reeling, fluttering, circling disabled down, down to the water.
quotations.context: On the empty beach at Grand Isle, out of season.
quotations.analysis: Mademoiselle Reisz's warning about weaklings fluttering back to earth arrives as an event in the landscape, twelve chapters later and without a word of commentary. Whether the reader takes it as Edna's verdict on herself or as something merely happening on the beach is left entirely open, and the sentence is placed between two blocks of prose about the sea.

quotations.text: How strange and awful it seemed to stand naked under the sky! how delicious! She felt like some newborn creature, opening its eyes in a familiar world that it had never known.
quotations.context: On the beach, having left her bathing suit on the sand.
quotations.analysis: Two exclamations with opposite charges in the same breath, and then a birth image at the end of a life. 'A familiar world that it had never known' is the whole novel in nine words: nothing around her has changed, and she is seeing it for the first time.

quotations.text: But they need not have thought that they could possess her, body and soul.
quotations.context: Thinking of Léonce and the children while swimming out.
quotations.analysis: The verb is the one from the wedding-ring and property scenes, and the objects are now her husband and her sons together. The sentence is in free indirect style, so the reader cannot tell whether it is a conclusion or a last piece of self-persuasion — which is where Chopin leaves the entire ending.

quotations.text: And you call yourself an artist! What pretensions, Madame! The artist must possess the courageous soul that dares and defies.
quotations.speaker: Mademoiselle Reisz
quotations.context: Imagined by Edna in the water, as the sneer Reisz would have given her.
quotations.analysis: The one standard Edna is still measuring herself against is delivered in a voice she is supplying herself, from a woman who is not present. It is the last piece of dialogue in the novel, and it is a rebuke — the book ends with its heroine inventing her sternest critic and then going on.

quotations.text: There was the hum of bees, and the musky odor of pinks filled the air.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book closes on a Kentucky garden from Edna's childhood, in the present tense of memory, with no statement about the water at all. Bees and flowers rather than drowning: Chopin ends on the sensory world that Edna's awakening began in, and refuses to write the sentence a reader is waiting for.

themes.name: The portrait he does not know he is painting
Respectability, and what it costs to keep up
Clerks, tradesmen and the people above
The Laurels, and the work of keeping it up

quotations.text: Why should I not publish my diary? I have often seen reminiscences of people I have never even heard of, and I fail to see—because I do not happen to be a ‘Somebody’—why my diary should not be interesting.
quotations.speaker: Charles Pooter
quotations.context: The whole of Pooter's preface, signed and dated from The Laurels, Brickfield Terrace, Holloway, before the diary proper begins.
quotations.analysis: The book's title is answered before the book starts, and the answer is a question nobody asked. Pooter argues from a real grievance — celebrated nobodies publish their memories, so why not an uncelebrated one — and the argument is perfectly sound; it is the tone that gives him away, the defensive dash, the sniff at ‘Somebody’ in inverted commas. He is the first of the two brothers' jokes and the last: the reader is about to agree with him, for two hundred pages, for reasons he would not accept.

quotations.text: I restrained my feelings, and quietly remarked that I thought it was possible for a city clerk to be a gentleman. He replied he was very glad to hear it, and wanted to know whether I had ever come across one, for he hadn’t.
quotations.context: Borset the butterman, drunk in the downstairs hall, has said he will be hanged if he serves City clerks any more.
