quotations.analysis: This is the book's subject stated in the first chapter by a man delivering butter. Pooter's sentence is a small masterpiece of self-defence: restrained, quietly, remarked, thought it was possible — four hedges in one line, so that the claim is barely made before it is knocked down. The riposte works because it accepts his terms and simply denies the evidence. Two sentences later he hears Borset fall over the scraper and is glad he never had it moved, and the entry ends with him thinking of a splendid answer he ought to have given, which he keeps for another occasion and never uses.

quotations.text: I don’t often make jokes, but I replied: “You’re talking a lot of dry rot yourself.” I could not help roaring at this, and Carrie said her sides quite ached with laughter. I never was so immensely tickled by anything I have ever said before. I actually woke up twice during the night, and laughed till the bed shook.
quotations.context: Gowing, who has complained about the smell of paint on every visit, announces that this time he distinctly smells dry rot.
quotations.analysis: The joke is thin and the reporting of it is enormous, and the disproportion is the comedy. Note the preface — I don't often make jokes — which he has already used once, eight days earlier, over the scraper and the scrape; it is not modesty but a flourish, a man rolling up his sleeves. Then four sentences of aftermath: roaring, aching sides, a superlative, and finally a night of it. The bed shaking in the dark is the detail that turns a weak pun into something close to tenderness, and it is also the exact measure of how little else there is to laugh at in Brickfield Terrace.

quotations.text: I thought I was the aggrieved party; but as I freely forgive you, you—feeling yourself aggrieved—should bestow forgiveness on me. … I have copied this verbatim in the diary, because I think it is one of the most perfect and thoughtful sentences I have ever written. I posted the letter, but in my own heart I felt I was actually apologising for having been insulted.
quotations.context: Cummings and Gowing left Pooter outside a public-house for the best part of an hour, and have written demanding an explanation of his conduct.
quotations.analysis: Three movements in one entry, and each undoes the one before. The sentence itself is a knot: a forgiveness that requires forgiving back, so that the injured party ends by asking pardon. Then comes the vanity, and the reason the reader gets to see the knot at all — he has copied it out because he is proud of it. Then the last line, which is the sharpest thing in the first half of the book, because it shows he knows. The diary form does all the work here. No other shape would let a man record his own cleverness and his own defeat in the same paragraph, in that order.

quotations.text: It’s concerning you both; for doesn’t it seem odd that Gowing’s always coming and Cummings’ always going? … I think this was one of the best jokes I have ever made.
quotations.speaker: Charles Pooter
quotations.context: Both friends have called on the evening of the red bath; Cummings has already said Funny as usual, without warmth.
quotations.analysis: The best-known joke in the book, and the laugh and the silence come in successive paragraphs. Carrie goes into fits and Pooter doubles up until the chair cracks; then the two men look at him without smiling, and Gowing calls a pun on a name wanting in taste. What makes it funny rather than painful is that Pooter never revises the verdict. The sentence stands in the diary unaltered.

quotations.text: My first thought was that I had ruptured an artery, and was bleeding to death, and should be discovered, later on, looking like a second Marat, as I remember seeing him in Madame Tussaud’s. My second thought was to ring the bell, but remembered there was no bell to ring. My third was, that there was nothing but the enamel paint, which had dissolved with boiling water.
quotations.context: Two days after painting the bath red, Pooter decides to treat a chill with a bath as hot as he can bear.
quotations.analysis: The structure is a countdown from tragedy to ironmongery, and the numbering does it: first, second, third, each thought smaller than the last. The middle step is the one to watch — the bell that has been broken since the first page, so that even the melodrama cannot be rung for. Marat is exactly the right reference for him, since he has not read about the murder but seen the waxwork, which is how the whole of Pooter's culture reaches him. Then the paragraph ends with the paint, and the business of the morning: he will tell Farmerson to come and paint the bath white.

quotations.text: I simply looked at him, and said coolly: “I never expected to see you here.” He said, with a loud, coarse laugh: “I like that—if you, why not me?” … Farmerson seized me rather roughly by the collar, and addressing the sheriff, said: “Let me introduce my neighbour, Pooter.” He did not even say “Mister.”
quotations.context: The supper-room at the Mansion House, where Pooter has just been slapped on the shoulder by the ironmonger who was to have repainted his bath.
quotations.analysis: Farmerson demolishes the evening in six words, and does it without malice, which is worse. Pooter's snub has assumed a ladder that the ironmonger simply does not believe in; and within five minutes a sheriff in full court costume has his arm round Farmerson's neck, so the ladder turns out not to exist. The last stroke is the smallest: the missing Mister. Pooter has spent four chapters and a great deal of money to be in that room, and he is introduced there as a neighbour by the man who mended his scraper, on first-name terms with people he cannot reach.

quotations.text: After professing to snub Mr. Farmerson, you permit him to snub you, in my presence, and then accept his invitation to take a glass of champagne with you, and you don’t limit yourself to one glass. You then offer this vulgar man, who made a bungle of repairing our scraper, a seat in our cab on the way home.
quotations.speaker: Caroline Pooter
quotations.context: The morning after the ball. Pooter has opened by asking, perfectly calmly and quietly, for a little explanation of his wife's conduct.
quotations.analysis: This is the only sustained attack on Pooter delivered by somebody who loves him, and it is the only one he transcribes in full. Carrie's method is a list in chronological order with no adjectives except vulgar, which is the word he would have used himself, and the sting is that every item is true and the reader has already seen it happen. The entry then does the thing that makes the book more than a set of jokes: he writes down the whole speech, calls himself humiliated, and does not answer it. Gowing comes in wearing two hats and calls it a lovers' quarrel.

quotations.text: “We have received two letters from Mr. and Mrs. Charles Pewter, requesting us to announce the important fact that they were at the Mansion House Ball.” I tore up the paper and threw it in the waste-paper basket. My time is far too valuable to bother about such trifles.
quotations.context: The third attempt to get his name into the Blackfriars Bi-weekly News list of guests; the second attempt printed him as Porter, so he wrote it out in capitals.
quotations.analysis: The paper has worked out what he is doing and printed it as news, with the phrase the important fact carrying the whole of the editor's opinion. The comedy then doubles back on him twice. He has written twice and ordered a dozen copies to send to friends, so the sneer is exactly earned; and his closing line about his time being too valuable arrives after three entries spent on nothing else. The misspellings are the crudest of jokes — Porter, Pewter — and the best, because a man whose name cannot survive a typesetter has no business worrying about the Lord Mayor.

quotations.text: Imagine my dismay when he replied with a loud guffaw: “It’s no use. If you want the good old truth, I’ve got the chuck!”
quotations.speaker: Lupin Pooter
quotations.context: Lupin has just announced that he has tendered his resignation at the bank, and his father has ordered him to sit down and withdraw it at dictation.
quotations.analysis: Two Englishes collide in one exchange. The father's is formal and futile — how dare you, sir; you will sit down immediately; amply apologising for your thoughtlessness — the language of a man who believes an employer can be written to. The son's is four syllables of slang that cancel the whole speech. The guffaw matters: Lupin is not ashamed, and the reader can see what Pooter cannot, that the resignation was a face-saving lie which his father's pomposity has just forced him to drop. Five days later Pooter records that being sacked for idleness is, on the whole, satisfactory.

quotations.text: I was a little vexed at everybody subsequently laughing at some joke which they did not explain, and it was only on going to bed I discovered I must have been walking about all the evening with an antimacassar on one button of my coat-tails.
quotations.context: An evening of card games with Mrs. James and Gowing, during which Lupin has led Gowing to a looking-glass and called the game monkeys.
quotations.analysis: The perfect emblem of the book, and Pooter files it without comment. The sentence is built to delay: a little vexed, a joke not explained, and then the discovery at bedtime, hours too late to do anything but write it down. An antimacassar is the most domestic object in the house, the cloth that protects a chair-back from hair-oil, and he has been dragging respectability's own furnishing round the room behind him. He works it out in the end, which is the part readers tend to forget. He simply works it out too late, every time, and keeps the record anyway.

quotations.text: I should very much like to know who has wilfully torn the last five or six weeks out of my diary. It is perfectly monstrous! Mine is a large scribbling diary, with plenty of space for the record of my everyday events, and in keeping up that record I take (with much pride) a great deal of pains.
quotations.context: The entry that follows a jump of two months. A burnt scrap in the grate turns out to be part of the diary.
quotations.analysis: The book eats itself, and the reader feels the hole before the explanation arrives, since the last entry was in August. Pooter's defence of the diary is his defence of himself — large, plenty of space, much pride, a great deal of pains — and the household's verdict is delivered by the fire: it was the handiest paper for lighting one. He never discovers who did it, and the inquiry runs through the servant, the charwoman and the sweep, all of whom deny it and none of whom is believed. The following day he admits that the missing weeks held nothing but rejection letters for Lupin.

quotations.text: I apologised for the foolery, but Mr. Perkupp said: “Oh, it seems amusing.” I could see he was not a bit amused.
quotations.context: The Pooters' first important party. Lupin and Frank Mutlar have just burst in as the Blondin Donkey, one of them whitened like a clown.
quotations.analysis: Three sentences, three levels of knowledge, and for once Pooter is on the reader's level. He sees the politeness for what it is, which is why the entry is not comic relief but the hinge of the chapter: the hour he has planned for since the invitations went out arrives while there is a pantomime donkey in the drawing-room. The economy is worth noticing — the joke needs no adjective, only the flat repetition of amusing and amused, with a negative dropped into it. Downstairs the table is a wreck, and the great man asks for soda water and is offered port.

quotations.text: When I returned to the parlour, Gowing was retailing his idiotic joke about the odd sock, and Carrie was roaring with laughter. I suppose I am losing my sense of humour.
quotations.context: The laundress has sent back an odd sock, and Gowing has suggested giving it to a poor man with one leg.
quotations.analysis: The saddest line in the book, and it is a joke. Gowing's remark is no better than anything Pooter has produced — arguably worse — and the difference is entirely in the delivery and in who is making it. Pooter's conclusion is exactly the wrong one, since his sense of humour is unimpaired; what has failed is his standing. The verb retailing carries the grievance: Gowing is selling the joke round the house, and Carrie, who has laughed at dry rot until her sides ached, is buying. Then Pooter goes back to complaining about Padge, which is what a man does when he cannot say the true thing.

quotations.text: I am sure it would prove quite as interesting as some of the ridiculous reminiscences that have been published lately. Besides, it’s the diary that makes the man. Where would Evelyn and Pepys have been if it had not been for their diaries? … Lupin, in a jeering tone, said: “If it had been written on larger paper, Guv., we might get a fair price from a butterman for it.”
quotations.context: At breakfast, after Carrie has said plainly that no publisher would take it and both she and Lupin have burst out laughing.
quotations.analysis: The book turns and looks at itself. Pooter's defence is the one he made in his preface, and it is not as silly as his family thinks: the diary did make Pepys. What he cannot see is the joke inside his own sentence, because it's the diary that makes the man is true of him in a way he would hate. Lupin answers by the weight of the paper.

quotations.text: I am a poor man, but I would gladly give ten shillings to find out who sent me the insulting Christmas card I received this morning. I never insult people; why should they insult me?
quotations.context: Christmas Eve. The handwriting on the envelope slopes the wrong way, and Pooter begins to work through his acquaintance.
quotations.analysis: Two of his favourite forms in one sentence: the declaration of poverty made just before an offer of money, and the reward for information, which he has already posted once, at the same rate, for the person who tore up his diary. The second sentence is a child's logic and is perfectly sincere. The payoff comes five days later, after a dream, a comparison of handwriting and a formal accusation: Carrie points out that the card was addressed to L. Pooter, and Lupin cheerfully admits he gets such cards, and sends them. The offence was never aimed at him at all.

quotations.text: My boy, as a result of twenty-one years’ industry and strict attention to the interests of my superiors in office, I have been rewarded with promotion and a rise in salary of £100. … “Having been in the firm of Job Cleanands, stock and share-brokers, a few weeks, and not having paid particular attention to the interests of my superiors in office, my Guv’nor, as a reward to me, allotted me £5 worth of shares in a really good thing. The result is, to-day I have made £200.”
quotations.context: A bottle of Jackson Frères has been opened at supper to celebrate news that father and son each claim to have.
quotations.analysis: The best-built joke in the book, and it belongs to Lupin. He stands up, takes his father's exact syntax and swaps in his own facts: twenty-one years becomes a few weeks, strict attention becomes not having paid particular attention, a hundred pounds a year becomes two hundred in a day. Nothing is said about what the parody means. The two sentences are left side by side for the reader to compare.

quotations.text: I was not so sanguine as to suppose, as you predicted, that I should get six or eight times the amount of my investment; still a profit of £2 is a good percentage for such a short time. … Lupin said, quite irritably: “You don’t understand. I sold your £20 shares for £2; you therefore lose £18 on the transaction.
quotations.context: The Parachikka Chlorates have collapsed. Lupin has just explained that he was fortunate to get two pounds for his father's holding.
quotations.analysis: A whole economy fits into a misread figure. Pooter hears the word profit and does his sum from the only kind of money he has ever handled, the kind that goes up by ten pounds a year; the possibility that an investment can return less than nothing has not occurred to him. The word irritably is beautifully placed — the son is annoyed at having to explain a loss he caused — and the sentence that follows completes the ruin by adding Cummings and Gowing, who will lose the lot. The eighteen pounds is roughly a fifth of the rise he was given six weeks earlier.

quotations.text: I made myself useful, and assisted several ladies to ices, remembering an old saying that “There is nothing lost by civility.” … “Your party’s had four suppers at 5s. a head, five ices at 1s., three bottles of champagne at 11s. 6d., a glass of claret, and a sixpenny cigar for the stout gentleman—in all £3 0s. 6d.!”
quotations.context: The East Acton Volunteer ball. Pooter has been handing round wine in an empty supper-room, assuming that a private invitation covers the food.
quotations.analysis: His one virtue is itemised and priced, and the bill is the funniest document in the book precisely because it is accurate. The proverb is doing the damage: he is not being generous, he is investing in a saying, and the waiter's list turns the investment into pounds, shillings and pence. The stout gentleman is Padge, who has said nothing all evening except that it is right, and whose cigar Pooter is now paying for. Three pounds and sixpence is a great deal of money for the household; he cannot cover it, gives his card, and resolves to keep the misfortune from Carrie so as not to spoil her evening.

quotations.text: I said to Mr. Finsworth: “Who is this jovial-looking gentleman? Life doesn’t seem to trouble him much.” Mr. Finsworth said: “No, it doesn’t. He is dead too—my brother.”
quotations.context: At Watney Lodge, Muswell Hill. Pooter has already said of a crayon portrait that the face looked pinched, and been told it was drawn after death.
quotations.analysis: The second blunder is the joke; the first only sets the trap. Having walked into one death, he crosses the room to a cheerful red face in a straw hat and volunteers the remark guaranteed to be wrong twice over. The comedy is in the host's flat too, quietly counting the bodies. This is the book at its most generous: not a fool, only a man in a strange drawing-room with nothing to say.

quotations.text: I am getting quite accustomed to being snubbed by Lupin, and I do not mind being sat upon by Carrie, because I think she has a certain amount of right to do so; but I do think it hard to be at once snubbed by wife, son, and both my guests.
quotations.context: He has tried to tell the room about a dream of burning ice, and been told by four people in turn that other people's dreams are of no interest.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a man drawing up the terms of his own defeat and finding them, on the whole, acceptable. The concession to Carrie is the heart of it — she has a certain amount of right to do so — which is both a joke about a henpecked husband and a genuine statement of how he sees his marriage. What he objects to is not the snubbing but the arithmetic: four at once is too many. The dream itself, blocks of ice on fire, is the single imaginative thing he produces in the book, and it is exactly what nobody will let him have.

quotations.text: The happy medium means respectability, and respectability means insipidness. Does it not, Mr. Pooter?” I was so taken aback by being personally appealed to, that I could only bow apologetically, and say I feared I was not competent to offer an opinion.
quotations.speaker: Mr. Hardfur Huttle, then Charles Pooter
quotations.context: Franching's dinner at Peckham. Huttle has been asked to explain the phrase happy medium, which his hostess offered as a pleasantry.
quotations.analysis: The book's case for the prosecution, delivered at a dinner table and addressed by name to the defendant. Huttle is rude, loud and largely right, and the Grossmiths give him the best rhetoric in the novel before letting him overreach: within a page he has insulted a deaf woman, the host's champagne and a man who spends his evenings playing dominoes with his wife, which is Pooter exactly. The reply is the finest thing Pooter ever says without meaning to. Bow apologetically and not competent to offer an opinion are the manners of the clerk, produced under direct attack, and they prove Huttle's point and answer it in the same breath.

quotations.text: I always feel people are happier who live a simple unsophisticated life. I believe I am happy because I am not ambitious.
quotations.context: The last lines of the chapter, written in bed after the dinner, following Carrie's remark that Huttle is exactly like Lupin.
quotations.analysis: Pooter's creed, stated plainly for once, straight after the man who despises it has finished talking. By itself the sentence is not ridiculous, and the book has been quietly showing that he is in fact happy. The placing undercuts it twice: he is ambitious, as chapter VI admits about getting his son into the firm, and he has just spent an evening trying to please a man with money.

quotations.text: I wrote him sixteen pages, closely written; he wrote me less than sixteen lines. … “Sir,—I totally disagree with you. Your son, in the course of five minutes’ conversation, displayed more intelligence than your firm has done during the last five years.
quotations.context: Perkupp has asked Pooter to write privately to Crowbillon, the firm's most valued client, and win him back. It took a whole day.
quotations.analysis: Pooter measures his own effort the only way he knows, by quantity, and the repetition of sixteen sets up the fall before the letter is even opened. Crowbillon's reply is a model of what he is up against: five lines, no courtesy, and a comparison of five minutes with five years that reverses everything the diary believes about long service. Pooter's response is not anger but a practical difficulty — he dare not show it to Perkupp and would not show it to Lupin — and he is left holding a document that proves his master wrong and his son right. He reports the contents to Perkupp in a modified form.

quotations.text: On the way home in the carriage, for the first time in my life, I was inclined to indulge in the radical thought that money was not properly divided.
quotations.context: Riding home in Murray Posh's carriage after dinner at Lupin's new rooms, having just been told what Posh has settled on his wife and his sister.
quotations.analysis: One sentence of political doubt in a book with no politics, and it is placed with great care: in a rich man's carriage, going back to a rented house in Holloway, at the end of an evening in which a necklace costing three hundred pounds has been mentioned. The hedging is the whole character — inclined to indulge in, and the word radical held at arm's length, as if the thought belonged to somebody disreputable. He does not develop it. The next paragraph is about a cab waiting outside his house, and the idea never appears again. Six days later he is given a house and the question is closed.

quotations.text: Mr. Perkupp, to my surprise, said: “Mr. Pooter, I will purchase the freehold of that house, and present it to the most honest and most worthy man it has ever been my lot to meet.”
quotations.speaker: Mr. Perkupp
quotations.context: The final entry but one. Pooter has just been thanked for the service he did the firm through Hardfur Huttle's American connection.
quotations.analysis: The ending refuses to be a punchline. Pooter has wanted two things throughout, his house and his employer's good opinion, and he is given both in one sentence, in the exact terms he would have chosen. It can be read as the comedy relenting or as the last irony, since a man's home is still a gift in another man's hands. The diary offers no verdict.

quotations.text: He and his brother are like plum-trees that grow crooked over standing-pools; they are rich and o'erladen with fruit, but none but crows, pies, and caterpillars feed on them.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: The Cardinal has just brushed Bosola off, though Bosola went to the galleys in his service.
quotations.analysis: The image condemns the brothers and the man who wants to feed on them in the same sentence. The trees are rich but crooked, rooted in stagnant water, and only scavengers profit, among whom Bosola at once counts himself: he would hang on their ears like a horseleech 'till I were full'. The malcontent's contempt and his appetite are one impulse.

quotations.text: Say, then, my corruption Grew out of horse-dung: I am your creature.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Ferdinand has offered Bosola gold to spy on the Duchess, then tells him he has also got him a post in her stables.
quotations.analysis: Bosola has just refused the gold as devils' wages, and he takes the job anyway. The bitter joke about horse-dung looks forward to the apricots ripened in the same stuff in Act II. A 'creature' was a dependant made by a patron's favour, and also a thing created: the word hands Ferdinand ownership of whatever Bosola is about to become.

quotations.text: Such weddings may more properly be said To be executed than celebrated.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Ferdinand and the Cardinal warn their sister against a secret remarriage.
quotations.analysis: The pun turns a wedding into a death sentence, and it is spoken before any wedding has taken place. It sounds like a courtier's quip, but Ferdinand is the one person in a position to make it literally true, and he does. The brothers share their warning so smoothly between them that the Duchess remarks the speech must have been 'studied'.

quotations.text: For I am going into a wilderness, Where I shall find nor path nor friendly clue To be my guide.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Her brothers gone, the Duchess sends Cariola behind the arras and waits for Antonio.
quotations.analysis: A moment earlier she said she would make her royal kindred her 'low footsteps'; now the confidence gives way to a clear sight of the danger. A 'clue' was a ball of thread, the kind Ariadne gave Theseus for the labyrinth, so the image admits that nobody has marked a way through what she is about to do. She goes in regardless, and that is the play's first definition of her courage.

quotations.text: The misery of us that are born great! We are forc'd to woo, because none dare woo us; And as a tyrant doubles with his words, And fearfully equivocates, so we Are forc'd to express our violent passions In riddles and in dreams
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Antonio has kept misreading her hints, and the Duchess stops hinting.
quotations.analysis: Rank reverses the order of courtship, and she sees the cost precisely: she must do the wooing, and do it in riddles. Comparing herself to a tyrant who equivocates is startling in a love scene and exact about her position, since she can marry only by using the authority that makes marriage impossible. 'Violent passions' is exactly what her brothers will accuse her of.

quotations.text: This is flesh and blood, sir; 'Tis not the figure cut in alabaster Kneels at my husband's tomb.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Antonio kneels, trembling, and the Duchess raises him.
quotations.analysis: The widow of convention is a stone figure kneeling on her husband's tomb for ever, and the Duchess refuses the part in so many words. The line sets living flesh against carved stone, and Act IV reverses it with deliberate cruelty: she is shown wax figures of her family, Cariola tells her she looks like 'some reverend monument', and Bosola comes to make her tomb.

quotations.text: Whether the spirit of greatness or of woman Reign most in her, I know not; but it shows A fearful madness.
quotations.speaker: Cariola
quotations.context: The last lines of Act I, spoken alone after the couple have gone to bed.
quotations.analysis: The only witness to the marriage is also its first critic. Cariola cannot tell whether the pride of a prince or the desire of a woman is driving her mistress, and she leaves the question with the audience. 'Fearful' means both frightening and full of fear, and the pity she offers in her next breath reads as a forecast.

quotations.text: Though we are eaten up of lice and worms, And though continually we bear about us A rotten and dead body, we delight To hide it in rich tissue
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: After mocking an old lady's cosmetics in prose, Bosola announces 'my meditation' and turns to verse.
quotations.analysis: The speech moves from prose to verse as it moves from satire to sermon, and its subject is the body under the silk. The sentiment is the old contempt of the world, but Bosola is about to spend the scene inspecting a pregnant woman for evidence, and the disgust he voices is also the professional stance of a man paid to treat bodies as information.

quotations.text: I have a trick may chance discover it, A pretty one; I have bought some apricocks, The first our spring yields.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola has listed the signs that the Duchess is pregnant: sickness, swelling, a loose gown.
quotations.analysis: He tests a theory with bait. The first apricots of the year, which he later tells her were ripened in horse-dung, become a pregnancy test, and her greed for them is taken as proof. The scene is comic in performance and invasive in substance: a woman's body is read without her consent, and the fruit brings on the labour it was meant to detect.

quotations.text: Though lust do mask in ne'er so strange disguise, She 's oft found witty, but is never wise.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola has read the child's horoscope and means to send the news to Rome.
quotations.analysis: The couplet closes the scene like a moral, and it is spoken by a spy pleased with his own cleverness. 'Witty' meant ingenious: the Duchess is quick enough to hide the birth and not careful enough to hide the paper. Bosola can imagine her marriage only as lust in disguise, which is her brothers' reading before they have heard a word.

quotations.text: Methinks I see her laughing,-- Excellent hyena! Talk to me somewhat quickly, Or my imagination will carry me To see her in the shameful act of sin.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: In Rome, with Bosola's letter in his hand, Ferdinand raves to the Cardinal.
quotations.analysis: He asks to be distracted from a picture he cannot stop painting, and then paints it: a strong-thighed bargeman, a labourer from the wood-yard, a squire carrying coals. The hyena, believed to laugh and to feed on the dead, makes his sister a beast. The Cardinal's dry 'With whom?' shows how little the other brother shares this particular obsession.

quotations.text: For know, whether I am doom'd to live or die, I can do both like a prince.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Brushing her hair, the Duchess talks to Antonio, not knowing that he has slipped out and Ferdinand has come in.
quotations.analysis: The boast is made to an empty room and answered by the wrong man, with a dagger and 'Die, then, quickly!' Before it she has joked about her brothers, her greying hair and more children; she ends on her rank, which is where Ferdinand strikes. That she can in fact do both like a prince is what Act IV sets out to prove.

quotations.text: 'Stay,' quoth Reputation, 'Do not forsake me; for it is my nature, If once I part from any man I meet, I am never found again.' And so for you: You have shook hands with Reputation, And made him invisible.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Ferdinand tells his sister what she has lost by marrying.
quotations.analysis: Love can be found among shepherds and Death in battles, but Reputation, once parted from, is gone for good. The formal fable, in the middle of a violent scene, shows what Ferdinand believes he is defending, and it is a thing that exists only in other people's opinion. The Duchess answers by asking why she alone, of all the princes of the world, should be 'cas'd up, like a holy relic'.

quotations.text: A politician is the devil's quilted anvil; He fashions all sins on him, and the blows Are never heard
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Alone, having just been told the secret, Bosola prepares to carry it to Ferdinand.
quotations.analysis: The 'politician', the stage schemer, is an anvil padded so that no hammer-blow is heard: every sin is shaped on him in silence. Bosola is describing himself as he goes to betray a woman who has just trusted him, and the next lines call his trade a 'base quality'. He sees his corruption exactly and continues with it.

quotations.text: The birds that live i' th' field On the wild benefit of nature live Happier than we; for they may choose their mates, And carol their sweet pleasures to the spring.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Banished from Ancona, with most of her household gone, the Duchess tells Antonio of a dream in which her diamonds turned to pearls.
quotations.analysis: The comparison removes rank altogether. Birds choose their mates without asking anyone and sing about it in the open, the two freedoms her greatness has denied her. The image looks forward to her prison, where she will tell Cariola that the robin and the nightingale 'Never live long in cages'.

quotations.text: Our value never can be truly known, Till in the fisher's basket we be shown: I' th' market then my price may be the higher, Even when I am nearest to the cook and fire.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Arrested by Bosola, who sneers at Antonio as 'One of no birth', the Duchess answers with a fable.
quotations.analysis: A dog-fish has rebuked a salmon for mixing with its betters; the salmon replies that both have escaped the same net, and that value is only known in the fisher's basket. It is her answer to rank: worth is fixed at death, not at birth, and the great are valued highest 'when they're most wretched'. She is describing her own case, and the next act bears her out.

quotations.text: Didst thou ever see a lark in a cage? Such is the soul in the body: this world is like her little turf of grass, and the heaven o'er our heads like her looking-glass, only gives us a miserable knowledge of the small compass of our prison.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola comes to the Duchess's prison disguised as an old man, and she asks him who she is.
quotations.analysis: The soul is a caged lark and the sky a looking-glass that shows only how small the cage is. The image is traditional and the application is exact, since he is speaking to a woman imprisoned in her own palace. His purpose, he says later, is to bring her 'By degrees to mortification', and what he offers is not comfort but the argument that nothing she is losing was worth having.

quotations.text: I am Duchess of Malfi still.
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Bosola has told her she must be 'some great woman, sure', since care has greyed her early and she sleeps worse than a mouse in a cat's ear.
quotations.analysis: Six words against everything Bosola has said about the body. 'Still' means both 'even now' and 'always', and it also suggests quiet, the composure she keeps against the noise of the madmen. She claims the title her brothers say she has forfeited, and Bosola answers that her rank is exactly what breaks her sleep. The scene lets both be true.

quotations.text: I know death hath ten thousand several doors For men to take their exits; and 'tis found They go on such strange geometrical hinges, You may open them both ways
quotations.speaker: Duchess
quotations.context: Bosola asks whether the manner of her death, the cord, does not terrify her.
quotations.analysis: She answers terror with geometry. Death is a building with countless exits, hinged both ways, and the method matters no more than which way a door swings. 'Exits' is a theatre word as well. The wit is the point: a woman about to be strangled refuses to let her killers set the tone, and asks only to be out of their 'whispering'.

quotations.text: Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Bosola shows Ferdinand the Duchess's body and asks, 'Do you not weep?'
quotations.analysis: Nine words in three clauses, none of them about what he feels. 'Dazzle' can mean blurred by tears or by too much light, and either way he cannot look. Then, for the first time, he gives reasons: they were twins, and he had hoped to gain 'An infinite mass of treasure by her death'. The line holds grief and guilt at the edge of speech.

quotations.text: I serv'd your tyranny, and rather strove To satisfy yourself than all the world: And though I loath'd the evil, yet I lov'd You that did counsel it; and rather sought To appear a true servant than an honest man.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Ferdinand has refused Bosola his reward and ordered him out of his sight.
quotations.analysis: The last line is the most exact self-judgement in the play. Bosola kept the act and the man who ordered it apart, loathing one and loving the other, and chose the look of loyalty over the fact of honesty. He says it to claim his pay; within a few lines, over the Duchess's body, he discovers that the distinction does not survive what it has done.

quotations.text: We are merely the stars' tennis-balls, struck and banded Which way please them.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola has stabbed a man in the dark, expecting an assassin, and learns that it is Antonio.
quotations.analysis: The man who spent the play choosing his masters now blames the stars. 'Banded' is a tennis term, struck to and fro, and the image makes human life a game played by someone else. It is an evasion, and also, in an act made of accidents, a fair description of what keeps happening. The audience saw who was coming; Bosola did not.

quotations.text: In all our quest of greatness, Like wanton boys whose pastime is their care, We follow after bubbles blown in th' air.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Dying, Antonio learns that his wife and two of his children have been murdered.
quotations.analysis: His last philosophy is the play's plainest statement of vanity. 'Our quest of greatness' takes in everyone, the brothers' pride, Bosola's hunt for preferment and his own rise by marriage, and the image of boys chasing bubbles makes the pursuit childish rather than wicked. His final wish is that his son should 'fly the courts' of princes altogether.

quotations.text: I am puzzl'd in a question about hell; He says, in hell there 's one material fire, And yet it shall not burn all men alike. Lay him by. How tedious is a guilty conscience!
quotations.speaker: Cardinal
quotations.context: The Cardinal is alone with a book, waiting for Bosola to help him move Julia's body.
quotations.analysis: The most composed character in the play is reading theology and cannot keep his mind on it. His puzzle, one fire that burns each sinner differently, is a question about proportion and judgement, and he puts the book down to admit that conscience is tedious. Then he describes a figure with a rake in his fish-ponds. The guilt he never showed has been at work all along.

quotations.text: My sister, O my sister! there 's the cause on 't. Whether we fall by ambition, blood, or lust, Like diamonds, we are cut with our own dust.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Mortally wounded, Ferdinand recovers his wits for a moment.
quotations.analysis: His last words go back to the beginning. His sister is the cause, and the couplet generalises it: ambition, blood and lust, the Cardinal's, the family's and his own, destroy the great as diamonds are cut with their own powder. The Duchess compared a widow who remarries to a diamond in Act I; the image returns to judge the men who objected.

quotations.text: These wretched eminent things Leave no more fame behind 'em, than should one Fall in a frost, and leave his print in snow; As soon as the sun shines, it ever melts, Both form and matter.
quotations.speaker: Delio
quotations.context: Delio arrives with the Duchess's son to find the Cardinal, Ferdinand and Bosola dead.
quotations.analysis: The great leave no more trace than a body's print in snow, and 'form and matter' melt together. The image answers every character who killed to protect a name or a line, and the final couplet names what does last: 'Integrity of life is fame's best friend'. Delio says it while presenting an heir, though the play has mentioned a son from the Duchess's first marriage, which leaves the ending less settled than it sounds.

quotations.text: “Whenever you feel like criticizing anyone,” he told me, “just remember that all the people in this world haven’t had the advantages that you’ve had.”
quotations.speaker: Nick's father
quotations.context: The advice Nick reports in the second sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The sentence sounds like generosity and is actually an instruction in class: it assumes both speaker and listener are on the advantaged side, and says nothing about what to do with that. Nick spends the novel among people who have had more advantages than he has, and never once applies the rule to them.

quotations.text: In consequence, I’m inclined to reserve all judgements, a habit that has opened up many curious natures to me and also made me the victim of not a few veteran bores.
quotations.context: Nick explaining the effect his father's advice has had on him.
quotations.analysis: The second half of the sentence gives the reason: suspending judgement is a technique for being told things. Within two pages he has called Tom's family enormously wealthy, Jordan incurably dishonest and the East a place he wanted in uniform, which is the contradiction the whole narration runs on — the reserve is a method, not a temperament.

quotations.text: it was an extraordinary gift for hope, a romantic readiness such as I have never found in any other person and which it is not likely I shall ever find again
quotations.context: The first description of Gatsby, given before the reader has met him.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is delivered in the opening pages, so the novel is not a mystery about whether Gatsby is admirable but an account of how Nick got there. 'Readiness' is the exact word: it names a capacity waiting for an object, which is what makes Daisy interchangeable with any sufficiently distant light.

quotations.text: ‘All right,’ I said, ‘I’m glad it’s a girl. And I hope she’ll be a fool⁠—that’s the best thing a girl can be in this world, a beautiful little fool.’
quotations.speaker: Daisy Buchanan
quotations.context: Daisy quoting what she said on waking from the ether after her daughter was born.
quotations.analysis: It is a quotation inside a quotation, which lets her disown it while saying it, and the setting matters: she is describing the hour in which her husband was elsewhere. The line is often read as cynicism about women, but it is a piece of career advice from someone who has calculated exactly what her own intelligence has been worth to her.

quotations.text: Involuntarily I glanced seaward⁠—and distinguished nothing except a single green light, minute and far away, that might have been the end of a dock.
quotations.context: Watching his neighbour stretch his arms towards the water at the end of the first chapter.
quotations.analysis: Three qualifications in one clause — nothing except, might have been — keep the light from meaning anything yet, which is precisely why it can later mean everything. Nick sees the gesture without the explanation, and the novel's method is set: the reader is given the reaching arms four chapters before the reason for them.

quotations.text: This is a valley of ashes⁠—a fantastic farm where ashes grow like wheat into ridges and hills and grotesque gardens; where ashes take the forms of houses and chimneys and rising smoke and, finally, with a transcendent effort, of ash-grey men, who move dimly and already crumbling through the powdery air.
quotations.context: The opening of the second chapter, describing the land between West Egg and New York.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is agricultural — a farm, wheat, gardens — applied to industrial waste, so the valley is described as growing what the city throws away. The sentence takes four clauses to arrive at the men, and by the time it does they are made of the same material as the landscape, which is the book's flattest statement about who is disposable.

quotations.text: The eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg are blue and gigantic⁠—their retinas are one yard high. They look out of no face, but, instead, from a pair of enormous yellow spectacles which pass over a nonexistent nose.
quotations.context: The hoarding above the valley of ashes, left by an oculist who moved away.
quotations.analysis: The measurements are given in the present tense and in yards, as though the reader might go and check, and the eyes are explicitly attached to nothing — no face, no nose, no oculist. George Wilson will later decide they are God's, and the novel's care in establishing that they are an abandoned advertisement is what makes his mistake so exact.

quotations.text: I believe that on the first night I went to Gatsby’s house I was one of the few guests who had actually been invited. People were not invited⁠—they went there.
quotations.context: The opening of the first party scene.
quotations.analysis: The verb is repeated three times in two sentences so that invitation, the basic transaction of hospitality, can be shown to have collapsed. Nick's one small distinction — he was asked — is what qualifies him to narrate, and it also tells the reader that the parties are not for the people at them.

quotations.text: “I hope I never will,” she answered. “I hate careless people. That’s why I like you.”
quotations.speaker: Jordan Baker
quotations.context: Jordan, who has just nearly hit a workman's coat with her car, explaining why bad driving does not worry her.
quotations.analysis: She has explained that it takes two to make an accident, so her own carelessness is safe until she meets another one — and then says she hates careless people. The word she introduces here is the one Nick will use, six chapters later, to sum up Tom and Daisy; she hands him the term for the novel's central charge while demonstrating the offence.

quotations.text: “You’re a rotten driver,” I protested. “Either you ought to be more careful, or you oughtn’t to drive at all.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: In the car with Jordan, on the way back from a party.
quotations.analysis: Driving is the novel's practical test of character, and every collision in it involves someone who thought the other party would take care. The exchange also establishes the alternative Nick is offering the reader — be careful or get out — which is exactly the choice he takes himself at the end by going home.

quotations.text: “If it wasn’t for the mist we could see your home across the bay,” said Gatsby. “You always have a green light that burns all night at the end of your dock.”
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: Showing Daisy the view from his own house, minutes after their reunion.
quotations.analysis: He tells her about the light in the flattest possible way — a fact about her property — and the sentence 'you always have' quietly admits five years of watching. This is the moment the symbol is handed over to its owner, and the next paragraph records what it cost him.

quotations.text: Now it was again a green light on a dock. His count of enchanted objects had diminished by one.
quotations.context: Nick watching Gatsby immediately after he has pointed the light out to Daisy.
quotations.analysis: 'Count' is an accountant's word, and it suggests Gatsby keeps an inventory of enchantments the way he keeps one of shirts. The loss is caused by getting what he wanted: the light only worked at a distance, and the whole tragedy is compressed into the arithmetic of that second sentence.

quotations.text: There must have been moments even that afternoon when Daisy tumbled short of his dreams⁠—not through her own fault, but because of the colossal vitality of his illusion.
quotations.context: The end of the reunion chapter, as Nick leaves the two of them together.
quotations.analysis: The exoneration is explicit — not through her own fault — which makes it much harder to read the novel as a case against Daisy. 'Vitality' gives the illusion a life of its own, something grown rather than held, and by this measure Gatsby's tragedy is not that he lost her but that no actual person could have been what he had spent five years building.

quotations.text: The truth was that Jay Gatsby of West Egg, Long Island, sprang from his Platonic conception of himself. He was a son of God⁠—a phrase which, if it means anything, means just that⁠—and he must be about His Father’s business, the service of a vast, vulgar, and meretricious beauty.
quotations.context: The chapter that finally gives James Gatz's history, seventeen years old on the shore of Lake Superior.
quotations.analysis: Two incompatible vocabularies are welded together: Platonic philosophy and the Gospel of Luke, both used to explain a boy changing his name. The aside — if it means anything — is Nick refusing to guarantee his own sentence, and the last three adjectives make the object of worship squarely commercial without withdrawing the religious language.

quotations.text: “Can’t repeat the past?” he cried incredulously. “Why of course you can!”
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: Answering Nick's suggestion that he should not ask so much of Daisy.
quotations.analysis: The adverb is the whole characterisation: he is not arguing, he is astonished that anyone would doubt it. Grammatically he treats the past as a direct object — something one performs again — and the rest of the novel is the demonstration that it is the one commodity his money cannot reach.

quotations.text: He wanted nothing less of Daisy than that she should go to Tom and say: “I never loved you.”
quotations.context: Nick explaining what Gatsby is actually asking for.
quotations.analysis: The demand is for a sentence, not an action, which tells the reader that Gatsby's project is editorial: he wants the record amended. When she cannot produce the words in Chapter 7 it is not cowardice but accuracy that stops her, and the failure of one clause brings down the entire five-year scheme.

quotations.text: “Her voice is full of money,” he said suddenly.
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: In Gatsby's house on the hottest afternoon of the summer, while Daisy is speaking in the next room.
quotations.analysis: Nick has spent two chapters failing to describe Daisy's voice and Gatsby settles it in five words, which is the one moment in the book where he sees more clearly than the narrator. It is also the diagnosis of his own defeat: what he loves in her is a sound produced by a security he was not born into and cannot purchase.

quotations.text: “They’re a rotten crowd,” I shouted across the lawn. “You’re worth the whole damn bunch put together.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: Leaving for work on the last morning of Gatsby's life, after a night of listening to the Louisville story.
quotations.analysis: Nick reports immediately afterwards that it was the only compliment he ever paid him, and that he disapproved of him from beginning to end — so the sentence is offered with the disapproval attached. The staging matters too: it is shouted across a lawn, at a distance, by a man on his way to the office, and it is the last thing Gatsby hears from anybody.

quotations.text: A new world, material without being real, where poor ghosts, breathing dreams like air, drifted fortuitously about
quotations.context: Nick's reconstruction of Gatsby's last hours, waiting beside a telephone that does not ring.
quotations.analysis: Everything solid in the novel is here declared unreal at the moment the illusion fails, and the ghosts are poor — the adjective does double duty for pity and for money. Nick admits he is guessing at all of this, so the most metaphysical passage in the book is explicitly an invention, made by a narrator about a man who invented himself.

quotations.text: “The poor son-of-a-bitch,” he said.
quotations.speaker: Owl Eyes
quotations.context: At the graveside, spoken by the drunk who admired the library in Chapter 3.
quotations.analysis: The only epitaph Gatsby gets comes from a man who went to one party and never met him, and it is four words of profanity. Set it against the two pages of lyric prose that close the book: the novel gives the plain human verdict first, and the grand one afterwards, and does not say which is truer.

quotations.text: They were careless people, Tom and Daisy⁠—they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money or their vast carelessness, or whatever it was that kept them together, and let other people clean up the mess they had made
quotations.context: After meeting Tom on Fifth Avenue and learning what he told George Wilson.
quotations.analysis: 'Things and creatures' declines to say people, which is how the sentence performs the carelessness it is describing. The judgement Nick promised on the first page to reserve is delivered here in the past tense, and the most damning phrase is the vaguest — 'or whatever it was' — because he has stopped trying to understand them.

quotations.text: gradually I became aware of the old island here that flowered once for Dutch sailors’ eyes⁠—a fresh, green breast of the new world
quotations.context: Lying on the beach at night before leaving the East for good.
quotations.analysis: The houses are made to melt away so that a seventeenth-century landscape can be laid over a twentieth-century one, and the colour green arrives from the dock light three hundred pages earlier. The move enlarges one man's obsession into a continental habit without ever quite saying that Gatsby stands for America.

quotations.text: Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgiastic future that year by year recedes before us.
quotations.context: The penultimate paragraph of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The verb 'recedes' does the work: the future is not ahead but retreating, so pursuing it is already a backward motion. Nick has also switched to the first person plural here, which quietly enrols the reader in Gatsby's error two sentences before the famous image of the boats.

quotations.text: So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: Two participles pulling opposite ways — beating forward, borne backwards — leave the sentence with no net motion at all, which is the exact shape of Gatsby's five years. 'We' has replaced 'he' by now, and the last word of a book about the future is 'past'.

quotations.text: “I’m thirty,” I said. “I’m five years too old to lie to myself and call it honour.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: Ending the affair with Jordan Baker, who has accused him of throwing her over on the telephone.
quotations.analysis: He turns his birthday into a moral unit of measurement, as though self-deception had an age limit, and the arithmetic quietly puts the honest years at twenty-five. Jordan's reply — that she thought he was an honest, straightforward person — is the novel's last word on his opening claim.

themes.name: A man with nobody to tell
Deep time, watched from a chair
Heaven and Hell, without a church
The woman who is already gone

techniques.name: The old house with a reputation

characters.name: The woman of the Sea of Sleep

quotations.text: I read, and, in reading, lifted the Curtains of the Impossible that blind the mind, and looked out into the unknown.
quotations.context: The editor describing his first reading of the manuscript.
quotations.analysis: The book's promise, made by a character rather than by the author. Capitalising the Curtains of the Impossible is Edwardian in the worst way and exactly right for a man who has just read something he cannot place.

quotations.text: I have the queer, faint, pit-water smell of it in my nostrils now as I write
quotations.context: Handling the manuscript before printing it.
quotations.analysis: A smell, not a sight, and it belongs to the pit the story will turn on. Hodgson authenticates his document with one physical sensation that the editor cannot get rid of, which is worth more than any amount of insistence that the tale is true.

quotations.text: The peasantry, who inhabit the wilderness beyond, say that I am mad.
quotations.context: The Recluse's first sentences in his own diary.
quotations.analysis: He raises the charge himself, in the third line, and disposes of it by explaining that he simply will not deal with people. The manoeuvre makes him sound reliable and also tells us that the only witness we will get has a reputation.

quotations.text: I have one friend, a dog; yes, I would sooner have old Pepper than the rest of Creation together.
quotations.context: Explaining his household: a sister, no servants, and the dog.
quotations.analysis: Hodgson plants the ending here, two hundred pages early. The rest of Creation is precisely what the last chapters take away, and the reader is told at the start which part of it the Recluse would have kept.

quotations.text: For a couple of centuries, this house has had a reputation, a bad one
quotations.context: Why the house was cheap.
quotations.analysis: The whole gothic inheritance, disposed of in a clause and followed immediately by the price. Hodgson is signalling that he knows the convention and is not going to spend the book on it.

quotations.text: the readers will but shake their heads, and be the more convinced that I was mad
quotations.context: On why he is writing the diary at all.
quotations.analysis: He anticipates his audience and writes anyway. The sentence also quietly establishes that he expects to be gone when it is read, which is the first hint that the manuscript will outlive him.

quotations.text: an enormous amphitheatre of mountains
quotations.context: Emerging from a chasm in the first vision.
quotations.analysis: The scale changes without warning and the prose does not raise its voice. Hodgson's method in the visionary chapters is to describe impossible geography in the tone of a walking guide.

quotations.text: a stupendous structure built apparently of green jade
quotations.context: The building at the centre of the arena.
quotations.analysis: One material, one colour, and the sentence that follows makes it his own house. The vision offers no interpretation, and the book's refusal to gloss its central image is the reason the image has survived a century.

quotations.text: in no particular, save in color and its enormous size, did the lonely structure vary from this house in which I live
quotations.context: Realising what he is looking at.
quotations.analysis: The clause is careful, legalistic and slightly clumsy, which is how a frightened man checks a fact. What it establishes is that the house is not merely haunted but duplicated somewhere else, and nothing in the novel ever qualifies that.

quotations.text: It was the face of a swine.
quotations.context: Looking down into the chasm at the first of the creatures.
quotations.analysis: Six words, full stop, no adjective. After pages of careful approach Hodgson gives the reveal the shortest sentence available, and the plainness is what makes it land.

quotations.text: he literally and actually crumbled into a mouldering heap of bones and dust
quotations.context: Nudging the sleeping dog with a foot, during the acceleration of time.
quotations.analysis: The adverbs are doing something unusual: literally and actually are a man refusing to be thought metaphorical. It is also the moment the cosmic chapters acquire a cost, because the reader was told on page one what the dog was worth.

quotations.text: that little hill of ash
quotations.context: Standing over what is left of Pepper.
quotations.analysis: Four words for a friend. The diminutive is what hurts, and it is also the book's measure of scale: against a dying sun, a life is a small heap on a study floor.

quotations.text: it was imperative she should leave me, before the Sun of Darkness
quotations.context: The woman explaining why she must go as the white orb is eaten across.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is hers, not his, and it is the only piece of vocabulary the book borrows from beyond. A sun that is darkness is a contradiction the novel does not resolve; it simply arrives again, larger, in the final chapters.

quotations.text: the pen has trailed away over the paper; possibly, through fright and weakness
quotations.context: The last footnote, on the unfinished word that ends the manuscript.
quotations.analysis: The book closes not on a vision but on a note about handwriting. After the death of the sun, the editor's evidence-based caution — possibly, through fright and weakness — is the most frightening sentence in it, because it is the only one that sounds reasonable.

themes.name: Fate and the will of Zeus
Home, and the city behind the wall

quotations.text: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled.
quotations.context: The opening of the poem.
quotations.analysis: The first noun is anger, and the sentence cares about its consequences rather than its cause: souls sent to Hades, bodies left for dogs and vultures. That last threat is not decoration. Whether a corpse is buried or eaten becomes the question the whole poem turns on, up to the ransoming of Hector. And 'the counsels of Jove' are fulfilled through this anger: the first sentence already puts a god's plan and a man's temper inside the same machine.

quotations.text: I came not warring here for any ill the Trojans had done me. I have no quarrel with them. They have not raided my cattle nor my horses, nor cut down my harvests on the rich plains of Phthia.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: In the assembly, after Agamemnon threatens to take Achilles' prize to make up for the one he must give back.
quotations.analysis: The most subversive thing anyone says in the poem is said in its first book. Achilles has no grievance against Troy; he is there to win satisfaction for Agamemnon and Menelaus, and his reward comes in the form of prizes. Once a prize can be confiscated, the whole contract is exposed. His refusal of the embassy in Book 9 grows out of this speech: if the war is not his quarrel, only honour kept him in it.

quotations.text: you bore me doomed to live but for a little season; surely Jove, who thunders from Olympus, might have made that little glorious. It is not so.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Alone by the sea after Briseis has been led away, Achilles calls on his mother.
quotations.analysis: Achilles' bargain is a short life in exchange for glory, and here he complains that he is being cheated on the glory. The phrasing is exact: the 'little season' is accepted, only the 'glorious' is in dispute. It is also the first time the most feared man in the army weeps, and he does it at the water's edge like a child calling for its mother. The poem never treats his tears as weakness.

quotations.text: Small wonder that Trojans and Achaeans should endure so much and so long, for the sake of a woman so marvellously and divinely lovely. Still, fair though she be, let them take her and go, or she will breed sorrow for us and for our children after us.
quotations.speaker: The elders of Troy
quotations.context: Helen comes to the Scaean gate to watch the duel that is to decide whose wife she is; the old men of Troy, too old to fight, see her approach.
quotations.analysis: The elders say two opposite things in two sentences and mean both. Her beauty explains ten years of war; she should be sent back anyway. It is the most generous verdict on Helen in the poem and it is spoken softly, among themselves. Notice who is judging: men past fighting, sitting on the tower 'like cicales', who will see their city burn for a decision nobody on the wall made.

quotations.text: Men come and go as leaves year by year upon the trees. Those of autumn the wind sheds upon the ground, but when spring returns the forest buds forth with fresh vines. Even so is it with the generations of mankind, the new spring up as the old are passing away.
quotations.speaker: Glaucus
quotations.context: Diomedes, meeting a stranger in battle, asks who he is before he fights him. Glaucus begins his answer by questioning the question.
quotations.analysis: A warrior asked for his pedigree replies that pedigrees are like leaves, and then gives his at great length. The simile is the poem's most famous statement of mortality, and a comment on heroic ancestry: what lasts is the kind, not the individual. Yet the genealogy that follows saves his life, because his grandfather turns out to have been the guest of Diomedes' grandfather. The leaves fall; the obligation survives.

quotations.text: it is you who bear the brunt of that toil that has been caused by my hateful self and by the sin of Alexandrus—both of whom Jove has doomed to be a theme of song among those that shall be born hereafter.
quotations.speaker: Helen
quotations.context: In Paris's house, Helen invites Hector to sit and rest; he refuses and goes to find his wife.
quotations.analysis: Helen is the one character who seems to know she is in a poem. Her sense that she and Paris exist to become 'a theme of song' is a bleak consolation: the suffering has a purpose, and the purpose is entertainment for people not yet born. Heroes fight so that songs will be sung about them. Helen, who had no choice, has worked out what being sung about costs, and she says it to the man who is paying.

quotations.text: He stretched his arms towards his child, but the boy cried and nestled in his nurse’s bosom, scared at the sight of his father’s armour, and at the horse-hair plume that nodded fiercely from his helmet.
quotations.context: At the Scaean gate, Hector reaches for his baby son Astyanax before returning to the battle.
quotations.analysis: The one warrior in the poem shown with a child is undone by his own equipment. Everything that makes Hector a hero — the bronze, the plume that 'nodded fiercely' — is exactly what a baby cannot read. The parents laugh, and Hector takes the helmet off: for a moment the poem shows a man choosing between his two roles and choosing the smaller one. A few lines later he picks the helmet up again.

quotations.text: Go, then, within the house, and busy yourself with your daily duties, your loom, your distaff, and the ordering of your servants; for war is man’s matter, and mine above all others of them that have been born in Ilius.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Hector's last words to Andromache before he goes back to the fighting.
quotations.analysis: Andromache has just given him sound advice about the weak point in the wall, and he answers by sending her to her loom. The sentence is a formula: the Odyssey gives it almost word for word to Telemachus, with 'war' changed to 'speech'. Here it is tender rather than rude, since he has just told her not to grieve before her time, but it draws the line the poem keeps. Men decide; women mourn the decisions. Book 24 gives the women the last word.

quotations.text: Then will one say hereafter as he sails his ship over the sea, ‘This is the monument of one who died long since a champion who was slain by mighty Hector.’ Thus will one say, and my fame shall not be lost.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Hector challenges the best of the Greeks to single combat, and sets terms for what will happen to the loser's body.
quotations.analysis: Hector pictures his fame as something a stranger will say about a tomb, and in doing so he lays down the rule the poem will later test: the winner keeps the armour and the body goes home to be buried. When he asks the same of Achilles in Book 22, Achilles refuses outright. The barrow he imagines is the Greek champion's; it does not occur to him that it may be his own, or that he may be denied one.

quotations.text: Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart; therefore I will say what I mean.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Odysseus has repeated Agamemnon's offer of gifts, leaving out Agamemnon's closing demand that Achilles submit to him as the more royal man.
quotations.analysis: Whether or not Achilles guesses what has been left out, he names the fault exactly, and he names it to the one man in the camp who most deserves it. Odysseus's own poem will celebrate the skill of saying one thing and hiding another. Achilles' refusal to do so is his integrity, and also his isolation: a man who says only what he means has no way to climb down.

quotations.text: My mother Thetis tells me that there are two ways in which I may meet my end. If I stay here and fight, I shall not return alive but my name will live for ever: whereas if I go home my name will die, but it will be long ere death shall take me.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Achilles tells the embassy that he will sail for Phthia in the morning.
quotations.analysis: The choice that defines Achilles is set out like a sum, and on this night he chooses the long life. He reverses the choice only when Patroclus dies. What makes the speech shocking is that it doubts the arithmetic heroes live by: glory is a name, and a name is worth less than a life that, as he has just said, 'can neither be bought nor harried back again'. He is the only man at Troy who knows the price for certain.

quotations.text: My good friend, if, when we were once out of this fight, we could escape old age and death thenceforward and forever, I should neither press forward myself nor bid you do so, but death in ten thousand shapes hangs ever over our heads, and no man can elude him; therefore let us go forward and either win glory for ourselves, or yield it to another.
quotations.speaker: Sarpedon
quotations.context: Sarpedon, prince of the Lycians and a son of Zeus, rouses his friend Glaucus to attack the Greek wall.
quotations.analysis: The clearest short account of why Homeric heroes fight. Privilege — the best seats, the fullest cups — is repaid by standing in front, and if men could not die there would be no point in courage at all. It is Achilles' argument from Book 9 turned inside out: because death is certain, glory is worth pursuing. Sarpedon dies at Patroclus's hands in Book 16, and his father, who could save him, lets him go.

quotations.text: You know no pity; knight Peleus was not your father nor Thetis your mother, but the grey sea bore you and the sheer cliffs begot you, so cruel and remorseless are you.
quotations.speaker: Patroclus
quotations.context: The Trojans are setting fire to the Greek ships. Patroclus comes to Achilles in tears and begs to be allowed to fight.
quotations.analysis: Patroclus disowns Achilles' parents on his behalf: no man and no goddess could have produced this, only rocks and the sea. It is the harshest thing said to Achilles by anyone who loves him, and it works where the embassy's gifts did not. Achilles gives way — not by fighting, but by lending his armour. The cruelty Patroclus names here is the quality that will make Achilles' revenge for him so terrible.

quotations.text: but as he was coming on like a god for a time, then, O Patroclus, was the hour of your end approaching, for Phoebus fought you in fell earnest.
quotations.context: Patroclus has driven the Trojans back towards their walls, killing nine men in each of three charges.
quotations.analysis: The narrator turns and speaks to Patroclus, as if to warn him, at the moment the warning is useless. The grammar changes the killing: the audience is put in the position of someone watching a friend walk into danger and unable to shout. 'Your end' is announced before we see how it comes. When it does, the poem's gentlest man is struck from behind by a god he never sees.

quotations.text: Poor things, why did we give you to King Peleus who is a mortal, while you are yourselves ageless and immortal? Was it that you might share the sorrows that befall mankind? for of all creatures that live and move upon the earth there is none so pitiable as he is.
quotations.speaker: Zeus (Butler's Jove)
quotations.context: Achilles' immortal horses stand motionless in the battle, heads bowed, weeping for Patroclus.
quotations.analysis: Looking at two grieving horses, the king of the gods arrives at the poem's bleakest general statement, and he says it about the race he rules. The horses were never meant to share human grief, and have caught it. Zeus's pity is real and changes nothing: he goes straight on to explain that the Trojans will keep killing until dark. The gods of the Iliad can feel for men without being moved to spare them.

quotations.text: Therefore, perish strife both from among gods and men, and anger, wherein even a righteous man will harden his heart—which rises up in the soul of a man like smoke, and the taste thereof is sweeter than drops of honey.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Told that Patroclus is dead, Achilles tells Thetis he will kill Hector, though he knows his own death must follow.
quotations.analysis: This is the nearest the poem comes to analysing its own subject. Anger is described from the inside as a pleasure — it rises 'like smoke' and tastes 'sweeter than drops of honey' — which is why it is so hard to give up. Achilles renounces his anger against Agamemnon in the same breath as he takes up a far worse one against Hector. He sees the mechanism clearly and cannot step out of it.

quotations.text: Meanwhile the people were gathered in assembly, for there was a quarrel, and two men were wrangling about the blood-money for a man who had been killed, the one saying before the people that he had paid damages in full, and the other that he had not been paid.
quotations.context: One of the scenes Hephaestus works into the new shield he makes for Achilles.
quotations.analysis: On the shield of the angriest man in the poem is a quarrel about compensation for a killing, argued in public and settled by elders, with a prize for whoever judges most fairly. It is the Iliad in miniature. Achilles refused Agamemnon's compensation in Book 9 and will accept Priam's in Book 24. The shield shows a city solving the problem its heroes cannot, and hands the picture to a man going out to kill.

quotations.text: but it was not I that did it: Jove, and Fate, and Erinys that walks in darkness struck me mad when we were assembled on the day that I took from Achilles the meed that had been awarded to him.
quotations.speaker: Agamemnon
quotations.context: At the formal reconciliation, Agamemnon speaks from his place rather than stepping into the middle of the assembly.
quotations.analysis: Agamemnon apologises by explaining that he is not to blame, and goes on to tell a long story about Folly deceiving Zeus himself. In the poem's theology this is not simply an excuse: gods do cloud men's minds. But it is convenient, and it is addressed to an army that has paid for his mistake with its dead. The Odyssey opens with Zeus complaining about precisely this kind of speech.

quotations.text: She wept as she spoke, and the women joined in her lament-making as though their tears were for Patroclus, but in truth each was weeping for her own sorrows.
quotations.context: Briseis, returned to Achilles at last, sees Patroclus's body and mourns him as the one Greek who was kind to her.
quotations.analysis: One sentence lets the captive women's mourning be seen for what it is: a public lament for a Greek hero that is really private grief for their own dead husbands, fathers and freedom. Briseis has just said that Achilles killed her husband and three brothers. The narrator does not comment further, but he has admitted that the women the heroes fight over are living through a war of their own.

quotations.text: Therefore, my friend, you too shall die. Why should you whine in this way? Patroclus fell, and he was a better man than you are.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Lycaon, a son of Priam whom Achilles once captured and sold, clasps his knees at the river and begs to be ransomed.
quotations.analysis: The word 'friend' is the most chilling thing in the passage. Achilles is not in a frenzy; he is calm, almost companionable, because he now includes himself among the dead-to-be, and goes on to say his own death will come 'at dawn or dark, or at the noontide'. Before Patroclus died, captives were sold. The same fact — that everyone dies — which will let him pity Priam in Book 24, is here his reason to show no mercy.

quotations.text: She told her maids to set a large tripod on the fire, so as to have a warm bath ready for Hector when he came out of battle; poor woman, she knew not that he was now beyond the reach of baths.
quotations.context: Andromache, at her loom in an inner room, has not yet heard that Hector is dead.
quotations.analysis: The poem cuts from the killing to a woman weaving flowers into a purple cloth, and the ordinary kindness of heating water for a tired husband becomes unbearable because we know more than she does. 'Poor woman' is the narrator stepping in. The bath matters for another reason: washing the body is the first rite of a funeral, and this body is being dragged through the dust towards the ships.

quotations.text: My doom has come upon me; let me not then die ingloriously and without a struggle, but let me first do some great thing that shall be told among men hereafter.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Hector has thrown his spear and turned for a second one, only to find that the brother at his side was Athene in disguise.
quotations.analysis: Tricked by a goddess and without a spear, Hector gives up on survival and falls back on the one thing he can still control: the story. It is the hope of his challenge in Book 7, fame spoken 'hereafter', now reduced to the manner of his death. After running three times round the walls, he turns and charges with his sword. The poem grants what he asks, since it is still telling it.

quotations.text: As when some cruel spite has befallen a man that he should have killed some one in his own country, and must fly to a great man’s protection in a land of strangers, and all marvel who see him, even so did Achilles marvel as he beheld Priam.
quotations.context: Priam, guided by Hermes, has entered Achilles' tent unseen, clasped his knees and kissed his hands.
quotations.analysis: The simile makes the wrong man a killer. It is Achilles who has killed and Priam who has lost, yet the comparison casts the old king as a murderer seeking refuge in a stranger's house. It fits someone else exactly: Patroclus, who as a boy killed a playmate over dice and was taken in by Peleus, as his ghost recalls in Book 23.
