By reversing the roles, the poem makes Achilles see a suppliant, and prepares the recognition between the two men.

quotations.text: Fear, O Achilles, the wrath of heaven; think on your own father and have compassion upon me, who am the more pitiable, for I have steeled myself as no man yet has ever steeled himself before me, and have raised to my lips the hand of him who slew my son.
quotations.speaker: Priam
quotations.context: The end of Priam's plea, after he has asked Achilles to think of his own old father, Peleus.
quotations.analysis: Priam rests his claim to pity on an act rather than a loss: he has done what no man has done before. The last clause holds the whole horror of the scene — a father's lips on the hand that killed his son. It also mirrors the poem's opening, where another old father, Chryses, came to the Greek camp with ransom for his child and was sent roughly away. This time the ransom is taken, and the father is fed.

quotations.text: The immortals know no care, yet the lot they spin for man is full of sorrow; on the floor of Jove’s palace there stand two urns, the one filled with evil gifts, and the other with good ones.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: After the two men have wept together, Achilles raises Priam from the ground and tells him to sit.
quotations.analysis: The youngest great man at Troy offers the oldest a philosophy, and it is not a comforting one. Zeus gives some men a mixture and some men only evil; nobody receives only good. Achilles applies it at once to Peleus and to Priam, which is the point: the speech is how he comes to see his enemy's father as his own. Grief is shared by everyone. Justice is not on offer.

quotations.text: Thus, then, did they celebrate the funeral of Hector tamer of horses.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the poem, after Hector's bones have been gathered into a golden urn and buried under a barrow.
quotations.analysis: A poem that began with the anger of Achilles ends with the funeral of the man he killed, and gives Hector the plainest of his fixed epithets, one that belongs to peacetime skill rather than battle. The fall of Troy, which everyone knows is coming, is left out. The poem stops at the one thing its first sentence feared would be denied: a body properly burned, mourned and buried.

themes.name: Town and country, and the double life
themes.canonicalName: Town and country, and the double life

themes.name: Diaries, letters and the written record
themes.canonicalName: Diaries, letters and the written record

quotations.text: I didn’t think it polite to listen, sir.
quotations.speaker: Lane
quotations.context: Answering Algernon's question about the piano, in the play's fourth line.
quotations.analysis: The servant declines to have heard something everyone in the theatre has just heard, and does it by appealing to manners rather than to fact. Within four lines Wilde has established the rule the whole play runs on: politeness is a technique for not knowing things.

quotations.text: The truth is rarely pure and never simple.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Pressing Jack to admit that Cecily exists.
quotations.analysis: The line is an epigram in defence of an interrogation, which is a peculiar use for it. Wilde puts the play's most quotable statement about truth in the mouth of the man currently telling the fewest lies, and follows it immediately with a joke about modern literature.

quotations.text: Divorces are made in Heaven
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: On marriage, moments before defending the cucumber sandwiches.
quotations.analysis: One word is swapped in a proverb and the sentiment is reversed without a syllable of argument. The line is also interrupted mid-breath by Algernon stopping Jack taking a sandwich, so that the epigram and the appetite share a sentence.

quotations.text: You have invented a very useful younger brother called Ernest, in order that you may be able to come up to town as often as you like. I have invented an invaluable permanent invalid called Bunbury, in order that I may be able to go down into the country whenever I choose.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Naming Jack's deception and matching it with his own.
quotations.analysis: The two fictions are laid out in parallel clauses, and the symmetry is the play's architecture in advance: town and country, brother and invalid, each man needing somewhere he is not. Note that both inventions are described as useful, which is the only virtue either man claims for them.

quotations.text: You don’t seem to realise, that in married life three is company and two is none.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Warning Jack that a married man will need Bunbury.
quotations.analysis: Two is company, three is none goes in and comes out reversed, so that adultery is described in the vocabulary of good manners. It is also a plot prediction: by Act II there are indeed three people in each engagement, and one of them does not exist.

quotations.text: I hate people who are not serious about meals. It is so shallow of them.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Interrupting a discussion of the evening's arrangements.
quotations.analysis: Seriousness, the quality the whole play is named for, is transferred to dinner, and shallowness becomes a charge against people who are not hungry. The joke works because Algernon means it entirely: his appetite is the one sincere thing in the comedy.

quotations.text: The fact is constantly mentioned in the more expensive monthly magazines, and has reached the provincial pulpits, I am told; and my ideal has always been to love someone of the name of Ernest. There is something in that name that inspires absolute confidence.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Explaining to Jack, before he has proposed, why she has decided to love him.
quotations.analysis: Her ideal is not a man but a set of syllables, and she supports it with the monthly magazines and the provincial pulpits, as though it were a matter of public opinion. Everything Jack has invented to make himself free has turned out to be the one condition he cannot meet.

quotations.text: To lose one parent, Mr. Worthing, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose both looks like carelessness.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: During the interview, on learning that Jack has lost both his parents.
quotations.analysis: Bereavement is reclassified as a lapse of organisation, and the balance of the sentence, misfortune against carelessness, does the reclassifying without an argument. It is the clearest example in the play of Wilde giving a monstrous position the rhythm of common sense.

quotations.text: A handbag?
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: On being told where Jack was found as a baby.
quotations.analysis: Two words, and they are the most famous in the English comic theatre because the actor has to decide the entire character on them. The line is a question that is not asking for information; it is a whole social order failing to accommodate a piece of luggage.

quotations.text: I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: On being told that Jack knows nothing.
quotations.analysis: Ignorance is given the vocabulary of horticulture and the protection usually reserved for virtue. The sentence that follows extends the compliment to English education on the grounds that it produces no effect whatsoever, which is Wilde attacking his own class from inside its drawing room.

quotations.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: Assessing Jack's Hertfordshire estate during the interview.
quotations.analysis: This is the play's one piece of genuine economics, spoken by its least reflective character: agricultural land in the 1890s really had stopped paying, and estates really were maintained for the position they conferred. The joke is that she states the whole agricultural depression as a social inconvenience.

quotations.text: Cecily, you will read your Political Economy in my absence. The chapter on the Fall of the Rupee you may omit. It is somewhat too sensational. Even these metallic problems have their melodramatic side.
quotations.speaker: Miss Prism
quotations.context: Leaving Cecily to her lessons while she walks with Dr Chasuble.
quotations.analysis: The collapse of the rupee had ruined real fortunes and salaries across the Empire, which is precisely why it is too sensational for a schoolroom. Wilde's governess protects her pupil from the one subject in the curriculum that describes the world she actually lives in.

quotations.text: The good ended happily, and the bad unhappily. That is what Fiction means.
quotations.speaker: Miss Prism
quotations.context: Describing the three-volume novel she once wrote.
quotations.analysis: A whole theory of the improving Victorian novel in fourteen words, delivered by the woman whose own carelessness with a perambulator will supply this play's ending. The capital letter on Fiction is doing the work: she is defining a genre, not describing a book.

quotations.text: I hope you have not been leading a double life, pretending to be wicked and being really good all the time. That would be hypocrisy.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: To Algernon, who is at that moment leading a double life in the other direction.
quotations.analysis: Hypocrisy is redefined as the pretence of wickedness, which inverts the standard Victorian charge exactly. Cecily is right about the double life and wrong about which way round it runs, and the audience is the only party in the garden that knows both halves.

quotations.text: You must not laugh at me, darling, but it had always been a girlish dream of mine to love someone whose name was Ernest.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: Accepting Algernon while explaining the condition she has always attached.
quotations.analysis: The second woman arrives at the identical requirement independently, and Wilde makes no attempt to explain the coincidence because the play is not interested in psychology. The effect is to turn a private preference into something more like a law of nature.

quotations.text: I never travel without my diary. One should always have something sensational to read in the train.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Producing documentary evidence during the tea-table confrontation with Cecily.
quotations.analysis: The diary is introduced as proof and described as entertainment in consecutive sentences, which tells the audience exactly how much the evidence is worth. Both women are now arguing from written records of events that never happened.

quotations.text: This is no time for wearing the shallow mask of manners. When I see a spade I call it a spade.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: At the height of the tea-table quarrel with Gwendolen.
quotations.analysis: The country girl claims plain speaking as a virtue, in a sentence that is itself a cliche about not using cliches. Gwendolen's reply, that she is glad to say she has never seen a spade, turns the claim into a statement about class within two lines.

quotations.text: I am glad to say that I have never seen a spade. It is obvious that our social spheres have been widely different.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Answering Cecily, marked in the text as spoken satirically.
quotations.analysis: She takes a dead metaphor completely literally and converts it into evidence of rank, which is the fastest piece of social violence in the play. The second sentence is delivered as a neutral observation, and that flatness is what makes it cut.

quotations.text: In matters of grave importance, style, not sincerity is the vital thing.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Agreeing with Cecily on how to receive the men's explanations.
quotations.analysis: This is the play's own defence, stated by a character as a rule of etiquette. It also inverts the usual hierarchy under which sincerity excuses a clumsy apology, and it arrives just before both women accept explanations they know to be worthless.

quotations.text: Never speak disrespectfully of Society, Algernon. Only people who can’t get into it do that.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: Rebuking her nephew during the negotiation over Cecily.
quotations.analysis: The defence of Society is conducted entirely by sneering at outsiders, which concedes the criticism while appearing to refuse it. Wilde, who was about to be put outside it himself, gives the line to the character with the most to lose from anyone examining the claim.

quotations.text: On the contrary, Aunt Augusta, I’ve now realised for the first time in my life the vital Importance of Being Earnest.
quotations.speaker: Jack
quotations.context: The last line of the play, answering the charge that he has been trivial.
quotations.analysis: The title arrives as a pun that has taken three acts to load: the quality and the name have become the same word, and the discovery that resolves everything is a matter of spelling. Wilde ends a comedy about sincerity by proving that the hero was accurate all along, and entirely by accident.

themes.name: Order, and who is allowed to defend it
Masks, and what is under them
What can be known from the back

techniques.name: An allegory that refuses to be solved
Everybody is on the same side

quotations.text: The suburb of Saffron Park lay on the sunset side of London, as red and ragged as a cloud of sunset.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: A real place — Bedford Park, where the aesthetes lived — described as weather rather than architecture. The simile makes the suburb look like something about to disperse, which is what happens to everything solid in the book.

quotations.text: An artist is identical with an anarchist… You might transpose the words anywhere. An anarchist is an artist.
quotations.context: Gregory, holding forth in the garden before Syme contradicts him.
quotations.analysis: The position Chesterton had spent two books arguing against, given to a character who means it and can phrase it. Putting the best version of the opposing case first is what stops the novel being a pamphlet.

quotations.text: The rare, strange thing is to hit the mark; the gross, obvious thing is to miss it.
quotations.context: Syme's answer to the claim that a railway timetable is unpoetic.
quotations.analysis: The sentence that turns the book's politics into an aesthetic. If order is the improbable achievement, then defending it is the adventure and the anarchist is merely the man who has noticed nothing.

quotations.text: Chaos is dull; because in chaos the train might indeed go anywhere, to Baker Street or to Bagdad. But man is a magician, and his whole magic is in this, that he does say Victoria, and lo! it is Victoria.
quotations.context: Syme, still arguing about trains.
quotations.analysis: The argument is made with a timetable, which is the joke and the point. Chesterton's defence of the ordinary never rests on the ordinary being safe — it rests on it being unlikely, and therefore worth guarding.

quotations.text: he was a poet of respectability
quotations.context: Reporting how Syme introduced himself to the Saffron Parkers.
quotations.analysis: Three claims in a row — poet of law, of order, of respectability — each more provoking to that audience than the last. The garden reacts as though he had fallen out of the sky, which tells you what kind of suburb it is.

quotations.text: the most dangerous criminal now is the entirely lawless modern philosopher.
quotations.context: The policeman in the dark room explaining why a force of philosophical detectives exists.
quotations.analysis: The premise of the plot, stated as policy. It also explains the book's structure: if the enemy is an idea, the detective has to be a man who can hold the idea and not be held by it, which is exactly Syme's difficulty.

quotations.text: The ordinary detective goes to pot-houses to arrest thieves; we go to artistic tea-parties to detect pessimists.
quotations.context: The same speech, describing the work.
quotations.analysis: The funniest sentence in the novel and a complete job description. It also quietly licenses the whole plot: if crimes can be detected in books of sonnets, then a poet is the right man to send.

quotations.text: the large face of Sunday grew larger and larger; and Syme was gripped with a fear that when he was quite close the face would be too big to be possible, and that he would scream aloud.
quotations.context: Walking towards the president's breakfast table.
quotations.analysis: A childhood fear of a museum mask, used to introduce the one character the book never explains. The threat is not violence but scale — something too large to be taken in, which is how the last chapter will describe God.

quotations.text: His face was very large, but it was still possible to humanity.
quotations.context: Syme sits down and risks a second look at Sunday.
quotations.analysis: Reassurance with a hole in it. 'Still possible' admits the standard is being stretched, and the rest of the book is spent finding out how far — by the last page the same face fills the sky.

quotations.text: a small blue card, on which was written, “The Last Crusade,” and a number, the sign of his official authority
quotations.context: Syme is issued with his credentials on leaving the police premises.
quotations.analysis: The badge of a modern police force is given a crusader's name, which is the book's whole method in an object: a bureaucratic detail that turns out to be a religious claim. Four more of these cards appear before the plot is done.

quotations.text: “I am a policeman,” said the Professor with his first broad smile
quotations.context: After a chase across London conducted at a shuffle.
quotations.analysis: The line arrives as the release of a long-held breath, and it is the second time the book has played this card. From here the reader stops fearing the conspiracy and starts wondering what is left to be afraid of.

quotations.text: Syme had for a flash the sensation that the cosmos had turned exactly upside down
quotations.context: When the Professor lays a police card on the table in front of him.
quotations.analysis: The reversal is felt as a change in the universe rather than in the facts, which is the book's characteristic scale. Nothing has happened except that a piece of card has appeared, and the world has inverted.

quotations.text: “Yes, I’m in the force right enough,” and he flicked a blue card towards them lightly as a matter of form.
quotations.context: Dr Bull, glasses off, greeting the men who had come to arrest him.
quotations.analysis: The third revelation is delivered with a shrug, and the comedy is in the casualness. The pattern is now so established that the novel has to find something else to frighten us with, which is exactly what it does.

quotations.text: “I am a detective from Scotland Yard,”
quotations.context: The Secretary, the last of the six to declare himself.
quotations.analysis: By this point the sentence is a punchline. The Central Anarchist Council has turned out to consist entirely of the police, which leaves the book with a chase and nobody to chase but its own president.

quotations.text: “What about Martin Tupper _now?_”
quotations.context: One of the notes Sunday drops behind him while being pursued across London.
quotations.analysis: The pursued god leaves nonsense messages for his hunters. The joke is aimed at a forgotten Victorian versifier, and its pointlessness is the point: the thing being chased will not engage on the chasers' terms.

quotations.text: Shall I tell you the secret of the whole world? It is that we have only known the back of the world. We see everything from behind, and it looks brutal.
quotations.context: Syme, in the balloon, trying to explain Sunday to the Secretary.
quotations.analysis: The book's own instruction for reading it. Everything that has seemed monstrous has been a rear view of something else, and the sentence turns a chase novel into an argument about how appearances are arranged.

quotations.text: “I am the Sabbath,” said the other without moving. “I am the peace of God.”
quotations.context: Sunday, asked at last who and what he is.
quotations.analysis: The answer names the day and claims the theology. It is also the moment the thriller stops working as a thriller: no pursuit can continue once the quarry has said this, and the remaining pages are given to the objection rather than the revelation.

quotations.text: I can forgive God His anger, though it destroyed nations; but I cannot forgive Him His peace.
quotations.context: The Secretary, refusing the reconciliation the others accept.
quotations.analysis: The strongest sentence in the book is given to the objection, not the answer. Chesterton lets the reconciliation be refused by the character the reader has come to trust most, and does not remove the refusal.

quotations.text: “Have you,” he cried in a dreadful voice, “have you ever suffered?”
quotations.context: Syme's question to Sunday, after Gregory's accusation.
quotations.analysis: The accusation the whole allegory has been travelling towards: whatever this figure is, has it paid anything? The question is asked by the man who has been most frightened, and the answer is the last line of the vision.

quotations.text: “Can ye drink of the cup that I drink of?”
quotations.context: Heard as a distant voice as the face fills the sky and everything goes black.
quotations.analysis: A question from Mark's gospel, given to the figure who has just been accused of never suffering, and offered instead of an explanation. The novel ends its vision on a text rather than a conclusion — which is why readers have argued about Sunday ever since.

quotations.text: There he saw the sister of Gregory, the girl with the gold-red hair, cutting lilac before breakfast, with the great unconscious gravity of a girl.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the book, after Syme wakes walking in a lane.
quotations.analysis: After a president the size of the sky, a girl with a pair of scissors. The nightmare is dismissed not by an argument but by breakfast, and the ordinary world is handed back with its gravity intact.

quotations.text: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad:
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: The opening line of the play, to Salarino and Salanio on the Rialto.
quotations.analysis: A comedy begins with a man announcing an unexplained depression, and the play never supplies the explanation — his friends propose his ships and then love, and he denies both. The refusal to account for it leaves a hole at the centre of the title role that every production has to fill with something.

quotations.text: so is the will of a living daughter curbed by the will of a dead father
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: In prose to Nerissa, listing the suitors she cannot refuse.
quotations.analysis: The sentence turns on one word used twice: 'will' as desire and 'will' as legal document. Portia's problem is stated as a pun, which is a warning about the kind of play this is — the trial in Act IV will also be won by a word that carries two meanings at once.

quotations.text: Still have I borne it with a patient shrug, For sufferance is the badge of all our tribe.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Answering Antonio's request for a loan by recalling how Antonio has treated him.
quotations.analysis: A badge in Venice was not a metaphor: Jews were required to wear identifying marks, and Shylock takes that fact and makes endurance itself the uniform. The shrug is the detail that does the work — a small physical gesture, repeated over years, standing in for everything he has swallowed.

quotations.text: 'Hath a dog money? is it possible A cur can lend three thousand ducats?'
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Quoting back to Antonio the names Antonio has called him.
quotations.analysis: He performs the insult rather than complaining of it, putting Antonio's own vocabulary into a speech Antonio has to stand and listen to. Quotation marks are a weapon here: the abuse is returned intact, with the arithmetic of the loan sitting inside it.

quotations.text: I am as like to call thee so again, To spit on thee again, to spurn thee too.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: His reply, immediately before asking for the loan anyway.
quotations.analysis: He does not deny a word of the account; he promises to repeat it. The couplet is the reason the bond is not simply a piece of villainy — the borrower has just told the lender to his face that nothing will change, and then asks to be lent the money as to an enemy.

quotations.text: Give him direction for this merry bond,
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Sending Antonio to the notary to seal the agreement.
quotations.analysis: 'Merry' is doing a great deal of work, and nobody in the scene challenges it. The forfeit is framed as a joke between men who have just exchanged threats, which is exactly what allows Antonio to sign it: a penalty that cannot be meant does not need to be feared.

quotations.text: Hie thee, gentle Jew. The Hebrew will turn Christian: he grows kind.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: As Shylock leaves to fetch the ducats.
quotations.analysis: 'Gentle' and 'gentile' were near-homophones, so the compliment is also a joke about conversion — and the joke turns out to be a prophecy the court will enforce at knife-point in Act IV. Antonio can praise the man only by imagining him becoming someone else.

quotations.text: Our house is hell, and thou, a merry devil, Didst rob it of some taste of tediousness.
quotations.speaker: Jessica
quotations.context: Saying goodbye to Launcelot, who is leaving her father's service.
quotations.analysis: Her complaint is not cruelty but dullness — the house is hell because it is tedious, and the clown made it bearable. It is the only account the play gives of what living with Shylock was like, and it comes from someone about to rob him.

quotations.text: All that glitters is not gold; Often have you heard that told: Many a man his life hath sold But my outside to behold:
quotations.speaker: Morocco
quotations.context: Reading the scroll found inside the golden casket, beside a skull.
quotations.analysis: The verse is in short rhyming lines, a nursery metre for a lesson everybody claims to know already, and the casket answers in the first person as though the gold were speaking. Morocco has just argued himself into gold by reasoning about what the world values — the scroll's point is that he was reasoning at all.

quotations.text: 'My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter! Fled with a Christian! O my Christian ducats!
quotations.speaker: Salanio
quotations.context: Salanio and Salarino imitating Shylock's behaviour in the street after Jessica's flight.
quotations.analysis: The audience never sees Shylock discover the loss; it is reported as an impersonation by a man doing the voice for a laugh. Whether the alternation of daughter and ducats is grief or greed depends entirely on how far you trust the reporter, and the play deliberately gives you no other witness.

quotations.text: I am a Jew. Hath not a Jew eyes? hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer, as a Christian is?
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: In the street, to Salarino, who has just asked what a pound of flesh is good for.
quotations.analysis: The argument is built entirely on the body, not on doctrine, and the repetitions of 'the same' make the shared ground impossible to refuse. It is in prose, which is why it sounds like a man talking rather than a set speech, and its logic is deliberately unfinished — everything so far has been about suffering, and the next sentence will apply the same equality to revenge.

quotations.text: The villany you teach me, I will execute, and it shall go hard but I will better the instruction.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: The end of the same speech, after the questions about bleeding and laughing.
quotations.analysis: He claims to be a pupil, which puts the responsibility on the teachers and leaves him doing the thing anyway. 'Better the instruction' is the sentence's cold centre: he intends not merely to match Christian revenge but to improve on it, and the play holds him to that promise in the courtroom.

quotations.text: So may the outward shows be least themselves: The world is still deceived with ornament.
quotations.speaker: Bassanio
quotations.context: Deliberating in front of the three caskets at Belmont.
quotations.analysis: He wins by distrusting appearances, having arrived in Belmont on borrowed money precisely in order to look the part. 'Still' means always, and the line indicts a world Bassanio has been working rather successfully; the play lets him say the true thing without noticing that it applies to him.

quotations.text: Which is the merchant here, and which the Jew?
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Her first words on entering the court in the gown of a doctor of laws.
quotations.analysis: The question establishes her impartiality and is also unanswerable by sight, which is the play's point about what Venice thinks it can see. She already knows which is which, so the line is a performance of neutrality by the one person in the room who has come to win.

quotations.text: The quality of mercy is not strain'd, It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven Upon the place beneath: it is twice blest; It blesseth him that gives and him that takes:
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Answering Shylock's question: on what compulsion must he be merciful?
quotations.analysis: The whole speech depends on mercy being uncompelled, which is a direct answer to the word 'compulsion' in Shylock's question. What follows in the scene contradicts it: the court will compel mercy out of Shylock at the price of his religion, and the word for what he receives will still be mercy.

quotations.text: My deeds upon my head! I crave the law,
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Refusing Portia's appeal and asking for judgment on the bond.
quotations.analysis: He takes the consequences onto himself in the words of a formula that Shakespeare's audience would have heard as an echo of the Gospel account of Christ's condemnation, and which was used for centuries to justify persecution. Giving Shylock that sentence is the harshest thing the play does to him, and he says it in the act of asking only for what he is owed.

quotations.text: Tarry a little; there is something else. This bond doth give thee here no jot of blood; The words expressly are 'a pound of flesh:'
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Stopping Shylock as he prepares to cut.
quotations.analysis: She has let the case run to the point of the knife before producing the objection, which means the trap was set several hundred lines earlier. Her method is not mercy but a stricter literalism than Shylock's own: he asked for what the words say, and she gives him exactly that and no more.

quotations.text: Nay, take my life and all; pardon not that: You take my house when you do take the prop That doth sustain my house; you take my life When you do take the means whereby I live.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: After the court has divided his estate and offered to commute the fine.
quotations.analysis: The repetition of 'take' four times in four lines turns the verdict into an inventory. He refuses the distinction the court is congratulating itself on — between killing a man and removing his livelihood — and the play gives him the argument without letting him win it.

quotations.text: Two things provided more, that, for this favour, He presently become a Christian;
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Stating his terms for giving up his half of Shylock's goods.
quotations.analysis: It is called a favour, and it is attached as a condition to a pardon Shylock cannot refuse. 'Presently' means at once: the man who has just been prevented from taking a pound of flesh is required to change religion on the spot, and the scene treats this as the merciful outcome.

quotations.text: I am content.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Asked by Portia whether he accepts the court's terms.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and then four more lines asking to be allowed to leave because he is not well. Antonio had used the same phrase twelve lines earlier while dictating the terms, so the play puts the identical sentence in two mouths in one scene and lets the difference between them stand without comment.

quotations.text: How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank! Here will we sit and let the sounds of music Creep in our ears:
quotations.speaker: Lorenzo
quotations.context: In the garden at Belmont with Jessica, waiting for Portia's return.
quotations.analysis: The last act opens by changing the weather completely: after four hundred lines of courtroom prose the play produces its most lyrical verse, and does it in the mouth of the man who organised the elopement and the theft. Shakespeare buys the comedy its ending with music, and the person who says she is never merry when she hears it is sitting next to him.

quotations.text: I am never merry when I hear sweet music.
quotations.speaker: Jessica
quotations.context: Her reply to Lorenzo's account of music's power over wild animals.
quotations.analysis: It is the last thing she says in the play. Lorenzo talks her out of it immediately, explaining that attentiveness only looks like sadness, and she does not answer — a silence that productions can play as agreement, exhaustion or something colder.

themes.name: Memory, medicine and the unwitnessed act

quotations.text: the Mohammedan conqueror, Mahmoud of Ghizni, crossed India; seized on the holy city of Somnauth; and stripped of its treasures the famous temple, which had stood for centuries⁠—the shrine of Hindu pilgrimage, and the wonder of the Eastern world.
quotations.context: The family legend of the diamond, as the letter-writer has heard it in camp.
quotations.analysis: The theft the English commit in 1799 is not the first: Collins puts an eleventh-century sack at the head of the book so that the stone arrives with a history of plunder already attached. The Epilogue returns to exactly this city, which turns the novel’s shape into a circle rather than a chase.

quotations.text: “The Moonstone will have its vengeance yet on you and yours!” He spoke those words, and fell dead on the floor.
quotations.context: The last of the three guardians, dying in the armoury doorway at Seringapatam.
quotations.analysis: The curse is the one supernatural claim in a novel that otherwise explains everything by paint, law and medicine, and Collins puts it in a language the narrator has to have translated for him. Every subsequent misfortune can be read as fulfilment or coincidence, and the book never adjudicates.

quotations.text: In the first part of Robinson Crusoe, at page one hundred and twenty-nine, you will find it thus written:
quotations.context: The opening sentence of Betteredge’s narrative.
quotations.analysis: A detective novel begins by citing another book by page number, and the citation is exact where everything else in Betteredge’s testimony will be approximate. Collins is announcing his method in the first line: this story will arrive as a document that quotes its sources.

quotations.text: When my spirits are bad⁠—Robinson Crusoe. When I want advice⁠—Robinson Crusoe. In past times when my wife plagued me; in present times when I have had a drop too much⁠—Robinson Crusoe. I have worn out six stout Robinson Crusoes
quotations.context: Betteredge explaining what the book is for.
quotations.analysis: The list runs from low spirits to marital trouble to drink, and the remedy never changes; six worn-out copies is the detail that turns a joke into a portrait of a life. It also plants a foundational story of English trade and mastery inside a novel about stolen colonial property, and Collins leaves the reader to notice.

quotations.text: trembling in a manner most remarkable to see, and which has given to it, among the people in our parts, the name of the Shivering Sand.
quotations.context: Betteredge describing the quicksand in the little bay below the house.
quotations.analysis: The name comes from the local people rather than from a map, which is how Collins keeps the place both real and slightly outside ordinary jurisdiction. The sand does the work a Gothic castle would once have done: it swallows a woman, hides the only physical evidence, and gives it back a year later intact.

quotations.text: here was our quiet English house suddenly invaded by a devilish Indian Diamond⁠—bringing after it a conspiracy of living rogues, set loose on us by the vengeance of a dead man.
quotations.context: Betteredge taking in what Franklin Blake has just told him about the legacy.
quotations.analysis: The sentence sets ‘quiet English house’ against ‘devilish Indian Diamond’ as though the two belonged to different worlds, which is the assumption the whole novel dismantles. The conspiracy of living rogues turns out to include an English barrister, and the vengeance of a dead man to be an English colonel’s.

quotations.text: Send the Diamond tomorrow (under guard of more than one man) to be cut up at Amsterdam. Make half a dozen diamonds of it, instead of one. There is an end of its sacred identity as The Moonstone
quotations.context: Murthwaite’s advice at the birthday dinner on how to end the danger.
quotations.analysis: The one solution offered that would actually work is refused because it would destroy the value of the stone as a stone. Murthwaite has identified precisely what makes the object dangerous — its sacred identity — and the English response is to bank it instead, which guarantees the rest of the plot.

quotations.text: One of these days (please God) I shall retire from catching thieves, and try my hand at growing roses.
quotations.context: The Sergeant’s first conversation on arriving, conducted with the gardener about grass walks.
quotations.analysis: Collins gives his detective a private life before he gives him a theory, and the roses are not a quirk but a measure: Cuff is at his most attentive and most accurate when the subject is not human. The same man will shortly read Rachel Verinder as a young woman in debt.

quotations.text: “Nobody has stolen the Diamond,” answered Sergeant Cuff.
quotations.context: Overheard by Betteredge at the threshold, in reply to Franklin Blake’s question.
quotations.analysis: The line is the first statement of the book’s real problem: not who took it, but whether taking it was a theft at all. Cuff means that Rachel has removed her own property to raise money; he is wrong about the person and right about the grammar, since the man who carried the diamond out of the room had no criminal intention either.

quotations.text: If there is such a thing known at the doctor’s shop as a detective-fever, that disease had now got fast hold of your humble servant.
quotations.context: Following Cuff down to the beach on the track of Rosanna Spearman.
quotations.analysis: Betteredge coins the phrase to excuse himself, and it names something the novel makes formally true: once Cuff begins asking questions, every detail in the house looks like a clue and every servant like a suspect. The word ‘fever’ also carries the warning — the appetite for a solution is what produces the wrong one.

quotations.text: having always a few tracts in my bag, I selected one which proved to be quite providentially applicable to the person who answered the door.
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: Waiting in the hall of her aunt’s London house.
quotations.analysis: The pamphlet is chosen for the servant who opened the door, which means a stranger has been diagnosed in the time it takes to cross a hall. Clack’s own word — providentially — does the work of concealing a judgement as a piece of divine good fortune, and she uses the same manoeuvre on every person in her narrative.

quotations.text: The chapters best adapted to female perusal are “Satan in the Hair Brush;” “Satan behind the Looking Glass;” “Satan under the Tea Table;” “Satan out of the Window”
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Describing the book she leaves for Lady Verinder to find.
quotations.analysis: The comedy is in the domestic inventory — brush, looking glass, tea table, window — which turns the devil into a fixture of the furniture. Collins is also making a point about method: Clack finds significance in ordinary household objects with exactly the confidence Sergeant Cuff brings to a smear of paint.

quotations.text: he will refrain from mentioning any personal objection which he may entertain to this species of literature
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter VI
quotations.context: One of the letters Collins prints inside Clack’s own narrative, refusing her extracts.
quotations.analysis: The editor of the record appears inside the record, and the reader watches the dossier being assembled and trimmed. Blake’s courtesy is lethal — he declines to mention his personal objection while mentioning it — and the exchange quietly tells us that every narrative in the book has passed through one man’s hands.

quotations.text: to be also capable of properly administering a trust (which, in my experience of the fair sex, not one in a thousand of them is competent to do)
quotations.reference: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: Explaining why Sir John’s will left everything to his wife.
quotations.analysis: The parenthesis is the whole point: Bruff praises Lady Verinder’s competence and generalises about her sex in the same sentence, without noticing the contradiction. Collins gives his most reliable witness a prejudice he cannot see, which is the exact defect the novel’s many-narrator structure exists to expose.

quotations.text: I looked back again at the letters. My own name. Plainly confronting me
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: Opening the tin case recovered from under the Shivering Sand and reading the mark on the nightgown.
quotations.analysis: Collins breaks the paragraph into fragments so that the sentence has to be read twice, which is what Blake is doing on the page. The buried evidence solves the mystery and destroys the investigator in the same instant, and the novel still has three hundred pages to run.

quotations.text: And, on the unanswerable evidence of the paint-stain, I had discovered myself as the thief.
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: The end of the same scene, with Betteredge walking towards him along the sand.
quotations.analysis: ‘Unanswerable’ is the word a lawyer would use, and Blake is applying the standard of proof he has been gathering testimony under. The sentence also fuses detective and criminal into one grammatical subject, which is the structural joke the entire second half depends on.

quotations.text: His gipsy-complexion, his fleshless cheeks, his gaunt facial bones, his dreamy eyes, his extraordinary parti-coloured hair, the puzzling contradiction between his face and figure which made him look old and young both together
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX
quotations.context: Franklin Blake’s first close look at Mr. Candy’s assistant.
quotations.analysis: Blake catalogues the features that have made a whole town refuse to employ Jennings and admits that his own first impression is unfavourable. The doubleness — old and young, black hair and white — is the book’s picture of a man read wrongly by everybody, which is precisely the condition Rachel and Rosanna are also in.

quotations.text: The one effectual palliative in my case, is⁠—opium. To that all-potent and all-merciful drug I am indebted for a respite of many years from my sentence of death.
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX
quotations.context: Jennings explaining his own illness to Franklin Blake.
quotations.analysis: The drug that lost Blake a night of his life is the same drug keeping Jennings alive, and the man who explains it is speaking from inside the experiment he is about to run. Collins, who took laudanum himself for years, refuses to let opium be either a poison or a miracle: it is a treatment with a stated limit.

quotations.text: It leaves her entirely mistress of her own decision. If she consents to assist the experiment, she consents of her own free will
quotations.context: From Jennings’s journal, on the letter he has drafted asking Rachel to permit the experiment.
quotations.analysis: Consent is written into the protocol before the laudanum is measured, by the one character the town has decided is disreputable. Set it beside the birthday dinner, where the first dose was administered to Blake as a practical joke without his knowledge, and the novel’s moral arrangement is complete.

quotations.text: And there, in the forehead of the deity, gleamed the yellow Diamond, whose splendour had last shone on me in England, from the bosom of a woman’s dress!
quotations.context: Murthwaite at the shrine in Kattiawar, watching the curtain drawn aside.
quotations.analysis: The last time the diamond was described it was on a woman’s dress at a birthday party, and Collins puts both settings into one sentence so the reader makes the comparison. The stone has not been recovered by anybody in the English narrative; it has simply gone back to where the Prologue took it from.

quotations.text: So the years pass, and repeat each other; so the same events revolve in the cycles of time. What will be the next adventures of the Moonstone? Who can tell?
quotations.context: The last sentences of the book.
quotations.analysis: A detective novel ends on an open question, and the question is not who did it but what happens next. The cycle Collins describes is the one the Prologue began — conquest, theft, restitution, conquest — and by refusing to close it he keeps the English portion of the story a single episode rather than the whole account.

themes.name: Loyalty and the audit of the household
Storytelling and who gets to tell it

techniques.name: The hero as his own narrator

quotations.text: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted
quotations.context: The opening of the poem.
quotations.analysis: The Iliad's first noun is anger; this poem's is a man, and an unnamed one. 'Ingenious' is Butler's word for the Greek polytropos, 'of many turns', which can mean much-travelled or much-twisting, and the sentence allows both. Note too what he is credited with: not killing, but visiting cities and learning customs. The hero is introduced as a kind of tourist with a sack of Troy behind him.

quotations.text: See now, how men lay blame upon us gods for what is after all nothing but their own folly.
quotations.speaker: Zeus (Butler's Jove)
quotations.context: Zeus opens the council of the gods, thinking of Aegisthus, who was warned not to murder Agamemnon and did.
quotations.analysis: The first speech in the poem is a complaint about being misjudged, and it sets the moral rules for everything after. People are warned; people ignore the warning; people pay. The crew and the suitors will both fit the pattern exactly. What the speech leaves out is Poseidon, whose persecution of Odysseus is about to be discussed and is not obviously anybody's folly but a god's temper.

quotations.text: Go, then, within the house and busy yourself with your daily duties, your loom, your distaff, and the ordering of your servants; for speech is man’s matter, and mine above all others
quotations.speaker: Telemachus
quotations.context: Penelope has asked the bard to stop singing about the Greeks' homecoming. Her son overrules her in front of the suitors.
quotations.analysis: It is the first time Telemachus has asserted himself and he does it against the wrong target, which is both comic and sad. The lines are nearly those Hector speaks to Andromache in the Iliad, with 'war' changed to 'speech': in this poem talk is the weapon. Penelope goes upstairs 'wondering', and keeps weaving — the loom he sends her back to is where the real resistance is happening.

quotations.text: we could see her working on her great web all day long, but at night she would unpick the stitches again by torchlight. She fooled us in this way for three years and we never found her out
quotations.speaker: Antinous
quotations.context: In the assembly, Antinous blames Penelope for the suitors' long stay: she promised to choose when the shroud for Laertes was done.
quotations.analysis: The story is told by her enemy, as an accusation, and it comes out as a tribute: three years, a hundred men, and they 'never found her out' until a maid told them. The web is a shroud, so she defers one man's funeral to defer her own remarriage. It is also the female version of her husband's craft. He makes things that hold — rafts, beds; she makes something that must never be finished.

quotations.text: I am quite aware that my wife Penelope is nothing like so tall or so beautiful as yourself. She is only a woman, whereas you are an immortal. Nevertheless, I want to get home, and can think of nothing else.
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: Calypso, ordered to let him go, asks whether she is really less attractive than his wife and reminds him that she can make him immortal.
quotations.analysis: This is diplomacy — he is speaking to a goddess who could still drown him — but it is also the poem's central choice, made in three sentences. He concedes every point of comparison and then says 'Nevertheless'. What he chooses is not the better woman but the mortal life: ageing, a particular island, a death. After the Iliad's heroes, who trade life for fame, here is one who turns down eternity for home.

quotations.text: there is nothing better in this world than that man and wife should be of one mind in a house. It discomfits their enemies, makes the hearts of their friends glad, and they themselves know more about it than any one.
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: Naked, filthy and holding a branch in front of himself, Odysseus ends his appeal to Nausicaa by wishing her a good marriage.
quotations.analysis: As rhetoric it is perfectly judged: a frightening stranger reassures a girl of marriageable age by praising marriage. But the Greek word behind 'of one mind', homophrosyne, describes what the poem will show in Book 23, where husband and wife turn out to think alike because each is testing the other. The last clause is the shrewdest — a good marriage is partly a secret, which is what the bed will be.

quotations.text: He wept as a woman weeps when she throws herself on the body of her husband who has fallen before his own city and people, fighting bravely in defence of his home and children.
quotations.context: At Odysseus's own request, Demodocus sings of the wooden horse and the sack of Troy. The guest breaks down.
quotations.analysis: The song is about his greatest success, and the simile puts him in the place of one of its victims: a Trojan widow, who in the following lines is beaten on the back with spears and led off to slavery. The poem does not say Odysseus feels guilt. It simply makes the sacker of cities cry in the shape of the sacked, and leaves the comparison there for the listener.

quotations.text: I am Ulysses son of Laertes, renowned among mankind for all manner of subtlety, so that my fame ascends to heaven.
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: After a whole book as an anonymous guest, Odysseus finally answers Alcinous's question and begins the story of his wanderings.
quotations.analysis: He has just heard a bard sing about him, so he knows the claim about fame is true, and he makes it without embarrassment: in this world reputation is a fact like height. What he is famous for is 'subtlety' — tricks. He is about to narrate four books in which that subtlety loses him twelve ships, and the boast in the first sentence frames how he wants the losses understood.

quotations.text: Cyclops, you ask my name and I will tell it you; give me, therefore, the present you promised me; my name is Noman; this is what my father and mother and my friends have always called me.
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: Odysseus has got Polyphemus drunk on unmixed wine. The giant asks his name so that he can give him a guest-gift.
quotations.analysis: The joke pays off when the blinded giant tells his neighbours that 'Noman is killing me' and they go home. In Greek there is a second pun underneath: a form of 'no one' sounds like metis, cunning, the hero's defining quality. Notice that he demands his 'present' in the same breath. Even while planning to blind his host, Odysseus is holding him to the etiquette of hospitality the Cyclops despises.

quotations.text: Cyclops, if any one asks you who it was that put your eye out and spoiled your beauty, say it was the valiant warrior Ulysses, son of Laertes, who lives in Ithaca.
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: From the ship, against the pleading of his crew, Odysseus taunts the blinded Cyclops a second time.
quotations.analysis: The escape worked because he was nobody; he cannot stand to stay nobody. Name, father and home address are exactly what a curse requires, and Polyphemus uses all three in his prayer to Poseidon a moment later. The poem's whole ten-year delay follows from this one sentence. It is the Iliad's hero, hungry for credit, breaking out of the Odyssey's survivor — and the crew, who begged him to be quiet, are the ones who pay.

quotations.text: you must take a well made oar and carry it on and on, till you come to a country where the people have never heard of the sea and do not even mix salt with their food
quotations.speaker: The ghost of Tiresias
quotations.context: In the land of the dead, the prophet tells Odysseus what he must do after he has killed the suitors.
quotations.analysis: Before the homecoming has happened, the poem announces that it will not be the end. He must walk inland until someone mistakes the oar for a winnowing shovel — until he reaches people for whom his entire story means nothing — and make his peace with Poseidon there. It is a strange, quiet idea: the man whose fame 'ascends to heaven' is sent to find the place where nobody has heard of him.

quotations.text: Thrice I sprang towards her and tried to clasp her in my arms, but each time she flitted from my embrace as it were a dream or phantom
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: Odysseus meets the ghost of his mother Anticleia, who has told him she died of longing for him.
quotations.analysis: He did not know she was dead; he learns it by seeing her among the ghosts. The triple attempt became a fixture of later epic, and Virgil borrows it twice. Here it is the first real cost of the twenty years presented to him in person. Cleverness is no use: for once he is reduced to grabbing at something, and the mother who could always be embraced is the one thing on the voyage he cannot hold.

quotations.text: I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man’s house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead.
quotations.speaker: The ghost of Achilles
quotations.context: Odysseus has congratulated Achilles on being honoured like a god in life and a great prince among the dead.
quotations.analysis: In the Iliad Achilles chose a short life and lasting glory; here the Odyssey lets him review the bargain and reject it. It is the later poem quarrelling with the earlier one, and doing so through its greatest hero. The speech also justifies Odysseus's own choice in Book 5. A hired labourer on someone else's farm is the lowest free rank there is, and Achilles would take it. Odysseus, in rags in Ithaca, more or less does.

quotations.text: No one ever sailed past us without staying to hear the enchanting sweetness of our song—and he who listens will go on his way not only charmed, but wiser
quotations.speaker: The Sirens
quotations.context: The crew row past with wax in their ears; Odysseus, tied to the mast, hears the song.
quotations.analysis: What the Sirens offer is not pleasure but knowledge: they go on to say they know everything that happened at Troy. In other words they offer to sing him the Iliad, with himself in it, for ever. The temptation is precisely fitted to a man who wept at Demodocus's song. The meadow around them is heaped with bones, and the danger is the one the whole poem worries at — a story so good you never go home.

quotations.text: that is why I cannot desert you in your afflictions; you are so plausible, shrewd and shifty.
quotations.speaker: Athene (Butler's Minerva)
quotations.context: On the beach in Ithaca, Odysseus has refused to believe even Athene that he is really home.
quotations.analysis: A goddess explains her loyalty, and the reasons are three words a moralist would use as charges. Butler's 'shifty' is sharper than most translators allow themselves and catches the tone: affectionate, amused, professional. She has just listened to him lie to her face and enjoyed it. The line tells us what kind of virtue this poem rewards — not honesty but wariness, the refusal to take even a homecoming on trust.

quotations.text: Stranger, though a still poorer man should come here, it would not be right for me to insult him, for all strangers and beggars are from Jove.
quotations.speaker: Eumaeus
quotations.context: The swineherd has called off his dogs, seated the beggar on his own bed-covering and been thanked for it.
quotations.analysis: The law of hospitality gets its plainest statement from a slave in a pig farm, with no audience and nothing to gain. That is the point: the suitors, noblemen in a palace, will throw furniture at the same beggar. The narrator marks the moment by addressing the swineherd directly — 'you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus' — a warmth the poem saves for him. Rank in the Odyssey is tested by what you do with a stranger.

quotations.text: There is no other Ulysses who will come hereafter. Such as I am, it is I, who after long wandering and much hardship have got home in the twentieth year to my own country.
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: Telemachus, seeing the beggar transformed, insists he must be a god and not his father.
quotations.analysis: Every other recognition in the poem rests on a token. This one cannot: Telemachus was a baby, there is no shared memory to appeal to, and the father can only say, in effect, I am all you are going to get. 'Such as I am' is a modest phrase from a man who announced his fame to the Phaeacians. The son has spent four books looking for a legend, and what arrives is this.

quotations.text: As soon as he saw Ulysses standing there, he dropped his ears and wagged his tail, but he could not get close up to his master.
quotations.context: At the gate of his own house Odysseus passes his old hunting dog, lying neglected and flea-ridden on a dung heap.
quotations.analysis: Athene's disguise works on every human being in Ithaca and fails on a dog, instantly. Argos is also a picture of the household — once swift, now lying in filth because 'the women take no care of him'. Odysseus has to wipe away a tear without Eumaeus seeing, and walk on; the dog dies as he goes in. The only recognition that costs him nothing in risk is the one he is not allowed to answer.

quotations.text: as soon as she began washing her master, she at once knew the scar as one that had been given him by a wild boar when he was hunting on Mt. Parnassus
quotations.context: Eurycleia washes the beggar's feet on Penelope's orders. He has turned away from the firelight, too late.
quotations.analysis: At the instant of discovery the poem stops and tells, at length, how the boy got the scar and how his grandfather Autolycus, 'the most accomplished thief and perjurer in the whole world', gave him his name. Only then does the foot fall into the basin. The digression is not a lapse in suspense; it says that identity is a history written on the body, which no goddess's disguise reaches.

quotations.text: There are two gates through which these unsubstantial fancies proceed; the one is of horn, and the other ivory.
quotations.speaker: Penelope
quotations.context: Penelope has told the beggar her dream of an eagle killing her geese; he assures her it means the suitors will die.
quotations.analysis: False dreams come through ivory, true ones through horn, and Penelope says she thinks hers was ivory. Then, in the next breath, she announces the contest of the bow for tomorrow. Either she has given up, or she has understood more from this stranger than she admits and is handing him his weapon. The poem does not settle it, and her refusal to hope aloud is of a piece with twenty years of caution.

quotations.text: strung it as easily as a skilled bard strings a new peg of his lyre and makes the twisted gut fast at both ends.
quotations.context: The suitors have all failed to bend the bow. The beggar turns it over, checks it for worm, and strings it.
quotations.analysis: At the moment he becomes a killer, he is compared to a poet. The string then 'sang sweetly under his touch', and his next words invite the suitors to 'song and dance'. The simile closes a circle drawn since Book 8: the man who wept at a bard's song and took over as narrator now plays an instrument of his own, and the performance that follows is the one the whole poem has been tuning for.

quotations.text: rejoice in silence; restrain yourself, and do not make any noise about it; it is an unholy thing to vaunt over dead men.
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: Eurycleia comes into the hall, sees the heaped corpses and her master spattered like a lion, and begins to cry out in triumph.
quotations.analysis: Iliadic heroes vaunt over the fallen as a matter of course, and Odysseus vaunted over the Cyclops to his cost. Here he has learnt, or the poem has: the suitors died by 'heaven's doom and their own evil deeds', and the killer presents himself as an instrument. It is a scruple of piety rather than mercy, though. His very next sentence asks the nurse which of the women have been disloyal.

quotations.text: as thrushes or doves beat against a net that has been set for them in a thicket just as they were getting to their nest, and a terrible fate awaits them, even so did the women have to put their heads in nooses one after the other and die most miserably.
quotations.context: Twelve maidservants who slept with the suitors are made to carry out the bodies and clean the hall; Telemachus then hangs them.
quotations.analysis: The narrative says they deserve it; the simile does not sound convinced. Small birds heading for their nest — for home, the poem's own highest value — are caught in a net. The next sentence, about their feet moving 'but not for very long', is as cold as anything in Homer. The women were slaves, and what choice they had is not discussed. The poem's justice and the poem's sympathy part company here, and both are left on the page.

quotations.text: There was a young olive growing within the precincts of the house, in full vigour, and about as thick as a bearing-post. I built my room round this with strong walls of stone and a roof to cover them
quotations.speaker: Odysseus
quotations.context: Penelope has told Eurycleia to move the master's bed out of the bedroom. Odysseus, for the only time in the poem, loses his temper.
quotations.analysis: It is a trap, and the master of traps walks into it: only the man who built the bed knows that one post is a rooted tree. His anger is the proof, because it is unplanned. The secret is apt as well as secure. He did not bring a bed into a house; he built the house around a living thing and made the marriage out of that. His fear that someone has 'cut down the olive tree at its roots' is the fear of the whole twenty years.

quotations.text: As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming towards the shore, when Neptune has wrecked their ship with the fury of his winds and waves
quotations.context: Penelope has accepted the proof of the bed; husband and wife hold each other and weep.
quotations.analysis: The simile begins as if it were about Odysseus — he is the one Poseidon wrecked, in Book 5, in nearly these terms — and then turns: 'even so was her husband welcome to her'. The shipwrecked swimmer is Penelope. In one comparison the poem gives her his ordeal and says that staying was a voyage too. It is the 'one mind' he wished on Nausicaa, enacted in the grammar of a sentence.

quotations.text: The fame, therefore, of her virtue shall never die, and the immortals shall compose a song that shall be welcome to all mankind in honour of the constancy of Penelope.
quotations.speaker: The ghost of Agamemnon
quotations.context: In Hades the dead suitors tell their story, and Agamemnon, murdered by his own wife, responds.
quotations.analysis: Undying fame in song is what Iliadic warriors die for, and here it is awarded to a woman for staying at home. The song Agamemnon predicts is, of course, the one we are reading. But his praise is narrow — 'constancy' — and the poem has shown a good deal more than that: nerve, deceit, and a test her husband failed to see coming. The dead king sees a faithful wife because a faithless one killed him.

quotations.text: Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, stop this warful strife, or Jove will be angry with you.
quotations.speaker: Athene (Butler's Minerva)
quotations.context: The suitors' families have armed to avenge them. Odysseus is swooping on them 'like a soaring eagle' when a thunderbolt lands at Athene's feet.
quotations.analysis: The poem ends by stopping its hero. Left to himself he would kill every man on the field, and the feud between the houses of Ithaca would run for generations; it takes Zeus's thunderbolt and a direct order to end it. The peace is imposed, not earned, which is honest. A poem that began with gods discussing human responsibility finishes by admitting that revenge has no natural stopping place.

themes.name: Winning a state and keeping it
What is done and what ought to be done
themes.canonicalName: What is done and what ought to be done

themes.name: The Church as a state among states

quotations.text: just as those who draw landscapes place themselves below in the plain to contemplate the nature of the mountains and of lofty places, and in order to contemplate the plains place themselves upon high mountains, even so to understand the nature of the people it needs to be a prince, and to understand that of princes it needs to be of the people.
quotations.context: Machiavelli answers in advance the charge that a man of low condition has no business instructing princes.
quotations.analysis: The comparison turns his lack of rank into his qualification: distance is what makes a subject visible. It is politely symmetrical, and the symmetry hides a cost to Lorenzo, since it implies that a prince cannot see what princes are like and needs somebody on the plain to tell him. The job application is folded inside the theory of knowledge.

quotations.text: men ought either to be well treated or crushed, because they can avenge themselves of lighter injuries, of more serious ones they cannot
quotations.context: From the argument that colonies are better than garrisons, because colonies injure only a few people and leave them too poor to retaliate.
quotations.analysis: This is the first sentence in the book likely to shock, and it arrives as an aside in a discussion of costs. The reasoning is actuarial: the question is not what men deserve but which injuries come back. The either and or leave no room for the ordinary middle course of governing, mild unfairness, which the sentence identifies as the dangerous one.

quotations.text: in the beginning of the malady it is easy to cure but difficult to detect, but in the course of time, not having been either detected or treated in the beginning, it becomes easy to detect but difficult to cure.
quotations.context: Praising the Romans for dealing with distant troubles before they became wars on Italian soil.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a chiasmus, with cure and detect changing places, so its form acts out the reversal it describes. The medical likeness makes statecraft a matter of diagnosis, which suits a writer whose trade was reading situations early. It also prepares the book’s case against fortune: most disasters called sudden were visible once to someone who was looking.

quotations.text: he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined
quotations.context: The general rule drawn from Louis XII’s career in Italy, after he has helped the Pope into the Romagna and Spain into Naples.
quotations.analysis: A chapter of detailed Italian politics is compressed into ten words that would fit any century. The reason given is psychological: power is conferred by either cleverness or force, and the man who receives it distrusts both in his benefactor. Read from Lorenzo’s side it is an odd thing for a petitioner to write, since it tells a prince to be wary of exactly the useful servant Machiavelli is offering to be.

quotations.text: there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things
quotations.context: Explaining why even the greatest founders had trouble at the start.
quotations.analysis: The explanation that follows is an analysis of interests, not of courage: those who did well under the old arrangement fight hard, and those who may do well under the new one help lukewarmly because they have not seen it work yet. It is one of the few passages in the book about reform rather than rule, and it accounts for why reformers so often turn to force.

quotations.text: Hence it is that all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed.
quotations.context: Just before Savonarola is named as the modern proof.
quotations.analysis: Prophet is the startling word. By choosing it Machiavelli puts Moses, whom he has just said one may not discuss, under the same law as Romulus: the people believed because they could be made to go on believing. Florentine readers had watched the unarmed case burn in their own piazza fifteen years earlier, so the generalisation rests on something the first audience had seen.

quotations.text: The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed.
quotations.context: Borgia has had his governor Ramiro d’Orco executed and left in the square at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife beside him.
quotations.analysis: Spectacle is exact: the killing is theatre, staged for an audience that hated the deputy and needed to fear the master. The two participles name the two effects a prince wants from a single act, gratitude and awe, and Machiavelli reports them as a critic reports a well-judged scene. The cruelty was Borgia’s policy throughout; the execution lets him disown it and profit from it together.

quotations.text: he told me that he had thought of everything that might occur at the death of his father, and had provided a remedy for all, except that he had never anticipated that, when the death did happen, he himself would be on the point to die.
quotations.context: Machiavelli, then a Florentine envoy in Rome, recalls talking to Cesare Borgia on the day Julius II was elected.
quotations.analysis: He told me is the only moment in the chapter where the author steps into the scene, and he does it to certify the one thing no planning covered. The sentence runs through a long list of provisions and then trips on except, which is how the career went. The book’s whole dispute between ability and fortune is here as an anecdote: a man can close every gap but the one he is standing in.

quotations.text: Yet it cannot be called talent to slay fellow-citizens, to deceive friends, to be without faith, without mercy, without religion; such methods may gain empire, but not glory.
quotations.context: The verdict on Agathocles, after a paragraph conceding that he owed nothing to fortune.
quotations.analysis: Anyone who thinks the book measures everything by success has to get past this sentence. Empire and glory are separated, and glory is withheld on grounds that are frankly moral. The awkwardness is that a few chapters later a prince will be told to break faith when he must; the difference seems to lie in the triple without, a life with no restraint at all as against a ruler who does wrong only under necessity.

quotations.text: For injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.
quotations.context: The practical conclusion about cruelty well used, drawn from Agathocles’ long and secure reign.
quotations.analysis: Harm and kindness are both described as things tasted, so the subjects are imagined as palates and government as a matter of dosage. The balance of the two clauses makes an unsettling idea sound like household economy. It is also a rule about time, which is this book’s real medium: the same quantity of pain is a different political fact when it is spread out.

quotations.text: The chief foundations of all states, new as well as old or composite, are good laws and good arms
quotations.context: The opening of the military chapters, as the book turns from kinds of state to means of defence.
quotations.analysis: Laws are named first and then dropped within two sentences, on the ground that good laws cannot exist where there are not good arms. The move tells a reader what kind of book this is: law, the usual subject of political writing, is treated as a consequence of force. Foundations is the book’s commonest figure, and here the building is every state there has ever been.

quotations.text: he who told us that our sins were the cause of it told the truth, but they were not the sins he imagined, but those which I have related.
quotations.context: On how easily Charles VIII overran Italy in 1494; the preacher is not named, and is usually taken to be Savonarola.
quotations.analysis: A sermon is accepted and rewritten in one sentence. Sin keeps its name and changes its content: the offence was not luxury or impiety but the hiring of other men to do the fighting. The following sentence sharpens it by saying that these were the sins of princes, so the moral vocabulary of the pulpit is kept and pointed at a political class.

quotations.text: Francesco Sforza, through being martial, from a private person became Duke of Milan; and the sons, through avoiding the hardships and troubles of arms, from dukes became private persons.
quotations.context: Evidence for the claim that war is the only art that belongs to a ruler.
quotations.analysis: One family supplies both halves of the proof, and the sentence is built as a mirror: private person to duke, dukes to private persons. The father is in the singular and the sons are a plural, as if decline needed no individuals. It is the book’s case against inheritance in miniature; a title passes to the next generation, and the quality that earned it does not.

quotations.text: how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done, sooner effects his ruin than his preservation
quotations.context: Machiavelli has just said he will depart from the methods of other writers and follow the real truth of the matter rather than the imagination of it.
quotations.analysis: The distance between is and ought is not denied, and it is not closed by lowering the ought; it is declared too wide to govern across. The argument is about survival, and ruin is its measure. What the sentence leaves unsaid is that a prince’s ruin is rarely his alone, which is the ground on which the chapters that follow will defend doing wrong.

quotations.text: Hence it is necessary for a prince wishing to hold his own to know how to do wrong, and to make use of it or not according to necessity.
quotations.context: The conclusion drawn at once from the gap between how men live and how they ought to.
quotations.analysis: Wrong is still called wrong. The sentence does not redefine evil as good, which would have been the easier and more comfortable course; it asks the prince to keep the ordinary moral names and act against them knowingly. Or not matters as much as the rest: what is recommended is a capacity held in reserve, governed by a necessity the prince must judge for himself.

quotations.text: it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.
quotations.context: The answer to the chapter’s question, given after saying that one should wish to be both.
quotations.analysis: The famous half of the sentence is conditional on the second half, and the word is safer, not better. The reasoning that follows is about who holds the lever: men love at their own pleasure and fear at the prince’s, so fear is the only bond he controls. The chapter then spends as long on avoiding hatred as on inspiring fear, a limit that the quoted version always loses.

quotations.text: men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony.
quotations.context: Advice that a prince who must execute someone should do it with clear justification and never touch the property.
quotations.analysis: The joke is grim and the sentence works as a restraint. It tells a prince that confiscation is more dangerous to him than execution, since killing needs a pretext and pretexts run out, while a ruler who has started seizing goods never lacks a reason to go on. The low view of human nature is put to a use that protects subjects from the commonest kind of tyranny.

quotations.text: it is necessary to be a fox to discover the snares and a lion to terrify the wolves.
quotations.context: From the passage on fighting by law, which is proper to men, and by force, which is proper to beasts.
quotations.analysis: Older advice to rulers had used the lion for courage and the fox as a warning. Machiavelli keeps both animals and makes them a division of labour, each covering the other’s weakness.
