The detail worth noticing is that the fox only discovers snares; cunning is presented first as a defence against a world of wolves and trappers, and the licence to break faith is drawn from that.

quotations.text: Alexander the Sixth did nothing else but deceive men, nor ever thought of doing otherwise, and he always found victims
quotations.context: The one recent example Machiavelli says he cannot pass over, in support of the claim that a deceiver will always find someone willing to be deceived.
quotations.analysis: The example chosen for successful lying is a pope, named without comment, in a book addressed to a family that then held the papacy. The exaggeration, nothing else and always, makes him less a person than a controlled experiment: a man who broke every oath and was believed at the next one. The lesson is about the audience’s appetite for being persuaded.

quotations.text: Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are
quotations.context: Explaining why a prince must take care that everything he says seems full of mercy, faith, humanity, uprightness and religion.
quotations.analysis: The argument is about the senses. The many judge by the eye, the few by the hand, and the few will not contradict the many while the state stands behind them. This is a theory of public opinion written before the phrase existed, and the you makes it personal: Lorenzo is being told that he is watched by a crowd, and that the crowd’s verdict is the one that counts.

quotations.text: He who will, therefore, carefully examine the actions of this man will find him a most valiant lion and a most cunning fox
quotations.context: Summing up Septimius Severus, who deceived one rival for the throne while he destroyed the other.
quotations.analysis: The image from the previous chapter is given a body, and the body is an emperor who was cruel to the people and died in power. Machiavelli does not hide that, and he does not simply recommend Severus either: the chapter ends by telling a new prince to take from him only what founding a state requires. The example is offered as a kit from which parts may be selected.

quotations.text: always using religion as a plea, so as to undertake greater schemes, he devoted himself with pious cruelty to driving out and clearing his kingdom of the Moors
quotations.context: From the account of Ferdinand of Aragon’s rise, offered as the pattern of a prince who wins esteem by great enterprises.
quotations.analysis: Pious cruelty is the most compressed phrase in the book, an adjective and a noun that ought to cancel each other and are made to cooperate. The chapter calls the example admirable and rare, and the praise is technical, as one might admire a well-made engine. A reader is left to decide whether the coolness is approval or the driest kind of exposure.

quotations.text: So it happens with fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her.
quotations.context: The end of the comparison between fortune and a river that floods the plain but can be banked and channelled in fair weather.
quotations.analysis: The river does not stop being violent; what changes is where the water goes. It is the book’s most hopeful image and its most civic, since dykes and canals are public works and the next paragraph calls Italy a country without them. Fortune is still a she who knows where the defences are missing, so the flood keeps something like a will.

quotations.text: fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her
quotations.context: The close of the chapter, after Julius II has been shown succeeding by rashness because rashness happened to suit his times.
quotations.analysis: The second image of fortune quarrels with the first. The river rewarded patient engineering; this figure rewards violence and youth, and it arrives just after the admission that no man can change his nature to match the times. It reads as a preference asserted once analysis has given out, and its brutality is of a piece with a book that pictures mastery as force throughout.

quotations.text: God is not willing to do everything, and thus take away our free will and that share of glory which belongs to us.
quotations.context: After listing signs borrowed from Exodus, the divided sea, the cloud, the rock and the manna, as omens favouring the Medici.
quotations.analysis: The miracles are produced and then told to stand aside, because the point is that the rest is up to the reader. It is the theology of chapter 25 restated for a devout audience: half is given, half must be taken. Glory, which was refused to Agathocles, returns as the prize, and the plural our quietly puts the author in the company that will share it.

quotations.text: To all of us this barbarous dominion stinks.
quotations.context: Near the end of the exhortation, after a run of questions asking what Italian would refuse a liberator.
quotations.analysis: After twenty-five chapters in the third person the book says us, and says it with the crudest verb it has used. The sentence is seven words long and follows a sequence of rising rhetorical questions, so it lands as a drop into plain speech. Whether the last chapter is the purpose of the whole or a flourish added to a technical work is the oldest argument about this book, and this line is the best evidence that the feeling was real.

themes.name: What the children are not told
Wages, hours and the people who keep the line
The railway as a living thing
A narrator who will not stay out of it

techniques.name: The gap where the fact should be
The narrator who talks to you

quotations.text: They were not railway children to begin with.
quotations.context: The novel’s first sentence.
quotations.analysis: The title is contradicted before the reader has finished the first line, and the tense does the work: were not, to begin with, implies a middle and an end already known to the teller. It also quietly warns that the railway is something that happened to these children rather than something they are, which is the difference between this book and an adventure story about trains.

quotations.text: “Of course they can. Girls are just as clever as boys, and don't you forget it! How would you like to be an engine-driver, Phil?”
quotations.speaker: Father
quotations.context: Peter has asked doubtfully whether girls can help to mend engines; his father is taking the toy apart on the table.
quotations.analysis: This is almost the last thing the father says before the knock at the door, and Nesbit puts it where it will be remembered. It licenses everything the girls do afterwards — the petticoat flags, the ride in the cab, the nursing in the tunnel — and it sets up the novel’s one real disagreement with itself, when Dr Forrest explains to Peter, as science, that girls are softer and weaker and have to be.

quotations.text: “Father's been called away--on business,” said Mother. “Come, darlings, go at once.”
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: The two gentlemen have gone, a cab has driven away, and she has come back into the room with her face as white as her lace collar.
quotations.analysis: The dash is the arrest. Everything before it is true and everything after it is a formula, and the pause in the middle is the only sign that a sentence is being assembled rather than spoken. Nesbit will keep this trick going for nine chapters: nothing said to the children is a lie, and nothing said to them is the truth either.

quotations.text: “If Mother doesn't want us to know she's been crying,” she said to herself as she heard through the dark the catching of her Mother's breath, “we WON'T know it. That's all.”
quotations.speaker: Bobbie
quotations.context: Their mother has come up late to kiss the sleeping children, and only Bobbie has woken.
quotations.analysis: Knowing is turned into something a child can decide to do or not do, which is a strange and precise idea to give an eleven-year-old, and the capitals on WON’T are the italics of a vow. Note the plural: we won’t know it. Bobbie appoints herself the keeper of a silence the other two have not been asked about, and she will keep it, alone, for the whole book.

quotations.text: “We're taking the useful ones,” said Mother; “we've got to play at being Poor for a bit, my chickabiddy.”
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Bobbie has noticed that the beautiful inlaid cabinet is being left behind and that they seem to be taking all the ugly things.
quotations.analysis: Play at, for a bit, and a nursery endearment: three softenings in one short sentence, and the capital P on Poor makes poverty a part in a game rather than a condition. The children take her at her word — Mother had told them more than once that they were quite poor now, but this did not seem to be anything but a way of speaking — and it takes three wet days in June and a refused fire to teach them otherwise.

quotations.text: “Oh!” said Roberta, drawing a long breath; “it was like a great dragon tearing by. Did you feel it fan us with its hot wings?”
quotations.speaker: Roberta
quotations.context: The children’s first close sight of a train, from the top of the fence at the bottom of the field, the morning after they arrive.
quotations.analysis: The simile is the child’s, not the narrator’s, and it is allowed to stand as a description of a real machine rather than being corrected. Everything the book later does with the railway grows from here: the 9.15 becomes the Green Dragon, the tunnel becomes its lair, and Phyllis decides in the dark of Chapter 11 that a train takes its own shape in there. Nesbit never says the children are wrong; she simply also teaches them what an injector is.

quotations.text: I am tired of calling Roberta by her name. I don't see why I should. No one else did. Everyone else called her Bobbie, and I don't see why I shouldn't.
quotations.context: An aside in brackets, dropped into the middle of a conversation about toy engines.
quotations.analysis: A narrator announcing that she has got bored of her own formality is a small joke, but it changes the book. From here the eldest child has two names, and Nesbit uses the split: Bobbie is the girl her family sees, Roberta the one she addresses when she is angry with herself in the tunnel. The aside also establishes that this teller will interrupt, admit preferences and keep back whatever she likes.

quotations.text: Well, it was just like that with the sorrow the children had felt at Father's going away, and at Mother's being so unhappy. It made a deep impression, but the impression did not last long.
quotations.context: The end of a long comparison with a finger poked into a crock of dough set by the fire to rise.
quotations.analysis: The simile is domestic, slightly greedy and entirely unsentimental, and it says the thing most books for children will not: that the young forget, and that the forgetting is elastic and healthy rather than callous. It is also a piece of housekeeping. Nesbit needs her children cheerful for eight chapters of larks, and this paragraph buys them without pretending the grief was shallow.

quotations.text: “I'm not a thief,” said Peter, as firmly as he could. “I'm a coal-miner.”
quotations.speaker: Peter
quotations.context: The Station Master has come out of the dark in a pair of old seaside sand shoes and taken him by the collar on top of the coal heap.
quotations.analysis: Peter’s defence is a real argument — he has reasoned that the outside of the heap might be stealing and the middle only mining — and he is brave enough to make it while being held by the jacket. The Station Master’s reply is the book’s plainest sentence about property: stealing is stealing, and what’s mine isn’t yours, whether you call it mining or whether you don’t. Eight chapters later a jury will decide what to call something a different man did not do.

quotations.text: He was a very nice-looking old gentleman, and he looked as if he were nice, too, which is not at all the same thing.
quotations.context: The first description of the passenger in the first-class carriage who waves back at the children.
quotations.analysis: A whole theory of appearances in eleven words, and one of the few moments where Nesbit’s adult irony is aimed at her adult reader over the children’s heads. The distinction matters later: this is a book in which a man’s good looks and good standing are what finally get another man out of prison, and the narrator has taken care to note that the two things are usually confused.

quotations.text: neither her own children nor you nor any other children in the world could ever understand exactly what it cost her to do it. Only some few of you, like Bobbie, may understand a very little bit.
quotations.context: Their mother has just given the children permission to walk on the railway line, having admitted that she did it herself as a girl.
quotations.analysis: The sentence turns from the story to the person holding the book and sorts them: most of you cannot understand this, a few of you can. It is a considerable thing to say to a child reader, and it identifies the quality the book values above bravery — the capacity to notice what an adult is paying. Bobbie is named as the type of it, which is why the narrator can later say, without embarrassment, that she is growing fond of her.

quotations.text: it's quite true that we're poor, but we have enough to live on. You mustn't go telling everyone about our affairs--it's not right. And you must never, never, never ask strangers to give you things.
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: The children have owned up to the letter and the hamper, and she has been angrier than they have ever known her, and then cried, and then apologised for being angry.
quotations.analysis: Two prohibitions are folded together here and only one of them is about money. Telling everyone about our affairs is the rule that governs the entire book, and it is being laid down by a woman whose own affairs include a husband in prison. The three nevers are the give-away: this is not household economy but a household under siege, and the children take away only the part about hampers.

quotations.text: “Or when the Judges THINK they've done wrong,” said Mother. “Yes, that's so in England. But in Russia it was different.”
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Peter has objected that people only go to prison when they have done wrong; his mother is explaining why a Russian writer was sent to Siberia.
quotations.analysis: The most exposed sentence in the novel, and the children walk straight past it. She corrects her son’s idea of justice, concedes that the correction applies to England, and then covers the concession with a contrast that lets her go on talking about somewhere else. The capitals mark the stress she puts on THINK; the full stop after England is where her own case is, and she steps over it.

quotations.text: “Yes,” said Mother, “upon all prisoners and captives. All prisoners and captives.”
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Bobbie has repeated the phrase back to her to check that she has it right, at the end of the evening the Russian arrives.
quotations.analysis: The words come from the litany, where they are safely general, and the mother is using the form of a prayer to say something she cannot say in her own voice. The repetition is the point: she says it once as instruction and once as her own petition, and the second time there is nobody in the sentence but her husband. Bobbie will quote it back in a letter six chapters later with the three words that close the circle — I see now.

quotations.text: “I--I don't know,” said Bobbie, angry with herself, but still clinging to that resolution of hers, not to see anything that Mother didn't mean her to see.
quotations.context: She has found her father’s clothes in the locked black trunk, worked out that he cannot have taken them with him, and blurted out a question about whether he is dead.
quotations.analysis: Not to see is a remarkable formulation, since she has already seen; what she is refusing is the inference. Nesbit is describing a discipline rather than an innocence, and the cost of it is in the phrase angry with herself. This is the technique of the whole novel stated as a character trait: the evidence is lying open in the room, and the decision is not to read it.

quotations.text: “Well, you see, you must take one side or the other. Same as with Liberals and Conservatives. The great thing is to take your side and then stick to it, whatever happens.”
quotations.speaker: Perks
quotations.context: Perks has been asked why he is on the side of the Japanese, having just agreed that the Russian government’s treatment of the exile was wicked.
quotations.analysis: This is the book’s only sustained piece of political comedy, and it is sharper than it looks. Perks has already said that the Station Master kept the story quiet because a man’s got to stand up for his own side whatever they does, and that foreigners are all tarred with the same brush. Taking a side and sticking to it is precisely what the jury in the father’s case has done, and Nesbit lets a porter explain the mechanism without once mentioning the trial.

quotations.text: “We never got any cherries, after all,” said Bobbie.
quotations.speaker: Bobbie
quotations.context: Walking home from the station after the cheering, while Peter and Phyllis congratulate themselves on having saved the train.
quotations.analysis: The others think her rather heartless, and the narrator lets that judgement stand for a chapter before explaining that Bobbie wakes screaming for months afterwards. The line is a small masterpiece of displacement: she cannot talk about the trustful engine rushing towards the mound, so she talks about fruit. It is the same manoeuvre her mother makes with Russia, learned from her without either of them noticing.

quotations.text: It just means that a person is able to know that you are unhappy, and to love you extra on that account, without bothering you by telling you all the time how sorry she is for you.
quotations.context: The narrator, having admitted that she is growing fond of Roberta, explains what is meant by the power of silent sympathy.
quotations.analysis: The definition is given in the plainest possible words and then undercut by the admission that follows it: this needs practice, it is not so easy as you might think. What is being praised is a skill, not a temperament, and the novel is unusual in treating tact as an achievement of the same order as stopping a train. The whole passage is addressed to you, so the reader is being taught as well as told.

quotations.text: “Oh, yes,” said Bobbie; “I think everyone in the world is friends if you can only get them to see you don't want to be UN-friends.”
quotations.speaker: Bobbie
quotations.context: The end of the barge day, after a man who twisted Peter’s ear has taken them the whole trip to Farley and back. Her mother answers, ‘Perhaps you’re right’, and sighs.
quotations.analysis: Nesbit gives her heroine the book’s most hopeful proposition and then puts an adult sigh immediately after it, which is the most efficient piece of undercutting in the novel. Bobbie’s rule has worked on a bargee, a porter and a Station Master; it has not worked on a jury, and her mother knows it. The coined word UN-friends is the giveaway that this is still a child’s formulation.

quotations.text: “I think,” said the clergyman, “it was what is sometimes called loving-kindness.”
quotations.speaker: The clergyman
quotations.context: Mrs Perks, going round the village to thank everyone, has asked whether what the children did was friendliness.
quotations.analysis: The chapter has spent twenty pages refusing the word charity — Perks will not have it, his wife says nobody would offer it to him, and the children did not mean it — so the right word has to be found by somebody with a professional vocabulary. Loving-kindness is a translation of a biblical term for covenant faithfulness, which is heavier than the tea-table it is used at; Nesbit slips in the one register in which a gift between unequals is not a humiliation.

quotations.text: The name of the man who had been tried was the name of her Father. The verdict was 'Guilty.' And the sentence was 'Five years' Penal Servitude.'
quotations.context: Bobbie has stopped at the level-crossing with a parcel of Perks’s old magazines and idly read the newspaper it is wrapped in.
quotations.analysis: Three flat sentences, each a fact from a legal record, and the shock is produced by the machinery of citation rather than by any emotion. The formula the name of the man was the name of her Father is exact: she is reading about a stranger until the last three words. Nesbit has arranged for the truth to arrive as waste paper, wrapped round a kindness done by a porter, and the bottom of the column is torn off.

quotations.text: “Are you going to tell the others?” Mother asked. “No.” “Why?” “Because--” “Exactly,” said Mother; “so you understand why I didn't tell you. We two must help each other to be brave.”
quotations.context: Bobbie has brought the cutting to her mother’s room and locked the door.
quotations.analysis: The reason is never given, by either of them, and the novel’s whole method is justified in a word and a half. Bobbie starts an explanation, finds she does not need one, and the trailing dash is accepted as an argument; the silence that has looked for ten chapters like evasion is revealed as the same choice the daughter has just made unprompted. It also promotes her: they are now two adults with a secret rather than a mother and a child.

quotations.text: “Nobody will listen,” said Mother, very bitterly, “nobody at all. Do you suppose I've not tried everything?
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Bobbie has just suggested explaining to the lawyers about the jealous subordinate who got her father’s place.
quotations.analysis: Very bitterly is the only such adverb attached to this character in the book, and it is earned. She has the explanation, she has the suspect, and she has no standing; the letters she writes to Members of Parliament and Editors of papers on a stranger’s behalf in Chapter 6 were presumably written on her husband’s behalf first. What eventually moves the case is not evidence but a railway director who happens to know some Russians and to read the papers carefully.

quotations.text: “SILLY little girl!” said Roberta to Bobbie, and felt better.
quotations.context: Alone in the tunnel with an unconscious boy, she has cut away his stocking, seen the broken leg and felt the ground go unsteady.
quotations.analysis: The two names are now two people, and the sterner one is put in charge. Nesbit explains in the next paragraph that Bobbie hates being called a little girl by anybody, even kindly, and allows Roberta to do it only when she is very angry with herself — so the insult is also a private joke and a way of standing up. It is the same machinery as her mother’s bravery, seen from inside and at eleven years old.

quotations.text: “Yes,” she said, “I do believe it--almost always--except when I'm so sad that I can't believe anything. But even when I can't believe it, I know it's true--and I try to believe. You don't know how I try, Peter.
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Peter has asked whether she really believes what she has just said about being characters in a book that God is writing.
quotations.analysis: A book for children that lets a mother admit she cannot always believe her own consolation is doing something unusual, and the three dashes are the hesitation written into the punctuation. The distinction she draws — I know it’s true and I try to believe — is the same distinction Bobbie makes between seeing and allowing oneself to have seen. It is also the closest the novel comes to saying out loud how tired she is.

quotations.text: “Oh! my Daddy, my Daddy!” That scream went like a knife into the heart of everyone in the train, and people put their heads out of the windows to see a tall pale man with lips set in a thin close line, and a little girl clinging to him with arms and legs, while his arms went tightly round her.
quotations.context: Three people get off the 11.54: a countryman with chickens, the grocer’s wife’s cousin, and the third.
quotations.analysis: Nesbit refuses the close-up. The reunion is shown from the carriage windows, at the distance of strangers, so that the reader is given the sound and then the picture other people see; the father is a tall pale man before he is anybody’s father, and his set lips record ten months that the book has declined to describe. It is the loudest moment in a novel that has been quiet on purpose, and it lasts one sentence.

quotations.text: I think we will not open the door or follow him. I think that just now we are not wanted there. I think it will be best for us to go quickly and quietly away.
quotations.context: The novel’s last paragraph. The father has gone in and the door has shut behind him.
quotations.analysis: The narrator who has interrupted, teased and confided for fourteen chapters closes by withholding one more thing, and this time names the reason. Three sentences beginning I think give the decision the feel of a judgement being made on the spot rather than a device prepared in advance. The book that is about what may properly be kept from people ends by keeping its own reunion from the reader, and walks off across the field.

books.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
books.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

themes.name: The living world, slimy and beautiful
Alone on a wide wide sea
The tale that has to be told
Prayer, chance and an unsteady providence

quotations.text: It is an ancient Mariner, And he stoppeth one of three.
quotations.context: The opening couplet, before anybody has spoken.
quotations.analysis: 'It is', not 'there was': the present tense puts the Mariner in front of us as something encountered, almost as a thing, and the same tense will return at the end when we learn he is still doing this. 'One of three' is never explained. Two men walk on into the wedding, and the poem's first act is a selection without a stated reason, which prepares for a story built on another.

quotations.text: He holds him with his glittering eye-- The Wedding-Guest stood still, And listens like a three years child: The Mariner hath his will.
quotations.context: The Mariner has been told to take his hand away, and does; this is what he uses instead.
quotations.analysis: The hand fails and the eye succeeds, so the hold is not physical and the guest's consent is not asked. Comparing a grown man to a three years child makes listening a return to helplessness. 'Hath his will' is a phrase of mastery, and it sits oddly on a man we later learn has no will of his own in the matter, since the tale compels him as he compels the guest.

quotations.text: As if it had been a Christian soul, We hailed it in God's name.
quotations.context: The albatross comes through the fog to a ship surrounded by ice, where no living thing has been seen.
quotations.analysis: The sailors greet the first creature they have met in the ice as one greets a person, and the 'as if' keeps the comparison honest: nobody claims the bird is a soul. What the line establishes is hospitality. The bird is received as a guest, fed, and called to, so that the shooting nine evenings later is a breach of welcome before it is anything more mysterious.

quotations.text: "God save thee, ancient Mariner! From the fiends, that plague thee thus!-- Why look'st thou so?"--With my cross-bow I shot the ALBATROSS.
quotations.context: The Wedding-Guest breaks in at the sight of the Mariner's face, and the answer closes the first part.
quotations.analysis: The confession is made in reply to a question about his expression, not about his conduct, and it answers 'why' with 'what'. The instrument comes first and the verb is the plainest available. There is no because, then or afterwards. Placing the act at the very end of the part, after a stanza of moonshine and vespers, gives it the abruptness of the thing itself, and the capitals are the text's way of letting the word ring.

quotations.text: For all averred, I had killed the bird That made the breeze to blow.
quotations.context: The first verdict of the shipmates, while the wind still holds but the bird no longer follows.
quotations.analysis: 'Averred' is a word for sworn testimony, and the crew use it twice, a stanza apart, for opposite findings: that he killed the bird that brought the breeze, and that he killed the bird that brought the fog. Their morality is a weather report. The poem quietly treats the second verdict as the fatal one, since approving the act afterwards is the only thing the two hundred ever do to deserve what follows.

quotations.text: We were the first that ever burst Into that silent sea.
quotations.context: The ship, running north with a fair wind, enters waters no ship has sailed.
quotations.analysis: For two lines the poem sounds like the voyage narratives Coleridge had been reading, with the explorer's boast of priority. 'Burst' is a violent verb for an arrival, and it rhymes inside the line with 'first', so that discovery and intrusion are heard as one sound. The silence they break into is about to become their own: in the next stanza the wind drops, and they speak only to hear something.

quotations.text: Day after day, day after day, We stuck, nor breath nor motion; As idle as a painted ship Upon a painted ocean.
quotations.context: The ship is becalmed under a copper sky.
quotations.analysis: The first line does what it describes, repeating itself because nothing has happened to report. The simile is stranger than it looks. A becalmed ship is compared to a picture of a ship, which is to say to art, and the comparison is a complaint: to be a painting is to be without breath. In a poem so concerned with what it is to be fixed by a tale, the image of people trapped in a representation is not idle.

quotations.text: Water, water, every where, And all the boards did shrink; Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink.
quotations.context: Thirst begins among the becalmed crew.
quotations.analysis: The line most people know is usually misquoted, and the true second line is the more exact observation: salt water and sun are shrinking the planks of the ship itself, so the sea surrounds them and is also pulling their shelter apart. The stanza is a riddle of abundance as deprivation. It prepares for Part IV, where the Mariner is surrounded by life and cannot be part of it until he sees it differently.

quotations.text: Instead of the cross, the Albatross About my neck was hung.
quotations.context: The close of Part II: the crew, too parched to speak, express themselves in an act.
quotations.analysis: The rhyme of 'cross' and 'Albatross' falls inside one line and makes the substitution audible. The passive voice matters: he does not take the bird up, it is hung on him by men who have themselves approved the killing, which makes this a scapegoating as much as a penance. Whether the bird is thereby likened to Christ, or whether the emblem of forgiveness has simply been replaced by the evidence of the offence, the line declines to say.

quotations.text: I bit my arm, I sucked the blood, And cried, A sail! a sail!
quotations.context: A shape has been sighted, and nobody on board has moisture enough in his mouth to call out.
quotations.analysis: To speak at all he has to drink from himself, and the poem sets down the fact in two short clauses without comment. It is the first time speech costs the Mariner blood, and it will not be the last: every later telling of the tale is wrung from him by a bodily agony. The hope he pays for so dearly is also mistaken, since the sail is the spectre-bark.

quotations.text: Her lips were red, her looks were free, Her locks were yellow as gold: Her skin was as white as leprosy, The Night-Mare LIFE-IN-DEATH was she, Who thicks man's blood with cold.
quotations.context: The Mariner sees the two figures on the skeleton ship as it comes alongside.
quotations.analysis: The first two lines are the stock portrait of a ballad heroine, and the third spoils it with a single noun. Red, gold and white are the colours of beauty, and white is also the colour of the disease, so the portrait turns on its own palette. The stanza runs to five lines because the name needs a line to itself. 'Thicks' is used as a verb, an old usage that makes the cold seem to act inside the listener's own veins.

quotations.text: The game is done! I've won! I've won!
quotations.context: Death and Life-in-Death have been casting dice on the deck of the hulk; this is her cry.
quotations.analysis: The poem's only glimpse of how sentences are passed in its universe is a game of chance, and the winner's glee is a child's. If the Mariner's survival is a prize in a dice game, then the moral economy of sin, penance and grace that he later describes has a rival explanation underneath it. The gloss of 1817 tidies this scene into a judgement; the verse leaves it as a throw.

quotations.text: And every soul, it passed me by, Like the whizz of my CROSS-BOW!
quotations.context: The last lines of Part III: two hundred men have dropped dead, and their souls leave their bodies.
quotations.analysis: Each part of the poem so far has ended on the bird or the weapon, and this one brings the weapon back as a sound. Two hundred deaths are heard as two hundred repetitions of the one shot, so that the simile does the accusing that no character has done aloud. The poem will not say where the souls go: they fled to bliss or woe, and the Mariner knows only that they went past him.

quotations.text: Alone, alone, all, all alone, Alone on a wide wide sea! And never a saint took pity on My soul in agony.
quotations.context: The Mariner has just reassured the Wedding-Guest that he is not a ghost, and resumes.
quotations.analysis: The first two lines contain almost nothing but one word and its near-rhymes: 'alone', 'all', 'a'. Long open vowels and the doubled 'wide wide' stretch the line out to the horizon it describes. The loneliness is then made vertical as well as horizontal, since no saint looks down either. He is not literally alone, as the next stanza cruelly points out; he has two hundred companions on deck.

quotations.text: The many men, so beautiful! And they all dead did lie: And a thousand thousand slimy things Lived on; and so did I.
quotations.context: Alone on deck among the bodies of the crew, looking from them to the sea.
quotations.analysis: The men are beautiful only now that they are dead; alive, they were evil looks from old and young. Against them he sets the slimy things and then, after a semicolon that works like a flinch, himself. The grammar files him with the creatures he despises. This self-disgust is the state from which he cannot pray, and the stanza needs to be remembered when the same creatures reappear transformed.

quotations.text: The moving Moon went up the sky, And no where did abide: Softly she was going up, And a star or two beside.
quotations.context: After seven days and nights under the dead men's curse, the Mariner looks up.
quotations.analysis: After stanzas clogged with rot, reek and curses, this one is almost empty, and the change of pace is the change of heart beginning. The moon is 'moving' and the Mariner is stuck; she abides nowhere and yet is accompanied, a star or two beside her, while he is fixed and alone. Nothing is asked of the image. It simply turns his eyes outward, and the water-snakes come two stanzas later.

quotations.text: O happy living things! no tongue Their beauty might declare: A spring of love gushed from my heart, And I blessed them unaware
quotations.context: The Mariner has been watching the water-snakes coil and swim in the shadow of the ship.
quotations.analysis: The turning point of the poem is an action its agent does not know he is performing. 'Unaware' is said twice in the stanza, and it matches the unexplained shooting exactly: he did not decide to kill and he does not decide to bless. 'A spring of love gushed' is water imagery arriving in a drought, and it comes from inside him before any rain falls. Note too that no tongue can declare their beauty, from a man whose whole later life is declaring.

quotations.text: The self same moment I could pray; And from my neck so free The Albatross fell off, and sank Like lead into the sea.
quotations.context: The end of Part IV, immediately after the blessing.
quotations.analysis: Prayer is not the cause of the release but its sign: the blessing came first and was not a prayer at all. The bird, which flew and perched and came to a call, leaves the poem as dead weight, and 'like lead' will be used once more, of the ship itself going down in Part VII. Both burdens sink, and neither sinking ends the matter, which is why this stanza closes a part and not the poem.

quotations.text: They raised their limbs like lifeless tools-- We were a ghastly crew.
quotations.context: The dead sailors rise without speaking and work the ship as it moves without wind.
quotations.analysis: The simile turns the men into the equipment they are handling, and then the pronoun does something worse: 'we'. The Mariner counts himself among them, hauling on a rope beside his own nephew's body. Life-in-Death has won him, and here the phrase is shown from the inside, as a living man doing a shift with corpses and unable to tell himself apart from the gang.

quotations.text: Quoth he, "The man hath penance done, And penance more will do."
quotations.context: The Mariner lies in a faint and hears two voices in the air discussing him; this is the softer one.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is passed in his hearing but not to his face, by speakers who are never identified, and it is the most exact statement of his condition in the poem: penance in the past tense and the future tense, with no present in which it is complete. The soft voice, as soft as honey-dew, delivers the harder news. Everything in Parts VI and VII should be read under this line.

quotations.text: Like one that on a lonesome road Doth walk in fear and dread, And having once turned round walks on, And turns no more his head; Because he knows, a frightful fiend Doth close behind him tread.
quotations.context: The spell of the dead men's eyes has just snapped, and the Mariner looks out over the sea again, but sees little.
quotations.analysis: The simile leaves the sea for a road on land, the place where we first met the Mariner, and describes a man who has looked once and will not look again. The fiend is never seen; knowledge of it is enough. The stanza takes six lines instead of four, so the reader, like the walker, is kept going past the point where rest was expected. Mary Shelley has Frankenstein quote it as he flees his creature.

quotations.text: "Ha! ha!" quoth he, "full plain I see, The Devil knows how to row."
quotations.context: The Pilot has fainted and the Hermit is praying, so the Mariner takes the oars of the rescue boat himself.
quotations.analysis: The boy's joke is the judgement of the ordinary world on the returning Mariner, and it is delivered in laughter by a child who is losing his mind as he speaks. The poem reports his madness in the present tense, in a subordinate clause, as a casualty nobody stops to count. It is a reminder that the tale harms those it touches, which bears on how we read the Wedding-Guest's condition at the end.

quotations.text: Since then, at an uncertain hour, That agony returns; And till my ghastly tale is told, This heart within me burns.
quotations.context: The Mariner has described how the Hermit's question forced the tale out of him, and explains what has happened since.
quotations.analysis: 'Uncertain' removes the last comfort of routine: the penance has no calendar. The burning has moved from the sky and the sea of Part II into his chest, so the tropics are now internal. 'Ghastly' is the word he used of the dead crew at the ropes, and he applies it to his own story. Telling brings relief, which means every listener is being used as medicine, and the Wedding-Guest is only the latest dose.

quotations.text: I pass, like night, from land to land; I have strange power of speech
quotations.context: The Mariner describes his life since the voyage and how he chooses, or is given, his listeners.
quotations.analysis: He compares himself to night, the thing that fell at one stride when the crew died, and the comparison makes him a natural force that arrives everywhere and stays nowhere. 'Strange power of speech' is as close as the poem comes to describing itself. Coleridge, a famous talker who held rooms for hours, gives the gift of eloquence to a man for whom it is a symptom.

quotations.text: He prayeth best, who loveth best All things both great and small; For the dear God who loveth us He made and loveth all.
quotations.context: The Mariner's farewell to the Wedding-Guest.
quotations.analysis: The rhythm goes nursery-simple and the diction could be a hymn for children, which is either the hard-won plainness of a man who has been to the bottom or a formula too small for what it follows. The poem gives grounds for both. The creed says God loves all; the narrative has shown two hundred men killed for a change of opinion. It is worth asking who needs this stanza more, the listener or the speaker.

quotations.text: A sadder and a wiser man, He rose the morrow morn.
quotations.context: The last two lines of the poem; the Mariner has gone, and the Wedding-Guest has turned from the bridegroom's door.
quotations.analysis: The poem ends on the listener, and the order of the adjectives is the verdict: sadder first. The stanza before says he went like one stunned and of sense forlorn, language closer to injury than to enlightenment. He has missed the wedding of his own kin to acquire this wisdom. If the Mariner's moral were the whole meaning, the guest ought to be gladder, and that gap is where the poem's interpretation properly begins.

themes.name: A sign that will not hold still
themes.canonicalName: A sign that will not hold still

quotations.text: which evidently found something congenial in the soil that had so early borne the black flower of civilized society, a prison
quotations.context: Describing the weeds on the grass-plot in front of the jail, in the book's opening paragraph.
quotations.analysis: The prison is called a flower, which makes punishment an organic product of settlement rather than a response to crime — and the chapter has already noted that every new colony lays out a graveyard and a jail before anything else. The rosebush beside the door arrives one sentence later, so the book's first image is a pair of flowers, one of them a building.

quotations.text: On the breast of her gown, in fine red cloth, surrounded with an elaborate embroidery and fantastic flourishes of gold-thread, appeared the letter A.
quotations.context: Hester's first appearance, coming out of the prison door with Pearl in her arms.
quotations.analysis: The sentence puts four clauses of craftsmanship in front of the letter itself, so the reader meets the needlework before the charge. Hester has been given a sentence and has answered it with her trade: the gold thread exceeds what the magistrates ordered, which is why the goodwives in the crowd are so angry about it.

quotations.text: “I will not speak!” answered Hester, turning pale as death, but responding to this voice, which she too surely recognized. “And my child must seek a heavenly Father; she shall never know an earthly one!”
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Refusing, from the scaffold, to name Pearl's father, after Dimmesdale has been ordered to exhort her.
quotations.analysis: The refusal is addressed to the man asking for it, and the narrator's aside — she recognised the voice — lets the reader in on the arrangement a hundred pages before the town gets there. Her second sentence is not defiance but a legal fiction, a father invented to fill an empty space on a record, which is the same manoeuvre Dimmesdale will use for seven years.

quotations.text: It irks me, nevertheless, that the partner of her iniquity should not, at least, stand on the scaffold by her side. But he will be known!⁠—he will be known!⁠—he will be known!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Spoken by the stranger in the crowd, who has not yet given anyone his name.
quotations.analysis: Three identical clauses, and each one is a promise rather than a prediction — he is describing work he intends to do. The irony is that he is standing in a crowd deciding not to be known himself, so the sentence that launches his revenge is also the moment he takes a false name.

quotations.text: she felt or fancied, then, that the scarlet letter had endowed her with a new sense
quotations.context: After Hester settles in a cottage on the edge of the settlement and begins to support herself by her needle.
quotations.analysis: 'Felt or fancied' is the book's characteristic hedge, offered before the claim rather than after it. The sense she acquires is a detector for concealed sin in respectable people, which is either a supernatural gift or the ordinary consequence of being the only person in town with nothing left to hide.

quotations.text: It was the scarlet letter in another form; the scarlet letter endowed with life!
quotations.context: Describing the crimson and gold tunic Hester has made for Pearl to wear to the Governor's hall.
quotations.analysis: Hester has dressed her daughter to match her own badge, which is either an act of defiance or a confession that she can no longer imagine the child apart from the crime. The exclamation mark belongs to the narrator, and it is worth noticing how often the adults in this book need Pearl to be a symbol rather than a three-year-old with good clothes.

quotations.text: “God gave me the child!” cried she. “He gave her in requital of all things else, which ye had taken from me. She is my happiness!⁠—she is my torture, none the less! Pearl keeps me here in life! Pearl punishes me too!
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Arguing against the magistrates' proposal to take Pearl away and have her brought up elsewhere.
quotations.analysis: She wins the argument by conceding the prosecution's case: yes, the child is a punishment, and that is the reason to leave her where she is. The two exclamations balance on the same verb, and the strategy is one Hester uses throughout — she never denies what the colony says about her, she simply refuses to draw its conclusions.

quotations.text: To the untrue man, the whole universe is false⁠—it is impalpable⁠—it shrinks to nothing within his grasp.
quotations.context: Explaining why Dimmesdale's visions of his dead parents and his congregation feel more solid to him than furniture.
quotations.analysis: The falsehood is described as spreading outward from the liar until it reaches the walls, which is a much stronger claim than that lying is wrong. It also explains the shape of Dimmesdale's sermons: the only thing he can still feel is the anguish, so the anguish is the only thing he can preach, and it is exactly what makes him beloved.

quotations.text: “Come up hither, Hester, thou and little Pearl,” said the Reverend Mr. Dimmesdale. “Ye have both been here before, but I was not with you. Come up hither once again, and we will stand all three together!”
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: On the scaffold at midnight, when no one in Boston is awake to see it.
quotations.analysis: Every word of this would be a confession at noon, and the sentence is grammatically identical to the one he will finally speak in Chapter 23. The only variable is the hour, which is the book's point about him: he has never lacked the words, only the daylight.

quotations.text: many people refused to interpret the scarlet A by its original signification. They said that it meant Able; so strong was Hester Prynne, with a woman’s strength.
quotations.context: After seven years of nursing the sick and clothing the poor.
quotations.analysis: The town has not forgiven her; it has relabelled her, which is cheaper. Note the passive shape of the reading — 'they said that it meant' — and note that the letter itself has not moved an inch: the same three stitches now certify a virtue, so the badge has proved capable of holding whatever the community needs it to hold.

quotations.text: Thou hadst great elements. Peradventure, hadst thou met earlier with a better love than mine, this evil had not been. I pity thee, for the good that has been wasted in thy nature!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: By the shore, when Hester tells him she means to break her promise of secrecy.
quotations.analysis: It is the fairest judgement anyone passes on Hester and it comes from the man ruining her lover, which is the novel's way of showing that accuracy is not the same as goodness. The conditional in the middle sentence also admits what the whole plot depends on: a marriage arranged between an old scholar and a young woman is where the evil actually started.

quotations.text: Ye that have wronged me are not sinful, save in a kind of typical illusion; neither am I fiend-like, who have snatched a fiend’s office from his hands. It is our fate. Let the black flower blossom as it may!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Refusing Hester's suggestion that he forgive, in the same conversation.
quotations.analysis: He describes his own vocation in the language of employment — he has taken over a post that belonged to a fiend — and then abolishes all responsibility by calling it fate. The image returns from the first page, where the prison was a black flower growing out of the soil of settlement; here revenge is a plant too, and the gardener denies having planted it.

quotations.text: Let men tremble to win the hand of woman, unless they win along with it the utmost passion of her heart!
quotations.context: The narrator, after Hester admits to herself that she hates her husband.
quotations.analysis: The warning is addressed to men in general and delivered in the imperative, which is as close as this narrator comes to taking a side. It also quietly relocates the novel's original sin from the forest to the wedding: the marriage was contracted without the wife's heart, and everything after it follows.

quotations.text: “Mother,” said little Pearl, “the sunshine does not love you. It runs away and hides itself, because it is afraid of something on your bosom. Now, see! There it is, playing, a good way off. Stand you here, and let me run and catch it. I am but a child. It will not flee from me; for I wear nothing on my bosom yet!”
quotations.speaker: Pearl
quotations.context: On the forest path, walking to the meeting with Dimmesdale.
quotations.analysis: A child's observation about where the light happens to fall becomes the most efficient statement of the book's premise, and the last word does the damage: 'yet' assumes she will wear one in time. Pearl has worked out the rule of her mother's world without being told it, and she expects to inherit it.

quotations.text: “Never, never!” whispered she. “What we did had a consecration of its own. We felt it so! We said so to each other! Hast thou forgotten it?”
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Answering Dimmesdale's question whether they are past hope.
quotations.analysis: She uses the vocabulary of the church to describe the act the church punished, and the tense is the point — 'had', not 'has', so she is defending the past rather than proposing a future. In 1850 this was the sentence reviewers objected to, and the novel neither retracts it nor lets her act on it.

quotations.text: There is one worse than even the polluted priest! That old man’s revenge has been blacker than my sin. He has violated, in cold blood, the sanctity of a human heart. Thou and I, Hester, never did so!
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: On learning that his physician and lodger is Hester's husband.
quotations.analysis: This is the moral scale the novel actually uses, and it is delivered by the man with the most to gain from it. 'In cold blood' is the operative phrase: the adultery is not excused, it is reclassified as a warm-blooded fault, while the sin the book cannot forgive is the deliberate, patient occupation of somebody else's inner life.

quotations.text: The scarlet letter was her passport into regions where other women dared not tread. Shame, Despair, Solitude! These had been her teachers⁠—stern and wild ones⁠—and they had made her strong, but taught her much amiss.
quotations.context: Explaining why Hester can contemplate flight and Dimmesdale cannot.
quotations.analysis: A punishment is redescribed as a travel document, which is the boldest reversal in the book — and then the final clause takes most of it back. 'Taught her much amiss' is the narrator declining to endorse his own heroine, and readers have been arguing ever since about whether that is Hawthorne's caution or Hawthorne's honesty.

quotations.text: The mystic token alighted on the hither verge of the stream. With a hand’s breadth farther flight it would have fallen into the water
quotations.context: Immediately after Hester unfastens the letter and throws it away among the leaves.
quotations.analysis: The narrator measures the miss in inches, which is the cruellest sentence in the chapter: the letter lands on this side of the brook, still retrievable, and so the whole flood of sunshine that follows is provisional. Pearl will make her pick it up within the hour, and the geography has already said she will have to.

quotations.text: “Is not this better,” murmured he, “than what we dreamed of in the forest?”
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: To Hester, as she supports him up the scaffold steps in front of the whole colony.
quotations.analysis: He is asking her to agree that public death is preferable to private escape, and she does not answer. The question is the last of his half-confessions: even at the end he needs the other person to pronounce the verdict, and Hawthorne withholds her reply so that the reader has to make it instead.

quotations.text: “Thou hast escaped me!” he repeated more than once. “Thou hast escaped me!”
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Kneeling beside the scaffold as Dimmesdale confesses.
quotations.analysis: The verb makes the physician a gaoler rather than an avenger, which is what he has been for seven years — the point was never to punish the man but to keep him. Within a year Chillingworth is dead, and the book says plainly that he had nothing else left to do, which is as close as it comes to defining what revenge costs the avenger.

quotations.text: Be true! Be true! Be true! Show freely to the world, if not your worst, yet some trait whereby the worst may be inferred!
quotations.context: The moral the narrator draws from Dimmesdale's case, and puts in quotation marks.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives and then an immediate discount: not the worst, only enough of a hint that the worst could be worked out. It is a morality of adequate disclosure rather than honesty, and the narrator has just spent a chapter reporting four incompatible accounts of the minister's chest — which suggests he knows how little inference can be trusted.

quotations.text: Here had been her sin; here, her sorrow; and here was yet to be her penitence.
quotations.context: Explaining why Hester comes back to the cottage on the edge of Boston years after she was free to leave.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses on the same adverb, and the tenses walk forward through them — had been, was, was yet to be — so the sentence turns a place into a chronology. The return is voluntary: the narrator notes that not the sternest magistrate would have required it, which makes the letter, at the very end, the only thing she has ever chosen to wear.

quotations.text: “On a field, sable, the letter A, gules.”
quotations.context: The last line of the book: the device carved on the slab that covers Hester and Dimmesdale.
quotations.analysis: The novel ends in heraldic French, a language of inherited honour, applied to a mark of shame — and the two words for the colours, black and red, are the only description of the grave we get. A punishment has become a coat of arms, which is either the final rehabilitation of the letter or proof that it will outlast everyone who tried to fix its meaning.

quotations.text: it seemed to me, then, that I experienced a sensation not altogether physical, yet almost so, of burning heat; and as if the letter were not of red cloth, but red-hot iron. I shuddered, and involuntarily let it fall upon the floor.
quotations.context: The narrator places the found scrap of embroidery on his own chest in the disused upper room of the Salem custom house.
quotations.analysis: The hedging is doing serious work — not altogether physical, yet almost so — and it establishes the rule for every marvel in the romance that follows. A man who will not commit himself to a sensation he has just had is the right narrator for a book whose final chapter cannot decide whether there was anything on Dimmesdale's chest at all.

quotations.text: the floor of our familiar room has become a neutral territory, somewhere between the real world and fairyland, where the Actual and the Imaginary may meet, and each imbue itself with the nature of the other
quotations.context: Describing moonlight in a room he cannot write in, near the end of the introductory sketch.
quotations.analysis: This is Hawthorne defining the romance as a form before he writes one, and the capital letters on Actual and Imaginary make it a diagram rather than a mood. It also explains why the novel keeps offering two explanations for everything: a neutral territory has to remain neutral, and a narrator who settled the meteor would have surrendered the ground.

themes.name: Freedom and what is mistaken for it

quotations.text: What cares these roarers for the name of king? To cabin: silence! trouble us not.
quotations.speaker: Boatswain
quotations.context: In the storm, ordering the king and his councillors below deck.
quotations.analysis: The play's first political statement is made by a working sailor to a monarch, and it is about the limits of titles. Within a hundred lines the audience learns that the storm was manufactured, so the one moment when rank genuinely counts for nothing turns out to have been arranged by a duke.

quotations.text: If by your art, my dearest father, you have Put the wild waters in this roar, allay them.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Her first words in the play, watching the wreck from the shore.
quotations.analysis: She knows at once that the storm is her father's doing, which tells the audience more about the household than any description could. The conditional 'if' is politeness rather than doubt, and the sentence ends in an imperative: the only person on the island who gives Prospero orders is fifteen.

quotations.text: What seest thou else In the dark backward and abysm of time?
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Testing how much Miranda remembers of her life before the island.
quotations.analysis: 'Backward' is used as a noun, which is not ordinary English then or now; the phrase makes the past a place you could fall into. He is checking the extent of her ignorance before deciding how much of it to repair, and the grandeur of the image conceals a piece of information management.

quotations.text: Hell is empty And all the devils are here.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Reporting how Ferdinand leapt from the burning ship.
quotations.analysis: Ariel is quoting a terrified boy, so the most famous line in the first act belongs to a character who never says it again. The joke underneath it is theological: the devils on this island are a spirit doing as it is told and a man who was once a duke.

quotations.text: Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains, Let me remember thee what thou hast promised, Which is not yet perform'd me.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: After performing the storm, before being sent out again.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is contractual rather than emotional: work has been done, a promise was made, the promise is outstanding. Prospero's answer is to recite the rescue from the cloven pine, which is the standard reply of an employer who would rather discuss gratitude than terms.

quotations.text: This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother, Which thou takest from me.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Answering Prospero's summons, before the quarrel about his attempt on Miranda.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the language of inheritance law — by his mother, therefore his — which is exactly how Prospero would argue for Milan. Nobody on stage disputes the facts; they change the subject to his conduct, and the play never returns to settle the question of title.

quotations.text: You taught me language; and my profit on't Is, I know how to curse. The red plague rid you For learning me your language!
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: The end of his argument with Prospero and Miranda about his education.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is delivered in fluent blank verse, which quietly contradicts it: he has plainly got more from the lessons than curses. 'Profit' is a merchant's word, and 'learning' here means teaching — the exchange is being audited, and the pupil finds it a bad bargain.

quotations.text: Full fathom five thy father lies; Of his bones are coral made; Those are pearls that were his eyes: Nothing of him that doth fade But doth suffer a sea-change Into something rich and strange.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Sung invisibly to Ferdinand, who believes his father has drowned.
quotations.analysis: The song tells a lie — Alonso is alive — in the gentlest possible form, turning a corpse into jewellery so that grief arrives already consoled. 'Sea-change' enters English here, and the whole lyric is an argument that loss can be transformation, which is the claim the last act will have to make good.

quotations.text: I' the commonwealth I would by contraries Execute all things; for no kind of traffic Would I admit; no name of magistrate;
quotations.speaker: Gonzalo
quotations.context: Imagining what he would do if he were king of the island.
quotations.analysis: The speech follows Florio's translation of Montaigne closely enough that the borrowing is visible, and Shakespeare stages it as a joke: Antonio and Sebastian point out that a commonwealth with no sovereignty has just been proposed by a man who began by saying he would be king of it. The mockery does not dispose of the idea, and the contradiction is the play's own.

quotations.text: And by that destiny to perform an act Whereof what's past is prologue, what to come In yours and my discharge.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Persuading Sebastian to murder the sleeping Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The line is now quoted as though it were wisdom about history; in the play it is a murderer's argument that the past is merely the warm-up and the killing is the real performance. 'Prologue' and 'act' are theatre words, put into the mouth of the man whose plot competes with Prospero's for control of the island's plot.

quotations.text: Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises, Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Reassuring Stephano and Trinculo, who have heard Ariel playing on an invisible pipe.
quotations.analysis: The drunkards are frightened and the so-called monster is the one who knows the island is safe. Shakespeare gives the play's most delicate verse to the character everyone on stage calls a beast, three minutes after he has explained how to drive a nail into a man's skull.

quotations.text: Remember First to possess his books; for without them He's but a sot, as I am, nor hath not One spirit to command
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Instructing Stephano on how the murder of Prospero must be done.
quotations.analysis: It is the most accurate piece of political analysis in the play, and it comes from the servant: the power is not in the man, it is in the library. Prospero lost Milan to his books and now holds the island by them, and the only character who understands the mechanism is the one with no share in it.

quotations.text: I am your wife, if you will marry me; If not, I'll die your maid: to be your fellow You may deny me; but I'll be your servant, Whether you will or no.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Proposing to Ferdinand at the log-pile, with Prospero watching unseen.
quotations.analysis: She proposes, sets out the alternatives and closes off the last of them: the grammar moves from a condition to a refusal to accept one. Having been given no information about her own life for twelve years, she takes the single decision available to her without consulting the man who arranged the meeting.

quotations.text: Our revels now are ended. These our actors, As I foretold you, were all spirits and Are melted into air, into thin air:
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Breaking off the wedding masque on remembering Caliban's conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: He is apologising to his son-in-law for a cancelled entertainment, and the apology grows into the play's largest statement about existence within eight lines. Note that he says 'as I foretold you': the consolation is that the disappearance was always in the design, which is true of a masque and is what he needs to believe about a dukedom.

quotations.text: We are such stuff As dreams are made on, and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The close of the same speech, before he admits his mind is troubled.
quotations.analysis: 'Made on' means made of, so human beings are built out of the same material as the vanished spirits — not that life resembles a dream but that it is cut from it. 'Rounded' can mean surrounded or finished off, and the line declines to choose, which is why it can be read as consolation or as the bleakest sentence in the play.

quotations.text: A devil, a born devil, on whose nature Nurture can never stick; on whom my pains, Humanely taken, all, all lost, quite lost;
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Alone, immediately after breaking off the masque.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is delivered by a man who has just spent years teaching the creature he says cannot be taught, and the repetitions — 'all, all lost, quite lost' — are those of someone arguing with himself. It is also the play's clearest statement of the position Miranda's existence contradicts.

quotations.text: Though with their high wrongs I am struck to the quick, Yet with my nobler reason 'gaitist my fury Do I take part: the rarer action is In virtue than in vengeance
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Immediately after Ariel says that he would pity the charmed courtiers if he were human.
quotations.analysis: The decision that ends twelve years of planning is made in four lines and prompted by a spirit. 'Rarer' means both more unusual and finer, which concedes that mercy is the less natural response; and the reason he gives is not that they deserve it but that it is the better piece of work.

quotations.text: But this rough magic I here abjure, and, when I have required Some heavenly music, which even now I do, To work mine end upon their senses that This airy charm is for, I'll break my staff, Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, And deeper than did ever plummet sound I'll drown my book.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Ending the long invocation of the elves of hills, brooks and groves.
quotations.analysis: He renounces the art in the middle of using it: the sentence that abjures magic also orders up the heavenly music that will disarm his enemies. The staff is broken, but the book is drowned deeper than any sounding line can reach, which is a peculiar precaution against an object he says he no longer wants.

quotations.text: How beauteous mankind is! O brave new world, That has such people in't!
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: On seeing the assembled courtiers for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The people she is admiring include the two men who set her adrift to die and a third who tried to murder his brother two days ago. Prospero's reply — three words, 'Tis new to thee — is the most economical piece of irony in Shakespeare, and it is the last thing he says to his daughter in the play.

quotations.text: Two of these fellows you Must know and own; this thing of darkness! Acknowledge mine.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Presenting the three conspirators to Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built to balance: two servants belong to the king, one belongs to me. 'Acknowledge' is doing a great deal of work — it can mean simply claiming a possession, or admitting a kinship, and the entire modern performance history of the play turns on which of those an actor decides to play.

quotations.text: As you from crimes would pardon'd be, Let your indulgence set me free.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The last two lines of the epilogue, spoken alone to the audience.
quotations.analysis: The man who has spent the play releasing or refusing to release other people ends by asking to be released himself, and the currency is applause. 'Indulgence' was also the word for a remission of punishment granted by the Church, so the audience is being asked to perform an absolution that the play's own theology could not quite supply.

themes.name: Innocence and what adults do with it
themes.canonicalName: Innocence and what adults do with it

themes.name: Class, service and who may speak
The frame, and how a story gets to us
themes.canonicalName: The frame, and how a story gets to us

quotations.text: The story had held us, round the fire, sufficiently breathless, but except the obvious remark that it was gruesome, as, on Christmas Eve in an old house, a strange tale should essentially be, I remember no comment uttered till somebody happened to say that it was the only case he had met in which such a visitation had fallen on a child.
quotations.context: The opening sentence, in the voice of the outermost narrator.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a hundred words long and arrives at its subject, a child, only at the very end, which is the book's method in miniature. Note also that the first thing we are told about the story we are about to read is that it is not the one being told.

quotations.text: If the child gives the effect another turn of the screw, what do you say to two children
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Offering his story in answer to one about a single haunted child.
quotations.analysis: The title is produced as a piece of after-dinner arithmetic: horror treated as a quantity that can be doubled. It also sets the terms on which everything that follows will be judged, because a story introduced as an intensification has to deliver one.

quotations.text: The story won’t tell
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Asked whether the story will say what the governess felt for her employer.
quotations.analysis: He is answering a question about motive, and the refusal is attributed to the manuscript rather than to himself. James thus establishes in the frame that the document is capable of not telling, and readers are warned before the first chapter that omission here is deliberate.

quotations.text: That she should never trouble him⁠—but never, never: neither appeal nor complain nor write about anything; only meet all questions herself, receive all moneys from his solicitor, take the whole thing over and let him alone.
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Describing the one condition attached to the post, which several other applicants had refused.
quotations.analysis: Every verb in the list is one the governess is forbidden to perform, and the accumulation makes the prohibition sound like a courtesy. The plot that follows is simply this sentence being kept: there is no adult she is permitted to consult, and she never breaks it.

quotations.text: He was incredibly beautiful, and Mrs. Grose had put her finger on it: everything but a sort of passion of tenderness for him was swept away by his presence.
quotations.context: Meeting Miles at the inn, the day after the school's letter arrives.
quotations.analysis: She decides the charge against him is impossible on the evidence of his face, and says so before she has asked him a single question. The verb swept away is worth keeping: her judgement of Miles is described from the start as something that happens to her rather than something she does.

quotations.text: Someone would appear there at the turn of a path and would stand before me and smile and approve.
quotations.context: Her habitual daydream during the free hour she takes in the grounds before dark.
quotations.analysis: This is the wish that the first apparition answers, and James puts it on the page a paragraph before Quint appears. The man she wants is the employer she has promised not to write to, so the figure on the tower arrives in a space her own longing has already prepared.

quotations.text: What arrested me on the spot⁠—and with a shock much greater than any vision had allowed for⁠—was the sense that my imagination had, in a flash, turned real.
quotations.context: The instant she catches sight of a man at the top of the tower.
quotations.analysis: The phrasing is doing two incompatible jobs at once: an imagination turning real is either a ghost or a symptom, and the sentence commits to neither. Almost every sighting in the book is worded with the same care.

quotations.text: So I saw him as I see the letters I form on this page
quotations.context: Insisting on the clarity of the first sighting.
quotations.analysis: She guarantees the apparition by comparing it with her own handwriting, which is the only thing the reader actually has. The comparison is meant as proof and works as a warning: everything we can see is the writing.

quotations.text: Quint was much too free.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Grose
quotations.context: Explaining why the valet was so often with the boy.
quotations.analysis: Four words, and they are the entire documented case against Peter Quint. Free is a word about rank as much as conduct, and the governess converts it into something much larger over the following chapters without ever being given more.

quotations.text: He was looking for little Miles.
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Concluding what Quint wanted when he looked in at the window.
quotations.analysis: She calls this a portentous clearness, and it is the first time she states a motive for an apparition rather than a fact about one. From here the sightings stop being events to be explained and become moves in a campaign she believes she has understood.

quotations.text: I was a screen⁠—I was to stand before them. The more I saw, the less they would.
quotations.context: Working out what her role in the household now is.
quotations.analysis: The image makes her heroism and her monopoly the same thing: standing in front of the children means standing between them and any other account of what is happening. The arithmetic in the second sentence is stated as a certainty and never once tested.

quotations.text: They’re not mine⁠—they’re not ours. They’re his and they’re hers!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Telling Mrs Grose what she has concluded about the children's good behaviour.
quotations.analysis: The children's goodness has been reinterpreted as evidence against them, which means no conduct of theirs can now count in their favour. Possession is stated grammatically, in four possessive pronouns, and the sentence takes them away from Mrs Grose as well.

quotations.text: For the love of all the evil that, in those dreadful days, the pair put into them. And to ply them with that evil still, to keep up the work of demons, is what brings the others back.
quotations.context: Answering Mrs Grose's question about why the dead should return.
quotations.analysis: Demons is the point at which her vocabulary leaves the household and enters theology, and the others is the phrase she now uses for people she has named. Once the case is put in these terms, any intervention at all can be justified as rescue.

quotations.text: You terrible, miserable woman!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Finding a figure seated at her own desk in the schoolroom.
quotations.analysis: She has just recorded the extraordinary chill of feeling that she was the intruder, and the outburst is what that feeling turns into. Both women have sat at this desk in charge of these children, which is why the insult lands so close to home.

quotations.text: She’s there, she’s there!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: At the lake, seizing Mrs Grose's arm and pointing across the water at Flora's back.
quotations.analysis: This is the one moment when the apparition is put to a public test, in daylight, with two other people present. Neither of them sees anything, and the governess's response is not doubt but a louder assertion, which tells the reader what kind of proof she is now capable of accepting.

quotations.text: Take me away, take me away⁠—oh, take me away from her!
quotations.speaker: Flora
quotations.context: Buried in Mrs Grose's skirts, moments after being asked where Miss Jessel is.
quotations.analysis: The child's only sustained utterance in the book is a plea to be removed from her protector, and the pronoun at the end is unambiguous. Whatever else is at Bly, this is the sentence the reader has to place any reading of the governess against.

quotations.text: I could only get on at all by taking “nature” into my confidence and my account, by treating my monstrous ordeal as a push in a direction unusual, of course, and unpleasant, but demanding, after all, for a fair front, only another turn of the screw of ordinary human virtue.
quotations.context: Steadying herself before dinner on the first day alone with Miles.
quotations.analysis: She reaches for the title herself, and applies it not to the horror but to her own endurance, as though virtue were a thing that could be tightened. The phrase quietly admits that what she is about to do to a ten-year-old is an extremity rather than a duty.

quotations.text: For there again, against the glass, as if to blight his confession and stay his answer, was the hideous author of our woe⁠—the white face of damnation.
quotations.context: The figure appears at the window just as Miles begins to answer her.
quotations.analysis: The apparition arrives precisely when a confession is about to be completed, which is convenient for the reading that it is a projection and equally convenient for the reading that it is a rival. James supplies no third possibility and no narrator to adjudicate.

quotations.text: Peter Quint⁠—you devil!
