quotations.speaker: Miles
quotations.context: His answer when asked whom he means by 'he'.
quotations.analysis: The line can be read two ways with no change of wording: the devil is either Quint at the window or the woman holding him. The governess takes it as her triumph and calls it his supreme surrender of the name, which is a phrase about an interrogation rather than a haunting.

quotations.text: We were alone with the quiet day, and his little heart, dispossessed, had stopped.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novella.
quotations.analysis: Dispossessed is the governess's word and it claims a success: the demon has been evicted. Placed between two commas in a sentence that ends with stopped, it also reads as the cause of death, and James lets both meanings stand without a syllable of comment from anyone outside her account.

themes.name: Country that does not know you are there
One man, one trail, no help
A divinity student in the bush

quotations.text: A considerable number of hunting parties were out that year without finding so much as a fresh trail
quotations.context: The story's first sentence, on the season's bad hunting.
quotations.analysis: It opens on an absence, and on men going home with stories. The whole tale is about what one party brought back instead of a trophy, and the first line quietly puts the reader among people who exaggerate.

quotations.text: This particular story, however, found no mention in his book on Collective Hallucination
quotations.context: Introducing Dr Cathcart.
quotations.analysis: The rationalist is given his credentials and his one omission in the same sentence, on page one. Everything he says for the next eight sections is read against a fact the reader has been handed in advance.

quotations.text: the vagaries of the human mind
quotations.context: What interests Cathcart besides moose.
quotations.analysis: His subject is named before the case arrives, so his diagnosis is available from the start. Blackwood is playing fair: the psychological reading is offered by the text itself and not smuggled in.

quotations.text: the “odor of lions” is the phrase with which he usually sums it all up
quotations.context: Simpson, years later, still trying to describe the smell.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is wrong for a Canadian forest and that is the point — the nearest thing he can reach for is an animal from another continent. Blackwood repeats the phrase three times across the story, so a smell becomes the creature's signature.

quotations.text: Wendigo’s somewhere around, doin’ a bit of swift traveling
quotations.context: Hank, explaining the smell to Simpson early in the trip.
quotations.analysis: The name arrives casually, in a guide's idiom, as a piece of weather. Introducing the creature as workaday local knowledge rather than as revelation is what makes the later sections unbearable.

quotations.text: Oh! oh! This fiery height! Oh, my feet of fire! My burning feet of fire
quotations.context: Défago's voice, heard once from far above the camp.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted sentence Blackwood wrote, and it does two things at once: it tells the reader that the man is airborne, and it puts the pain of it in his own mouth. The exclamations are the only moment the prose loses its composure.

quotations.text: They were big, round, ample, and with no pointed outline as of sharp hoofs
quotations.context: Simpson examining the second set of prints in the snow.
quotations.analysis: A description by elimination: not a moose, not a caribou, not a bear. The adjectives are so neutral that they do the work of a scream, because the one thing the reader wants — what made them — is exactly what the sentence refuses.

quotations.text: These mysterious writings left in the snow by the unknown creature that had lured a human being away from safety
quotations.context: Simpson following the trail alone.
quotations.analysis: Writings, not tracks. Once the snow is a text the story's method is clear: Simpson is reading, the reader is reading over his shoulder, and the horror is a problem of interpretation rather than of sight.

quotations.text: several Indians had “seen the Wendigo” along the shores of Fifty Island Water
quotations.context: Hank finally explaining why Défago did not want to hunt there.
quotations.analysis: The information that would have changed everything arrives after the event, from the man who talked his friend into going. Blackwood puts local knowledge in quotation marks, which is both the story's method and the fairest charge against it.

quotations.text: for the Wendigo is simply the Call of the Wild personified, which some natures hear to their own destruction
quotations.context: Cathcart, breaking a long silence by the fire.
quotations.analysis: The doctor's neatest formulation, offered to fill a pause rather than because he believes it settles anything. It is a good line, it is almost certainly wrong, and the story gives it to the cleverest man present.

quotations.text: It calls you by name right ’nough
quotations.context: Hank's answer to the doctor's theory.
quotations.analysis: Seven words that dispose of a paragraph of psychology. The bushman does not argue with the theory; he adds a detail it cannot accommodate, and the detail is the one Simpson heard outside the tent.

quotations.text: But Défago surely had already told you all these details of the Wendigo legend, my dear fellow
quotations.context: Cathcart pressing his nephew on where the images came from.
quotations.analysis: The suggestion theory, put politely and in the form of a question. It is the explanation most readers would reach for, and Blackwood has it stated by a professional so that nobody can accuse the story of ducking it.

quotations.text: It’s a moss-eater, is the Wendigo
quotations.context: Hank, after the figure at the fire has gone.
quotations.analysis: The detail is grotesque rather than grand, and that is why it convinces: nobody inventing a terror puts moss in it. It also sets up the last section, where a man in a bed pulls wads of it out of his cheeks.

quotations.text: a damned moss-eater
quotations.context: What the recovered Défago says about himself before he dies.
quotations.analysis: Hank's phrase comes back out of the mouth of the man it was used about, with an idiot smile attached. The repetition is the story's proof: the same words in two places nobody could have coordinated.

quotations.text: bereft of mind, memory and soul, had gone with it
quotations.context: The narrator's summary of what became of the guide.
quotations.analysis: Three nouns, in order of increasing loss, and then the flat verb. For a story that refuses to describe its monster, this is as close as it comes to saying what the monster does.

quotations.text: The terror of a whole race drove him
quotations.context: Punk covering three days' travel without stopping, after the thing walks into camp.
quotations.analysis: The cook is the only person in the story who acts on what he knows, and the narrator explains him in a single sentence that is also the story's most uncomfortable. Inherited knowledge is treated as evidence and its holder is given no voice at all.

quotations.text: Défago had “seen the Wendigo.”
quotations.context: The last sentence of the story.
quotations.analysis: It closes on the local phrase, in quotation marks, refusing to translate it into the doctor's language or the student's. After eight sections of competing explanations the story ends by using the one it started with and declining to gloss it.

themes.name: A place with no use for people
Older explanations, and why they fail
Marks in sand, marks in skin

techniques.name: Ground described until it becomes a character
A narrator arguing with his own story

quotations.text: across it may be seen in large straggling letters the word Sümpfe, meaning marshes
quotations.context: Describing how the region appears on a map.
quotations.analysis: The place is introduced as a blank with a label. Starting from cartography rather than from atmosphere is a deliberate move: the reader is told the marshes are a real, mapped, unremarkable feature before being told anything else about them.

quotations.text: they somehow give the impression that the entire plain is moving and alive
quotations.context: On the willow bushes in the wind.
quotations.analysis: An observation any camper might make, and the whole story is contained in it. Blackwood never has to claim the willows are alive; he describes what they look like and lets the impression do the work for the next twenty thousand words.

quotations.text: I can liken it to nothing so much as to the sound of an immense gong, suspended far up in the sky
quotations.context: The first sustained description of the sound over the marshes.
quotations.analysis: The simile is reached for and admitted to be inadequate — I can liken it to nothing so much as. Every sensory detail in the story arrives with that qualification, which is how a writer builds dread out of a noise he never identifies.

quotations.text: the way a sound in the fourth dimension is supposed to come
quotations.context: The Swede, explaining why the humming seems to be inside him.
quotations.analysis: Blackwood reaches for the popular science of 1907 rather than for folklore, and the borrowed phrase does something folklore could not: it makes the thing geometrical. The horror is no longer a spirit but a direction nobody can point in.

quotations.text: All my life, he said, I have been strangely, vividly conscious of another region—not far removed from our own world in one sense, yet wholly different in kind
quotations.context: The Swede beginning the explanation he has been holding back.
quotations.analysis: The man introduced as having no imagination turns out to have carried this since childhood. Putting the story's cosmology in the mouth of its most literal character is the reason the reader accepts it.

quotations.text: these beings who are now about us have absolutely nothing to do with mankind, and it is mere chance that their space happens just at this spot to touch our own
quotations.context: Rejecting both the spirit of the elements and the old gods as explanations.
quotations.analysis: The sentence that separates this story from every haunting before it. Gods and spirits can be appeased because they want something from us; these do not, and the island is not a chosen place but a coincidence. Lovecraft took his whole subject from this paragraph.

quotations.text: A sacrifice, a victim, might save us by distracting them until we could get away
quotations.context: Answering the question of what can be done.
quotations.analysis: He follows it with an image of wolves stopping to eat the sleigh dogs, and then with the observation that there is no other victim available. The reader works out what he is proposing about a page before the narrator does.

quotations.text: It’s the willows, of course. The willows mask the others, but the others are feeling about for us.
quotations.context: Explaining what the bushes have to do with it.
quotations.analysis: A word from stagecraft: the willows are scenery hiding what is behind them. Feeling about for us is worse than searching — it makes the hunt blind, patient and impersonal, which fits everything else he has just said.

quotations.text: If we let our minds betray our fear, we’re lost, lost utterly.
quotations.context: The rule for getting through the night.
quotations.analysis: Fear is reclassified as a leak. In most horror stories courage is a virtue; here it is a technical requirement, and the repetition of lost is the only place the Swede's own composure slips.

quotations.text: Do not refer to them by name. To name is to reveal
quotations.context: Cutting his companion off mid-question.
quotations.analysis: The oldest idea in folklore, stated as an operating procedure. It also explains the story's method: the things in the willows are never named by the narrator either, so the prohibition governs the prose as well as the characters.

quotations.text: Our thoughts make spirals in their world
quotations.context: Asked whether they must avoid even thinking of them.
quotations.analysis: Six words that give the other region a physics. Thought is visible there, and has a shape, which means the two men can be tracked by the one thing they cannot switch off.

quotations.text: For one thing—the steering paddle’s gone
quotations.context: The Swede's first report of the morning.
quotations.analysis: Delivered quietly, and it is the sentence that ends any possibility of leaving. Blackwood takes the escape route away with a piece of missing equipment rather than a locked door, and the practical consequence — the Danube in flood without a rudder — is spelled out at once.

quotations.text: There, you see an attempt to prepare a victim for the sacrifice
quotations.context: Looking at the tear in the bottom of the canoe.
quotations.analysis: He is reading the damage as intention, and the reader cannot prove him wrong. The correction that follows — two victims rather — is worse than the claim, because it means he has already counted himself in.

quotations.text: absolutely determined to find an explanation for everything
quotations.context: The narrator, calling after the Swede with a theory about the wind.
quotations.analysis: He tells us his own method in one phrase, and it is not scepticism but need. Every explanation he offers is available to the reader as well, which is what makes the story unsettling rather than silly: you are invited to use the same defence and to watch it fail.

quotations.text: Their mark!
quotations.context: The Swede, on his knees beside the body.
quotations.analysis: Two words, twice, and they are the only naming in the story — a possessive pronoun with nothing attached to it. The horror is that a pronoun turns out to be enough.

quotations.text: how the skin and flesh were indented with small hollows, beautifully formed, and exactly similar in shape and kind to the sand-funnels that we had found all over the island
quotations.context: As the current turns the corpse to face them.
quotations.analysis: The proof arrives as a match between two sets of measurements, and the word beautifully is the most frightening thing in the sentence. The narrator's habit of exact observation, which has been his defence all along, is what finally convicts him.

quotations.text: turning over and over on the waves like an otter
quotations.context: The last clause of the story, as the body is carried into midstream.
quotations.analysis: The comparison returns to an animal the two men had argued about seeing days earlier, and the evidence leaves with the current. Nothing is resolved, nobody can be told, and the story ends on a simile borrowed from its own unreliable middle.

themes.name: Home, and the claim it keeps
Halls, holes and the lower orders
The motorcar against the old road
Wonder, and the gift of forgetfulness
themes.canonicalName: Wonder, and the gift of forgetfulness

quotations.text: Spring was moving in the air above and in the earth below and around him, penetrating even his dark and lowly little house with its spirit of divine discontent and longing.
quotations.context: The third sentence of the novel, while Mole is still at work with the whitewash.
quotations.analysis: The season is the subject of the sentence and Mole merely the place it reaches, which sets up a book in which characters are acted on by weather, smells and calls rather than by decisions. ‘Divine discontent’ is a phrase from the pulpit and the essay, and it arrives four lines before the word ‘Bother!’ — the two registers of the whole novel established on its first page.

quotations.text: he suddenly flung down his brush on the floor, said, “Bother!” and “O blow!” and also “Hang spring-cleaning!”
quotations.context: The moment Mole abandons the house he has spent all morning cleaning.
quotations.analysis: Three exclamations in ascending order of daring, and all of them mild: the most rebellious thing Mole can say is a word about housework. The comedy is that a life is being abandoned in the vocabulary of a slightly cross uncle, and the novel keeps that gap between small language and large events all the way to the battle at the end.

quotations.text: there is nothing⁠—absolute nothing⁠—half so much worth doing as simply messing about in boats.
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Rowing Mole downstream on the morning they meet.
quotations.analysis: The famous sentence is usually quoted as ‘absolutely nothing’; Grahame wrote ‘absolute nothing’, and the slight wrongness is part of Rat’s dreamy delivery, which trails off a line later into ‘messing—about—in—boats; messing—’. The philosophy being proposed is the refusal of purpose, and the sentence enacts it by losing its own thread.

quotations.text: “There’s cold chicken inside it,” replied the Rat briefly: “coldtonguecoldhamcoldbeefpickledgherkinssaladfrenchrollscresssandwichespottedmeatgingerbeerlemonadesodawater⁠—”
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Mole asks what is in the fat wicker luncheon basket.
quotations.analysis: The spaces are removed so that the list is read at the speed Rat says it, and the effect is of a rope of food paying out without a breath. ‘Briefly’ is the joke: the narrator calls a sixteen-item catalogue brief because for Rat the river’s abundance genuinely goes without saying.

quotations.text: “Beyond the Wild Wood comes the Wide World,” said the Rat. “And that’s something that doesn’t matter, either to you or me. I’ve never been there, and I’m never going, nor you either, if you’ve got any sense at all. Don’t ever refer to it again, please.
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Mole has asked what lies past the smoke on the horizon.
quotations.analysis: Rat answers a question about geography with a prohibition, and the sentence that closes the subject — ‘Don’t ever refer to it again, please’ — is the politest thing in the book and the most frightened. Chapter 9 will collect on it: the animal who refuses to discuss the world outside turns out to be the one most easily carried off by a stranger’s description of it.

quotations.text: They found him in a sort of a trance, a happy smile on his face, his eyes still fixed on the dusty wake of their destroyer. At intervals he was still heard to murmur “Poop-poop!”
quotations.context: The motorcar has just put the caravan in the ditch and disappeared down the road.
quotations.analysis: The car is converted into a sound and the sound into a possession: Toad has learned the vocabulary of the new machine before he has touched one. ‘Their destroyer’ is the narrator’s word, not Toad’s, and it keeps the wrecked cart and the terrified horse in view while the joke is being made.

quotations.text: “Glorious, stirring sight!” murmured Toad, never offering to move. “The poetry of motion! The real way to travel! The only way to travel!
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: Still sitting in the road where the car has left him.
quotations.analysis: ‘Never offering to move’ is placed inside a speech about motion, and the contradiction is the whole of Toad: his enthusiasms are states of mind rather than activities. The three exclamations escalate from description to doctrine in nine words, which is how every one of his conversions is reported.

quotations.text: I want to show you the world! I’m going to make an animal of you, my boy!
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: Persuading Rat to come on the caravan expedition.
quotations.analysis: ‘Make a man of you’ is the phrase the sentence is built on, and swapping in ‘animal’ is the book’s only direct joke about its own premise. It also reveals Toad’s theory of friendship: other people are raw material for his current enthusiasm, which is why he never notices that Rat has said no.

quotations.text: he thought that he had never seen so far and so intimately into the insides of things as on that winter day when Nature was deep in her annual slumber and seemed to have kicked the clothes off.
quotations.context: Mole setting out alone for the Wild Wood on a cold, still afternoon.
quotations.analysis: A sentence of grave Latinate observation ends with somebody kicking off the bedclothes, and the joint is invisible. This is Grahame’s characteristic move — the natural world made domestic rather than sublime — and it explains why a wood can be terrifying in this book without ever becoming supernatural.

quotations.text: We river-bankers, we hardly ever come here by ourselves. If we have to come, we come in couples at least; then we’re generally all right.
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Comforting Mole in the hollow tree after finding him in the snow.
quotations.analysis: ‘We river-bankers’ is the first time the book names a class, and it does so to explain where that class does not go. The reassurance is really a set of rules of caste — passwords, signs, sayings which have power and effect — and the Wild Wood is dangerous chiefly because it belongs to animals who have not been introduced.

quotations.text: “People come⁠—they stay for a while, they flourish, they build⁠—and they go. It is their way. But we remain.
quotations.speaker: Badger
quotations.context: Explaining that his house is built in the cellars of a city that once stood where the Wild Wood now grows.
quotations.analysis: The dashes let the whole of human history pass in a single line, and the verbs get shorter as it goes. ‘But we remain’ is the book’s one moment of geological time, and it quietly reverses the usual arrangement in which animals are temporary and people permanent.

quotations.text: Home! That was what they meant, those caressing appeals, those soft touches wafted through the air, those invisible little hands pulling and tugging, all one way!
quotations.context: On the winter road, when Mole catches the smell of the house he abandoned in Chapter 1.
quotations.analysis: The summons is written entirely as touch — appeals, touches, hands — so that homesickness arrives as a physical assault rather than a thought. Grahame delays the explanation for a whole paragraph after the word ‘Home!’, which reproduces the order in which Mole himself works it out.

quotations.text: directly facing them was Mole’s little front door, with “Mole End” painted, in Gothic lettering, over the bellpull at the side.
quotations.context: Rat following Mole down the long passage to the house he left in the spring.
quotations.analysis: Gothic lettering over a bellpull is suburban gentility rendered in a hole in the ground, and it tells you what Mole was before he met the river. The detail also does the work that Mole’s tears could not: the house is shown to be modest, cared for and named by its owner, all in one line.

quotations.text: he looked in the very eyes of the Friend and Helper; saw the backward sweep of the curved horns, gleaming in the growing daylight; saw the stern, hooked nose between the kindly eyes that were looking down on them humorously
quotations.context: Dawn on the island, at the end of the night search for Otter’s son.
quotations.analysis: The god is never named in the chapter, only titled, and the description is built out of a repeated ‘saw’ that turns looking into a liturgy. Note the adverb ‘humorously’ dropped into the middle of an awe-struck sentence: even here Grahame will not let the sublime arrive without a domestic detail to steady it.

quotations.text: “Afraid?” murmured the Rat, his eyes shining with unutterable love. “Afraid! Of Him? O, never, never! And yet⁠—and yet⁠—O, Mole, I am afraid!”
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Mole has whispered the question while both animals are crouching on the island.
quotations.analysis: The speech contradicts itself twice in eighteen words and means all three positions at once, which is a precise account of religious awe rather than a muddle. It is also the only time in the novel that Rat, the competent one, is given a sentence he cannot finish.

quotations.text: For this is the last best gift that the kindly demigod is careful to bestow on those to whom he has revealed himself in their helping: the gift of forgetfulness.
quotations.context: A breeze crosses the island and both animals lose the memory of what they have seen.
quotations.analysis: The vision is removed from the characters by the narrator rather than by them, and the colon lands on ‘forgetfulness’ as though it were a reward. This is why the chapter leaves no trace on the plot: Grahame has decided that an experience of this kind cannot be carried back into a book about picnics and motorcars.

quotations.text: “And you, you will come too, young brother; for the days pass, and never return, and the South still waits for you. Take the adventure, heed the call, now ere the irrevocable moment passes!
quotations.speaker: The Sea Rat
quotations.context: The end of the Sea Rat’s account of his travels, told over a meal on the riverbank.
quotations.analysis: The rhythm is deliberately liturgical — three clauses, then a command, then a warning — and it works on Rat precisely because he has no counter-vocabulary for it. Set beside Chapter 7, the chapter is unnerving: the same trance-like language that produced a god here produces a travel brochure.

quotations.text: It is true that he sucked a good deal more than he scribbled; but it was joy to the Mole to know that the cure had at least begun.
quotations.context: After Mole has held Rat down through his fit and then put paper and pencil in front of him.
quotations.analysis: Wanting to go to sea is treated here as an illness with a treatment, and the treatment is writing poetry. It is the most revealing sentence in the book about its own making: the longing is real, the departure is impossible, and what is left is a man at a desk sucking a pencil.

quotations.text: “Ho, ho!” he said to himself, as he marched along with his chin in the air, “what a clever Toad I am! There is surely no animal equal to me for cleverness in the whole world!
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: Walking away from the barge, having just stolen the barge-woman’s horse.
quotations.analysis: Every escape in the second half has been arranged by somebody else — a girl with a dress, an engine-driver, a gipsy with cash — and Toad’s self-congratulation edits all of them out. The narrator lets him do it at length and then puts him in a river, which is the book’s standard method of argument.

quotations.text: The Toad⁠—came⁠—home!
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: The refrain of the song Toad composes in his bedroom before the banquet, and sings twice over.
quotations.analysis: The dashes are stage directions for a singer pausing to be admired, and the third person is the point: Toad writes about himself as a public event. The chapter is called ‘The Return of Ulysses’, and the returning hero’s first act is to compose his own ballad.

quotations.text: “Badger’s was the master mind; the Mole and the Water Rat bore the brunt of the fighting; I merely served in the ranks and did little or nothing.”
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: Disengaging himself from Otter’s embrace at the banquet.
quotations.analysis: It is an accurate account of the battle, delivered by the one animal who has never given an accurate account of anything. The modesty is a new performance rather than a new character, and the narrator confirms it two lines later by noting how closely Toad watches Badger and Rat for their reaction.

quotations.text: He was indeed an altered Toad!
quotations.context: After Toad has declined to make a speech or sing a song at his own banquet.
quotations.analysis: One sentence, one paragraph, and an exclamation mark that could be admiration or disbelief. The reform is real enough to be observed and light enough to be withdrawn, which is why the book can end with a promise about motorcars that nobody in the room believes.

themes.name: Time and what it cannot mend
The women who hold the line
themes.canonicalName: The women who hold the line

themes.name: Court and country, tragedy and comedy
themes.canonicalName: Court and country, tragedy and comedy

quotations.text: Too hot, too hot! To mingle friendship far is mingling bloods. I have tremor cordis on me: my heart dances; But not for joy; not joy.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: An aside, the instant Hermione succeeds in persuading Polixenes to stay.
quotations.analysis: This is the whole onset of the jealousy, and it occupies four lines. 'Tremor cordis' is a physician's term, so he reaches for a diagnosis before he reaches for an accusation; the repetitions — too hot, mingle and mingling, not for joy, not joy — are a man arguing with something already decided.

quotations.text: But to be paddling palms and pinching fingers, As now they are, and making practised smiles, As in a looking-glass, and then to sigh, as 'twere The mort o' the deer
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Continuing the aside, describing what he can see across the stage.
quotations.analysis: Everything he lists is something the audience can watch happening, which is what makes the scene so uncomfortable to stage: a director must decide how much of this is true. The hunting horn blown at a deer's death was a stock image for the sigh after sex, so the innuendo is doing the work that evidence cannot.

quotations.text: A sad tale's best for winter: I have one Of sprites and goblins.
quotations.speaker: Mamillius
quotations.context: Beginning a story for his mother and her ladies, moments before the guards arrive.
quotations.analysis: The play takes its title from a child's game and then interrupts it for good: he gets two lines further before his father walks in. Placing the phrase here rather than in the happy fifth act makes the title a description of Acts I to III, not of the ending.

quotations.text: There may be in the cup A spider steep'd, and one may drink, depart, And yet partake no venom, for his knowledge Is not infected: but if one present The abhorr'd ingredient to his eye, make known How he hath drunk, he cracks his gorge, his sides, With violent hefts.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: On being told that Polixenes and Camillo have fled by ship.
quotations.analysis: It is a brilliant image and it proves nothing whatever: the argument is that knowing makes the poison work, which conveniently means his own conviction is itself the evidence. He ends the sentence with 'I have drunk, and seen the spider', having drunk nothing and seen only two men leaving in a hurry.

quotations.text: You speak a language that I understand not: My life stands in the level of your dreams, Which I'll lay down.
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: At her trial, answering the charge of conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: 'In the level of' is an archery term — she is standing in the line of his aim — and the aim is a dream. Leontes answers by taking the word off her: 'Your actions are my dreams', which is the play's most compact statement of how a delusion defends itself.

quotations.text: if powers divine Behold our human actions, as they do, I doubt not then but innocence shall make False accusation blush and tyranny Tremble at patience.
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: The opening of her defence, before the court.
quotations.analysis: She makes blushing and trembling the business of the accusers rather than the accused, which reverses the whole physical vocabulary of a trial. The conditional at the start — 'if powers divine behold' — is the risk she is taking, and within a hundred lines Apollo answers it, and Leontes refuses the answer.

quotations.text: Hermione is chaste; Polixenes blameless; Camillo a true subject; Leontes a jealous tyrant; his innocent babe truly begotten; and the king shall live without an heir, if that which is lost be not found.
quotations.speaker: An Officer
quotations.context: Reading the sealed oracle aloud in the courtroom.
quotations.analysis: Five flat verdicts and then one condition, and the condition is the plot of the last two acts. Everything before the final clause is in the present tense and settled; the play's whole second half hangs on the word 'if', which is the only uncertainty Apollo allows.

quotations.text: Apollo's angry; and the heavens themselves Do strike at my injustice.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: One line after a servant reports that his son is dead.
quotations.analysis: The delusion that survived a god's direct testimony collapses the moment a child dies, which is a brutal piece of arithmetic on the play's part. Note that he still makes the news about himself — the heavens are striking at his injustice, not at Mamillius.

quotations.text: What studied torments, tyrant, hast for me? What wheels? racks? fires? what flaying? boiling? In leads or oils? what old or newer torture Must I receive, whose every word deserves To taste of thy most worst?
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Returning to the court with the news that the queen is dead.
quotations.analysis: She lists the punishments before she delivers the news, which is a way of making it impossible to silence her: every torment has already been named and accepted. The word 'tyrant' is placed inside the first question, where a king's title would go.

quotations.text: The day frowns more and more: thou'rt like to have A lullaby too rough: I never saw The heavens so dim by day. A savage clamour! Well may I get aboard! This is the chase: I am gone for ever.
quotations.speaker: Antigonus
quotations.context: On the Bohemian coast, having just laid the baby down; the next line of the text is the stage direction.
quotations.analysis: 'A lullaby too rough' is addressed to an infant he is abandoning in a storm, and it is the gentlest thing said in three acts. The last four words are both a cry of terror and a piece of plain information, and the stage direction that follows them is the most famous in the language.

quotations.text: Heavy matters! heavy matters! but look thee here, boy. Now bless thyself: thou mettest with things dying, I with things newborn.
quotations.speaker: Shepherd
quotations.context: To his son, who has just described the shipwreck and the bear, while holding the baby he has found.
quotations.analysis: The play's structure is stated out loud by a man who has no idea he is describing it: one half of the stage has a wreck on it and the other half a child. It is also the only line in Shakespeare that could serve as a definition of tragicomedy, and it is given to a shepherd in prose.

quotations.text: My father named me Autolycus; who being, as I am, littered under Mercury, was likewise a snapper-up of unconsidered trifles.
quotations.speaker: Autolycus
quotations.context: Introducing himself to the audience on the road to the sheep-shearing.
quotations.analysis: Mercury was the god of thieves and of eloquence, and Autolycus in Homer was his son; the name is a joke for anyone who has it and a good name for a pedlar for anyone who has not. 'Littered' is a word for animals, and he applies it to himself without complaint.

quotations.text: You see, sweet maid, we marry A gentler scion to the wildest stock, And make conceive a bark of baser kind By bud of nobler race: this is an art Which does mend nature, change it rather, but The art itself is nature.
quotations.speaker: Polixenes
quotations.context: Disguised at the sheep-shearing, arguing with Perdita about grafted flowers.
quotations.analysis: The argument is that human art is one of nature's own methods, and it is unanswerable — Perdita simply says 'So it is' and then refuses to do it anyway. The joke is savage: within forty lines the same speaker will forbid his noble son to marry a baser stock and threaten the girl with death.

quotations.text: O Proserpina, For the flowers now, that frighted thou let'st fall From Dis's waggon! daffodils, That come before the swallow dares, and take The winds of March with beauty
quotations.speaker: Perdita
quotations.context: Wishing she had spring flowers to give the young women at the feast.
quotations.analysis: Every flower in the speech is one she does not have, so the loveliest passage in the play is a list of absences. Proserpina was also a daughter stolen from her mother and returned for half the year — Perdita invokes her own story without knowing it, which is the closest the play comes to telling her who she is.

quotations.text: when you do dance, I wish you A wave o' the sea, that you might ever do Nothing but that; move still, still so, And own no other function
quotations.speaker: Florizel
quotations.context: Praising Perdita as she moves among the guests.
quotations.analysis: 'Move still, still so' means keep moving and keep still at once, which is what a wave does and what a statue cannot — the play will collect on that image in the last scene. The wish is also faintly alarming: he would like her to do nothing else ever, and the speech turns her actions into a series of held poses.

quotations.text: No more such wives; therefore, no wife: one worse, And better used, would make her sainted spirit Again possess her corpse, and on this stage, Where we're offenders now, appear soul-vex'd, And begin, 'Why to me?'
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Refusing, in front of Paulina, the court's suggestion that he remarry.
quotations.analysis: He imagines his dead wife returning to reproach him, in a theatre, on a stage — and two scenes later she does return, without reproaching him at all. 'Where we're offenders now' turns the court into a playhouse and the living into the guilty party, which is exactly the arrangement of the final scene.

quotations.text: Chide me, dear stone, that I may say indeed Thou art Hermione; or rather, thou art she In thy not chiding, for she was as tender As infancy and grace.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: The first words spoken after Paulina draws the curtain.
quotations.analysis: He asks the statue to scold him and then decides its silence is more like her, which lets him have the rebuke and the forgiveness at once. Everything he says in this scene is addressed to an object, and the audience has been given no more information than he has.

quotations.text: So much the more our carver's excellence; Which lets go by some sixteen years and makes her As she lived now.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Explaining why the statue looks older than the queen Leontes remembers.
quotations.analysis: The wrinkles are the play's proof that the reconciliation is not a reversal: the sixteen years are carved into the object everyone is looking at. It is also a very good lie, and the audience is invited to notice that a sculptor who aged his subject would be doing something no sculptor does.

quotations.text: It is required You do awake your faith. Then all stand still; On: those that think it is unlawful business I am about, let them depart.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Before calling for music and telling the statue to descend.
quotations.analysis: The instruction is given to the people on stage and, unavoidably, to the people watching them: a theatre audience is always being asked to do this, and here the request is made out loud. 'Required' is the hardest word in the sentence — not invited, not encouraged, and with an exit offered to anyone who will not.

quotations.text: O, she's warm! If this be magic, let it be an art Lawful as eating.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Taking Hermione's hand as she steps down from the pedestal.
quotations.analysis: Three words settle a question the whole scene has hung on, and they are about temperature rather than identity. The comparison he reaches for is eating — the most ordinary bodily fact available — which quietly refuses the supernatural reading while leaving it standing.

quotations.text: That she is living, Were it but told you, should be hooted at Like an old tale: but it appears she lives, Though yet she speak not.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: As Hermione embraces Leontes and the others ask where she has been.
quotations.analysis: The play calls its own plot ridiculous for the third time, and the defence is that this one is being seen rather than reported. It is also an exact description of what the audience is doing: accepting on stage what it would hoot at in a story, which is the difference the last act is built to demonstrate.

quotations.text: You gods, look down And from your sacred vials pour your graces Upon my daughter's head!
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: Her first words after sixteen years, spoken once Paulina has turned her towards Perdita.
quotations.analysis: She speaks to the gods, then to her daughter, and never once to her husband — the reunion the play has been building towards turns out to be with the child. Her only explanation is that she preserved herself because the oracle gave hope the baby was alive, which makes the marriage a piece of unfinished business the play leaves alone.

themes.name: What women are allowed to do

quotations.text: This is the story of what a woman’s patience can endure, and what a Man’s resolution can achieve.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: The first sentence of the preamble.
quotations.analysis: Two virtues, two sexes, and the capital letters fall on Man and not on woman. The book then reverses the assignment without ever amending the sentence: it is Marian who acts and Walter who spends years waiting for a date to be proved, and the formula stands at the front of the file like an uncorrected heading.

quotations.text: the story here presented will be told by more than one pen, as the story of an offence against the laws is told in Court by more than one witness⁠—with the same object, in both cases, to present the truth always in its most direct and most intelligible aspect; and to trace the course of one complete series of events, by making the persons who have been most closely connected with them, at each successive stage, relate their own experience, word for word.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: The preamble, setting out how the narrative to follow has been assembled.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is to a court, and it promises the reader a jury’s job. What the sentence does not mention is the person who chose the witnesses and set them in order; ‘word for word’ guarantees the accuracy of each statement and says nothing about the selection.

quotations.text: There, in the middle of the broad bright high road⁠—there, as if it had that moment sprung out of the earth or dropped from the heaven⁠—stood the figure of a solitary woman, dressed from head to foot in white garments, her face bent in grave inquiry on mine, her hand pointing to the dark cloud over London, as I faced her.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: On the Finchley Road at the end of a July night, the moment a hand touches his shoulder.
quotations.analysis: The repeated ‘there’ holds her in place for a whole clause before the sentence admits what she is, and the two alternatives offered — out of the earth or down from the heaven — are both supernatural. She is described entirely by her clothes and her gesture; the novel will spend six hundred pages establishing that she also has a name.

quotations.text: Done! She has escaped from my asylum. Don’t forget; a woman in white. Drive on.
quotations.speaker: The proprietor of the asylum
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Called down from a chaise to a policeman on the Finchley Road, minutes after Walter has put the woman into a cab.
quotations.analysis: Four sentences, and the only description offered is a colour. The policeman asks what she has done and is answered with a word that means the opposite of an offence, which is the novel’s first demonstration that a certificate does the work a charge would otherwise have to do.

quotations.text: She left the window⁠—and I said to myself, The lady is dark. She moved forward a few steps⁠—and I said to myself, The lady is young.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter VI
quotations.context: Meeting Marian Halcombe for the first time, before she turns round.
quotations.analysis: Two clauses of movement, each answered by a verdict, as though a face were arriving in instalments. The syntax is a piece of physiognomy in action, and the paragraph that follows — swarthy, masculine, almost a moustache — shows the method failing on the one person in the book most worth reading correctly.

quotations.text: I am nothing but a bundle of nerves dressed up to look like a man.
quotations.speaker: Frederick Fairlie
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Frederick Fairlie’s narrative
quotations.context: Asked by his servant how he is, on the morning Fosco’s messenger arrives.
quotations.analysis: He describes himself as an assemblage rather than a person, and does it with obvious pleasure. Collins gives him his own narrative precisely so that this self-portrait can be volunteered rather than reported: the man whose refusal to be troubled costs his niece her name is allowed to explain himself, and does.

quotations.text: Seriously and sorrowfully I repeat here the parting words that I spoke at Limmeridge House:⁠—No daughter of mine should have been married to any man alive under such a settlement as I was compelled to make for Laura Fairlie.
quotations.speaker: Vincent Gilmore
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Vincent Gilmore’s narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Closing his narrative, having failed to persuade Mr Fairlie to protect Laura’s twenty thousand pounds.
quotations.analysis: He puts his objection on the record, draws the document anyway, and then quotes himself in the past tense at the end of his own statement — which is what a professional man does when he expects to be asked about it later. It is the most accurate picture of legal helplessness in the novel: he sees the clause, names it, and signs.

quotations.text: No man under heaven deserves these sacrifices from us women. Men! They are the enemies of our innocence and our peace⁠—they drag us away from our parents’ love and our sisters’ friendship⁠—they take us body and soul to themselves, and fasten our helpless lives to theirs as they chain up a dog to his kennel.
quotations.speaker: Marian Halcombe
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s diary, Chapter II
quotations.context: To Laura, who has just said that she means to go through with the marriage for her father’s sake.
quotations.analysis: The simile is domestic and brutal: a wife is a dog chained to a kennel, and the verbs — drag, take, fasten — are all transitive with women as their object. It is the most explicit political statement in the novel, and Collins gives it to a woman writing privately in a diary she does not expect anyone to read.

quotations.text: The fool’s crime is the crime that is found out, and the wise man’s crime is the crime that is not found out.
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: At Blackwater Park, arguing after dinner that crimes cause their own detection is a piece of claptrap.
quotations.analysis: The antithesis is perfectly balanced and completely circular: the only evidence of a wise crime is that you have never heard of it. Fosco is describing the plan he is about to execute, out loud, to the woman who will try to stop him, and the pleasure of saying it is what he cannot forgo.

quotations.text: English Society, Miss Halcombe, is as often the accomplice as it is the enemy of crime.
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: Continuing the same argument, having just accused John Bull of finding other people’s faults faster than his own.
quotations.analysis: The foreigner is given the outsider’s privilege of describing the host country’s machinery, and the sentence turns out to be a plot summary: the conspiracy works because respectable people accept a certificate. Collins puts his own thesis in the villain’s mouth, which is a cheap trick that works.

quotations.text: Women can resist a man’s love, a man’s fame, a man’s personal appearance, and a man’s money, but they cannot resist a man’s tongue when he knows how to talk to them.
quotations.speaker: Marian Halcombe
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, Chapter V
quotations.context: In her diary, after an evening in which Fosco has deliberately charmed the table.
quotations.analysis: She writes the sentence as a general law and includes herself in it, which is the honesty that makes her diary worth reading. The list ascends from love to fame to appearance to money and then breaks the pattern: the irresistible thing is not a possession at all but a technique.

quotations.text: The illness of our excellent Miss Halcombe has afforded me the opportunity of enjoying an unexpected intellectual pleasure.
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, postscript
quotations.context: Written at the foot of Marian’s diary, which breaks off mid-sentence when the fever takes her.
quotations.analysis: The violation is done entirely in the register of a compliment, and the reader discovers it at the same moment as the page is turned. It is also a formal outrage: the novel’s most private document is annotated by its antagonist, which tells you exactly how safe any of these testimonies are.

quotations.text: Sacred to the Memory of Laura, Lady Glyde, wife of Sir Percival Glyde, Bart., of Blackwater Park, Hampshire, and daughter of the late Philip Fairlie, Esq., of Limmeridge House, in this parish. Born March 27th, 1829; married December 22nd, 1849; died July 25th, 1850.
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, the narrative of the tombstone
quotations.context: The inscription on the Fairlie monument in Limmeridge churchyard, given as a narrative in its own right.
quotations.analysis: Collins lets a piece of carved stone take a turn as narrator, and it is the only witness in the book that cannot be cross-examined. Three dates — born, married, died — are all it offers, and the last of them is the lie on which everything depends and, eventually, the thing that breaks the case open.

quotations.text: Dead to her uncle, who had renounced her; dead to the servants of the house, who had failed to recognise her; dead to the persons in authority, who had transmitted her fortune to her husband and her aunt; dead to my mother and my sister, who believed me to be the dupe of an adventuress and the victim of a fraud; socially, morally, legally⁠—dead.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: Opening the Third Epoch, standing in a world where the woman beside him is officially buried.
quotations.analysis: Four clauses, each beginning with the same word and each naming a different authority — a guardian, the servants, the officials who transferred her fortune, and his own family. The three adverbs at the close rank the kinds of death from softest to hardest, and it is the legal one the rest of the novel has to attack.

quotations.text: she must have started on the twenty-sixth, and must have come to London one day after the date of her own death on the doctor’s certificate. If we can prove that date, we prove our case against Sir Percival and the Count.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Working out with Marian what evidence would actually overturn the conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: The rescue turns on a single day. Nobody needs to recognise Laura, and nobody’s word about her is worth anything; what is required is a document showing she travelled after she died. Collins makes the emotional climax of his novel an argument about a calendar, which is the most Victorian thing about it.

quotations.text: I was struck by the insecurity of the place in which the register was kept. The door of the press was warped and cracked with age, and the lock was of the smallest and commonest kind. I could have forced it easily with the walking-stick I carried in my hand.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter IX
quotations.context: In the vestry at Old Welmingham, as the clerk produces the marriage register.
quotations.analysis: A baronetcy is kept in a warped cupboard behind a lock that a man could break with a walking-stick, and Collins gives us the exact means to hand. The register is the same kind of object as the gravestone and the death certificate: a piece of writing that makes a person, kept somewhere nobody guards.

quotations.text: Chemistry especially has always had irresistible attractions for me from the enormous, the illimitable power which the knowledge of it confers. Chemists⁠—I assert it emphatically⁠—might sway, if they pleased, the destinies of humanity.
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Count Fosco’s narrative
quotations.context: Opening his written confession, composed at Walter’s dictation and at his own leisure.
quotations.analysis: Asked for a confession, he delivers a prospectus. The dash before ‘I assert it emphatically’ is the sound of a man who cannot let a sentence go without applauding it, and this vanity is exactly what Walter has counted on: the document he needs is produced because Fosco cannot bear to write a dull one.

quotations.text: That conception involved nothing less than the complete transformation of two separate identities. Lady Glyde and Anne Catherick were to change names, places, and destinies, the one with the other⁠—the prodigious consequences contemplated by the change being the gain of thirty thousand pounds, and the eternal preservation of Sir Percival
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Count Fosco’s narrative
quotations.context: Describing the moment he first understood what could be done with the resemblance.
quotations.analysis: He calls it a conception, as though it were a piece of composition, and prices it in the same clause: thirty thousand pounds and a secret kept. The three nouns he exchanges — names, places, destinies — go from the trivial to the absolute without a change of tone, which is the whole character in one list.

quotations.text: I passed on my way the terrible dead-house of Paris⁠—the Morgue. A great crowd clamoured and heaved round the door. There was evidently something inside which excited the popular curiosity, and fed the popular appetite for horror.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s conclusion, Chapter II
quotations.context: In Paris, walking towards Notre Dame, some days after Fosco has left England.
quotations.analysis: The Count’s death is delivered as a piece of tourism: a crowd, a queue and an overheard conversation. Collins refuses his villain a scene, and the body is identified by a mark cut into the arm — another inscription, in the one place where a name could not be forged.

quotations.text: The long, happy labour of many months is over. Marian was the good angel of our lives⁠—let Marian end our Story.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s conclusion, Chapter III
quotations.context: The last sentences of the novel, after Marian has held up the child who is the heir of Limmeridge.
quotations.analysis: The labour of months is the writing, not the living, so the book ends by announcing that a file has been closed. He calls Marian the good angel and hands her the last word in a sentence he himself is writing, which is generosity and editorial control performing the same gesture.

books.title: The Yellow Wall-Paper and The Giant Wistaria
books.author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

themes.name: A journal that cannot be checked
Hiding things in a house without privacy

techniques.name: A narrator who cannot be checked

quotations.text: It is very seldom that mere ordinary people like John and myself secure ancestral halls for the summer.
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the journal.
quotations.analysis: A social joke, told by someone pleased with her luck. It establishes the voice the story will use throughout — light, self-deprecating, interested in appearances — and the gothic set-up is delivered as a piece of good fortune rather than a warning.

quotations.text: John is a physician, and perhaps—(I would not say it to a living soul, of course, but this is dead paper and a great relief to my mind)—perhaps that is one reason I do not get well faster.
quotations.context: A few lines into the journal, explaining why she is not improving.
quotations.analysis: The most important sentence in the story is delivered in a parenthesis, in a whisper, and immediately hedged with perhaps. She knows the cause, cannot say it aloud, and says it to paper — which is why the paper has to be dead before it is safe.

quotations.text: You see he does not believe I am sick!
quotations.context: After quoting the diagnosis her husband and brother agree on.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation mark is doing the work of an argument she is not allowed to make. Being disbelieved, not being ill, is the condition the story is about, and it is stated plainly on the first page and never taken seriously by anyone in the house.

quotations.text: If a physician of high standing, and one’s own husband, assures friends and relatives that there is really nothing the matter with one but temporary nervous depression—a slight hysterical tendency—what is one to do?
quotations.context: Explaining why her own account of herself carries no weight.
quotations.analysis: The shift to the impersonal 'one' is the sound of someone arguing in a register that might be listened to. The two roles — physician and husband — are stacked deliberately, because each is used to settle what the other cannot.

quotations.text: So I take phosphates or phosphites—whichever it is—and tonics, and journeys, and air, and exercise, and am absolutely forbidden to “work” until I am well again.
quotations.context: Listing the treatment.
quotations.analysis: The list runs on as though the items were equivalent, then arrives at the one that matters, with 'work' in quotation marks — his word, handed back. Her uncertainty about the medicine is comic; her certainty about the ban is not.

quotations.text: Personally, I believe that congenial work, with excitement and change, would do me good.
quotations.context: Her own view of what would help, offered once.
quotations.analysis: 'Personally' is the word of someone whose opinion is a matter of personality rather than evidence. Her prescription is the opposite of his in every particular, and the story's ending is the demonstration that she was right.

quotations.text: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage.
quotations.context: After admitting she believes the house is haunted.
quotations.analysis: Eleven words that describe a marriage and excuse it in the same breath. 'Of course' and 'one expects' are the story's method: the narrator supplies the defence before the reader can object, and the defence is the evidence.

quotations.text: He is very careful and loving, and hardly lets me stir without special direction.
quotations.context: Describing the daily regime.
quotations.analysis: Care and control are stated as one thing, because in this house they are. The sentence can be read as gratitude or as a description of custody, and the story never chooses — it simply keeps producing examples.

quotations.text: I don’t like our room a bit. I wanted one downstairs that opened on the piazza and had roses all over the window, and such pretty old-fashioned chintz hangings! but John would not hear of it.
quotations.context: On being given the top-floor nursery instead.
quotations.analysis: The only choice she asks to make in the whole story, and it is refused with a reason about windows and beds. Everything that follows happens because she is in this room rather than that one.

quotations.text: The color is repellant, almost revolting; a smouldering, unclean yellow, strangely faded by the slow-turning sunlight.
quotations.context: Her first sustained description of the wallpaper.
quotations.analysis: This is expert writing, and the story knows it: rhythm, three adjectives that refuse to settle, and a last clause that turns light itself into a stain. The woman who is not fit to hold a pen produces the best prose in the house.

quotations.text: It is dull enough to confuse the eye in following, pronounced enough to constantly irritate and provoke study
quotations.context: On the pattern itself.
quotations.analysis: A description of the paper and of her situation in one clause: dull enough to be maddening, marked enough to demand attention. 'Provoke study' is the giveaway — she has been forbidden intellectual work and has found some anyway.

quotations.text: There is a recurrent spot where the pattern lolls like a broken neck and two bulbous eyes stare at you upside-down.
quotations.context: Cataloguing the pattern's features.
quotations.analysis: The first body in the paper is a corpse, seen upside down and looking back. The observation is offered in the same matter-of-fact tone as the colour, which is how the story moves from decoration to horror without changing register.

quotations.text: But John says if I feel so I shall neglect proper self-control; so I take pains to control myself—before him, at least, and that makes me very tired.
quotations.context: After admitting she cries at nothing.
quotations.analysis: The performance of wellness is itself exhausting, and she is the only person who can see the cost. 'Before him, at least' quietly announces that there are now two versions of her: the one in the room and the one in the journal.

quotations.text: at night in any kind of light, in twilight, candlelight, lamplight, and worst of all by moonlight, it becomes bars!
quotations.context: On what the sub-pattern looks like after dark.
quotations.analysis: Four kinds of light, listed in the order they fall on the wall, and then the word the room has been asking for. The bars are real — the windows have them — so the paper is not inventing the cage, only repeating it.

quotations.text: There are things in that paper that nobody knows but me, or ever will.
quotations.context: As her interest in the paper becomes private property.
quotations.analysis: Knowledge is the one thing the household has not taken, so she hoards it. The sentence is triumphant and isolating at once, and from here on the story's secrecy is her doing rather than theirs.

quotations.text: The front pattern does move—and no wonder! The woman behind shakes it!
quotations.context: The moment the pattern is explained.
quotations.analysis: A design becomes an event: something is behind it and is trying to get out. 'No wonder' is the tone of a problem solved, which is why the sentence is frightening — she is not raving, she is concluding.

quotations.text: Sometimes I think there are a great many women behind, and sometimes only one, and she crawls around fast, and her crawling shakes it all over.
quotations.context: Watching the paper by daylight.
quotations.analysis: The figure multiplies and the story widens: one woman behind a pattern is a haunting, a great many is a social fact. The sentence is the closest the story comes to naming who else is in rooms like this.

quotations.text: I always lock the door when I creep by daylight.
quotations.context: Immediately after describing the woman creeping outside.
quotations.analysis: The two figures merge here, in a subordinate clause, without announcement. The narrator has begun doing what she has been describing, and the journal records it as a sensible precaution.

quotations.text: I am getting angry enough to do something desperate.
quotations.context: After John refuses again to leave the house early.
quotations.analysis: The word 'angry' arrives late and is followed by a plan rather than a complaint. The story's last movement begins here: everything after this sentence is action.

quotations.text: Life is very much more exciting now than it used to be.
quotations.context: On the change in her days since the paper began to move.
quotations.analysis: She was told that excitement and change would harm her and has found both by herself, in a locked room, with a wall. The sentence is cheerful, and the cheerfulness is the most alarming thing in the story.

quotations.text: “I’ve got out at last,” said I, “in spite of you and Jane! And I’ve pulled off most of the paper, so you can’t put me back!”
quotations.context: Spoken to John through the door he has just opened.
quotations.analysis: The only speech she makes in the story, and the first sentence in it without a hedge. 'Jane' appears nowhere else: readers have taken it for her own name, for Jennie misprinted, and for the self she has just left behind. The victory and the disaster are the same act.

quotations.text: Now why should that man have fainted? But he did, and right across my path by the wall, so that I had to creep over him every time!
quotations.context: The last lines of the story.
quotations.analysis: The doctor is unconscious on the floor and the patient is still moving. Calling him 'that man' completes the reversal, and the mild puzzlement of the question is what makes the ending land: she has got past him, and does not much wonder why.

themes.name: Work, idleness and who is doing it
Clerks, swells and a crowded river

quotations.text: I plodded conscientiously through the twenty-six letters, and the only malady I could conclude I had not got was housemaid’s knee.
quotations.context: J. has gone to the British Museum to read up on hay fever and has worked through the whole medical dictionary.
quotations.analysis: The joke is built like a proof. J. goes through the alphabet as a conscientious student would, so the absurd conclusion arrives by method, and the one exception becomes the punchline. The next paragraph improves it: he feels slighted not to have housemaid’s knee, then grows less grasping and decides to do without. Hypochondria becomes acquisitiveness, a man collecting diseases. And the missing one is a servant’s complaint, the ailment of kneeling to scrub, which a man who never does that could hardly catch.

quotations.text: 1 ten-mile walk every morning. 1 bed at 11 sharp every night. And don’t stuff up your head with things you don’t understand.
quotations.speaker: J.’s doctor
quotations.context: The end of the prescription, which a chemist has just handed back unmade; it begins with a pound of beefsteak and a pint of bitter beer every six hours.
quotations.analysis: The prescription is funny because of its form. It is set out like a dosage, with quantities and hours, so the chemist reasonably cannot make it up; the medicine is steak, beer, exercise and bed. Then the last line drops the formula and speaks plainly, and it is aimed at the reading-room where J. caught his diseases. The doctor is the book’s first straight man, and he diagnoses the whole party: nothing is wrong that fresh air and fewer books will not cure.

quotations.text: From my earliest infancy I have been a martyr to it. As a boy, the disease hardly ever left me for a day. They did not know, then, that it was my liver. Medical science was in a far less advanced state than now, and they used to put it down to laziness.
quotations.context: The chief symptom in the liver-pill circular is a general disinclination to work of any kind.
quotations.analysis: The deadpan keeps the vocabulary of medicine while the facts describe idleness. Martyr, disease, medical science are solemn words; the symptom is not wanting to work, and the old treatment was a clump on the head, which J. admits often worked. The reader supplies the diagnosis the narrator refuses to make. It is also the book’s first statement of its real subject: three young men who call their boredom overwork and prescribe themselves a holiday.

quotations.text: There’s nothing for me to do. Scenery is not in my line, and I don’t smoke. If I see a rat, you won’t stop; and if I go to sleep, you get fooling about with the boat, and slop me overboard. If you ask me, I call the whole thing bally foolishness.
quotations.speaker: Montmorency
quotations.context: George has proposed the river and the other two have agreed; the dog lodges an objection.
quotations.analysis: Montmorency is the only member of the party allowed to speak without irony, and his objections are exact: a rowing holiday offers a dog no rats, no smoking and no scenery he cares for. The comedy is in the register. J. gives him the grumble of a man dragged on somebody else’s holiday, and through him the book says what none of the men will admit about their plan. The motion is then carried three to one, like a committee vote, and the minority report is the accurate one.

quotations.text: we fall asleep beneath the great, still stars, and dream that the world is young again … Harris said: “How about when it rained?”
quotations.context: J. and George favour camping out, and J. describes a night by the river in a single long, lyrical sentence.
quotations.analysis: The sentence runs for most of a page, through the moon’s sister’s kiss and the wiles of painted civilisation, and Harris answers it in five words. The fall works only because J. writes the passage in earnest enough to carry the reader a little way. It also sets out the friendship: J. supplies the feeling and Harris the practical question, and the book gives Harris the better of it, since the next two pages describe exactly what happens to a tent in the rain.

quotations.text: That’s Harris all over—so ready to take the burden of everything himself, and put it on the backs of other people.
quotations.context: Harris has offered to make the list, provided J. gets the paper, George the grocery catalogue, and somebody the pencil.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a trap that closes in its last clause. It opens as praise, ready to take the burden of everything himself, and the final phrase reverses it without any change of tone. That shape, a generous start and a treacherous finish, is one of Jerome’s commonest devices. It also doubles back on the speaker. A page later J. rescues Harris from overwork by giving the paper, the pencil and the catalogue to the others and announcing that he will do the work.

quotations.text: “There you are,” he would say, stepping heavily off the chair on to the charwoman’s corns, and surveying the mess he had made with evident pride. “Why, some people would have had a man in to do a little thing like that!”
quotations.speaker: Uncle Podger
quotations.context: Midnight. The picture is up, crooked, and the wall for yards round looks as if it has been smoothed with a rake.
quotations.analysis: The boast is funny because the reader has watched the evening: seven helpers, a lost coat, a cut finger, a smashed thumb, a hammer through the plaster. The charwoman’s corns and the evident pride share a sentence, the cost and the satisfaction side by side. Would say marks the habit; this is a man who does it every time. The digression is told as a portrait of Harris but works as a model of the whole trip: a small job, a household mobilised, and a man sure of his own competence standing on somebody’s foot.

quotations.text: You will have time to think as well as to work. Time to drink in life’s sunshine—time to listen to the Æolian music that the wind of God draws from the human heart-strings around us—time to— I beg your pardon, really. I quite forgot.
quotations.context: George’s rule for packing, only what we can’t do without, has grown into a sermon about throwing life’s lumber overboard.
quotations.analysis: A sensible remark about hampers becomes a sermon, the sermon a list of the lumber people carry through life, and the list a lyrical catalogue of sunbeams and forget-me-nots. Then the voice breaks off mid-phrase and apologises. The bathos is aimed at J.: he has been caught preaching, and I quite forgot implies he does it often. The sermon is not simply mocked, though. Its advice, a light boat, one or two friends, someone to love, is the book’s sincerest statement, and Jerome lets it stand before he laughs at the man making it.

quotations.text: My friend got rid of them, at last, by taking them down to a sea-side town, and burying them on the beach. It gained the place quite a reputation. Visitors said they had never noticed before how strong the air was, and weak-chested and consumptive people used to throng there for years afterwards.
quotations.context: The end of the story of the Liverpool cheeses, told to support George’s rule that no cheese goes in the hamper.
quotations.analysis: The cheese story is a digression inside a digression, and each stage is the same joke at a larger scale: the smell wakes a somnambulist cab-horse into a gallop of four miles an hour, empties a railway carriage, drives a wife and children to a hotel, sickens the bargemen and outrages a coroner. The ending turns the escalation into advertising. A resort’s bracing air is a buried cheese, and the invalids who flock there are the book’s hypochondriacs seen from outside. Deadpan keeps it all plausible: nobody in the story ever admits the absurdity.

quotations.text: Anyhow, if he wasn’t the 11.5 for Kingston, he said he was pretty confident he was the 9.32 for Virginia Water, or the 10 a.m. express for the Isle of Wight, or somewhere in that direction, and we should all know when we got there. We slipped half-a-crown into his hand, and begged him to be the 11.5 for Kingston.
quotations.context: At Waterloo, after porters, the station-master and the traffic superintendent have each named a different platform.
quotations.analysis: Nobody at Waterloo knows where any train goes, and Jerome escalates the ignorance in lists: platform two, platform one, the local, the Southampton express, the Windsor loop, and now the driver’s own three candidates. The solution is not information but a bribe, and begged him to be the 11.5 treats a train as something a man can choose to become. The joke is about the new machinery of Victorian leisure, timetables and officials, and how little it resembles the order it promises. The train turns out to be the Exeter mail.

quotations.text: In 2288 people will gush over it. The making of such dogs will have become a lost art. Our descendants will wonder how we did it, and say how clever we were. We shall be referred to lovingly as “those grand old artists that flourished in the nineteenth century, and produced those china dogs.”
quotations.context: Carved oak in a Kingston shop, papered over in blue to make the room cheerful, has set J. thinking about what makes an antique.
quotations.analysis: The musing ends in the future. J. has described his landlady’s china dog without mercy, its expression amiability carried to verge of imbecility, and now imagines it dug up legless and admired in a glass case. The comedy is a transfer of value by time: he mocks the collectors of his own day by imagining their descendants, and the prophecy has partly come true, since Victorian pottery dogs are collected now. History in the book is often like this, less a record of greatness than a trick of distance.

quotations.text: Harris drew out his map again, after a while, but the sight of it only infuriated the mob, and they told him to go and curl his hair with it. Harris said that he couldn’t help feeling that, to a certain extent, he had become unpopular.
quotations.context: Harris’s story of taking a country cousin into the Hampton Court maze, which he had studied on a map and thought too simple to be worth the twopence.
quotations.analysis: Understatement is the joke. The scene has built a crowd of twenty lost people, a woman with a baby who calls Harris an impostor, and return after return to the centre; to a certain extent, he had become unpopular is the mildest possible summary. The phrasing is Harris’s own, reported by J., so it is also a portrait: Harris survives humiliation by describing it in the language of a committee. The maze is a small model of the river trip, a simple route, a confident guide and a map that makes things worse.

quotations.text: And Harris never sees what an ass he is making of himself, and how he is annoying a lot of people who never did him any harm. He honestly imagines that he has given them a treat, and says he will sing another comic song after supper.
quotations.context: J. has just set out Harris’s performance at a party as a little play, with stage directions for the nervous pianist.
quotations.analysis: The performance itself turns on a muddle. Harris announces the Judge’s song from Trial by Jury, starts the First Lord’s from HMS Pinafore, and fuses the two, so that called to the Bar collides with office-boy to an attorney. The audience roars, and he takes the laughter as a compliment. This sentence adds the moral: Harris does not know, and everyone else does. That gap between a man’s view of his performance and the room’s is the comic engine of the whole book, and J. applies it to everyone except himself.

quotations.text: There may be tow-lines that are a credit to their profession—conscientious, respectable tow-lines—tow-lines that do not imagine they are crochet-work, and try to knit themselves up into antimacassars the instant they are left to themselves.
quotations.context: George has been handed the tow-line, which J. coiled with great care, and it has turned into a tangle in his hands.
quotations.analysis: Jerome gives the rope a moral character. It is not merely tangled; it imagines itself crochet-work, and the hope that some tow-lines may be conscientious and respectable is phrased like a character reference for a servant. Personification lets the men blame the rope for their own clumsiness, which is the book’s steady view of equipment: every object has a will, and it is against them. The domestic comparison matters too. The river is meant to be an escape from the drawing-room, and the rope turns into drawing-room needlework.

quotations.text: That is the only way to get a kettle to boil up the river. If it sees that you are waiting for it and are anxious, it will never even sing.
quotations.context: The first night at Picnic Point. The canvas is at last up, and the kettle has been put on in the nose of the boat and ignored.
quotations.analysis: The proverb says a watched pot never boils. Jerome takes it literally and builds a method on it: the kettle can see and overhear, so the men must turn their backs and shout that they would rather have lemonade, at which it boils over in pique.
