The joke is the seriousness of the instructions, written like a manual. Like the tow-line, the kettle is a character with a temper, and later Montmorency attacks one by the spout and loses.

quotations.text: A bolder hand might have turned the game even at that point. Had it been a Richard there! the cup of liberty might have been dashed from England’s lips, and the taste of freedom held back for a hundred years.
quotations.context: J.’s imagined June morning of 1215, with King John arriving to be rowed across to the island where the Charter waits.
quotations.analysis: For two pages the comedy stops. J. fills Staines with soldiers and the river with barges, in a present-tense pageant of casques and banners, and writes it straight, excited exclamation and all. The history is the popular kind, a nation’s liberty turning on one king’s nerve. Its placing is the joke. The chapter closes on the cornerstone of England’s temple of liberty, and the next one opens with George asking whether J. would mind helping to wash up.

quotations.text: I was sitting on the bank, conjuring up this scene to myself, when George remarked that when I was quite rested, perhaps I would not mind helping to wash up; and, thus recalled from the days of the glorious past to the prosaic present, with all its misery and sin, I slid down into the boat and cleaned out the frying-pan with a stick of wood and a tuft of grass, polishing it up finally with George’s wet shirt.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the chapter, straight after the pageant of Magna Charta.
quotations.analysis: This is the fall the pageant was built for. The glorious past and the prosaic present, with all its misery and sin, are mock-solemn phrases, and the sentence then descends through a stick of wood and a tuft of grass to its last words. The shirt is a callback: J. dropped it in the river that morning, was furious at George’s laughter until he saw whose shirt it was, and then laughed so much he dropped it again. The bathos works because Jerome let the reader believe in the barons for a while, and because George, the man who interrupted, supplies the dishcloth.

quotations.text: We beat it out flat; we beat it back square; we battered it into every form known to geometry—but we could not make a hole in it.
quotations.context: There is no tin-opener, and a tin of pineapple has already defeated a pocket-knife, a pair of scissors, a hitcher and a mast.
quotations.analysis: The episode is written as a battle, with wounds, a weapon and a survivor who keeps his crushed straw hat as a relic. This sentence is its climax, and the list does the work: flat, square, every form known to geometry, then the plain clause that nothing has changed. Afterwards the tin acquires a dent like a mocking grin and is flung into the river with curses, like a defeated enemy. Three men and a missing tin-opener become a war of the world against its users, and the users lose.

quotations.text: I do hate steam launches: I suppose every rowing man does. I never see a steam launch but I feel I should like to lure it to a lonely part of the river, and there, in the silence and the solitude, strangle it.
quotations.context: Leaving Marlow just before Henley week, when launches are going upstream in numbers, some towing houseboats.
quotations.analysis: J. speaks for every rowing man and wishes on a machine the death of a villain in a melodrama, lured, isolated and strangled. The violence is a joke of proportion, like the tombstone he would make from a notice-board in chapter VIII, but the grievance behind it is real: launches belonged to people with money, and they whistled rowing boats out of the way. The chapter then describes the three drifting across the channel with their backs turned. Three chapters later J. is towed by a launch, and his opinions turn inside out.

quotations.text: It is not that I object to the work, mind you; I like work: it fascinates me. I can sit and look at it for hours. I love to keep it by me: the idea of getting rid of it nearly breaks my heart.
quotations.context: Harris has proposed that George and J. should scull while he steers, and J. feels he is doing more than his share.
quotations.analysis: The paradox works because fascinates is the right word used wrongly. Work becomes first a spectacle, something to watch for hours, and then a possession, kept, dusted and never touched. Every clause sounds like an industrious man’s boast and describes an idle one. J. never concedes the point. He goes on to observe that every man in a boat believes he is doing everything, and does not apply the rule to himself, which is the book’s method with its narrator in one paragraph.

quotations.text: It is very delightful being towed up by a launch. I prefer it myself to rowing. The run would have been more delightful still, if it had not been for a lot of wretched small boats that were continually getting in the way of our launch.
quotations.context: At Reading lock a steam launch belonging to friends of J. takes them in tow almost as far as Streatley.
quotations.analysis: The chapter argument calls this the irritating behaviour of small boats, and the joke is that J. now speaks as he said launch-owners speak. In chapter XIII small boats were a noble resistance; now they are wretched and ought to be run down now and then to teach them a lesson. Jerome never points out the reversal. He leaves the reader to remember, which is how the book treats its narrator throughout: not exposing him, only placing his opinions where they can be compared.

quotations.text: Six shillings a week does not keep body and soul together very unitedly. They want to get away from each other when there is only such a very slight bond as that between them.
quotations.context: The story of the drowned woman they have found in the river, as J. learned it afterwards.
quotations.analysis: The book’s one real death is told as a sentimental tract, a fallen woman shut out by respectable relations, and yet the comic habit of phrasing survives in it. Not keeping body and soul together very unitedly is a turn on a cliché, the same move Jerome makes about cheese and kettles. Here it lands as bitterness: twelve hours a day for twelve shillings, half of it for the child. The passage shows what the comic voice is made of, and it sits between a launch towing three men on holiday and a recommendation of Streatley for a few days’ stay.

quotations.text: And so it would have been strange and unaccountable, if it had been a stuffed trout, but it was not. That trout was plaster-of-Paris.
quotations.context: George has climbed on a chair to look at the trout in the inn parlour and brought the case down.
quotations.analysis: The fish story is a comic form with a fixed shape, in which every angler’s fish grows. Jerome runs it four times in the inn parlour, the weight rising from eighteen pounds to thirty-four, before the landlord tells the real history. Then George falls on the case, the trout breaks into a thousand fragments, or nine hundred, and the last line reverses everything: the object at the centre of five confident stories was never a fish. The joke catches the reader too, who had been sorting the true account from the false.

quotations.text: Our feet were undoubtedly the leading article in that photograph. Indeed, very little else was to be seen.
quotations.context: A memory of a crowded lock at Hampton Court, where a photographer was taking a picture of all the boats.
quotations.analysis: The photograph is a story about posing. George hides his feet and arranges his expression; J. leans on the hitcher with a curl over his forehead and a touch of cynicism, which I am told suits me. Then the boat’s nose catches under the lock timbers, and the camera records them on their backs with their feet in the air. Leading article is newspaper language for the main story, applied to four boots. Vanity and its exposure end up on a single plate, and nobody else will buy a copy.

quotations.text: We pretended, at first, that we enjoyed it. We said it was a change, and that we liked to see the river under all its different aspects. We said we could not expect to have it all sunshine, nor should we wish it. We told each other that Nature was beautiful, even in her tears.
quotations.context: The first day of rowing back down from Oxford in the rain.
quotations.analysis: In the rain the three try to keep up the tone of the book’s own lyrical passages and cannot. Each we said is a line from the sentimental guide to nature, variety, not all sunshine, beautiful even in her tears, and the repetition sounds like people agreeing in order to keep their spirits up. The purple passages of the earlier chapters are here turned into dialogue and exposed as things one says. The chapter has just offered its own fine writing about the river in rain, and this puts it in brackets.

quotations.text: “Well,” said Harris, reaching his hand out for his glass, “we have had a pleasant trip, and my hearty thanks for it to old Father Thames—but I think we did well to chuck it when we did. Here’s to Three Men well out of a Boat!”
quotations.speaker: Harris
quotations.context: Supper in a London restaurant after the Alhambra, with the rain splashing in the street outside.
quotations.analysis: The book ends with the holiday abandoned and its own title turned round. Harris thanks Father Thames in a toastmaster’s phrase and then undoes the whole project in a slang verb, chuck. It is the last bathos and the most honest, since the trip has consisted largely of things going wrong and the best evening in it is spent in town. Montmorency, who voted against the river in chapter I, stands at the window and barks his agreement, so the minority report is carried at last.

themes.name: Friendship and the test of it
Service, and the people who go on doing it
Knowing the answer and not using it

quotations.text: When Fortune in her shift and change of mood Spurns down her late beloved, all his dependants, Which laboured after him to the mountain's top Even on their knees and hands, let him slip down, Not one accompanying his declining foot.
quotations.speaker: Poet
quotations.context: Describing to the Painter the poem he has brought to the house to sell.
quotations.analysis: The Poet summarises the next four acts before any of them have happened, then hands the manuscript to the man who will fall. 'Let him slip down' is the exact verb: nobody pushes, everyone simply stops holding on. What the scene refuses is a clean division between corrupt flatterers and honest art, because the diagnosis is itself for sale.

quotations.text: I gave it freely ever, and there's none Can truly say he gives if he receives.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Refusing the five talents Ventidius has come to the banquet to repay.
quotations.analysis: Good ethics and ruinous accounting. By defining a gift as something that cannot be handed back, Timon puts every friend permanently in his debt and forbids them to clear it. That is precisely the position they use against him in Act III, when there is nothing written anywhere that says they owe him a talent.

quotations.text: O you gods, what a number of men eats Timon, and he sees 'em not! It grieves me to see so many dip their meat in one man's blood
quotations.speaker: Apemantus
quotations.context: At his own table at the first banquet, refusing Timon's food.
quotations.analysis: Apemantus turns the dinner into cannibalism with one verb: not eat with Timon but eat Timon. It is the play's governing image of consumption and it is literally true of the estate, which the guests are working through course by course. He says it aloud, at the table, in front of everyone, and nothing whatever follows.

quotations.text: I should fear those that dance before me now Would one day stamp upon me. 'T has been done. Men shut their doors against a setting sun.
quotations.speaker: Apemantus
quotations.context: Watching the masque of Amazons that Cupid has brought into the banquet.
quotations.analysis: The couplet has the shape of a proverb and the function of a prophecy: in 3.4 Timon finds his own doors shut against him from the inside. 'Stamp' keeps the dancing in view, so that the feet entertaining him now are the feet that will be on him, and the line is spoken over music nobody else stops hearing.

quotations.text: His promises fly so beyond his state That what he speaks is all in debt; he owes For every word.
quotations.speaker: Flavius
quotations.context: Aside, while Timon sends out for the casket of jewels.
quotations.analysis: Flavius makes speech itself a form of borrowing. Timon's generosity is verbal before it is financial — he gives away the bay courser because a guest praised it in passing — so every sentence draws on an account already empty. It is the most precise thing said about him in the play, and it is said to nobody at all.

quotations.text: If I want gold, steal but a beggar's dog And give it Timon, why, the dog coins gold.
quotations.speaker: A Senator
quotations.context: Going through his ledger at home, and deciding to call in what Timon owes.
quotations.analysis: The senator has found the mechanism and states it as a recipe: worthless object in, gold out. His is the first voice to treat Timon's bounty as a market and not a virtue, and the calculation ends with an order to fetch the bonds and fill in the dates. Athens does not set out to ruin Timon; it simply notices him.

quotations.text: Ah, when the means are gone that buy this praise, The breath is gone whereof this praise is made. Feast-won, fast-lost
quotations.speaker: Flavius
quotations.context: Laying the accounts before Timon at last, after the creditors have been sent from the door.
quotations.analysis: Praise is made of breath and paid for with dinners, so when the dinners stop the praise simply evaporates; the metaphor is physical, not moral. 'Feast-won, fast-lost' compresses the whole of Act III into four words, and the two senses of fast — quickly, and going without food — sit one on top of the other.

quotations.text: For by these Shall I try friends. You shall perceive how you Mistake my fortunes. I am wealthy in my friends.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Answering Flavius, who has just shown him that the land is sold and the debts unpayable.
quotations.analysis: He has been told he is ruined and he hears an opportunity. 'Try' means test, and he is right that a test is coming; what he has wrong is which way it will go. The line is the hinge of the play, and the confidence in it is why the three refusals of Act III land as hard as they do.

quotations.text: this is no time to lend money, especially upon bare friendship without security. Here's three solidares for thee. Good boy, wink at me, and say thou saw'st me not.
quotations.speaker: Lucullus
quotations.context: To Flaminius, who has come with an empty box to ask for fifty talents.
quotations.analysis: 'Bare friendship' is the entire refusal in two words: friendship stripped of collateral is not a thing a man lends against. Lucullus then tries to buy a servant's eyesight for three small coins, which is the rate he puts on a house he has dined in for years. Flaminius throws them on the floor and curses the meat in him.

quotations.text: But I perceive Men must learn now with pity to dispense, For policy sits above conscience.
quotations.speaker: First Stranger
quotations.context: After watching Lucius refuse the servant, having just heard him call Lucullus shameful for doing the same.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is given to a man with nothing at stake — he says he never tasted Timon in his life — which is what makes it a judgement on Athens and not a grievance. To dispense with something is to do without it. Pity has become an optional expense, and the strangers are watching a city decide it can no longer afford one.

quotations.text: And with their faint reply this answer join: Who bates mine honour shall not know my coin.
quotations.speaker: Sempronius
quotations.context: Refusing the fourth request, after being told that Lucullus, Lucius and Ventidius have all said no.
quotations.analysis: Sempronius is the only one who does not trouble to sound sorry. Being asked last is the injury; the money is incidental to it. 'Bates' means lessens, and by rhyming honour against coin he states the exchange rate he is working to. The servant, left alone, calls it a man striving hard to appear foul, which will do for the whole act.

quotations.text: Knock me down with 'em! Cleave me to the girdle. … Cut my heart in sums! … Tell out my blood.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Breaking out of his own house among the creditors' servants and their bills.
quotations.analysis: Three short answers to three bills, each turning a sum into an injury to the body. 'Tell out' means count out, so blood is being reckoned in the units that money is reckoned in: the metaphor the play has been building since the first banquet is finally spoken by the man it is about. Within twenty lines he has ordered another dinner.

quotations.text: Banish me? Banish your dotage, banish usury, That makes the Senate ugly.
quotations.speaker: Alcibiades
quotations.context: Sentenced to exile for pressing the senate a second time to spare a soldier's life.
quotations.analysis: He takes their verb and turns it three times, and the third turn names what is actually wrong with the room: the men refusing mercy are lending at large interest. It is the same charge the Timon plot brings against Athens, said out loud in the senate house, and it gets him thrown out of the city instead of answered.

quotations.text: May you a better feast never behold, You knot of mouth-friends! Smoke and lukewarm water Is your perfection.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Uncovering the dishes at the second banquet.
quotations.analysis: 'Mouth-friends' is the play's best coinage: friends who exist at a table and no further than the mouth. Warm water is what a feast leaves when the food is taken out of it, the honest substance under the sauces, and 'perfection' means completion — the finished form of what they always were. He then throws it in their faces.

quotations.text: Timon will to the woods, where he shall find Th' unkindest beast more kinder than mankind.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Turning at the city wall for a last look before leaving Athens.
quotations.analysis: He speaks of himself in the third person, as though reading his own epitaph early. The play on kind — a species, and kindness — carries the argument: the beast is kinder because it was never of his kind. Apemantus takes the comparison apart in 4.3 by showing that every beast in the list is prey to some other beast.

quotations.text: Poor honest lord, brought low by his own heart, Undone by goodness! Strange, unusual blood When man's worst sin is he does too much good!
quotations.speaker: Flavius
quotations.context: Alone, after dividing his own last money among the dismissed servants.
quotations.analysis: This is the most generous reading of Timon in the play and it comes from the one man entitled to be bitter about him. 'Blood' here means temperament. Flavius does not claim the giving was wise, only that the fault in it was goodness, and the exclamation marks are the sound of a bookkeeper running out of categories.

quotations.text: Thus much of this will make Black white, foul fair, wrong right, Base noble, old young, coward valiant.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Digging for a root outside his cave, and turning up gold instead.
quotations.analysis: Six reversals in two lines with no verbs between them, so that the transformations happen as fast as the words are said. Gold is not being called evil here; it is being called a translator, able to exchange any value for its opposite. Marx quoted the speech in 1844 and again in Capital for exactly that claim about money.

quotations.text: This yellow slave Will knit and break religions, bless th' accursed, Make the hoar leprosy adored, place thieves And give them title, knee, and approbation With senators on the bench.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: The same speech, a few lines on, with the gold in his hands.
quotations.analysis: Calling gold a slave and then listing what it commands is the joke inside the image: the thing that serves is the thing that rules. 'Knee' and 'approbation' were the currency of Act I, when the lobbies filled with tendance, and here the same bowing is bought openly. He buries most of the gold and keeps out enough to go on proving the point.

quotations.text: The middle of humanity thou never knewest, but the extremity of both ends.
quotations.speaker: Apemantus
quotations.context: In the wood, in the middle of the insult match that ends with a stone being thrown.
quotations.analysis: The sharpest criticism of Timon in the play, and the reason it is hard to call him a tragic hero: there is no scene in which he learns anything, only a switch from one absolute to its opposite. Apemantus has earned the observation by occupying the same extreme for years and knowing exactly what it is worth.

quotations.text: The sun's a thief and with his great attraction Robs the vast sea; the moon's an arrant thief, And her pale fire she snatches from the sun
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Giving gold to three bandits, and proving to them that theft is universal.
quotations.analysis: A piece of real natural philosophy — evaporation, reflected light, the tides — recruited to tell three robbers that nothing they do is exceptional. It talks one of them out of the trade, which is the last thing Timon wants; he means to make them worse. Nabokov took the title of a novel from the phrase in the third line.

quotations.text: I do proclaim One honest man, mistake me not, but one; No more, I pray, and he's a steward.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: To Flavius, who has found him in the wood and wept at the sight of him.
quotations.analysis: The concession is fenced on both sides — 'but one', 'no more, I pray' — because a second honest man would wreck the argument he has built his exile on. That the one should be a steward, a paid servant with no reason left to stay, is the quietest rebuke in the play to everything Timon believed about brothers commanding one another's fortunes.

quotations.text: Why, I was writing of my epitaph; It will be seen tomorrow. My long sickness Of health and living now begins to mend And nothing brings me all things.
quotations.speaker: Timon
quotations.context: Refusing the senators who have come to the cave to offer him command of Athens.
quotations.analysis: Health and living are the disease and dying is the cure, and the inversion is held perfectly steady across three lines. 'Nothing brings me all things' is the last of his reversals and the calmest of them: he has stopped cursing and started arranging. It is also the only preparation the play gives for a death it keeps offstage.

quotations.text: Here lies a wretched corse, of wretched soul bereft. Seek not my name. A plague consume you, wicked caitiffs left! Here lie I, Timon, who alive all living men did hate. Pass by and curse thy fill, but pass and stay not here thy gait.
quotations.speaker: Alcibiades
quotations.context: Reading aloud at the gates from the wax impression a soldier has taken off the tomb by the sea.
quotations.analysis: Two epitaphs printed as one, contradicting each other inside four lines: the first forbids you to seek his name and the second gives it. Both stand in North's Plutarch as separate inscriptions, one said to be Timon's own and one by the poet Callimachus. The collision has been read as a sign of unfinished work and as a last joke by a man who could not stop giving.

quotations.text: Bring me into your city, And I will use the olive with my sword, Make war breed peace, make peace stint war, make each Prescribe to other, as each other's leech.
quotations.speaker: Alcibiades
quotations.context: The last speech of the play, immediately after the epitaph has been read out at the walls.
quotations.analysis: The play ends with the one man who can tell one Athenian from another. 'Leech' means physician, so war and peace are set to treat each other, and the balanced clauses do on the page what the terms do in the city. It is a settlement and not a reconciliation: nobody is forgiven, and the cure is mutual restraint.

themes.name: Law, and what is left when it goes
Aaron, and the language Rome uses
Rites, and what they are worth

quotations.text: Wilt thou draw near the nature of the gods? Draw near them then in being merciful. Sweet mercy is nobility's true badge.
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Kneeling in the street, begging Titus to spare her eldest son Alarbus.
quotations.analysis: She argues in Rome's own vocabulary, and she argues well: nobility, the gods, mercy as a mark of rank. Titus answers with the word religiously and burns the boy anyway. Everything Tamora does for the rest of the play is licensed by the fact that she asked properly first and was refused on a technicality of rite.

quotations.text: O cruel, irreligious piety!
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: As her son is led off to be hacked apart and burned on the Andronici tomb.
quotations.analysis: Four words that hold the play's whole difficulty. Titus has just used the word religiously to justify the killing, and she hands it straight back with cruel attached. The line concedes that the sacrifice is genuinely pious and insists that piety is what makes it monstrous, which is the charge Rome never answers.

quotations.text: Thou art a Roman; be not barbarous.
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Kneeling with Titus's sons, begging him to let Mutius be buried in the family tomb.
quotations.analysis: Marcus means it as a compliment and the play hears it as a question. Roman and barbarous have been opposed since the first scene, where Chiron said Scythia was never half so barbarous as this. The distinction has already collapsed: the Roman thing and the barbarous thing were the same act, performed at the same tomb, an hour earlier.

quotations.text: These words are razors to my wounded heart.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: After Saturninus has sneered at Lavinia as a changing piece and at Titus's sons as lawless.
quotations.analysis: The first blade in a play full of them, and it is only a figure of speech. By Act III the metaphors have all come true: hands actually come off, tongues actually go, and the razor is a real knife held by a father over two bound men. Titus's language keeps predicting the stage business that arrives to replace it.

quotations.text: I'll find a day to massacre them all, And raze their faction and their family, The cruel father and his traitorous sons, To whom I sued for my dear son's life
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Aside to Saturninus, while publicly urging him to forgive Titus.
quotations.analysis: The double voice is the whole of her method: aloud she is reconciling the court, under her breath she is naming a date. Note what she lists as the grievance. Not the war, not the captivity, not the yoke; the refusal of a kneeling woman in the street. She is precise about the debt, and she collects on exactly that account.

quotations.text: Vengeance is in my heart, death in my hand, Blood and revenge are hammering in my head.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Refusing Tamora's invitation to lie down with her in the wood.
quotations.analysis: Tamora has just spent twenty lines on birds, shade and a golden slumber. Aaron cuts across her pastoral with three body parts and a verb from a forge. Hammering makes revenge a trade with tools and a rhythm, and it tells the audience who is actually running the plot: not the empress, but the man refusing her for a morning's work.

quotations.text: Hadst thou in person ne'er offended me, Even for his sake am I pitiless.
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Answering Lavinia, who has begged her in the name of Titus's mercy to Tamora herself.
quotations.analysis: Lavinia's argument is that Titus spared Tamora's life, so Tamora owes the daughter something. The reply concedes the debt and converts it: precisely because Titus is the father, the daughter is the payment. Hadst thou in person is the cruellest part. Tamora states outright that Lavinia has done nothing, and will suffer for that reason.

quotations.text: So, now go tell, an if thy tongue can speak, Who 'twas that cut thy tongue and ravished thee.
quotations.speaker: Demetrius
quotations.context: The first words of the scene, as the brothers leave Lavinia in the wood.
quotations.analysis: The play opens its most notorious scene with a taunt built on the mechanics of the crime. Philomela in Ovid was silenced and still wove the truth; Demetrius thinks he has closed that loophole by taking the hands as well. The rest of the act, and most of the next two, is the play proving him wrong by a staff and a sandy plot.

quotations.text: Write down thy mind, bewray thy meaning so, An if thy stumps will let thee play the scribe.
quotations.speaker: Chiron
quotations.context: Joining his brother's mockery before they leave her alone.
quotations.analysis: A joke that the play takes literally and turns into the instrument of his death. Two acts later Lavinia does play the scribe, guiding a staff with her stumps and her mouth, and writes his name. Chiron names the method by which he will be identified, bound, gagged and bled over a basin. Few taunts in Shakespeare are repaid so exactly.

quotations.text: Fair Philomela, why she but lost her tongue, And in a tedious sampler sewed her mind; But, lovely niece, that mean is cut from thee
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Alone with Lavinia in the wood, in the middle of his forty-line speech over her.
quotations.analysis: The word but is doing terrible work here: Philomela only lost her tongue. Marcus reaches for a literary precedent and finds it insufficient, which is the most honest thing in the speech. The scene has divided readers for two centuries, because the verse is beautiful and a woman is bleeding through all of it while a man looks for the right comparison.

quotations.text: Why, foolish Lucius, dost thou not perceive That Rome is but a wilderness of tigers? Tigers must prey, and Rome affords no prey But me and mine.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Telling his banished son that exile is good fortune.
quotations.analysis: Titus gave this city his sons, his arm and the empire, and here he sees it plainly for the first time. Wilderness is the sharp word: not a corrupt Rome to be reformed, but no Rome at all, a wood with animals in it. He has just come from the forest where his daughter was attacked, and he no longer distinguishes the two places.

quotations.text: Let fools do good, and fair men call for grace, Aaron will have his soul black like his face.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Leaving with Titus's severed hand, having just told the audience the sons are already dead.
quotations.analysis: He takes Rome's insult and makes it a rhyme and a policy. Fair men call for grace pins the hypocrisy: the same city that equates whiteness with virtue has just cheated an old man out of his hand. Aaron chooses the identity Rome has assigned him and turns it into something he owns, which is not the same as agreeing with it.

quotations.text: Why dost thou laugh? It fits not with this hour.
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Immediately after Titus responds to the arrival of his sons' heads with laughter.
quotations.analysis: Marcus speaks for the part of the audience still trying to keep the genre steady. Titus's answer is that he has no tears left, which is not madness but accountancy: grief has a supply and it has run out. The laugh is the moment the play stops being a tragedy of suffering and becomes a tragedy of planning.

quotations.text: Thou shalt not sigh, nor hold thy stumps to heaven, Nor wink, nor nod, nor kneel, nor make a sign, But I of these will wrest an alphabet
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: At the family dinner, promising Lavinia that he will learn to read her.
quotations.analysis: The tenderest speech he makes, and it is also a claim of ownership over her meaning. Wrest is a violent verb for a loving promise: he will force a language out of her body whether the signs are offered or not. The play gives her a father who will not stop attending to her and never once asks her a question she could answer.

quotations.text: Pardon me, sir; 'twas a black ill-favoured fly, Like to the empress' Moor; therefore I killed him.
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Explaining himself after Titus has accused him of murder for swatting a fly at dinner.
quotations.analysis: Marcus invents the excuse on the spot and it works instantly: Titus takes the knife and stabs the dead fly twice more, once for Aaron and once for Tamora. The scene shows grief turning into method, and it shows the family's racism in its most casual form, offered as a joke to calm a distressed old man.

quotations.text: Stuprum. Chiron. Demetrius.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Reading aloud what Lavinia has written in the sand with a staff held in her mouth.
quotations.analysis: Three words, one of them Latin, and the play's only piece of direct testimony. Stuprum is the legal term, not a cry: she names the crime in the language of the courts that failed her, then names the men. After two acts of other people describing her, this is Lavinia speaking, and it takes a stick, a patch of sand and both her stumps.

quotations.text: Coal-black is better than another hue In that it scorns to bear another hue; For all the water in the ocean Can never turn the swan's black legs to white
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Defending his newborn son against Chiron, Demetrius and the nurse sent to kill it.
quotations.analysis: The argument is that black keeps its own colour and white cannot. Fifteen lines later Chiron says he blushes at the family shame, and Aaron pounces: a treacherous hue that betrays the counsels of the heart. It is the one speech in the play where blackness is a boast, made by a man holding a newborn in one arm and a scimitar in the other.

quotations.text: My mistress is my mistress; this my self; The vigour and the picture of my youth. This before all the world do I prefer; This maugre all the world will I keep safe
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Asked whether he will betray Tamora to protect the child.
quotations.analysis: He drops the empress in half a line and never mentions her again with any warmth. The repetition of this, three times, keeps pointing at the baby in his arms while the sentence gets shorter and harder. Aaron is the only character in the play who chooses a living child over an inherited quarrel, and he is the one buried alive for it.

quotations.text: And sith there's no justice in earth nor hell, We will solicit heaven and move the gods To send down Justice for to wreak our wrongs.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Handing out bows and arrows with letters tied to them, to be shot into the emperor's court.
quotations.analysis: He has already sent men to dig for Justice underground and to drag the sea for her. The logic is perfectly sound and the method is ridiculous, which is how this play does madness: not confusion, but a rational man following a failed system to its last address. The arrows land in the palace, and Saturninus reads them as libel.

quotations.text: But I have done a thousand dreadful things As willingly as one would kill a fly, And nothing grieves me heartily indeed But that I cannot do ten thousand more.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: On a ladder with a rope round his neck, having just listed his crimes to Lucius.
quotations.analysis: The comparison reaches back to Act III, where a killed fly reduced Titus to fury and then to knife-work. Aaron uses the same insect to measure indifference. He has bought his son's life with this confession and spends the rest of it refusing the remorse that would make the bargain look like repentance.

quotations.text: Know thou, sad man, I am not Tamora; She is thy enemy, and I thy friend. I am Revenge, sent from th' infernal kingdom
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: At the door of Titus's study, dressed as Revenge with her sons as Rape and Murder.
quotations.analysis: She thinks she is exploiting his madness and she is walking into his kitchen. Titus has already told her he knows her by his own stump, and he lets the disguise stand because it hands him her sons. The old morality figures knock at the door, the play lets them in, and then butchers two of them behind it.

quotations.text: Why, there they are, both baked in that pie, Whereof their mother daintily hath fed, Eating the flesh that she herself hath bred.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Asked by Saturninus to fetch Chiron and Demetrius to the banquet.
quotations.analysis: The line is delivered as information, in answer to a polite request, by a man dressed as a cook. Daintily does the damage: it makes Tamora a guest with manners while she finishes her sons. Three lines later he stabs her, and the revenge that began with a boy burned on a tomb is settled over dinner in under thirty seconds.

quotations.text: I am no baby, I, that with base prayers I should repent the evils I have done. Ten thousand worse than ever yet I did Would I perform, if I might have my will. If one good deed in all my life I did, I do repent it from my very soul.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Sentenced by Lucius to be set breast-deep in earth and starved.
quotations.analysis: His last speech refuses the scaffold conversion an Elizabethan audience expected and an Elizabethan gallows usually produced. The final couplet is a joke with a real fact inside it: he did do one good deed, and everyone on stage is looking at it, because the baby he saved is alive in Lucius's household while he goes into the ground.

quotations.text: O, let me teach you how to knit again This scattered corn into one mutual sheaf, These broken limbs again into one body
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Speaking down to the people of Rome from the upper stage, with four fresh bodies below.
quotations.analysis: The old civic language comes back for the ending: the state as a sheaf, the state as a body. Broken limbs is a metaphor that has been literal for three acts, and an audience that has watched hands and heads come off cannot hear it as figure any more. Marcus asks Rome to reassemble itself using the vocabulary that failed it.

quotations.text: And hither am I come A prologue arm’d, but not in confidence Of author’s pen or actor’s voice, but suited In like conditions as our argument
quotations.speaker: Prologue
quotations.context: The opening speech, after the ships have been counted and the six gates of Troy named.
quotations.analysis: A prologue normally comes out in a black cloak to ask for goodwill. This one comes out in armour and refuses to ask, saying the costume matches the subject. The line also tells the audience how to take everything that follows: the play will be defensive, combative and uninterested in being liked, and it ends by leaving the verdict to chance.

quotations.text: Fools on both sides! Helen must needs be fair, When with your blood you daily paint her thus.
quotations.speaker: Troilus
quotations.context: Alone after Pandarus has walked out on him, hearing the alarum from the field.
quotations.analysis: Painting a woman's face was a byword for cosmetic fraud, and Troilus makes the paint blood: Helen's beauty is manufactured daily by the men dying for it. It is the sharpest thing said about the war, and it is said by the man who will stand up in council an act later and argue that she must be kept.

quotations.text: Women are angels, wooing: Things won are done; joy’s soul lies in the doing.…Men prize the thing ungain’d more than it is.
quotations.speaker: Cressida
quotations.context: Alone at the end of her first scene, after her uncle has spent the afternoon selling Troilus to her.
quotations.analysis: Her first private words are a piece of market analysis, and they are about herself as the commodity. She has worked out that her value lasts exactly as long as she withholds it, which makes her caution a business decision and not coldness. The play then takes the decision out of her hands by trading her for a prisoner.

quotations.text: Take but degree away, untune that string, And hark what discord follows! Each thing melts In mere oppugnancy
quotations.speaker: Ulysses
quotations.context: Answering Agamemnon's question about what is wrong with the Greek army after seven years.
quotations.analysis: The image is a lute string: loosen one and the whole instrument is out of tune. It is the most orderly statement of hierarchy in Shakespeare, and it is a diagnosis with a plan attached, delivered by a man who is about to rig a lottery. Nothing in the speech is untrue, and nothing in the play is run by it.

quotations.text: And appetite, an universal wolf, So doubly seconded with will and power, Must make perforce an universal prey, And last eat up himself.
quotations.speaker: Ulysses
quotations.context: The end of the same speech, describing what follows when power turns into will and will into appetite.
quotations.analysis: The chain is deliberate: power, will, appetite, and then a wolf that runs out of everything else and starts on itself. Ulysses means it politically, but the image is the one the rest of the play keeps reaching for, in Thersites's lechery, in Troilus's boundless desire, and in Achilles feeding his eyes on Hector's body before he kills him.

quotations.text: Let Helen go. Since the first sword was drawn about this question, Every tithe soul ’mongst many thousand dismes Hath been as dear as Helen—I mean, of ours.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Opening the Trojan council on whether to return Helen and end the war.
quotations.analysis: A disme is a tenth, the tithe taken by the church, and Hector uses it to count the dead: one in ten of many thousands, and each of them worth as much as she is. The arithmetic is unanswerable and he supplies the qualification himself — of ours — which quietly concedes that the calculation is tribal before it is moral.

quotations.text: What’s aught but as ’tis valued?
quotations.speaker: Troilus
quotations.context: Interrupting Hector's argument that Helen is not worth what she costs to keep.
quotations.analysis: Five words that reduce every question in the play to a market. Troilus is arguing that worth is conferred by the buyer, which is convenient for a council that has already paid, and fatal to him personally: if value is only what somebody will give, then Cressida is worth one Antenor, and a sleeve is worth whatever Diomedes decides.

quotations.text: But value dwells not in particular will: It holds his estimate and dignity As well wherein ’tis precious of itself As in the prizer.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: The immediate reply to Troilus in the Trojan council.
quotations.analysis: Hector's answer is the philosophical one: a thing has worth in itself as well as in the eye of whoever prizes it, and to make the service greater than the god is idolatry. He is right, he wins the exchange, and he then votes with his brothers anyway, which is the moment the play's whole argument about value is revealed to be unenforceable.

quotations.text: Hector’s opinion Is this, in way of truth. Yet, ne’ertheless, My spritely brethren, I propend to you In resolution to keep Helen still
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Closing the debate, immediately after proving that the law of nature and of nations requires Helen's return.
quotations.analysis: The hinge of the play turns on two words. He has established the truth, in way of truth, and then leans the other way because the dignity of the family is engaged. Nothing has been refuted. The council simply prefers its own reputation to its own reasoning, and Troy is destroyed by a man who could see the answer perfectly well.

quotations.text: All the argument is a whore and a cuckold—a good quarrel to draw emulous factions and bleed to death upon.
quotations.speaker: Thersites
quotations.context: Leaving Achilles's tent as the Greek generals arrive.
quotations.analysis: Argument means the plot of a play as well as the matter of a dispute, so Thersites is reviewing the drama he is standing in. Ten years, sixty-nine ships and every famous name in the Greek world reduced to two people and their adultery. The play never answers him, and every later scene supplies more evidence for the prosecution.

quotations.text: This is the monstruosity in love, lady, that the will is infinite, and the execution confin’d; that the desire is boundless, and the act a slave to limit.
quotations.speaker: Troilus
quotations.context: In the orchard, answering Cressida's suggestion that lovers promise more than they can deliver.
quotations.analysis: He thinks he is paying love a compliment and he is describing the machinery that will break them both. Will and desire are limitless, performance is not, and the gap between them is where every vow in the play goes. Cressida has just made the same point as a joke about lions and hares, and she is the one who will be blamed for proving it.

quotations.text: If I be false, or swerve a hair from truth, When time is old and hath forgot itself, When waterdrops have worn the stones of Troy…‘As false as Cressid.’
quotations.speaker: Cressida
quotations.context: In the orchard, answering Troilus's vow that lovers will swear by his name.
quotations.analysis: She invents her own curse and gets it exactly right, which is the strangest thing in the play. The condition she sets is geological — Troy worn away by water, cities swallowed by oblivion — and the punishment is that one phrase outlives all of it. By 1602 the phrase already existed, so the audience is watching a woman coin a proverb she is standing inside.

quotations.text: let all constant men be Troiluses, all false women Cressids, and all brokers between Pandars.
quotations.speaker: Pandarus
quotations.context: Witnessing the lovers' oaths and joining his own name to them before taking the pair to a bed.
quotations.analysis: All three names had already become common nouns by the time the play was written, and Pandarus hands them over as though the language were waiting for his permission. The joke is that only his own prediction is neutral: constancy and falsehood are still to be proved, but a pander is a pander in the act of speaking.

quotations.text: Time hath, my lord, a wallet at his back, Wherein he puts alms for oblivion, A great-siz’d monster of ingratitudes.
quotations.speaker: Ulysses
quotations.context: Working on Achilles outside his tent, after the generals have walked past him without speaking.
quotations.analysis: A wallet here is a beggar's satchel, worn behind so the owner cannot see into it, and what goes in are the good deeds already done. Ulysses is telling a soldier that his past is charity thrown to a monster who will not remember it. It is the most persuasive speech in the play and it fails: Achilles moves only when Patroclus is killed.

quotations.text: One touch of nature makes the whole world kin— That all with one consent praise new-born gauds, Though they are made and moulded of things past
quotations.speaker: Ulysses
quotations.context: The same speech, explaining why the Greek camp has transferred its admiration to Ajax.
quotations.analysis: The first line is quoted at funerals as a statement about common feeling. In place it means the opposite: the trait all humanity shares is a weakness for the newest shiny thing, and the gauds are second-hand at that. Ulysses is flattering a man by telling him the world is fickle, which is itself the technique he is describing.

quotations.text: I speak not ‘Be thou true’ as fearing thee, For I will throw my glove to Death himself That there’s no maculation in thy heart
quotations.speaker: Troilus
quotations.context: Parting from Cressida at Pandarus's house, an hour before she is handed over.
quotations.analysis: He has already said be thou true twice and will say it twice more, and each denial that he is afraid makes the fear plainer. Maculation is a stain, a word from theology rather than love talk. Cressida's exasperated reply, that she will be true, is the last promise she makes in Troy, and she keeps it for about a day.

quotations.text: There’s language in her eye, her cheek, her lip, Nay, her foot speaks; her wanton spirits look out At every joint and motive of her body.…Set them down For sluttish spoils of opportunity, And daughters of the game.
quotations.speaker: Ulysses
quotations.context: As Cressida is led away, immediately after the Greek commanders have kissed her one by one.
quotations.analysis: He has just taken part in the general kissing and refused her one himself, and he now reads her body as a text anybody may open. Nestor's verdict, a woman of quick sense, is what provokes it. The speech decides Cressida's reputation for the audience four hundred lines before she does anything, and it is delivered by the play's most reliable observer.

quotations.text: The end crowns all; And that old common arbitrator, Time, Will one day end it.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Answering Ulysses, who has told him the walls of Troy must kiss their own feet.
quotations.analysis: Hector is being courteous and is also refusing the prophecy: he will not argue about the future, he will leave it to time. The audience knows Troy falls, so the calm is unbearable rather than wise. He has three scenes to live, and the end that crowns him is an unarmed man in a field being surrounded by twenty soldiers.

quotations.text: Troilus, farewell! One eye yet looks on thee; But with my heart the other eye doth see. Ah, poor our sex! this fault in us I find, The error of our eye directs our mind.
quotations.speaker: Cressida
quotations.context: Alone, after Diomedes has taken the sleeve and gone.
quotations.analysis: Her only soliloquy since the first act, and it is an admission with the terms already set: the fault is the eye's, and the eye belongs to a sex, not to her. Whether that is honesty, self-excuse or the language she has been given by the men watching her is the argument the scene exists to start. She does not appear again.

quotations.text: Bi-fold authority! where reason can revolt Without perdition, and loss assume all reason Without revolt: this is, and is not, Cressid.
quotations.speaker: Troilus
quotations.context: Still hidden with Ulysses, a few lines after watching Cressida hand the sleeve to Diomedes.
quotations.analysis: The syntax breaks up because the thought will not close: two authorities, the eyes and the vows, each fully convincing, and no way to prefer one. It is the play's central sentence and its hardest, and it is spoken by a man who has argued for four acts that things are worth whatever we decide they are worth.

quotations.text: Lechery, lechery! Still wars and lechery! Nothing else holds fashion.
quotations.speaker: Thersites
quotations.context: Left alone when Troilus and Ulysses have gone, at the end of the scene he has spent commenting on.
quotations.analysis: He has watched the same scene the audience has and this is his summary of it, offered as the closing remark on the whole story. Holds fashion means stays in style, so even the two constants are being treated as a passing taste. The line is usually the one productions build their design around, and the play gives it to a man everybody hits.

quotations.text: Mine honour keeps the weather of my fate. Life every man holds dear; but the dear man Holds honour far more precious dear than life.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Refusing Andromache and Cassandra, who have knelt to keep him from the field.
quotations.analysis: To keep the weather is to hold the windward side in a sea fight, the advantage position. Hector is saying his honour has the better of his fate, and the play gives him four scenes before the Myrmidons prove otherwise. The lines are noble and are also the reason he dies: he has sworn an oath to appear, and the oath outranks every warning he has been given.

quotations.text: Come here about me, you my Myrmidons; Mark what I say. Attend me where I wheel; Strike not a stroke, but keep yourselves in breath…It is decreed Hector the great must die.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Briefing his own men in the middle of the battle, after the death of Patroclus.
quotations.analysis: Eight lines of tactical instruction: stand round me, save your wind, and when I find him make a fence of your weapons. Decreed sounds like fate and means his own order. The single combat the whole play has been arranging, with heralds, a lottery and a trumpet, is replaced here by a squad briefing, and nobody in the camp objects afterwards.

quotations.text: Brethren and sisters of the hold-door trade, Some two months hence my will shall here be made.…Till then I’ll sweat and seek about for eases, And at that time bequeath you my diseases.
quotations.speaker: Pandarus
quotations.context: The last lines of the play, spoken alone after Troilus has driven him off.
quotations.analysis: Hold-door trade is brothel-keeping, and sweat is the sweating-tub used to treat the pox, so the will he promises is a diagnosis. He addresses the audience as colleagues, which the Bankside houses made an easy joke, and then leaves them the one thing he has. No other play of Shakespeare's ends by making the theatre a beneficiary.

quotations.text: If music be the food of love, play on; Give me excess of it, that, surfeiting, The appetite may sicken, and so die.
quotations.speaker: Orsino
quotations.context: The first lines of the play, to his musicians.
quotations.analysis: He is not asking for music because he enjoys it; he wants to overeat until he is sick of the feeling. The metaphor treats love as an appetite that can be killed by indulgence, and eight lines later he stops the music because it is not as sweet as it was — an attention span the whole play measures him by.

quotations.text: What country, friends, is this?
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Her first line, on the coast, having just survived the wreck.
quotations.analysis: Five words that establish everything: she has no idea where she is, no standing, and no information. The Captain's answer, 'This is Illyria, lady', is the last time anybody in the play addresses her as a woman until the final scene.

quotations.text: Whoe'er I woo, myself would be his wife.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: An aside, having agreed to carry Orsino's suit to Olivia.
quotations.analysis: A single rhymed line closing the scene, and the first statement of the play's central knot. Three days into her employment she is already in the position the rest of the comedy depends on, and she tells the audience rather than anybody on stage — which is where she will keep it for four acts.

quotations.text: Oh, you are sick of self-love, Malvolio, and taste with a distempered appetite.
quotations.speaker: Olivia
quotations.context: Rebuking her steward for sneering at Feste's wit.
quotations.analysis: The diagnosis is delivered in the same appetite imagery Orsino used in the first scene, so the play's two kinds of self-absorption are made to rhyme. It is also the reason the forged letter will work: his mistress has told him publicly what his weakness is, and Maria is listening.

quotations.text: Make me a willow cabin at your gate, And call upon my soul within the house; Write loyal cantons of contemned love And sing them loud even in the dead of night;
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Answering Olivia's question: what would you do if you loved as your master does?
quotations.analysis: Asked what she would do, she describes a courtship nobody in the play is actually conducting — noisy, sleepless, unembarrassed — and it is the moment Olivia falls. The irony is exact: the speech is convincing because Viola means it, and she means it about somebody else.

quotations.text: Disguise, I see, thou art a wickedness, Wherein the pregnant enemy does much.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Alone, having realised what Olivia's returned ring means.
quotations.analysis: She blames the costume rather than herself, and the 'pregnant enemy' is the devil, ready and resourceful. It is the only moral judgement anybody passes on the disguise in the whole play, and she passes it on herself before anyone else has noticed there is a problem.

quotations.text: How will this fadge? my master loves her dearly; And I, poor monster, fond as much on him; And she, mistaken, seems to dote on me.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: The same soliloquy, setting out the triangle.
quotations.analysis: 'Monster' is the word she chooses for being both sexes at once, and it is harsher than anything her enemies say about her. The three clauses are perfectly parallel, which makes the impasse look like a diagram: everyone is loving in the right direction and at the wrong person.

quotations.text: O time! thou must untangle this, not I; It is too hard a knot for me to untie!
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: The couplet that ends the soliloquy and the scene.
quotations.analysis: The cleverest person in the play admits she has no plan, and the comedy takes her at her word: nothing she does resolves anything, and the knot is cut by her brother walking on stage in Act V. It is an unusual thing for a Shakespearean protagonist to say, and the play never contradicts it.

quotations.text: Trip no further, pretty sweeting; Journeys end in lovers meeting, Every wise man's son doth know.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: Singing 'O mistress mine' to Sir Toby and Sir Andrew at midnight.
quotations.analysis: A love song sung to two drunks by a professional, ending on the flattest possible authority — every wise man's son knows it, which is to say it is a commonplace. The next stanza's point is that youth does not last, and the play's three marriages are all arranged by people in a hurry.

quotations.text: Art any more than a steward? Dost thou think, because thou art virtuous, there shall be no more cakes and ale?
quotations.speaker: Sir Toby
quotations.context: To Malvolio, who has come down in his nightgown to stop the singing.
quotations.analysis: Two questions, and the first one is the real argument: rank, not morality, is what Sir Toby thinks settles the matter. The line is often quoted as a defence of pleasure against puritanism, but in context it is a gentleman telling a servant to remember his place, and the joke depends on that as much as on the ale.

quotations.text: A blank, my lord. She never told her love, But let concealment, like a worm i' the bud, Feed on her damask cheek: she pined in thought, And with a green and yellow melancholy She sat like patience on a monument, Smiling at grief.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Asked by Orsino for the history of the sister she has just invented.
quotations.analysis: She describes her own situation to the man responsible for it, in the third person and the past tense, and he asks whether the girl died. 'A blank' is the exact word for a history nobody was told, and the statue image is chosen for stillness: she is describing the one thing she is not allowed to do, which is act.

quotations.text: I am all the daughters of my father's house, And all the brothers too: and yet I know not.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Answering Orsino's question of whether her sister died of love.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is literally true, riddling and heartbreaking at once: she is the only surviving child and, in her clothes, both the daughter and the son. 'And yet I know not' is her hedge about her brother's death, and it is the nearest she comes to hope in the first half of the play.

quotations.text: be not afraid of greatness: some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em.
quotations.speaker: Malvolio
quotations.context: Reading Maria's forged letter aloud in the garden, watched from behind a box-tree.
quotations.analysis: Maria's cleverest stroke is that the sentence says nothing at all: it covers every possible route upward and so confirms whichever one the reader already believes in. Feste quotes it back at him in the last scene, which turns a flattering commonplace into the epitaph of the joke.

quotations.text: Then think you right: I am not what I am.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: To Olivia, who has just said she thinks the same of Cesario.
quotations.analysis: It is a confession that cannot be heard as one, and it is deliberately a step short of a lie. The formula inverts the name God gives himself in Exodus, and Shakespeare gives the same construction to Iago; here it costs its speaker something instead of arming her.

quotations.text: Love sought is good, but given unsought better.
quotations.speaker: Olivia
quotations.context: Declaring herself to Cesario, having abandoned discretion.
quotations.analysis: She makes a proverb out of her own position — unasked love is worth more — at the moment she is doing the asking. The line is a rhymed couplet in a scene that keeps slipping between prose and verse, and the shift into sententious rhyme is exactly how a formal woman gives herself permission.

quotations.text: Nothing that is so is so.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: To Sebastian, whom he takes for Cesario and who denies knowing him.
quotations.analysis: Six words that state the plot: the fool is mistaken about the man in front of him and is nevertheless exactly right about the world he is in. He arrives at the formula by a run of sarcastic denials, which means the truest sentence in the play is produced by accident.

quotations.text: Or I am mad, or else this is a dream:
quotations.speaker: Sebastian
quotations.context: After Olivia has stopped the brawl and invited him into her house.
quotations.analysis: He is offered a countess, a household and a marriage by a stranger, and his response is to check his own sanity — the same question the household is at that moment putting to Malvolio in the dark. The play runs both tests in the same act and reaches opposite verdicts.

quotations.text: Madman, thou errest: I say, there is no darkness but ignorance; in which thou art more puzzled than the Egyptians in their fog.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: Disguised as Sir Topas the curate, speaking to Malvolio through the door of a dark room.
quotations.analysis: The proposition is a scholastic commonplace and it is being used to gaslight a man who has correctly observed that he is shut in the dark. Feste has put on a false beard nobody can see, which makes this the one disguise in the play worn purely for the pleasure of the wearer.

quotations.text: An apple, cleft in two, is not more twin Than these two creatures. Which is Sebastian?
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Seeing Viola and Sebastian on stage together for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The recognition is given not to the twins or the lovers but to Antonio, who has most to lose by it — he has just been calling Viola a traitor. The homely image of a cut apple lands in the middle of the play's most formal verse, and his question is the one the whole comedy has been withholding.

quotations.text: and thus the whirligig of time brings in his revenges.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: Revealing to Malvolio that he was Sir Topas, and reminding him of his own insults.
quotations.analysis: A whirligig is a child's spinning toy, which makes cosmic justice into something that goes round because somebody set it going. He has been waiting since Act I for this, and the sentence admits that the punishment was personal rather than corrective.

quotations.text: I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you.
quotations.speaker: Malvolio
quotations.context: His exit line, leaving the final scene.
quotations.analysis: The last words of the only character who refuses the comedy's settlement, and he walks off stage with them unanswered. Olivia's reply — that he has been most notoriously abused — concedes the point, and Orsino sends somebody after him, which is not the same as putting it right.

quotations.text: When that I was and a little tiny boy, With hey, ho, the wind and the rain, A foolish thing was but a toy, For the rain it raineth every day.
quotations.speaker: Feste
quotations.context: Alone on the empty stage after everyone else has gone in.
quotations.analysis: The song walks a life from childhood to marriage to drunkenness to old age, and each stanza ends with the same weather. It is the only Shakespearean comedy that finishes with a solitary figure singing about how little difference the ending has made, and the refrain is what the audience takes out into the street.

themes.name: Law, debt and property in people
Flight and the geography of freedom
themes.canonicalName: Flight and the geography of freedom

quotations.text: Well, I’ve got just as much conscience as any man in business can afford to keep
quotations.speaker: Haley
quotations.context: The trader, over wine, negotiating the sale of Tom and the child Harry.
quotations.analysis: Conscience is presented as an overhead, priced like any other, and the joke is that the speaker is entirely sincere. Stowe puts the novel's economic case in its first pages and in the mouth of its least reflective character, so that everything said later by thoughtful men is an elaboration of a trader's small talk.

quotations.text: a delicately formed hand and a trim foot and ankle were items of appearance that did not escape the quick eye of the trader, well used to run up at a glance the points of a fine female article.
quotations.context: Eliza has come into the parlour on an errand and gone out again.
quotations.analysis: The sentence begins as a conventional novelistic description of a pretty woman and ends in the vocabulary of livestock, with 'items' and 'points' and 'article' doing the turn. The reader is made to notice that they have been looking at her in the same way the trader has, one clause earlier.

quotations.text: I always thought that I must obey my master and mistress, or I couldn’t be a Christian.
quotations.speaker: Eliza
quotations.context: To George, who has told her he intends to escape.
quotations.analysis: She states the doctrine she has been taught as a condition of her faith, and within four chapters she will break it with a child on her hip. The novel gets its Christian readers to abandon that teaching by letting a good woman hold it first, and then making obedience unthinkable.

quotations.text: It is a sin to hold a slave under laws like ours
quotations.speaker: Mrs Shelby
quotations.context: On learning that her husband has sold Tom and Harry to settle a debt.
quotations.analysis: The qualification is the whole sentence: it is the laws that make it a sin, which leaves open the idea of a slavery conducted decently. Stowe gives her heroine the argument most of her readers actually held, and then spends forty chapters dismantling it by following the paperwork.

quotations.text: God helping me, I crossed on the ice
quotations.speaker: Eliza
quotations.context: In Senator Bird's kitchen, answering the disbelief of everyone in the room.
quotations.analysis: The novel's most spectacular action is reported afterwards, flatly, by the person who performed it, and the room's astonishment does the work that description would. Note that she credits God and the syntax credits herself: the main verb is hers, and the help is a subordinate phrase.

quotations.text: It’s a shameful, wicked, abominable law, and I’ll break it, for one, the first time I get a chance
quotations.speaker: Mrs Bird
quotations.context: To her husband, who has voted for the Fugitive Slave Act.
quotations.analysis: Three adjectives and then a plan, which is the order Stowe wants her readers to follow. The chapter is constructed so that the opportunity arrives within the hour, and the senator who defended the law in the abstract is soon driving a wagon through the mud at midnight.

quotations.text: Mr. Wilson, you have a country; but what country have I, or anyone like me, born of slave mothers?
quotations.speaker: George Harris
quotations.context: In an inn, in disguise, to his former employer from the factory.
quotations.analysis: The question is put to a sympathetic man who has just advised obedience to the law, and it works by simple grammatical contrast: you have, what have I. Stowe lets George reject the national argument rather than appeal to it, which is why he ends the novel outside the United States.

quotations.text: I’ll fight for my liberty to the last breath I breathe. You say your fathers did it; if it was right for them, it is right for me!
quotations.speaker: George Harris
quotations.context: The end of the same speech, having announced that he is armed.
quotations.analysis: He does not ask for the revolution's principles to be extended to him; he points out that they already cover his case and dares his listener to deny it. An American readership in 1852 could refuse the claim only by unsaying its own founding story, which is precisely the trap the sentence sets.

quotations.text: The trader, therefore, sat discontentedly down, with his little account-book, and put down the missing body and soul under the head of losses!
quotations.context: After a woman whose child Haley has sold has gone over the side of the steamboat.
quotations.analysis: A suicide is recorded as a bookkeeping entry, and the sentence adopts the ledger's own calm until the last three words. 'Body and soul' is the trade's own phrase used against it: the column exists because the law allows a soul to be entered as stock.

quotations.text: His heart was exactly where yours, sir, and mine could be brought, with proper effort and cultivation.
quotations.context: Of Haley, who has just watched a mother lose her child without interest.
quotations.analysis: The narrator turns from the trader to the reader mid-paragraph and includes herself in the indictment, which stops the sentence from being a simple accusation. 'Cultivation' is the word a Victorian reader would apply to their own moral improvement, redeployed here to describe the process of learning not to care.

quotations.text: You loathe them as you would a snake or a toad, yet you are indignant at their wrongs.
quotations.speaker: Augustine St Clare
quotations.context: To his cousin Ophelia, on the difference between northern and southern feeling.
quotations.analysis: The line is aimed past Ophelia at the book's actual readership, most of whom lived north of the Ohio and had subscribed to an antislavery paper. Stowe puts her sharpest attack on her own supporters into the mouth of a slaveholder, which makes it harder to dismiss and impossible to enjoy.

quotations.text: This cursed business, accursed of God and man, what is it?
quotations.speaker: Augustine St Clare
quotations.context: Beginning a long explanation of slavery to Ophelia, in his own house, with his own servants in it.
quotations.analysis: He asks the question rhetorically and then answers it in the language of force rather than of race: because I am strong and he is weak, therefore I may. The speech is the most complete argument in the novel, and it is given to the one man in a position to act who never does.

quotations.text: never had no father nor mother, nor nothin’. I was raised by a speculator, with lots of others.
quotations.speaker: Topsy
quotations.context: Answering Ophelia's questions about where she comes from.
quotations.analysis: The scene is played for comedy and the answer is a statement of fact about the domestic trade, which is exactly the difficulty Topsy presents. 'Raised by a speculator' names the only parent the market provided, and the sentence is funny and unanswerable in the same breath.

quotations.text: I would die for them, Tom, if I could
quotations.speaker: Eva St Clare
quotations.context: To Tom in the garden, having heard the stories of the people in the household.
quotations.analysis: The conditional is doing something odd: she is already dying, and the novel is about to spend a chapter arranging her death as a redemptive event. Stowe's sentimental machinery is at its most exposed here — a child's willingness to die is offered as the emotional equivalent of the political act nobody in the house will perform.

quotations.text: Mas’r, if you mean to kill me, kill me; but, as to my raising my hand agin anyone here, I never shall
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: Refusing Legree's order to flog a sick woman in the field.
quotations.analysis: The refusal is not to be beaten but to beat, and that distinction is the whole of Tom's position: he concedes the body and withholds the act. Legree's plantation runs on making the enslaved police each other, so one man declining to strike is a structural problem rather than a moral gesture.

quotations.text: No! no! no! my soul an’t yours, Mas’r! You haven’t bought it
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: Answering Legree's demand to know whether he is not his master's, body and soul.
quotations.analysis: Legree has just cited scripture and a purchase price; Tom answers the property claim in property language, conceding the sale and disputing what was in it. The triple 'no' is the only moment in the novel where Tom raises his voice, and he does it about a point of law.

quotations.text: I’ve been on this place five years, body and soul, under this man’s foot; and I hate him as I do the devil!
quotations.speaker: Cassy
quotations.context: Telling Tom what the plantation is, on the night after his first flogging.
quotations.analysis: She uses the same phrase Tom has just refused to concede, and she concedes it, which measures the distance between them. Stowe gives Cassy the plainest hatred in the book and does not require her to repent of it, even while the novel is arranging Tom's forgiveness.

quotations.text: in the judgment day, I will stand up before God, a witness against those that have ruined me and my children, body and soul!
quotations.speaker: Cassy
quotations.context: The end of her account of her own life, told to Tom in the first person.
quotations.analysis: She does not ask the reader for pity; she declares herself a witness in a proceeding that has not yet opened. It is the strongest claim to legal personality in the novel, and it is made by a woman whose testimony no court in Louisiana would have heard.

quotations.text: I’ll give ye all the work of my hands, all my time, all my strength; but my soul I won’t give up to mortal man.
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: To Legree, who has told him he is broken and offers him a place as an overseer.
quotations.analysis: The offer on the table is promotion — Legree wants Tom to drive the others — so the refusal is of power rather than of suffering. The list of what he concedes is long and specific, which makes the single withheld item look like a legal reservation rather than a pious formula.

quotations.text: they can see to it that they feel right
quotations.context: In the concluding remarks, answering the question of what any individual can do.
quotations.analysis: It is the most-quoted sentence in the book and the most criticised, because it makes the reader's inner state the unit of political action. Read in context it is less passive than it sounds — the paragraph goes on to talk about influence and atmosphere — but the novel does end by asking for feeling and leaving the legislation to follow.

quotations.text: And say, mothers of America, is this a thing to be defended, sympathized with, passed over in silence?
quotations.context: The closing appeal, after a page addressed to farmers, sailors and shipowners by region.
quotations.analysis: Stowe names her actual constituency last and most directly, and the three verbs run from active approval to mere silence, closing every available position. The fiction has been put down by this point: the last chapter is a pamphlet, and the novel has been its evidence.

quotations.text: not surer is the eternal law by which the millstone sinks in the ocean, than that stronger law, by which injustice and cruelty shall bring on nations the wrath of Almighty God!
quotations.context: The last sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is to a physical certainty, so judgement is presented as mechanics rather than as a threat. Nine years before the first shots, Stowe ends a domestic novel by telling the United States that the consequence is already in motion and that repentance is the only variable left.
